The Morrisites in brief Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, began recording revelations in Utah in the late 1850s. On April 6, 1861, he organized his own church at South Weber, and his followers gathered at Kington Fort on the Weber River. In June 1862 a territorial posse besieged the fort for three days; Morris was killed at the surrender, others died in the siege, and the men were taken prisoner and later tried. After Governor Stephen S. Harding pardoned those convicted in 1863, the Morrisites scattered: to Soda Springs, Idaho, under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor; to Carson Valley, Nevada, and San Francisco; to Omaha and Council Bluffs; to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla; and to the Deer Lodge Valley in Montana, where the last organized Morrisite church lasted until George Johnson’s death in 1954. This guide gathers the records they left and what has been written about them. Read the chronology and the place pages for the story, the essential works below for the movement’s own texts and its standard history, Teachings for what the Morrisites believed, and Questions for what is still unsettled.

Four ways in History A dated chronology from 1857 to the present, the places of the movement from South Weber to Racetrack, and what the Morrisites taught. Family history

Looking for a Morrisite ancestor? Look up the name. The name index lists everyone on the 1861–62 roll and everyone else the sources name, with links to every place the guide mentions them. Try other spellings: the roll was printed from Danish, Swedish, Welsh and English names, and clerks spelled them as they heard them. The search box at the top of every page searches the whole site. Read what the guide has found. On the roll, a name may carry a note on what the sources say, a FamilySearch link, a tag for the men taken at Kington Fort in 1862, or a link to a person page with a life, family on the roll and sources. Check the family in Family Tree. FamilySearch links marked “probable” are likely but not certain; Family Tree is shared and editable, so check its sources before relying on it. See where the records are. The place pages gather what the guide holds on each place the family lived. Repositories lists the archives that hold Morrisite papers, court files and land records, and Documents lists what can be read online. Share what your family knows. Letters, photographs, family histories and corrections are welcome; see Share records. Descendants have already filled in parts of this guide.

Core texts

Essential works The movement’s own scripture, a later compilation from within the movement, a modern collection of its leaders’ writings, and the only book-length history of it. Primary text · 1886 The Spirit Prevails Joseph Morris’s revelations, articles, and letters, recorded from 1857 to 1862 and published after his death by his follower George S. Dove. It holds more than 300 revelations, making Morris one of the most prolific revelators in Mormon history. For his followers it was scripture. Read online: Internet Archive · Google Books. Both are free scans of the University of California copy (684 pages), which lacks pp. 1–3; for those pages, including the start of the “History of Events,” see the Harvard copy (Internet Archive). Primary text · 1899 Gems of Inspiration A Collection of Sublime Thoughts by Modern Prophets, compiled by John R. Eardley, a leader of the Montana church after Williams’s death, and printed in San Francisco by Joseph A. Dove in 1899. It shows how the movement kept and passed on its prophetic writings a generation after Morris. Read online: Internet Archive. Primary texts, collected · 2026 The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations Edited by Kirk Watson. Writings of Joseph Morris, George Williams, William W. Davies, George S. Dove and James Dove, among them Davies’s pamphlets, hymns and 1882 interview and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation (1892). It is the only collection that puts the later leaders’ writings beside Morris’s, and the main source for the guide’s Teachings page. It also transcribes twelve of Morris’s letters to Brigham Young, 1858–60, his earliest surviving writings; see the dated list with catalog links on the Documents page. Independently published, 267 pages. Buy: Amazon (paperback and Kindle). The standard history · three editions C. LeRoy Anderson’s history of the Morrisites 1981 For Christ Will Come Tomorrow: The Saga of the Morrisites 1988 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites, 2nd ed. 2010 Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited), the final edition. Buy from the publisher · Digital edition (member libraries) Anderson, a sociologist at the University of Montana, built the book on Morrisite papers found in a Deer Lodge attic and on the records of Andrew Hendrikson, who presided over the Montana church from 1886 to 1921, kept by his family. His research files are the core of the Morrisite collection at USU. The 2010 edition is in print in paperback and as an ebook. Please buy it from Utah State University Press, an imprint of the University Press of Colorado; buying from the publisher supports keeping the book in print.
History
Chronology The main events, from Morris’s revelations through the Montana congregations to later claimants and the present.

The movement at a glance How the Morrisite congregations descended from one another, where many members went, and the later groups that drew on the tradition without descending from it. Not drawn on the chart. Some breaks and claims left no lasting body, or none that can be traced. S. P. Guhl, who founded a congregation in Copenhagen on Williams’s authority, broke with him in 1871; whether its members followed Guhl is not known (1870–71). Williams wrote in 1876 that Guhl and J. J. Poulsen had “fell, gathering themselves up to Omaha again” (Williams to Hendrikson, September 26, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876). In 1868 Williams called “Dow, Davies, Gudmanson” rebels (probably Alexander Dow, William W. Davies and Gudmund Gudmundson), and in 1875 wrote that John Parson, R. J. Livingstone, Davies, Dove or Dow “and others” had set up “a business of their own.” That year Joseph Warner of South Weber travelled among the scattered Saints in California, claiming “the Presidency of the Apostleship” and foretelling Joseph’s coming at Weber in June 1876 (Who was “Brother Warner”?), and Barnet Moses Giles, a claimant from outside the movement, wrote to the Omaha members (1875). One of those he wrote to was Nels Damander, who had hosted the Council Bluffs councils and had been made a bishop’s counselor in Montana in 1872; in July 1873 Damander turned against Williams, saying that “Cainan was a Man like Brigham Young to lead the People astray,” and by September 1876 he had written to Williams in repentance (Church History Library, MS 31876). Hendrikson’s own mail went to Council Bluffs in Damander’s care, about 1871 (envelope, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1869–1871, MS 31876), and in December 1877 the Danish council in Montana heard that a member had taken Damander’s and Niels Jensen’s part against the church (council minutes, December 2, 1877, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). By 1888 Parson was leading a mission of his own, appointed, John R. Eardley told the Montana court, by “a new prophet called Dr. Poulson of Oakland” (court minutes, May 10, 1888, Church History Library, MS 32226); he died in 1892. In Montana the church had run as two stakes under Williams since 1874: William James’s Stake No. 1 and Andrew Hendrikson’s Danish-speaking Stake No. 2. On May 10, 1877, Hendrikson, James and Rasmus Rasmussen agreed that neither stake would go into the other’s ground; members could move between them, and in 1878 a dispute involving a member of Stake No. 1 was sent to James to settle (council minutes, 1877–1878, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Besides the 1886 James split, a high priest at Warm Springs broke with the Race Track court in 1891 (Chronology). The Doves’ own list of 1879 names seven claimants after Morris, in order: Williams, Livingston, Davies, Gudmundson, Parson, Warner and George S. Dove (A Voice from the West, pp. 13–15). Solid line: organizational succession or movement of members. Dashed line: a later claimant with a documented contact or borrowing, not a line of succession.

The groups over time The same story on a time scale. After 1862 no single leader held the movement together: Anderson counts more than a dozen men who contended for leadership over the next twenty years, and several groups existed side by side. Each lane is a group; the divisions within it are its leaders or phases. Lighter shading means the dates are approximate, and a lane that fades out has no known end. Arrows show members moving from one group to another. Point to or tap the chart to see which groups existed in a given year; select a lane to read more.

t: The groups, with dates and sources Morris’s church 1861–1862. Organize…
s: The groups, with dates and sources Morris’s church 1861–1862. Organized April 6, 1861, later called the Church of the Firstborn (see Glossary); Morris killed June 15, 1862. Soda Springs (Morristown) 1863–1872. Settled May 20, 1863, under Connor's protection. After five frozen harvests most settlers left; a few, among them the Niels Andersons, stayed for life (Anderson, pp. 159–64). Nevada: Carson Valley and Carson City 1863–1878. Livingstone, Parson, the Doves and Eardley organized here in 1863–64; Cainan made Parson president at Carson in August 1864. The Carson Valley News still wrote of “the Morrisites” of the valley in 1877 (Anderson, ch. 13; Carson Valley News, 1877). Cainan’s claim to lead 1862–1882. Claimed the succession from the autumn of 1862 on the strength of visions of April and August 1862; led by correspondence, never visited Montana, and died in England in 1882 (Anderson, ch. 12). Omaha and Council Bluffs 1868–1880. Fifteen members at Omaha and twelve at Council Bluffs in January 1869; forty-two and twenty-seven by October 1871. Many later moved on to Montana (Anderson, ch. 15). Saints of the Most High, Montana 1866–1969. Morrisites arrived from 1863 and gathered under Cainan in the late 1860s and 1870s; the council called itself the Saints of the Most High by 1873. William James presided until 1886; George Thompson was then elected president, though he spent much of his time in England, and Andrew Hendrikson presided in Montana from 1886 to 1921 and George Johnson to his death in 1954, with which the church came to an end (Anderson, pp. 212, 214); survivors still gathered at the Lord’s House in 1969, the year USU’s finding aid gives for its formal disbanding. Kingdom of Heaven 1864–1888. Davies, in Montana from 1864, claimed a divine call in January 1866 and led about forty followers to Walla Walla in 1867. The community broke up after members sued him in 1880–81 (Anderson, ch. 14). Parson’s kingdom 1874–1885. Parson visited Davies in 1872–73, was impressed, then set up his own kingdom in San Francisco on April 7, 1874. How long it lasted is not known (Anderson, chs. 13–14). Church of the Firstborn (the Doves) 1874–1910. George Dove claimed leadership from 1874; the Doves published from 1879 to 1892, including The Spirit Prevails (1886), and visited Montana in 1885. Holzapfel, cited by Anderson, says the church lasted until 1910 (Anderson, ch. 13). Later claimants. James Brighouse’s Order of Enoch (1884) has no traced Morrisite link; Leland Jensen’s Missoula group (from the 1970s) drew on Cainan’s Deer Lodge prophecy without descending from the church. Neither is drawn.

t: 15 Dec 1823Joseph Morris is born at Burwardsley, Cheshire, England, “b…
s: 15 Dec 1823Joseph Morris is born at Burwardsley, Cheshire, England, “brought up near the borders of Wales,” the fifth of seven children (The Spirit Prevails (1886), “History of Events,” p. 2, which spells it “Burswardly”). The day, December 15, is the same in every source; the year is not. The records made in his lifetime point to 1823: he was 23 when he married in February 1847 (Mottram in Longdendale, St. Michael, marriage register, 1844–1848, p. 205, no. 410 (Cheshire Archives and Local Studies)) and 27 in the census of August 1850 (1850 U.S. census, St. Louis, Missouri, Ward 5, p. 214, enumerated August 5, 1850); in the 1841 census, which rounded teenagers’ ages down, he is “15” (see 1842–1853). A Sons of Utah Pioneers questionnaire of 1990, drawing on George Morris’s papers, also gives December 15, 1823. The Spirit Prevails gives 1824, and George’s statement that he was killed in June 1862 “in the 38th year of his Age” fits 1824 (George Morris reminiscences, Church History Library, MS 1614, p. 115); the Church History Biographical Database gives 1822, with no source shown (“Joseph Morris (1822–1862),” accessed November 21, 2026). His baptism at Burwardsley has not yet been found, which would settle it. George, the eldest of the family, was born at Handley, a few miles away. New 1842–1853Joseph Morris’s early life, as his elder brother George tells it. Joseph joined the church in England, “I think in 1842,” received the gift of tongues and used it unwisely, and was badly burned by fire damp, the explosive methane gas of the coal mines. He married Mary Thorp and emigrated to St. Louis, where he worked on a river steamboat; after a serious illness he became, George writes, “very flighty and Visionary,” and in Pittsburgh he made himself president of a small branch. He reached Salt Lake City in the fall of 1853 with his wife and one child and lived for a time with George, who rejected his claims (George Morris reminiscences, Church History Library, MS 1614, pp. 115–20, 179; see Documents). The Morrisites’ own history, written from the other side, agrees on nearly all of this and adds detail: he worked as a hired lad among the farmers, became a collier at eighteen, and was “badly burned in a mine explosion which disabled him for one year”; he married Mary Thorpe in England; he was a fireman on a steamboat at St. Louis for about two years; at Pittsburgh the branch accepted his doctrine and made him president, but “owing to some dissatisfaction he resigned”; and in Salt Lake City he spent about six months with George digging wells, making adobes and fencing (The Spirit Prevails (1886), “History of Events”, p. 2). The two differ on his baptism: George thought it was in 1842, while the Morrisite history says he was baptized at Dukinfield “at the age of twenty-three,” about 1848. Which is right is not settled. The Church History Biographical Database dates the marriage to Mary Thorpe February 15, 1847, and names their child, Anna Eliza Morris. It lists Mary and the child in the Moses Clawson company of 1853, notes that Joseph is not on that company’s roster, and quotes George that “he drove a team for some one across the plains” to pay his way (Church History Biographical Database, “Joseph Morris (1822–1862),” accessed November 21, 2026; no sources shown on the page). Contemporary records bear out the outline. In the 1841 census at Dukinfield, Cheshire, a household headed by Joseph “Morreys,” 40, shoemaker, holds George, 25, shoemaker; William, 20, coal miner; Joseph, 15, coal miner; Mathew, 12; and Jane, four months: George’s brothers by name, the year before George emigrated (1841 census, Dukinfield, Cheshire, HO 107/109/12, p. 17, The National Archives). On February 15, 1847, in the parish church at Mottram in Longdendale, “Joseph Moris,” 23, bachelor, collier, of Stayley, married “Mary Thorp,” 20, spinster, weaver, of Stayley; both fathers were shoemakers, Joseph Moris and Thomas Thorp, and bride and groom both signed with a mark (Mottram in Longdendale, St. Michael, marriage register, 1844–1848, p. 205, no. 410 (Cheshire Archives and Local Studies)). In August 1850 Joseph Morris, 27, and Mary Morris, 23, were living in St. Louis with Ann Thorpe, 50, and William Thorpe, 27, all born in England (1850 U.S. census, St. Louis, Missouri, Ward 5, p. 214, enumerated August 5, 1850). Three children born to them died in infancy: Ann, born at Newton Moor, Hyde, on December 28, 1847; Sarah Jane, born June 26, 1849; and Joseph, born December 16, 1851, the last two at St. Louis (Merrill D. Beal, Henry Allen Beal and George Washington Bean: Pioneers on the Utah Frontier (Garland, Utah: V. W. Johns, 1971), p. 35); only Joseph is in the 1850 household. Their daughter, Ann Eliza, was born on the way west on September 2, 1853, at “Greenwood, Wyo,” according to her death certificate, which names her parents as Joseph Morris and Mary Thorpe; she married Alfred Pehrson and died at Ephraim, Utah, on June 3, 1939 (Utah certificate of death, Sanpete County, 1939, State Board of Health file no. 57625). New

t: Mar–Apr 1854A petition for divorce in Sanpete County. On April 6, 1854…
s: Mar–Apr 1854A petition for divorce in Sanpete County. On April 6, 1854, the probate court of Sanpete County, Judge George Peacock presiding, “took up the following case, Joseph Morris vs Mary Morris, Petition for Divorce”; the case was “investigated,” and the papers were filed in the clerk’s office and marked E (Sanpete County Probate Court, Minutes, vol. A, 1852–1866, p. 6; FamilySearch DGS 007638304, image 15). The minute does not record the outcome; in 1853 and 1854 the clerk often entered only that a case had been investigated and its papers filed, and the papers themselves have not been found. The petitioner is the later prophet. George Morris writes that his brother came to Utah in the fall of 1853 with his wife, Mary Thorp, and that she left him there (George Morris reminiscences, Church History Library, MS 1614, pp. 115–20). In the running narrative of his own life George is more exact: Joseph “lived with mee thro the winter,” and “in the Spring he went down South to his wifes Brother where she left him and he returned alone in the summer of 54” (MS 1614, p. 80). That agrees with the court record and with Mary’s staying in Sanpete, rather than with the Morrisite account below that she went back to Salt Lake City. John Banks, drawing on George S. Dove’s manuscript history of Morris, adds that after about six months with George he went south to San Pete in the spring of 1854, that his teaching got him into trouble there, and that the bishop caused his wife to leave him and take their property back to Salt Lake City (Banks, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” University of Utah thesis, 1909, p. 5; the same account is printed in The Spirit Prevails (1886), “History of Events”, p. 2). In March 1854 the Deseret News printed two seventies quorum reports that list a Joseph Morris of Great Salt Lake City, the 12th Quorum’s (March 2, 1854, p. 2) and that of the 37th Quorum, organized January 12, 1854 (March 30, 1854, p. 3); there were other men of the name in Utah, and neither entry has been confirmed as his. Kirk Watson found the divorce entry and the two lists (correspondence with the editor, November 2026). Mary stayed in Sanpete. On July 4, 1854, three months after the petition, she married Henry Beal at Ephraim (W. H. Lever, History of Sanpete and Emery Counties, Utah, Ogden, 1898, p. 302; Ephraim Enterprise, February 23, 1911, p. 4). Beal was later mayor of Ephraim and president of the Snow Academy; they had seven children, and Morris’s daughter Ann Eliza was raised in their household (Merrill D. Beal, Henry Allen Beal and George Washington Bean: Pioneers on the Utah Frontier (Garland, Utah: V. W. Johns, 1971), p. 35). Their daughter Mary Jemima was the mother of Henry Thorpe Beal Isaacson, a counselor in the First Presidency to David O. McKay from 1965 to 1970: the first wife of the Morrisite prophet was the grandmother of a Latter-day Saint general authority, who was not himself a descendant of Morris. Mary Thorpe Beal died at Ephraim on September 12, 1905, aged 78, having lived there, her death certificate says, for 51 years (Utah certificate of death, Sanpete County, 1905, registered no. 18). New

t: 5 Jul 1854Ordained a high priest at Great Salt Lake City. The membersh…
s: 5 Jul 1854Ordained a high priest at Great Salt Lake City. The membership record of the High Priests Quorum enters a Joseph Morris as ordained at G.S.L. City on July 5, 1854, and enrolled in the quorum the same day, by J. L. Haywood [probably Heywood] and A. Hoagland; the entry gives no birthplace or parents (High Priests Quorum record of members, 1845–1871, Church History Library, CR 1000 2, p. 21). Morris himself later wrote that he had received an ordination on earth “to the office of a high priest” “in the High Priests’ Quorum, Great Salt Lake City,” which he said only acknowledged an ordination first received in heaven (Eardley, Gems of Inspiration, p. 53). His own statement names the same quorum, and the date falls after his spring in San Pete (see Mar–Apr 1854). Kirk Watson found the quorum entry and the passage (correspondence with the editor, November 2026).

t: 1855A second marriage. Morris marries the widow Elizabeth Mills, who l…
s: 1855A second marriage. Morris marries the widow Elizabeth Mills, who leaves him “in about six months”; he goes “from place to place, endeavoring to find employment,” and is often not paid for his work (The Spirit Prevails (1886), “History of Events”, p. 2). George Morris names the marriage without a date: they “soon parted” (MS 1614, p. 119). New

t: Oct–Dec 1856In the handcart rescue? Not confirmed. The Church History …
s: Oct–Dec 1856In the handcart rescue? Not confirmed. The Church History Biographical Database lists a Joseph Morris, under its entry for this man, as serving in the rescue companies sent out from October 7 to December 15, 1856, to bring in the Willie and Martin handcart companies and the wagon trains stranded in Wyoming (Church History Biographical Database, “Joseph Morris (1822–1862),” accessed November 21, 2026). The page shows no source, and there was more than one Joseph Morris in Utah, so this is not yet confirmed as the later prophet. It would fit his whereabouts: he was in the Salt Lake Valley between his marriage to Elizabeth Mills in 1855 and Provo in early 1857. New

t: Jan–Apr 1857Morris at Provo in the Reformation. The Provo minutes show…
s: Jan–Apr 1857Morris at Provo in the Reformation. The Provo minutes show Morris disciplined during the Reformation. On January 1 he confessed before the congregation that he had spoken what was not true and was forgiven on condition that he make his wrongs right; on January 4, on Bishop E. H. Blackburn’s motion, he was cut off from the church “for lying.” On January 10 Blackburn presented him as “an altered man,” and on January 18 Morris confessed that he had been “the tool of the Devil” and was forgiven unanimously. On April 15 he was before the High Priests quorum again, testifying that he spoke by the Holy Ghost and accusing the quorum of wanting to destroy him (Provo Utah Central Stake general minutes, vol. 10, 1855–1860, Church History Library, LR 9629 11, pp. 627, 631, 657, 676, 817). His first revelation in The Spirit Prevails is headed “Provo, Utah, Spring of 1857” (No. 1, p. 9). Kirk Watson found these minutes and pointed out the date of the first revelation (correspondence with the editor, November 2026). The Morrisite history says that at Provo he married Elizabeth Jones, was rebaptized and sent out as a teacher, and that the bishops opposed his speaking and “commanded his wife to leave him, which she did” (The Spirit Prevails (1886), “History of Events”, p. 3); George Morris likewise says that at Provo “they made a teacher of him,” that he married “Elize Jones,” and that “those in Athoraty” separated them (MS 1614, p. 119). New

t: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint chu…
s: 1857–1862Joseph Morris, an English convert to the Latter-day Saint church, records the revelations later gathered as The Spirit Prevails. He writes repeatedly to Brigham Young. No written reply is known; Anderson reports that the first letter, dated December 7, 1857, bears a penciled note on its margin, “He’s weak minded.” The church’s answer comes in February 1861 (next entry). The Spirit Prevails dates the first revelation to the spring of 1857 at Provo (previous entry); Forscutt dates it to the fall of 1857, the season of the Utah War, the Mountain Meadows Massacre and the Reformation, and sets the movement’s beginning among them: “then the Mountain Meadow Massacre took place—then Morrisism planted its foundations” (Forscutt, Sketch, pp. 7–11; see Teachings).

t: Nov 1859George S. Dove moves Morris from American Fork to Salt Lake Ci…
s: Nov 1859George S. Dove moves Morris from American Fork to Salt Lake City, where, by the Morrisites’ own history, he stays “in a vacant house and lot in the First Ward” and receives “the revelation called the Keys of the Priesthood” (The Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” p. 3). The Doves’ earlier printing of 1879 dates the move to November 1859, says that George’s father, James Dove, had refused several times to allow it, and places the revelation “in an old wagon box covered with canvass, in the same lot with the house he [George] occupied, in the first Ward”; it adds that of the church’s leaders only Heber C. Kimball urged Brigham Young to hear him (George S. and James Dove, A Voice from the West, San Francisco, 1879, p. 6). Both accounts then send him to Slaterville, in the spring of 1860 (The Spirit Prevails) or the fall of 1859 (1879). The date of “Keys” is uncertain: Emanuel Strom’s Swedish copy dates it at South Weber, December 12, 1860 (see the Teachings).

t: 19 Nov 1860Morris leaves Slaterville for South Weber. Catherine V. Wai…
s: 19 Nov 1860Morris leaves Slaterville for South Weber. Catherine V. Waite, writing in 1866, gives the date: on November 19, 1860, Morris set out on foot “from Slatersville, a settlement in Weber County … to the Holy City” to deliver two letters to Brigham Young, his life having been threatened and he driven from his home, and on the way met John Cook, brother of Bishop Richard Cook (C. V. Waite, The Mormon Prophet and His Harem, Cambridge, MA, 1866, p. 122). By the account William W. Davies gave in 1882, the people of Slaterville, northwest of Ogden, had set a day to drive Morris out; he would not go at their order, but prayed, and the day brought “a destructive wind that blew down houses,” so that night found him still there, which he and his followers took as an answer to prayer. The next day he set out for Salt Lake City and on the road met John Cook, brother of Bishop Richard Cook, who invited him to South Weber, “late in the fall of 1860.” Davies says Morris had been driven from seventeen homes in three years; that of the church’s leaders only Orson Pratt would receive him; and that he was called “the Dreamer, or Praying Joe.” He described him as “a stout, square built, powerful man, about five feet six inches in hight,” whose dark brown hair, never cut, “hung in seven ringlets upon his shoulders,” with a small mouth, thin lips, an aquiline nose and “a mild blue eye”; meek, slow of speech, never known to laugh, though he would smile “in a way that made one like the man” (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, Whitman, Columbia and Garfield Counties, Portland, 1882, pp. 370–71; Davies’s recollection of twenty years later. Other accounts have Morris brought to South Weber after John Cook met him near the Warm Springs; see the roll note for John Cook). Dec 1860The Reorganized Church’s True Latter Day Saints’ Herald prints an unsigned letter from Weber County. The writer says many there acknowledge “Brother Joseph’s” right to lead the church and wishes to join “the organization where young Joseph is at the head.” This is two months before the excommunications at South Weber; the letter does not mention Morris (True Latter Day Saints’ Herald 1, no. 12 [December 1860]: 292; see Teachings).

t: 11 Dec 1860Morris writes to Brigham Young that he has “waited with gre…
s: 11 Dec 1860Morris writes to Brigham Young that he has “waited with great patience” for Young to open the way for him, in vain, and is “now compelled to come up whether the way is open or not.” He has visited “the homes of a few of the twelve” and was not satisfied with their spirit: “if I had have been some great lawyer or doctor … I should have been better received.” A revelation follows, addressed to the “rebellious shepherds of my flock”: “I have sent my Servant up unto you for the last time, and if you open the way for him it will be well with you, but if you do not I will cut both you and your seed off from the Earth forthwith” (address to President Brigham Young, December 11, 1860, fair copy, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 192–93, Community of Christ Library Archives; not in The Spirit Prevails). With the address of September 22, 1860 (P11-1 f5, and a second copy in f1) and that of December 21 (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 667 and after), it is one of three letters Morris sent Young that autumn.

t: 21 Dec 1860A prophecy “to the inhabitants of Utah” foretells a mighty …
s: 21 Dec 1860A prophecy “to the inhabitants of Utah” foretells a mighty work beginning in 1861 with the leaders of the church. It promises a temple in the land of promise, but no endowments “in this place,” for “my saints shall not remain here long.” When the people have returned to that land, Joseph is to be given power to write “a law which shall govern the nations of the earth” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 30, pp. 40–41). A manuscript copy of this passage is among the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f6).

t: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meetin…
s: 11 Feb 1861The apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff hold a meeting at South Weber to “regulate” the branch. On Taylor’s motion, seconded by Woodruff, sixteen of Morris’s followers are cut off from the church, among them Bishop Richard Cook, his brother John Cook, John Parson and Robert Farley. Woodruff wrote his account that day. Asked to state his belief, Cook said he believed in Joseph Morris as “a Prophet whom God has raised up to lead this Church & kingdom,” did not believe Brigham Young had had any revelation “more than any sectarian Priest,” and that the church would “ownly be known in name in 10 years unless God does raise up a Prophet.” Morris was then sent for and spoke for about half an hour: Joseph Smith “was ordained of man while He Joseph Morris was ordained of the Father, & held six times more keys of the Priesthood than Joseph did,” and he was “the seventh Angel.” Taylor answered him. Woodruff then told the meeting that Morris “had been cut off from the Church twice for Adultery in the Territory” and had spent “about one year with a woman whose husband was crazy”; Morris denied it, and Bishop Chauncey W. West said that it was true. After the vote Philo Allen was named to preside over the rest of the branch, which was joined to Ogden (Wilford Woodruff journal, February 11, 1861, MS 1352, Church History Library, pp. 119–20, transcribed at the Wilford Woodruff Papers). Morris’s name is not on the list of the sixteen. A Morrisite account printed thirty years later says the test put to the branch was to testify that Brigham Young was a “Prophet, Seer and Revelator,” and that “seventeen men and women” declined, willing to own him as president of the church but not as a prophet. It has Lot Smith and about twenty armed men come with the apostles, an “old man of the name of Watts” propose that the dissenters’ throats be cut, and Bishop Cook ask whether he was “under the flag of the United States” or “among savages,” after which Taylor proposed excommunication (“The Morrisite Tragedy,” letter 8 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 19, 1891, p. 3; see Newspapers). The Latter-day Saint side has a later version of the same exchange. In 1893 Orson F. Whitney wrote that “President Wilford Woodruff states” that at this visit Morris, asked about his claims, “replied that he was Gabriel, Michael, Moses, etc.,” and that Woodruff answered: “Well, when the angel Gabriel comes to blow his horn I don’t think he’ll stay around here for thirty days, living with another man’s wife, as you have been doing.” Whitney added that Morris “had previously been cut off from the Mormon Church for adultery,” and that after the visit “the entire community was excommunicated for apostasy” (Orson F. Whitney, History of Utah, vol. 2 (Salt Lake City, 1893), p. 50 n.). Correction: this entry said that Woodruff’s journal records no exchange with Morris and does not name him; it does both. The core of Whitney’s story, the charge of adultery put to Morris’s face at the meeting, is in the journal written that day. The details are not: the journal has Morris claim to be the seventh angel, not Gabriel, Michael and Moses (his claim to be Moses is otherwise first attested at the Foreshadowing of May 1862); it has “about one year,” not thirty days; and sixteen were cut off, not “the entire community,” and the church grew afterwards. The two earlier excommunications for adultery are Woodruff’s assertion; no record of them has been found for this guide, and Morris denied the charge about the woman. His earlier wives had left him or been separated from him before he came to South Weber (Anderson, Revisited; see the roll note for Mary Morris), and he did not marry Mary Olsen until August 1861. Whitney’s chapter otherwise follows Richard W. Young’s account of 1890, written from the posse’s side. 6 Apr 1861Morris organizes his church at South Weber with six members and calls his followers to gather at Kington Fort, an abandoned 1853 settler fort there (Anderson, Revisited, p. 66). Two days earlier a revelation named Richard Cook and John Parson as the first men called, Parson to preside over those who would hold the apostleship, because it was necessary to call these two “in order to commence an organization” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 56, pp. 78–79). Josiah D. Price’s journal names the six whom Morris baptized on April 6: Richard Cook, John Cook, Nathan Brooks, John Firth, William Kendell and Moses Bryne (written “Burnes”), all of them high priests except Bryne (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). On its name, see the Glossary. May–Jun 1861An informer’s report sent to Brigham Young describes Morris’s Sunday meetings. On May 12 six people are confirmed by three men laying on hands together, Morris, Richard Cook and John Parson, and Cook gives “an explanation of the diagram.” Morris says: “I say now I profess to be the Seventh Angel. The seventh thousand years is now ushered in. Joseph held the 6th seal of the 6th dispensation.” Parson reads a revelation of May 11 commanding “those who believed in him (Morris) to gather forthwith to South Weber.” On May 26 Morris says that “one month would not elapse before the judgments of God would be poured out” (“Doctrines of the Morrisites, May 12, 1861,” informer’s report, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). At Manti, in Sanpete County, the ward’s Sunday meetings took notice. On May 26 David Candland, newly come from Great Salt Lake City, warned against “apostacy even in our midst,” referred to “Little Joseph” (Joseph Smith III, who had taken the lead of the Reorganized church in 1860) and a “man named Morris,” and “reasoned against the folly of their pretenses”; on July 7 Bishop Moffat said that he “did not know what the New Prophet Morris and followers were at,” and called their pretensions “Tomfoolery”; on July 14 Father Snow spoke on “the False Prophet, Morris, n

t: 1–6 Jan 1862Three revelations of the week after the coming promised fo…
s: 1–6 Jan 1862Three revelations of the week after the coming promised for December 31 failed, none of them printed in The Spirit Prevails, record Morris quarrelling with the voice that spoke through him. On January 1 Christ answers his fear that he is “an enemy to truth, and a friend to falsehood,” “a traitor to you because of the many disappointments”: the promises about the time of the deliverance “have failed, because they were intended to fail”; “if I had told them the naked truth, I could not have led them on at all … I had to mention dates” (fair copy, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 250–55). On January 5 the revelation repeats Morris’s complaints that the people have “suffered long enough” and will “deny everything that I have revealed,” and that if they are held longer, “you will oppose me!” On January 6, with wood left for two or three days and snow falling: “You insult me beyond all manner of reason!” and, “In the course of a few more days, you will witness many thousands of the inhabitants of this territory lying dead upon the ground” (copies on loose sheets, Nos. 177 and 178, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f2, Community of Christ Library Archives). The revelation of January 6 printed in The Spirit Prevails (No. 195) is a different text.

t: Jan–Apr 1862Forscutt’s diary continues. William Richards, a Welsh memb…
s: Jan–Apr 1862Forscutt’s diary continues. William Richards, a Welsh member at Box Elder, is carried off at night by masked men and let go only on his oath never to return; W. P. and W. W. Thomas, hearing he has been killed, flee to the camp at Weber. In late January Niels Jacobsen Geertzen, “an Apostle of the new faith,” leaves the camp and returns five days later, confessing; he loses his apostleship and is received among the priests. In February Forscutt is writing a history of the church at the fort and needs “Rev. Book No 1 to make some quotations … for the History.” On February 1 Col. P. C. Merrill tells the miller at Kay’s Ward not to grind James Peacock’s wheat: “Starve ’em out.” On February 6 William Jones, arrested by Constable Burton over the taking of a hat in November, is rescued by men from the camp. In March Peter J. Moss is arrested, tried at Farmington and sentenced to forty days at hard labor; on March 27 Joseph Astle is shot when a cocked gun is drawn through brush, and Forscutt describes him laid out for burial. On April 28, Forscutt notes, seven women whipped Christian Lundgreen in the fort: he had “turned traitor” and helped Mortensen’s wife get away by night. From April 24 the diary is in Forscutt’s own shorthand, not yet transcribed (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62 (“Pettitt’s Pocket Diary for 1860”), Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University; see Questions). 12 Feb 1862The members swear the oath to the kingdom of God, to keep all the laws of God and the counsels of his prophet, given and to come. They swear it twelve at a time, by Josiah D. Price’s account: the apostles first, then the high priests and the priests of Aaron, then their wives in the same order, and last the boys and girls, as the revelation of January 25, 1862, directed (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 208–209; Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Price had recorded that the saints consecrated their property on December 30, 1861.

t: 25–27 Feb 1862A revelation orders the quorum of the twelve disorganize…
s: 25–27 Feb 1862A revelation orders the quorum of the twelve disorganized: John Parson, its president, is “a traitor to me,” and only those who will uphold Morris “with all their power” are to meet in his council. Two days later Christ allows that Parson has “done much good in preaching” but cannot yet “detect false spirits,” and promises to place over the apostleship “a person whose birthright is great,” with Parson, “inasmuch as” he is faithful, as his counsellor (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 229–230, pp. 431–36; manuscript copies, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 216–17, and f2, pp. 221–23, Community of Christ Library Archives). 1 May 1862Six captains are chosen at Kington Fort, each to drill ten men. That day, by Josiah D. Price’s account, Morris, Richard Cook, John Banks and John Parson rode before the company as the four horsemen of Revelation 6, on white, red, black and pale horses, with a sword, a pair of balances and the book of revelations, which were explained to the people as judgment, justice and mercy (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). 26 May 1862The men are reorganized into three companies of high priests and four of priests of Aaron, and each swears an oath as a soldier to defend the kingdom; Price swore it that day (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Morris’s revelation on the army of the kingdom provides for seven companies under captains (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 534–35).

t: 16 May 1862The “First Division of the Soldiers of Israel” is formed, w…
s: 16 May 1862The “First Division of the Soldiers of Israel” is formed, with Morris as Captain at Arms, John Fred. Klingbeck as Lieutenant at Arms, and seven captains, John Nielson, Andrew Lee, John E. Jones, Christian Nielsen, Andrew M. Mason, Niels Peterson and P. C. Klemgaard, each over twelve men; a second division of three companies follows. Officers and soldiers swear to defend “the Law of God” and obey their commander. Richard W. Young printed the oath and the rosters, 142 men in all, in 1890 (Documents).

t: 30 May 1862Foreshadowing Day. Twelve generals ride around the fort, th…
s: 30 May 1862Foreshadowing Day. Twelve generals ride around the fort, the first four on white, red, black and pale horses, followed by seven companies of armed infantry, with Morris as the representative of Jesus (The Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” pp. 6–7; Anderson, Revisited, pp. 116–17). Price records the order of march, Morris first, then Cook, Banks and Parson and the rest in the order of their baptism, in black coats, white waistcoats, trousers and gloves and black hats, and copies the declaration made by William Harris in the bishop’s robe (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). An onlooker, Eli Smith, wrote three days later that Morris rode “his old white horse,” its mane braided into seven braids, in a hat with “seven crowns upon the top of it” and a sword in his hand; Richard Cook, “his first Counsellor,” rode beside him with a sword, and John Banks carried “a pair of small balances”; Parson, “president of the twenty-four apostles,” carried “the Book of the Revelations.” They marched round seven times, shouting “Hosanna to God and the Lamb,” and in the afternoon the lesser priesthood marched with William Harris at their head. Smith also reported talk in the camp of a day appointed for “the slaying of the prisoners” (Eli Smith to Christopher Layton, June 2, 1862, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). W. P. Thomas, writing to his wife in Welsh that evening, adds that the riders went round seven times with Morris in military dress and seven more with him in his robe, the rod in his left hand and a sword in his right; that the crowns on the leaders’ hats ran from seven on Morris’s, six on Cook’s and five on Banks’s down to one on John E. Jones’s; that twelve of the Aaronic priesthood rode with rods, “a foreshadow of the twelve princes of Israel”; and that he had washed Morris’s horse the day before and that morning plaited its mane into seven skeins with white ribbons. He dated the letter “Friday 29”; Foreshadowing Day fell on Friday the 30th (W. P. Thomas to his wife and children, Weber, “Friday 29” [May 30, 1862], Welsh, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, folder 21, images 12–13, Church History Library; translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). Richard W. Young, in 1890, from former Morrisites, has Morris wave his rod on a carpeted platform and say, “Be it known to all the earth that I am Moses,” and a banner reading “Peace and prosperity to our friends—death and destruction to our enemies” (The Contributor 11, no. 8 (June 1890): 283). See Where did the rituals come from?

t: Jun 1862A revelation copied as “No. 276, June 13, 1862,” and headed “w…
s: Jun 1862A revelation copied as “No. 276, June 13, 1862,” and headed “why he has never cut off any people,” explains that this is “unlawful”: the Father is not president over this world, “Adam is,” the “Loyal President over this Earth,” and “one god cannot controll another gods world” except through the one who holds its ruling power. “Your Enemies are now comming fast upon you but fear them not … I Permitted them to come thus far in order to try my People.” The copy’s date and number do not agree (its numbering would place it between June 7 and 12); it is not in The Spirit Prevails (fair copy, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 215–16, Community of Christ Library Archives). 11 Jun 1862Acting Governor Frank Fuller orders General Daniel H. Wells to furnish the territorial marshal, Henry W. Lawrence, and his deputies, Robert T. Burton and Theodore McKean, “a sufficient military force” to act as a posse in serving Third District Court writs for the arrest of “Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis County.” The order survives in a copy Wells made in 1871 (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, document 1,215, Utah State Archives; page image on FamilySearch). 13 Jun 1862A territorial posse under Robert T. Burton arrives at Kington Fort about 10 a.m.; one of its members, John G. Chambers, puts it at “about 500 men,” with artillery. Howard Egan carries a white flag; when no notice is taken, the cannon open fire. “The first ball killed two women & wounded a third” in the bowery, where Morris was reading a revelation (Chambers; Forscutt also saw two women dead). Jared Smith of the posse is killed. Two men, one of them “Eardley,” leave the fort with their families under a white handkerchief (John G. Chambers, “Siege of Morris fort, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). The Morrisite letters of 1891 add that the notice was carried in by a boy herding the camp’s cows, giving the five men named in the writs thirty minutes to give themselves up, and that the cannon ball struck the meeting while the notice was being read, killing an old woman and a younger one with a baby in her lap, who was unhurt, and wounding a girl in the jaw. They tell of Egan’s men coming in through the fields on the east, and give Egan’s own account, as he told it to Morrisites at Deep Creek in 1863: that he led the Salt Lake City men, fired on the tents from the east until the Morrisites drove them back, and then withdrew and did not return (“The Morrisite Movement” and “The Morrisite Tragedy,” letters 7 and 8 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 12 and 19, 1891, p. 3). 14 Jun 1862Rain falls all day. That evening the posse fires the Ogden cannon and “the ‘Old Sow,’” a large gun sent up from Salt Lake City (Chambers). The same day the acting governor, Frank Fuller, writes to Burton that “the shedding of blood in resistance to civil authority renders execution of the law imperative”: “Let your acts still be tempered with mercy, but see that the Laws are vindicated” (copy, Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). 15 Jun 1862A Sunday. About eighteen men of the posse take a log cabin near the entrance of the fort, and Peter Wahler is killed. A rolling battery of willows on wagon wheels is then brought forward; by Chambers’s account the Morrisites took it for a mine and panicked, while other accounts have it tipping over in the mud or pushed up to the wall (see Kington Fort). That morning Morris delivers a revelation promising deliverance “which ever way it comes”: either the posse will be turned aside, or angels will hold the men so that “all the guns would soon be still”; Christ must “unveil” himself “in the course of a few hours” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 304; a manuscript copy is in the Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f5). A white flag goes up, and the people are called together to the tune “In a cottage near a wood.” Morris is killed at the surrender; George Thompson, one of the fort’s people, wrote in 1869 of the moment “when Joseph fell by the School house” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, July 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874). Most accounts say John Banks, wounded, died in custody that evening; Chambers writes that Burton “with his aides killed Morris & Banks, and two women” (see Who died at Kington Fort?). The siege ends that evening, and the men are listed as prisoners “Sunday, June 15, 1862 – 7 p.m.” (John G. Chambers, “Siege of Morris fort, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; “Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). 16 Jun 1862Of 149 men taken, counting Morris and Banks, 49 are discharged at the fort: 41 mostly older men, among them Nathan Brooks, Erick Eliason and Ole Olsen, and eight who had “surrendered during the engagement on the 13, 14 & 15 June,” among them Mark H. Forscutt, John R. Eardley, John E. Jones, William James, Griffith Thomas, William Lloyd and Joseph Moss Jr. (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; second copy in Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1). That day Fuller ordered that only “all able bodied men among your prisoners, capable of bearing arms, and who have been found in resistance to civil authority” be held for the court, and congratulated Burton on “the small number of casualties to your force” (copy, Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). That day Briant Stringham brought Morris’s scepter, two others and his crown to the Historian’s Office in Salt Lake City, where they were shown to hundreds; Wilford Woodruff copied the inscriptions and described Morris’s scepter as five feet long, eight-sided and tipped with iron, and the crown as “tin pain

t: 18–19 Jun 1862The 98 prisoners are examined before Judge Kinney, who t…
s: 18–19 Jun 1862The 98 prisoners are examined before Judge Kinney, who tells them they are “not to be tried but to be Examined.” Burton testifies that he waited ninety minutes for an answer before firing, and that at the surrender Morris called on all “who will stand by me to the death” to lift their hands; when they rushed, “as He would not stop I stoped him with my revolver,” and of the two women shot he said he “vary much regret[ted]” it “but it could not be helped.” Alexander Dow tells the court he believes Morris “as much a Prophet as he was before he died.” Kinney says he had let the writ of May 22 “rest 19 days” before acting, and binds the men over on $1,500 bail each, standing bail for one another, with an interpreter for those who do not speak English (Wilford Woodruff’s notes of the hearing, Wilford Woodruff journal, January 1, 1860 – October 22, 1865, MS 1352, Church History Library, transcribed at the Wilford Woodruff Papers, June 18, 1862). In the end Richard Cook is fined and jailed for contempt, Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson are held in prison, and ninety-five other men are bound over for the March 1863 term (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). 24–25 Jun 1862In Salt Lake City, by an entry the Historian’s Office copied from its “Documentary History of the Church,” “Parsons,” very probably John Parson, read to the Morrisites “(so it is reported)” an epistle in which Brigham Young told the bishops to employ and feed any of them who were willing to work; Parson told the others that they had been “grandly humbugged,” and that he meant to go to work and advised them all to do the same. The next day Young sent Dr. Jeter Clinton to the jail to dress the wounds of the Morrisite prisoners, and sent flour to feed them (Journal History, June 24 and 25, 1862, CR 100 137, Church History Library). Both entries are the church’s own record, written from the other side.

t: 29 Jun 1862Brigham Young, preaching in the Bowery on apostasy, says th…
s: 29 Jun 1862Brigham Young, preaching in the Bowery on apostasy, says that had he had his own way he would have left the Morrisites alone, but Judge Kinney “thought the Law must be honored,” and warns that no one is to baptize any of them without his consent (Wilford Woodruff journal, January 1, 1860 – October 22, 1865, MS 1352, Church History Library, transcribed at the Wilford Woodruff Papers, June 29, 1862).

t: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-de…
s: Mar 1863In Salt Lake City, seven Morrisites are convicted of second-degree murder: Peter Klemgard is sentenced to fifteen years, Christian Neilsen to twelve, and Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason to ten; John Parson and John E. Jones are acquitted. The other prisoners are fined $100 each for resisting arrest (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Ten had been indicted for murder on March 19, Richard Cook, John Parson and John E. Jones among them; twenty of those bound over in June did not appear and forfeited their bail; and Lot Smith testified for the prosecution and Mark Forscutt for the defence in the trial for resisting process (Deseret News, March 18, p. 8, and March 25, p. 5, 1863). The Deseret News called the pardon a “flagrant outrage” (April 1, 1863, p. 5). The new territorial governor, Stephen S. Harding, pardons them all a few days later. Harding later recalled that no Mormon signed the petitions for pardon but Bill Hickman, who rode fourteen miles at night to sign, and that Bishop Woolley warned him he “could not answer for my safety” if he pardoned the men (Bill Hickman, Brigham’s Destroying Angel (New York, 1872), p. 216; see The Morrisite War). During the trials, on March 8 and 24, believers in Great Salt Lake City received a prophecy in tongues, “given by L. B.” and interpreted by “Br. B.”: they would be “gathered together again,” a “reorganisation of the faithful” would soon take place, those in prison would be “delivered as Daniel,” and “the Records hidden in the earth” would soon be in their hands (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f5). It is the earliest dated Morrisite text yet found from after the siege. May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) A writer who camped beside that train at Deep Creek, the Overland Mail station kept by Howard Egan, remembered six-mule army wagons carrying two Morrisite families each, bound for Fort Churchill under a lieutenant, with Richard Cook among them; Egan, who had been with the posse in 1862, gave them a supper and a dance (“The Morrisite Movement,” letter 7 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 12, 1891, p. 3). Some Morrisites had spent the winter at Camp Douglas, cutting wood for the troops. John L. Bear, driving a Swiss brother’s ox team, reached Soda Springs “on the 3rd of June, 1863,” to snow that night; the settlers lived in dugouts, Captain Black’s men brought logs, flour and bacon, and “all felt happy to be out of Brigham’s dominion.” James Bowman, who had lost his wife at Weber, helped Bear start a Sabbath school, and later kept a store on the lot Alexander Dow left when he moved to St. Louis (Johann L. Baer, autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 31–36). 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895; Bear himself was baptized into the Reorganized Church at Malad on November 29, 1869, organized a branch at Soda Springs, and wrote a pamphlet, one copy for each Morrisite family still there, on “the fallacy and non fullfillment of many of Joseph Morris revelations”; some burned it unread, but by his account most of the Soda Springs Morrisites joined the Reorganization in time (autobiography, MS 10240, pp. 41–42; no copy of the pamphlet is known); in 1890 John R. Eardley reported that Brother Emmons of the Montana church had been baptized and that Mrs. Emmons meant to follow (see the roll). 1865–66Morrisites are meeting in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana. On March 4, 1866, Sven Olson Hagg writes from Deer Lodge City that he has spent the winter with L. C. Larsen and his family, and helped Larsen build a new house “hvori vi nu holder forsamlinger” (“in which we now hold meetings”). God has begun “to pour out the power of his Spirit upon some of his children right here in Deer Lodge Valley, where the beginning (of the Kingdom) shall be founded.” The first to receive it, he says, was “his servant William D.”, president of the Aaronic priesthood, standing “in Abel’s place” by birthright. This was William W. Davies, whose community later dated its era from January 24, 1866. Williams himself used the name: in 1870 he wrote of “the President of Abel’s Priesthood,” whose duty was to see that the Saints met and “to settle any dispute,” and of filling an inactive brother’s place “with one of Abel’s Priesthood for the time being” (Williams to Hendrikson, July 10 and October 27, 1870, Church Hist

t: Nov 1865Writing from Salt Lake City to William James and John R. Eardl…
s: Nov 1865Writing from Salt Lake City to William James and John R. Eardley, Williams breaks into verse on the siege, his own poem in his own hand. It begins, on the pattern of Byron’s “The Destruction of Sennacherib” (“The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold”): “The Mormons came down like a wolf on the fold / On a morning in June that was glittering like gold.” Its lines tell of the cannon, of “the shrieks of the children and cries of the maid / Whose chin was torn off by the fierce cannonade” (Mary Christoffersen, later Mary Anderson, who testified in 1879 that a cannon ball took off her chin), and of a babe “torn from the breast by a bombshell’s embrace”; it ends with a prayer that “Seth,” Morris, “may be loosed.” Williams left it unfinished: “Here I end not that the Muse tires but that you may share the honor of placing in verse the terrible scene of immortal Weber; finish the tragedy yourselves.” It is a partisan poem written three years after the events, the earliest Morrisite telling of the siege so far found in verse (Williams to James and Eardley, G.S.L., November 1865, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and John R. Eardley, 1864–1867; readings from the manuscript, some words uncertain). 29 Mar 1866In the Deer Lodge Valley a revelation dated March 29, 1866, set down as the heavenly hosts speaking to a “son of man,” declares that Margaret Thomas “shall be classed with the head as long as she lives on the earth,” and tells William [P. Thomas] that he is “an instrument, in the hands of the Lord to turn many souls unto him” and that “those that are in this valley knows that light surrounds and that truth is in you.” He is to bless people when led to, “whether they shall ask or not.” A doom on anyone who might oppose her had been “given through your mouth” on January 21, 1866. The paper is unsigned and not in Williams’s hand; it may record a revelation through Thomas himself. With Hagg’s letter of the same month, it shows spiritual gifts claimed in the valley in 1866 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882).

t: 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a th…
s: 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, setting baptism aside for a covenant vow (Watson, p. 124), leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment. 1867Almerin Grow is making converts to Williams’s faith in St. Louis. Mark H. Forscutt, there as a Reorganized Church missionary, meets in April a Mr. Clarke “tinged with Morrisism, thro’ the teachings of Alminn [Almerin] Grow,” and in June a Mrs. Hill, “baptized by Grow into the Canaanistic faith – an outgrowth of Morrisism” (Mark H. Forscutt, journal, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University, April 18 and June 6, 1867). Dec 1867The Montana Saints, through S. P. Guhl, invite Williams to spend the winter with them, Guhl promising to send his expenses; the money does not come, and Williams warns, “let no man escape with your money.” He appoints Guhl “to preside this winter in Virginia & elsewhere,” addresses William James as “the President,” and announces that “the second Section of Cainan’s ministry is now open.” Those who fall away may go to the Pope, to Wesley or to Luther, “or sink with Doctor Davy,” that is, William W. Davies (Williams to James, December 12, 1867, docketed “Cainan’s Sixth Epistle in the Second Section,” and to Eardley, December 1867, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and John R. Eardley, 1864–1867). 1868Early in the year Williams, in Salt Lake City, thanks the Montana Saints for money sent “by Bro P. Thomas.” S. P. Guhl’s promise to send for him has come to nothing (“he tells me his horses were stolen”), his “family are very sick,” and someone is taking up a land claim for him near the Saints; George Thompson is already in England. Williams explains that by ministers he had sent “to Montana & Idaho” who “had cursed the saints instead of blessing them” he meant “the rebels Dow, Davies, Gudmanson and not … Bro Ghul,” that is, probably Alexander Dow, William W. Davies and Gudmund Gudmundson, the apostle of 1861: George Thompson wrote in 1869 of “Poor Brother Dow,” “Poor Livingstone,” “Poor Goodman Goodmunsen, poor W. W. Davis and others of the Weber House, good men,” who had been “deceived by supernatural manifestations” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874). He signs “Cainan for the Lord’s sake, George Williams.” On December 14 he writes to “Bro. James & Saints of the Most High in Montana”: William James’s group is already in Montana and uses the name later borne by the Montana church. Williams wishes to visit “my beloved brethren & sisters in Montana” but has been “kept from coming,” for “the rebel who have entered my flock in Montana has laid a snare for Cainan’s life,” one he calls “the seventh born son,” who has “seduced others” but whom he does not name; “Joseph the first & Joseph the Second fell a sacrifice to plots.” Instead he is “called to travel to the States & Europe” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1868).

t: Oct 1868W. W. Blair, president of the Reorganized Church’s Pacific mis…
s: Oct 1868W. W. Blair, president of the Reorganized Church’s Pacific mission, tells its California conference at San Francisco: “In Nevada I saw many old Saints (Morrisites). As a general thing they are good people who have been deceived,” led astray “by seducing spirits,” but now “beginning to look at the matter in a favorable light,” and “friends to our cause.” The word in parentheses is cramped and its reading not certain (minutes of the semiannual conference, California District, October 6–9, 1868, p. 7, P19 f34, Community of Christ Library Archives). The conference’s Carson City District then had branches at Carson City, Franktown and Jack Valley, where Cook’s and Parson’s Nevada Morrisites lived. 1869George Williams leaves Utah for England, passing through Omaha from January 18 to February 5, where the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations are organized on his authority (see Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places); a year later he writes from Loughborough that it was “now one year since I left the continent of America”; his wife and children stay in Salt Lake City, and he asks the Montana members to send help for “my little ones” (Williams to the Saints of the Most High in Montana, January 10 [?], 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876). By June he is at Ashwicken, near King’s Lynn, Norfolk, writing to the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs, where Rasmus Rasmussen is “the presiding Bishop.” George Thompson is with him at Ashwicken that summer, and William P. Thomas and a Brother James come to England too: Thompson writes on July 29, 1869, to “Beloved Brethren W. P. and D. J.,” one at Llanybyther in Wales and the other at Derby. That summer Thompson, then a shoemaker at Ashwicken, lost touch with Williams from his letter of July 30 until September 10, when Williams wrote that he had “worked & preached and lectured in the field, harvest field, at night, on Sundays … with thieves for my companions”; S. P. Guhl had left Lynn for Hull and Denmark in July, meaning to publish a paper there (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874, July 29 and September 13, 1869). In September and October Williams writes from near Betchworth Castle, Surrey, “often in different parts of the Country”; on October 13 he writes that Thompson, “like a rock unto me,” will leave for Wales on October 20 to help Thomas, “then I am alone in England as far as the old Weber House is concerned,” and asks that letters be sent to him in care of W. P. Thomas at Llanybyther, Carmarthenshire. His letter of December 24 is headed, apparently, from Llanybyther; “in England the Priesthood are united in love and in effort,” though the seed “certainly is falling on stony ground” (Williams to the Omaha church, September 16, October 13 and December 24, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869). The Omaha minutebook names him: on June 2, 1869, Guhl left for Denmark with “2 Welsh brethren, William P. Thomas, a High Priest, and an Aaronic Priest Daniel James,” called “to go to Wales on mission.” In March 1870 Williams writes that “Bro Thomas & Bro James,” having “attended the heavenly call,” are “now permitted to return to their families in Montana” by way of Omaha. In May he reports the English followers “preaching on the building of the temple in this nation in our meetings on Sundays,” with the sacrament “not refused to any we know that are our real friends”; in December he writes that “the Lord is raising up a set of men to pull down Brigham’s cruel rule; I wish them success but beware of their infidel reasoning,” apparently of the Godbeites (Williams to Hendrikson and Rasmussen, May 1870, and to Hendrikson, December 28, 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870). In April 1871 he thanked Hendrikson for sending the Salt Lake Tribune, the Godbeites’ new paper: it “contains some sound principles, but you will know how to sort the errors; it is also a powerful engine against the Tyrant of Salt Lake” (Williams to Hendrikson, April 1871, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1871). In September 1870 he gives his own account of Almerin Grow, who had walked from California to Salt Lake on hearing of him, was told of “his mission to the Sultan & Priesthood of Mahommet,” and was later “sent to Constantinople & Jerusalem,” returning “without my consent”; Grow himself wrote from San Francisco in August 1870 that he had come overland, met “the assembly at Omaha,” and “did more in Turkey than any other living man could have done,” having “made up my mind to die in the streets of Constantinople rather than fail in my mission,” and that James Dove “has been with Davis but has left him” (Almerin Grow to Williams, August 29, 1870, enclosed with Williams to Hendrikson, September 21, 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870); by 1878, John R. Eardley reported from California, Grow was preaching against Williams and “up George Dove” at San Juan (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880) (Williams to the Omaha church and to Andrew Hendrikson, 1869–70; George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869; and the Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876). Danish-language congregations keep membership and account books in Omaha, Nebraska, and Council Bluffs, Iowa. Their registers show Andrew Hendrikson, born at Ondrup, Jutland, on July 29, 1843, baptized “in the Missouri River” at Omaha on January 22, 1869, by Rasmus Rasmussen and Hans Knudsen (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871,” Council Bluffs, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

t: 1870–71Williams’s followers in Denmark. As early as November 1868 the …
s: 1870–71Williams’s followers in Denmark. As early as November 1868 the Latter-day Saint mission president in Copenhagen, Jesse N. Smith, wrote that “the Morrisites have some half crazy representatives here, who occasionally pick up some poor worn out Mormon of ours,” recalling Wilford Woodruff’s saying that “the Morris sieve was the coarsest” of all the sieves used to sift the Saints (Jesse N. Smith to George A. Smith, November 3, 1868, George A. Smith papers, MS 1322, Church History Library, images 40–41). S. P. Guhl, who had sailed for Denmark in June 1869, and J. P. Lorentzen found a congregation of “the Most High Saints” in Copenhagen, preaching publicly there from January 1, 1871, in a hall in Adelgade, and supporting themselves by their own work; Lorentzen, Guhl and C. B. Berg form a committee to publish tracts (letter from Copenhagen, February 10, 1871). By November 1871 Guhl has broken with Williams. Writing from Denmark on November 5 to Mikkel Christiansen and “Seth’s disciples,” he says they had organized the church in Scandinavia on Williams’s orders but have now “rejected him from our hearts and our assemblies,” objecting to Williams’s oaths (“God’s law says thou shalt not swear at all”), to his appointing one leader after another “to further his speculations to get money,” and to his claim to the Urim and Thummim, which Guhl says he “never had, or else lost” (known from Andrew Hendrikson’s copy, made at Fremont in March 1872: Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1869–1871; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Guhl was back in Omaha, again under Williams, by 1874 (see the roll note).

t: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under Ge…
s: 1870sMany members regather in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, under George Williams, the “Prophet Cainan,” who claims to be Morris's successor. In July 1874, following a revelation in Williams’s epistle from Ashby of April 6, that “my Servant W. James take charge of those that are convenient unto him, and my Servant A. Henrickson take charge of those convenient unto him, and there shall be two Stakes under one Head, even my own chosen Servant Cainan,” the Montana church is divided into two stakes (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1874–1875; William P. Thomas brought the epistle from the post office and read it to the Saints one Sunday): Stake No. 1 on Warm Spring Creek, which met at a meeting house at Willow Glen under William James, and Stake No. 2 at Race Track under Andrew Hendrikson (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories). Stake No. 2’s own minutes record its founding general meeting on July 12, 1874. Hendrikson spoke to “the brothers and sisters who had chosen to be under his presidency”: they lived in two places, Warm Spring and Deer Lodge, about equally many in each, and Jens Jensen was appointed to preside over the meetings at Deer Lodge. From then on only members of “our organization” were to sit in its councils, not those of “the other organization” (general meeting, July 12, 1874, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Hendrikson was living at Race Track by February 1878. A local history of Anaconda dates the first Morrisite settlers in the valley to 1863, among them William Price Thomas on Warm Springs Creek, east of the later townsite; has a group under William James arriving in 1867 as others left; and describes a caravan of thirteen covered wagons that came in June 1871, part of a larger migration from Iowa, Nebraska, Utah and Idaho: Scandinavian families, mostly Danes, with English, Scottish and Welsh believers. It places the two congregations in the upper valley near Lost Creek and near Race Track Creek, with about eighty members in all (Patrick F. Morris, Anaconda, Montana, 1997, pp. 15–17). Williams’s letters from England direct the move from Omaha: in September 1871 “Bro Merrick” sets out for Montana “with his cattle,” in the spring of 1872 Williams sends “instructions for gathering up to Montana,” and by December 1872 Andrew Hendrikson’s mail goes to the Warm Spring Creek post office (Williams to Hendrikson and the Omaha church, 1871–72, MS 31876). Not everyone left Nebraska at once. A branch at Fremont met in Andrew Peterson’s house in November 1871, and in March 1873 Peterson wrote to Hendrikson that the Fremont members hoped to come to Montana that summer and were trying to sell their place (MS 31876, Minutes, 1871, and Minutes, 1872–1873). Williams himself was in England, living by 1876 in George Thompson’s house at Walthamstow, Essex: “I am now writing in Bro Thompson’s house where I have been tarrying some weeks” (to William James, July 13, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876). 2 Aug 1871Williams sends instructions for the gathering to Montana. Andrew Hendrikson had asked “the object of gathering together in Montana”: “it is our Lords Command that his Chosen People may come together to receive blessings Spiritual & temporal and the order of both Priesthoods,” with a temple “prepared to receive the ministering angels of our God.” The Saints need not all live in one place, but should be “in organized companies, that is, families near together, acknowledging one head set to preside”; William James is to preside, “taking the High & holy Priesthood, their first Quorum, himself & Counsellors, then as they are found to stand in twelve.” If John Merrick takes his cattle up to Montana, Hendrikson may go with him (Williams to Hendrikson, Loughborough, August 2, 1871: the English original, pages 5–10 only, is filed in Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1872–1873; Hendrikson’s complete Danish copy, made at Omaha on August 28, 1871, is in the folder for 1871).

t: 22 Sep 1872At the house of William P. Thomas on Warm Spring Creek, the…
s: 22 Sep 1872At the house of William P. Thomas on Warm Spring Creek, the Montana Saints meet “for the purpose of Organizing the Church of Jesus Christ of the Saints of the Most high,” following a general epistle Williams sent from England in August. William James is appointed president, with W. P. Thomas and Andrew Hendrikson as counselors; Rasmus Rasmussen is ordained bishop, with Daniel James and Nels Damander as his counselors; Peter Staffenson is to preside over the second quorum of Seventies; and Margaret Thomas is reordained “as the Lady elect to preside over the Female Order.” A revelation through Williams of August 22 had called James “on a Mission to Nevada,” leaving his counselors in charge, and he left in haste “with a Teamster down to Corrine.” A copy of the revelation, dated August 20, sent him to Austin, Nevada, to help “my son J. D. Bowen,” whose affairs were about to fall into trouble, so that his property might be “saved from those who are looking for speculation profit,” and to bring him back to Montana. Bowen wrote to William P. Thomas from Austin in October 1874 that he had since lost everything, but that Cainan had “sent his servant” two years before to try to save his property (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas, 1871–1874; translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). A second meeting on November 10 “complete[s] the organization” by ordaining six men to the Seventies. The minutebook’s title page dates the emigration of “the Saints of the Most high from the States of Iowa and Nebraska” from the summer of 1871 (minutebook, September 1872–January 1874, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library). Two dolls that belonged to Peter Staffanson’s granddaughters Myrtle and Evelyn Staffanson are at the Copper Village Museum and Art Center in Anaconda (see Images, MO-IMG-105 and 106). 1873The Montana council minutes, kept in English this year, show the church at Warm Springs while its leaders are away. William James is on “his Mission in Nevada.” Williams calls William P. Thomas “on a Mission to Salt Lake,” and he appoints Andrew Hendrikson by letter “to take the Presidency, assisted by the Bishop and his Counselors,” while both are absent (May 5, 1873). In March a committee of four tries a quarrel between Thomas and Daniel James over the line between their lands and Daniel James’s cattle, set on by dogs as they passed Thomas’s place. It tells the two to forgive each other, but Thomas rejects the ruling as “Develish talke.” In July, Damander, who had hosted the Council Bluffs councils, turns against Williams, saying “Cainan was a Man like Brigham Young to lead the People astray.” James takes back the presidency on July 20. In September the council meets privately at Rasmus Rasmussen’s house to keep Thomas out and agrees to report him to Williams; Thomas, Williams’s appointed first counselor and “our second man in authority,” is to be left alone until Williams answers.
