In December the sisters in the town of Deer Lodge complain that Margaret Thomas did not invite them to the sisters’ feast at Warm Springs (council minutes, March–December 1873 and January 12, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876). In California the same year, George Dove, who with his father James had followed Williams and then Davies, begins receiving communications and organizes a Church of the Firstborn of about thirty people (Watson, p. 198). James Dove’s own account places the Davies years in San Francisco: back there in January 1868, he “found a few who had accepted W. W. Davies,” joined them and preached among them; it does not say whether he accepted Davies’s claims himself, nothing so far places the Doves at Walla Walla, and by 1892 he wrote of Davies with open hostility (James Dove, A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, [1892], pp. 3, 6, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892). James Dove’s own account puts the organizing a little later: George’s communications began the year before John Parson set up his “kingdom” in San Francisco on April 7, 1874, and only after that did “the word of the Lord” come “that we were to organize into a church called the Church of the Firstborn,” with five baptized first and about twenty-nine members (James Dove, A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, [1892], pp. 4–5, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892).

t: Jul–Aug 1873The RLDS missionary Charles W. Wandell, waiting in Califor…
s: Jul–Aug 1873The RLDS missionary Charles W. Wandell, waiting in California to sail for Australia, preaches at San Juan, Monterey County, where he counts “about twelve Morrisites.” They show him the first two chapters of Williams’s St. Ann’s Hill records, which they hold to be “the sealed portion of the plates of the Book of Mormon,” containing “the record of John” the Revelator, and tell him the translation is finished and will soon be published; he sends a partial copy to Joseph Smith III (Henry A. Stebbins Papers, P24 f26–f28, Community of Christ Library Archives). See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?

t: 1874In Carson Valley, Nevada, a man “from Montana or Idaho” brings “a …
s: 1874In Carson Valley, Nevada, a man “from Montana or Idaho” brings “a message or a prophecy, one of Morris’ revelations,” and about thirty Morrisites and about as many members of the Reorganized Church’s Mottsville branch meet to hear it in a schoolhouse. At the testimony meeting a Sister Cook, “who had been a Morrisite, but had not long since been baptized into the Reorganized Church,” speaks in tongues, and the interpretation states “the calling of young Joseph to take his father’s place.” D. R. Jones, recalling the meeting in 1908, wrote that she was the only one of the Morrisite families who came from Utah in 1862 to join the branch, which was organized in February 1869 with about twenty-five members; he calls her Mary Cook, but she was very probably Margaretta Cook of the roll, baptized in Nevada in 1873 (Saints’ Herald 55, May 27, 1908, p. 524).

t: 1874–75In England, John R. Eardley has come to Williams “with his belo…
s: 1874–75In England, John R. Eardley has come to Williams “with his beloved wife & family and quickly engaged in business” (Williams to Margaret Thomas, July 27, 1874). Williams still means to come to Montana: in April 1874 he asks about crops, prices, the chance of “a Railway coming thro either from the States or from Ogden,” and “when I come where do you intend to put me for a while” (epistle of April 6, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1874–1875). About January 24, 1875, Williams leaves Ashby for George Thompson’s house at 1 Aglan Place, Shernhall Street, Walthamstow. Thompson, writing to William P. Thomas on January 31, asks: “Have you heard of Brother Warner? He claim[s] to have seen Bro Joseph & to be sent to warn the brethren to gather to Weber, that the Shepherds of Utah will be cut off in 1875 & the Saints be gathered to Weber in 1876. I fear this is too sweet to be true”; and, “I am looking for him & at Weber.” On May 10, 1875, Williams answers such prophecy: “if one cometh saying to Seth cometh to Weber in such a time or times or half a time, the chart & compass of a righteous judgment is gone.” In the same letter he warns against a man who “can keep putting off the coming of Jesus until years has passed away,” and writes that “John Parsons, Livingstone, Davy, Dove [or Dow] and others, after admitting the legal Priesthood of Cainan, fell and attempted a business of their own; these failed and did not do very much injury” (“Davy” is probably Davies, whom Williams elsewhere calls “Doctor Davy”) (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). In November 1875 John R. Eardley reported from Hollister, California, that “Bro. Warner—the German brother” had been through that country warning the Weber Saints “to prepare for the coming of Bro. Joseph next June” (John R. Eardley to William James, Hollister, California, November 9, 1875, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William James, 1874–1875). Brother Warner was almost certainly Joseph Warner of South Weber, a German-born Morrisite who testified in 1879 that a vision of Joseph Smith had got him cut off from the Latter-day Saint church (see Who was “Brother Warner”?).

t: 20 Apr 1875Barnet Moses Giles, who that year published at Salt Lake Ci…
s: 20 Apr 1875Barnet Moses Giles, who that year published at Salt Lake City The Pure Testimony, claiming the presidency of the Latter-day Saint church by descent from Israel, writes to Nels Damander “and all the faithful Brethren and Sisters” in the Omaha region. He is glad they have received “the Books which i have Sent to you,” teaches that “Father adam” is “the only god whom we aught to worship,” and counsels them to make their own sacrament wine, to wash one another’s feet on the first Sunday of the month, and to be ready “to go to build up and to redeem Zion,” adding that nothing of consequence will happen before “(Saul) that is Brigham” has finished his work (copy “Writen By Josephine Jensen,” Church History Library, MS 31876, Niels Jensen record, 1870–1879; for the pamphlet, Singerman, Judaica Americana, entry 2504). 18 Jun 1876At Genoa, Nevada, “a very small gathering” of Morrisites meets in the court house to hear Robert Roberts, who claims to be the Prophet Daniel and tells the town that the child “who is to ‘run’ the Kingdom of God on earth” is already born at Walla Walla. R. J. Livingston opens with an account of “his experiences and sufferings in the cause” (Carson Valley News, June 23, 1876, p. 3). Roberts was William W. Davies’s missionary; Livingston left Genoa for Walla Walla on May 28, 1877 (Carson Valley News, May 29, 1877, p. 3).

t: 2 Jul 1876In San Francisco, George S. Dove organizes his own Church of…
s: 2 Jul 1876In San Francisco, George S. Dove organizes his own Church of the Firstborn “on the morning of the 2d of July, 1876,” with five baptized: George S. Dove, his father James Dove, John Neilson, Joseph Taylor and Joseph A. Dove. Later baptisms the Doves recorded include “mother White, formerly mother Jones,” who had sheltered Morris at Slaterville in 1860, and “mother Dove” (June 9, 1877), Jemima and Margaret Spencer (July 7, 1877) and Elizabeth Hughes (September 22, 1878). In 1879 the Doves listed the claimants who had followed Morris: George Williams; John Livingston in Nevada, with Parson and Cook as counsellors; William W. Davies; Gudmund Gudmundson, with a few short revelations at Sacramento; John Parson in San Francisco, with John Petrie and George S. Dove and seventeen people, “most of them gathered previously by James Dove”; Joseph Warner, who said Morris would return to Weber in June 1876; and George S. Dove himself (George S. and James Dove, A Voice from the West, San Francisco, 1879, pp. 13–15, 22, 26; see Documents). 1876The Danish council minutes for the year show the Montana church meeting monthly in members’ houses at Warm Springs, Deer Lodge and Dempsey Creek, with Andrew Hendrikson presiding and Jens Jensen reading the minutes. Williams, who in April wrote that he had been “very sorrowful … because of the strife, the unfriendliness, the unforgiveness, the disputings” in Montana (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877), has sent William James away on a mission and directed that Daniel James look after James’s stake; when James suspected that the mission was meant “to get rid of you,” Williams wrote that “no such thought could emanate from me” (Williams to James, July 13, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1876–1878). When James returns in August with a letter from Williams, he reads Williams’s word “convenient” to mean that he should preside over the members at Warm Springs and Hendrikson over those at Deer Lodge; the council holds that the two stakes must stay as they are until Williams sends further instructions. In November a letter from Williams asks Hendrikson to call together the brethren “of both priesthoods” to propose a form of government with officers; the council proposes no change. In December it excludes Peter Nelsen, who said he had no faith in Cainan’s mission, from “Jesu Christi Kirke af den Høiestes Hellige,” the Church of Jesus Christ of the Most High Saints (council minutes, January–December 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Rasmus Rasmussen, visiting Williams in England that spring, carries back his letter of April 23 to Margaret Thomas, received June 23; in it Williams says he is holding back further “Chapters of the records” because of the disunion. In October Williams writes to Margaret of “the difficulty of your Husband”: “I cannot think he would be so unwise as to endanger his character; no one can help accusations which go for nothing unless proved”; Thomas had long since stopped writing to him (Williams to Margaret Thomas, April 23 and October 10, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). That December a grand jury at Deer Lodge indicted “Wm. P. Thomas” for assault “with intent to do great bodily injury”; he was tried in the district court, and on December 21 “the jury returned verdict of not guilty and prisoner discharged” (New North-West, December 15, 1876, p. 3; December 22, 1876, p. 3; January 5, 1877, p. 3). This was very probably William P. Thomas of Warm Springs, Williams’s former first counselor; the reports do not name the person assaulted. Williams, told of it in England, wrote in August 1877 of “such a serious charge before a court where his life was in jeopardy” and of Thompson’s distress that Thomas “could be guilty of such hideous crimes,” and complained that a note of Thompson’s to Thomas had been used “to bring persecution on the faithful” (Williams to Hendrikson, August 8, 1877, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877). 1877Williams settles the dispute of 1876: the word “convenient” meant that each member “may choose the Stake convenient to their feelings & opportunities of attending,” under “two distinct Presidencies, not interfering one with the other.” In the same letter of January 11 he asks that February 14, his birthday, be kept as “a day of rejoicing,” and that Sister Rasmussen be ordained “High Priestess” for Stake No. 2. In April he sends William James instructions for a white linen robe and creates “the Court of the Lord’s House,” to meet every May 10; in August he adds a court every November 10. In October he asks for a building “to carry out Temple ordinances,” and moves that the court commit William Davies, S. P. Guhl, James and George Dove and one other “to outer darkness for one thousand years,” to be sanctioned “with both hands uplifted, saying Amen.” In August Williams writes of the “serious charge” that William P. Thomas had faced the winter before (see 1876), and asks that musical talent be encouraged “within limits”: a brother “wasting his talent for Music with the earthly throng” should instead “get up little schools and learn the young.” That summer Rasmus Rasmussen wrote to him of “the Indians in anger coming down upon our friends in Deer Lodge,” during the Nez Perce War; in October Williams wrote that he had been “daily expecting to hear … in hope to allay our uncertainty regarding the mischief expected from Indians,” and that “Bro George & Bro Britt [?] of Weber are with me.” (Williams to Hendrikson, January 11 and August 8, 1877; to James, April 2, 1877; to James, Hendrikson and the Montana Saints, October 12, 1877; Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877, and Lett

t: 13 Nov 1878S. W. Wood, a missionary of William W. Davies, calls at the…
s: 13 Nov 1878S. W. Wood, a missionary of William W. Davies, calls at the Sun office in New York with a proclamation “that the Messiah had come,” on his way to announce it in England. He says Davies learned in Montana in 1866 that he was the Standard of Israel and then the Comforter; that the society near Walla Walla, which “some call … Redemptionists,” keeps a tabernacle, a meeting house and a press; and that the Messiah, “the Father’s Son,” was born in 1868 and is ten years old. The second-advent preacher Stephen H. Tyng Jr. tells the paper he has had “documents from the organization at Walla Walla” (“Mr. Wood of Walla-Walla,” The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878, p. 1; Chronicling America). 1879Robert T. Burton, indicted for the killing of Isabella Bowman during the surrender (in 1870, an indictment voided in 1872, and again in 1877), is tried in the Third District Court from February; on March 7, after forty-six hours, the jury finds him not guilty (Salt Lake Herald, March 8, 1879, p. 3). Morris’s brother George, a Latter-day Saint high priest who had rejected Joseph’s claims, attended the trial and wrote afterward that “there was no nesesity to shed one Drop of Blood” and “no attempt made to take them prisoners alive” (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 198–99).

t: 6 Jan 1879Writing from Walthamstow to William James and the “Saints of…
s: 6 Jan 1879Writing from Walthamstow to William James and the “Saints of the Most High in Stake No. 1 on the Sides of the North in Montana,” George Williams says that the region where they live is “the Sides of the North” (Psalm 48:2), where “the City of the great King” will come down before the Lord’s coming: “you are the pioneers.” He sets no date. The same letter calls the Lord’s House, then building, “my first House of Prayer on the Sides of the North” (Andrew Hendrickson’s copy of 1883, letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881, MS 31876, Church History Library). It is “not the only House of Prayer for Montana; finish it and it will be revealed to you how to raise another more easily at the proper time.” Williams still hoped to come: “if our Merciful God will release me I shall be there to help. How long, dear & Merciful Father, am I required to be a Hunter & a witness for you?”; Peter Staffanson, he had heard, “has a waggon & wishes to ride me round” (same letter, original, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881). See Teachings.

t: 1879–81The Walla Walla press turns on William W. Davies. In August 187…
s: 1879–81The Walla Walla press turns on William W. Davies. In August 1879 the Walla Walla Watchman prints a long exposé: Davies has set himself up as a “prophet of God,” keeps a camp at the foot of the Blue Mountains, claims a child who is the Savior of the world, and has taken money from a blind man who came from San Francisco hoping to be healed (summaries in the Puget Sound Argus, August 28, 1879, p. 4, and the Spokan Times, September 4, 1879). When Davies’s sons die of diphtheria in February 1880, the Watchman calls the elder “the Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called” (Daily Intelligencer (Seattle), March 4, 1880, p. 3, reprinting the Walla Walla Watchman). In December 1880 and January–February 1881 the claims of former members are heard before Judge W. G. Langford as referee, and the Walla Walla Statesman reports the testimony: George Lee, seventy, who had lived fifteen months in the camp and believed “that the boy Jesus would control and rule the Kingdom of God on earth for his father”; D. V. Lambert, brought in by Davies’s missionaries Robert Roberts and Thomas Parker at San Francisco; and the former Morrisite captain Peter C. Klemgard, on the stand more than two days (Walla Walla Statesman, January 1, 1881, p. 2; February 5, 1881, pp. 3–4; checked against the page images; see Repositories for the case file). 1880In Chicago, Mark Hill Forscutt, a former Morrisite apostle now serving as an RLDS minister, baptizes James Brighouse (August 5) and confirms him (August 8), having baptized Mrs. Brighouse in July and preached the funeral of their infant child. In December Forscutt nominates Brighouse as a teacher in the branch. (Forscutt journal, 1880–1881, Vault MSS 811.) Four years later Brighouse founds the Order of Enoch. 1880–81The Race Track council meets in the Lord’s House. In January the council arranges how the 14th of February is to be kept: a meeting in the Lord’s House at half past ten, with those at Deer Lodge and Warm Spring, too far to come, meeting that day in members’ houses. In March 1880 word comes through Rasmus Rasmussen that a son of Williams has died and that Williams hopes to send his family to Montana; the council votes to help them when they come, and in September it reports that “the Lord’s Servant’s daughter” has arrived, the brethren having helped with her fare. On May 10 a joint meeting appoints August 9, the anniversary of the dedication, as “a Social Meeting in the Lords House (Conference),” and William James, robed, administers the sacrament and looks for the coming of Christ in 1891 (see Teachings). At the end of May the council decides that meetings at Warm Spring will be “every other meeting Danish and every other English,” with an English meeting and the Sunday school in the afternoon, because the members “saw the need to practise themselves in the English language”; for the Fourth of July at Deer Lodge, Emanuel Strom is asked to bring his violin. On July 14, 1881, Williams appoints George Thompson in writing to “officiate in his stead for the present and until his recovery,” and Thompson asks the Montana church to lay the appointment “before the Saints for their approval or disapproval” (Thompson to the Montana brethren, August 21, 1881, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881). In September 1881 Hendrikson reads the council “an Epistle from Cainan which George Thompson had written,” and in November members object that John R. Eardley has preached against brandy and tobacco in a public meeting; Hendrikson says Eardley has “gone to extremes” (minutes, 1880–81, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1880 and Minutes, 1881; translation from the Danish generated by Claude, except the meeting of May 10, 1880, which is in English).

t: 1881–90The Reorganized Church gathers members in the Deer Lodge Valley…
s: 1881–90The Reorganized Church gathers members in the Deer Lodge Valley. Its Deer Lodge Branch register opens with baptisms by W. W. Blair in the valley on August 21, 1881. Joseph C. Clapp, who in 1886 offers the Morrisites the use of the new RLDS meeting house in Deer Lodge City, baptizes at Deer Lodge and Willow Glen from 1886 to 1890, among others three men who had been Morrisites at Omaha: Peter Nielsen (1887), Niels Jensen (1890) and Niels Thorkelsen (1890) (Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District, #228, Community of Christ Library Archives; Record of members, 1869–1872, MS 32226, Church History Library). See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?

t: 1882–83Williams dies in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 ye…
s: 1882–83Williams dies in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 year,” after about two years of great pain from “an enlargement of the bone” in his shoulder joint; George Thompson, who had done his writing for him, still knew of no one “appointed to fill his place” in August 1883 (Thompson to William P. Thomas, August 9, 1883, MS 31876). The movement splits among rival successors. In Montana, where the church is known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High, Williams had directed that William James, its local president, be put before the church a year after his death: “Let the organisation remain as it is, for twelve months after my decease, then let brother James be placed before the whole Church when assembled at the years end, and if sustained by uplifted hand, there let him remain, and so on, from year to year” (Williams to the Montana brethren, January 29, 1882, Church History Library, MS 31876). An envelope he addressed to James, postmarked at New York on March 26, bears the words “I leave you in charge after my decease.” In his last weeks George Thompson, who lived near him in Walthamstow, answered the Montana church’s questions for him: on March 23, 1882, he wrote that “Bro Cainan is no better but gradually getting weaker & weaker,” and that if Williams named no one to replace a Sister Rasmussen in her office, the church should choose someone “and we will confirm your choice” (MS 31876). A week earlier, on March 16, Sister Theodora had written for him to Margaret Thomas of “my martyrdom out of sight of my family,” asking her to befriend his daughter Adelaide, then in Montana, “being absent from her Mother and Sisters” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). The same day he wrote to William James that Adelaide, living with the Daniel James family, “is now a member with you,” thanked Sister Daniel James, “the Sister who offered me a home if I could come to Montana,” for five dollars sent “in the time of my affliction,” and welcomed James’s hint of a match between Adelaide and his son: “our generations might meet and go down through time together; tell me his age, is he steady and likely to make a good husband” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1879–1882). The match did not take place: Adelaide never married, and William R. James married Elizabeth Frances Emmons at Deer Lodge in 1886 (FamilySearch Family Tree, KWJ8-P3L; L6V6-ZNQ; California Death Index, ark:/61903/1:1:VPQR-KCV). On April 25, 1883, a general assembly in the Lord’s House sustains James by 19 votes to 10, and he chooses Andrew Hendrikson and John R. Eardley as counselors. Several of the minority, among them Erick Eliason and Lars Beck, refuse to accept the vote, and the Race Track bishop, Rasmus Rasmussen, who will not sustain James, keeps the church’s records and is suspended (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories). On May 26 the Race Track council removes those who would not accept the vote: Hendrikson said that the teachers “had left us of their own will, because they were not satisfied with the president election and the organization of this church.” Peder Jansen and Lars Beck are released as teachers, Erik Eliason as deacon and keeper of the Lord’s House, and Jens Jensen as Hendrikson’s counselor and scribe; the Jensens, the Becks, the Jansens, Hans Golde, Eliason and Peder Just are released “from membership and the church’s obligations,” since they “had separated themselves from us.” George Johnson is made bishop of the stake, and a Sunday school and a fortnightly prayer meeting are begun (minutes, May 26, 1883, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1883–1884; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). By February 1884 Johnson reports “no disorder among the Saints such as ther were before the separation” (minutes, February 24, 1884, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1883–1884). (Eardley, later a stake president, leaves Montana about 1900.) In the Danish-speaking stake at Race Track, the council minutes record the other side of the vote: in December 1882 Andrew Hendrikson read Williams’s last instructions that, if no new servant of the Lord came before the anniversary, the church might “selv … vælge en Leder for Kirken” (“itself choose a leader for the church”); in February 1883 he said that since “Cainan havde recommenderet Wm. James” he would uphold him, while Lars Beck said he could not see that choosing a president would do them any good (Race Track council minutes, December 30, 1882, and February 24, 1883, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). George Dove leads the California congregation. 1884The yearly assembly of April 25, at which Williams had directed that William James be put before the church “from year to year,” becomes a dispute. James and Andrew Hendrikson set it aside; John R. Eardley holds that Williams’s words, “Let the organization remain as it is for twelve months after my decease; then let Bro. James be placed before the whole church,” meant a vote every year, not “I leave you in charge” for life, and George Thompson in England takes his side (Eardley to Hendrickson, April 24 and 25, 1884, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1880–1889). 1884A later claimant. James Brighouse, breaking from the RLDS Church, organizes the Order of Enoch in Independence, Missouri, a small commune with Lars Peterson whose main tenet is celibacy. After breaking with the Petersons he has a vision on July 21, 1885 (The Voice of the Seventh Angel, part 1, p. 28, a reference supplied by Kirk Watson; Internet Archive). Returning to Utah, he proclaims himself the embodiment of the Second Coming and the “One Mighty and Strong,” and only then, as far as Kirk Watson can tell, teaches reincarnation. Brighouse had been brought into the RLDS Church in 1880 by the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forsc

t: 25 Jan 1885Joseph Smith III writes to John Parson after a meeting betw…
s: 25 Jan 1885Joseph Smith III writes to John Parson after a meeting between them, quoting Morris’s revelation of May 4, 1861, on the Reorganization (The Spirit Prevails, No. 64), asking whether Parson or Richard Cook had represented the Weber body after Morris, and urging him to join the Reorganized Church. Smith counts 281 revelations of Morris by the Doves’ Olive Branch and calls Morris’s followers “divided” (Joseph Smith III Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, pp. 148–51, Community of Christ Library Archives). 1885George S. and James Dove of the California congregation preach in Salt Lake City and the Cottonwoods, baptizing ten on September 14, then go on to Montana in October. At Willow Glen and Deer Lodge they hold meetings, baptize W. P. Thomas and L. C. Larson on October 26, and speak in the Deer Lodge courthouse; John R. Eardley orders James Dove out of his store, and at Race Track the members refuse them the Lord’s House and agree not to hear them. By the Doves’ account, “a number of brethren” in Montana pressed George S. Dove to publish Morris’s revelations “just as they were written”; it took him about seven months, “as the revelations were in a very disordered condition,” and The Spirit Prevails appeared in 1886 (James Dove, A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, [1892], pp. 6–13, in Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892). In November the Montana council disowned the Doves as “pretenders” in the New North-West.

t: Jan 1886Writing from Stuart, Montana, on January 18, the RLDS missiona…
s: Jan 1886Writing from Stuart, Montana, on January 18, the RLDS missionary J. C. Clapp, whose “Montana notes” had given offence by what they said of the Doves, calls the Morrisites of the Deer Lodge Valley “an honest, industrious people” and adds: “The great and most damaging difference is in respect to the right of presidency” (Saints’ Herald 33, 1886, pp. 86–87).

t: 1886At the yearly general assembly in the Lord’s House at Race Track, …
s: 1886At the yearly general assembly in the Lord’s House at Race Track, Montana, on April 25, George Thompson of London is elected president of the church; William James, who had claimed the presidency for life “by birthright,” resting on Williams’s envelope “I leave you in charge,” stays away. Eleven members who decline to sustain Thompson are given thirty days to do so. At a court meeting on May 10 James is suspended “for the crimes of usurpation of authority, and heresy,” and John R. Eardley is put over the Warm Spring Creek stake (Church History Library, MS 32226; see Repositories); Daniel James is suspended too, as a teacher and member, “for rebellion against the teachings, laws and authority of the church.” A separate tally of the April vote lists seventeen votes for Thompson, women and girls among them (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1886–1887). Those who held out were led by the officers of Stake No. 1, William M. James as stake president, Peter Steffanson as bishop and Daniel James as teacher; six of them met and sustained William James as their president, and rumors went round that “John the Revelator” was coming (Eardley to Hendrickson, May 2, 1886, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1880–1889). That December Thompson was living in England, writing to the Montana brethren from Thornwood Common, Epping, Essex (MS 31876). Thompson is probably the last general president. Andrew Hendrikson, a Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, presides over the Montana Morrisites from 1886 until his death on July 3, 1921. 1886The Spirit Prevails, a collection of Morris’s revelations, articles, and letters, is published by George S. Dove & Company. 1887At the “Annual President Election” in the Lord’s House on April 25, Hendrikson reminds the church that “some time ago we thought that the Church would never be left without a Prophet,” and that Williams had told them to “allow the Majority to rule.” George Thompson is sustained as president of the church, John R. Eardley as president of Stake No. 1, Hendrikson as president of Stake No. 2, and George Johnson as bishop for the church; three trustees are appointed for the Lord’s House, which “under the new law” was otherwise “liable for Taxation” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1886–1887). 1887In March John R. Eardley reports that “we are to have the Doves here again on the 17th,” to the unease of some members, two years after the church had disowned them. He is also in touch with the followers of David Whitmer: Whitmer has sent a postcard promising pamphlets, the Expositor has printed an article on the “Church of Christ” signed “P.J.” and a dedicatory prayer by John Parson, and Brother Emmons, on a visit to Missouri, means to call on Whitmer at Richmond and go on to Independence and Lamoni. Joseph Smith III has written to Eardley of a proposed new place of worship opposite the Temple Lot at Independence. Later that month Eardley sails for England, where his mother is ill, planning to see Thompson and, on his way, the Kirtland Temple, Lamoni, Independence and “Father Whitmer”; Brother Strom is to conduct the meetings while he is gone (Eardley to Hendrickson, March 11 and 18, 1887, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1880–1889).

t: 1886–90John Parson is baptized into the Reorganized Church at Oakland …
s: 1886–90John Parson is baptized into the Reorganized Church at Oakland by Joseph Smith III (December 12, 1886, in the church record; February 23, 1886, in the Oakland branch record). In 1888 H. P. Brown of Oakland accuses him of spiritualism; Smith refuses to sanction Dr. P. W. Poulson’s book “Light of Messiah” and its “Order of Messiah,” in which Parson had been offered the place of “Third general,” and Parson returns his certificate of appointment in July. He is expelled on April 1, 1890 (Henry A. Stebbins to Richard Ferris, November 20, 1891, HASLB7, pp. 236–37; Joseph Smith III Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, pp. 287–319, Community of Christ Library Archives). The Montana council takes his case as a sign of waning confidence in Smith (MS 32226, minutebook, May 10, 1889). 1888–89George Thompson, still president of the church, writes from Thornwood Gate, Epping, that he is “here alone on an island,” uncertain how the parable of the ten virgins will be fulfilled, and wary of spiritualism: “I shall stick to the chosen few.” In January 1889 Eardley subscribes for himself and Hendrikson to The Return, a Whitmerite paper he calls “a thorn in the side of the Reorganized Church.” That winter he is chief clerk of the Council of the 16th Legislative Assembly at Helena (Thompson to Eardley, October 7, 1888, and February 17, 1889; Eardley to Hendrickson, January 7 and March 8, 1889, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1880–1889).

t: Mar 1890Writing from Deer Lodge on March 4, J. C. Clapp says he has be…
s: Mar 1890Writing from Deer Lodge on March 4, J. C. Clapp says he has been preaching to the Morrisite brethren and was welcomed by “Peter Stafferson and family, Niels Jenson and family, James Emmons and family and Andrew Peterson and family.” “Father James, who has been the president of that part of the people called Canaanites, has been very sick.” He adds: “I baptized brother and sister Emmons” (Saints’ Herald 37, 1890, p. 184). James M. Emmons had joined the Morrisites in California; by his obituary he came west in 1862 and moved his family to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1881 (Saints’ Herald 51, 1904, p. 677; see the Montana register).

t: Feb 1891At Olney, Washington, John Davis baptizes into the Reorganized…
s: Feb 1891At Olney, Washington, John Davis baptizes into the Reorganized Church “an aged man named Hastings,” very probably Winter Hastings of the roll, who had joined the Morrisites in Utah and “was with Joseph Morris when he was shot” (Saints’ Herald 38, 1891, p. 134; see The siege). 1891The year that William James had named in 1880 for the coming of Christ passes. On November 10 Hendrikson tells the court that they had long expected “the ‘winding up scene’” this year, and Eardley proposes moving the Lord’s House nearer the members, since “the apostasy of so many of the Saints in Race Track” had left it out of the way (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1891; see Teachings). Writing to the court beforehand, Eardley called 1891 “the year in which we have been led to expect so much.” That spring John Parson, now leading a mission of his own, wrote to Eardley that the work under his charge would be “established this year.” From May 31 to August 2 the Sunday Salt Lake Tribune printed ten letters on the Latter-day Saint church signed “The Elder,” under the running title “Charity for the Mormons,” which Eardley said were Parson’s; the first spoke of 1891 as “a year of expectancy of great things,” and the seventh to ninth told the Morrisite story (see Newspapers). By October Parson had visited the Saints in the Deer Lodge Valley. In December Eardley wrote that a high priest whose ordination had been only temporary was “in open rebellion” against Hendrickson and the court, preaching at Warm Springs and meeting with others there; he feared that only a handful might be left as witnesses (Eardley to Hendrickson, June–December 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1891). 1892In San Francisco, James Dove publishes A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites for the California congregation, and A Treatise on Re-Incarnation or Re-Embodiment, which Kirk Watson calls the earliest book on the subject in the wider Mormon tradition (Watson, pp. 199, 208–64). A printed copy of A Few Items survives among Hendrickson’s letters at the Church History Library. On June 13, the thirtieth anniversary of the posse’s arrival at Weber, the former apostle John Parson dies of pneumonia at the Larsens’ ranch near Deer Lodge; Eardley calls the death “a great shock” that “undermines many of my calculations, and some of the predictions of Weber!” (Eardley to James Dove, June 18, and to Hendrickson, July 3, 1892, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892). 1893As the Salt Lake Temple nears its dedication on April 6, Eardley writes that “Joseph Morris prophesied it never would be completed,” and that he has been watching to see whether Morris spoke “by the spirit” or “by his own presumption”; no such prophecy has been found in The Spirit Prevails, whose revelations place the temple in Jackson County. On August 9, the church’s feast day, Peter Helstrom’s wife and some children are to be baptized at Race Track (Eardley to Hendrickson, February 28 and July 27, 1893, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1893–1901). 1894After the division of 1891–92, Eardley hears that Staffanson and Mrs. Daniel James have agreed to let his group use “the meeting house” part of the time; which building is meant is not clear (Eardley to Hendrickson, March 28, 1894, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1893–1901). 1901Eardley calls the members together with Hendrickson and George Johnson on April 25 “to prevent if possible the threatened collapse of God’s little church,” reminding Hendrickson that it “is not my Church, nor your Church” and that they are only its stewards (Eardley to Hendrickson, April 22, 1901, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1893–1901). It is the latest dated crisis in the church’s papers at the Church History Library.

t: 1902At Deer Lodge, the RLDS apostle William H. Kelley preaches “seven …
s: 1902At Deer Lodge, the RLDS apostle William H. Kelley preaches “seven miles out of town for the Morrisites or Canaanites,” Brother Christoffersen driving him out; “Elder A. Hendrickson was in charge and invited me to occupy the morning hour” (Saints’ Herald 49, 1902, p. 898).

t: Jan 1924George W. Thorburn of the Reorganized Church writes that he is…
s: Jan 1924George W. Thorburn of the Reorganized Church writes that he is “living right in a settlement of the Morrisites; some of them have been baptized in the recent past” (Saints’ Herald 71, January 23, 1924, p. 88).

t: Sep 1925A visitor from the RLDS reunion in Montana drives “via Dempsey…
s: Sep 1925A visitor from the RLDS reunion in Montana drives “via Dempsey” to photograph “a neat-looking, small building labeled over the entrance, ‘The Lord’s House,’” “the only church building owned by the Morrisites,” and calls on Andrew Hanson, “a little Dane, eighty-one years old,” and his sister Mrs. Bernard (Saints’ Herald 72, September 23, 1925, p. 1012).

t: 1921–1954George Johnson, Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty yea…
s: 1921–1954George Johnson, Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years and likewise never a Latter-day Saint, presides at the Lord’s House until shortly before his death on April 29, 1954, at ninety-eight. Anderson calls him the last official Morrisite leader: by the 1940s fewer than a dozen members were active, and with Johnson’s death the church came to an end and the Lord’s House was boarded up (Revisited, pp. 212, 214). His funeral was conducted by an Episcopal priest, and the local paper called the Morrisite church “almost extinct these days” (Silver State Post, May 7, 1954, p. 7; see Newspapers).

t: 1969Surviving Morrisites, all of the second or third generation, gathe…
s: 1969Surviving Morrisites, all of the second or third generation, gather at the Lord’s House on August 9, the anniversary of its dedication and one of the church’s two feast days; by then, Anderson writes, the gatherings were more social than religious (Revisited, p. 218). Utah State University’s finding aid for the Morrisite collection says the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High officially disbanded in 1969, and the description of Anderson’s papers says meetings were held irregularly until then; Anderson himself dates the end to 1954. See How and when did the Montana church end? Its records, its descendants, and the Racetrack church remain.

t: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (19…
s: 1981–1988C. LeRoy Anderson publishes For Christ Will Come Tomorrow (1981) and Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (1988), the first book-length histories. 1990A later claimant. Neal Chase, interpreter for Leland Jensen’s Missoula-based sect, the Bahá’ís Under the Provisions of the Covenant, publishes Ezekiel’s Temple in Montana. Drawing on Anderson’s book, he cites George Williams’s prophecy that Christ would come in the Deer Lodge Valley, identifies the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge (where Jensen was held from 1969) as Ezekiel’s temple, and dates the fulfillment to August 9, 1969, Jensen’s first full day in prison. Jensen already taught that the prison was Ezekiel’s temple; his followers say they first learned of the Morrisites and Williams on a trip to Deer Lodge in 1990. Anderson finds that the book attributes far more prophetic ability to Williams than he had, and that there is no substantive proof the 1969 gathering anticipated the Second Advent (Revisited, pp. 216–18). The sect was not Morrisite in origin; it adopted Morrisite prophecies as confirmation of its leader’s mission. 1996–2010After Jensen’s death in 1996 the sect divides over leadership, with Chase leading one faction; lawsuits continue to about 2010.

t: 2006A monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site is dedicated at …
s: 2006A monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site is dedicated at South Weber. 2010Anderson’s final edition, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited), is published. July 2012Descendants of Morrisite families hold a reunion in Deer Lodge; the property owners allow them to visit the Racetrack church. 2026Kirk Watson publishes The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations, collecting writings of Morris, Williams, Davies, and the Doves. The Racetrack church still stands, in declining condition (see the condition record under Images).
History
Places Sites connected with the movement, and what can be seen at each today. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008

Kington Fort South Weber, Utah Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. Not all the people in the fort were from South Weber. Holley (2008) names eleven men from Slaterville and Marriott, about nine miles to the northwest, among the prisoners of June 1862, and two of the family groups on the roll, Cowan–Bull and Higham, were Slaterville families (see “Families on the roll” on the roll page). A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The date cannot be his death: a Joseph Warner, sixty-two, born in Germany, a widowed laborer, was living at South Weber in 1880 (1880 U.S. census, South Weber, Davis County, ED 16), and he died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September (Davis County Court minutes, October 2 and October 30, 1893, pp. 462, 470 (County court minutes, 1852–1893, FamilySearch film 484601, item 2, DGS 7579269)). The date is a modern guess. In 1979 Werner’s grave was unmarked (Standard-Examiner, May 9, 1979, p. 75); Leonard Bowman of South Weber said in 1983 that he had learned two years before where Werner was buried and had a marker made for him (Salt Lake Tribune, April 28, 1983, p. 75), and in 1984 that marker read “Joseph Werner Morrisite, died about 1870” (Lakeside Review, North Edition, May 23, 1984, p. 2). The present flat markers were laid by a Boy Scout troop copying the older ones, about twenty years ago by the city’s account (the photograph is earlier than February 2004), and the date came over from Bowman’s marker. The city’s cemetery records do not support it: Mattie G. Ray’s compiled list, typed in 1998, enters “Werner, Joseph” with no dates, as the “only Morrisite to stay in South Weber,” and the plot map puts him in lot 20, on the south row. The city, drawing on Norma Earl Allred’s compilation of South Weber families, also regards the date as an error; Allred adds that several people she talked to had been told stories about “the old Morrisite that lived by or at the fort” (Norma Earl Allred, comp., South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952 (2004), Attachment 3) (South Weber City cemetery records, sent to the editor by Lisa Smith, November 16, 2026). He was almost certainly the “Brother Warner” who in 1875 prophesied a gathering to Weber (see Who was “Brother Warner”?). The same records place other Morrisites in or by the cemetery. Two were buried outside the fence near its northeast corner, because residents did not want them inside; one was “Bella Bowman,” very probably Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender (see Who died at Kington Fort?). Charles Patton Bowman (1865–1872), son of John and Agnes Bowman, both on the roll, is buried in lot 40. Bendt Nielsen, who died on July 15, 1862, a month after the siege, is buried in lot 24 (same records). He was not a casualty of the siege: a family history by his granddaughter May Nielsen Christensen makes him a Latter-day Saint convert from Denmark who died on his farm at South Weber, the second burial in the cemetery (Lakeside Review, September 18, 1990, p. 9). The city’s history of the cemetery notes “at least one burial” from the war of 1862. In 1908 Henry Firth, who had lived at South Weber in the Morrisite years, showed John Banks what was left of the fort wall and the site of Morris’s house, and pointed out fifteen unmarked mounds in the old village cemetery that he said held Morrisites killed in 1862 (Banks, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” 1909, p. 2). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) Two traditions of the siege survive in undated papers kept by the city, their authors unknown, and neither has been found in a contemporary account. Local tradition: a dissenter was chained in a log shed for three weeks and escaped his Danish guard near Weber Canyon; the story may echo the detention of the three departing members. Local tradition: the posse fired pieces of cut wagon tire from the hill near Uintah, and a boy on a white horse was sent to stop the firing (South Weber City files, “Morrisite Movement” and “Morrisite War Incident”). Family tradition: the first cannon ball, a

Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement; John L. Bear, who left for Missouri in 1870, remembered “about 30 families” when they first came and “about 10” by then, and sold his two log houses, stables and yards to Erick Eliason for $350 (Johann L. Baer, autobiography, circa 1908, typescript, MS 10240, Church History Library, p. 47). Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir.

Carson City & California Nevada · California The western congregations, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails and led the California church after 1882. In May 1863 Connor gave 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City in an empty quartermaster’s train bound there for stores (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). VisitNo surviving sites identified for this guide. Information welcome.

Omaha & Council Bluffs Nebraska · Iowa Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. Their own minutebook, written up at Omaha in May 1871, tells how they began. Jens Jacob Poulsen, “a High Priest of the Weber House,” was sent ahead by George Williams to gather the scattered Morrisites, and spent about a year there. Williams himself arrived in Omaha on January 18, 1869, “from his home in South Cottonwood in Utah,” on his way to England, held meetings in Omaha and Council Bluffs, and left on February 5 with Poulsen and a Brother Mortensen, who went on to Denmark. On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, S. P. Guhl, newly come from Montana, organized the church on Williams’s authority: Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, under Carlton Fellows, with Hans Nielsen over the Scandinavians at Crescent City, since the Danes “were not satisfied” to have an American president; and Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for all the Saints west of the Missouri, under Jens Jensen, with a district at Florence under Niels Jensen. Rasmus Rasmussen became the first bishop. A conference at Omaha on April 6, 1869, sustained “George Williams, called of the Lord Cainan,” as “our Prophet, Seer and Revelator,” and on May 30, as Guhl left on a mission to Denmark, Andrew Hendrikson was appointed to preside, with Jens Jensen and Hans Nielsen as counselors (minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In March 1871 the church gave up its yearly conferences, which Hendrikson said Guhl had brought in “in likeness with the Mormons’ custom” and Williams had never commanded, and met instead in councils in members’ houses and in “social gatherings.” That May one of its leaders, Sister Marie Mortensen, whom Williams had called the congregation’s “High Priestess” in 1870 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870), joined the Reorganized Church, and Hendrikson had the early records copied into a book, “for many of us must be called hence and go to other places.” The last entry is dated June 4, 1871, at Jens Jensen’s house in Omaha. Most of the congregation moved to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1871–72. Those who stayed were courted by other churches: by 1874 Danish “Josephites” of the Reorganized Church were challenging S. P. Guhl to debate, and a Danish Adventist missionary had baptized several “of our brothers and friends”; O. P. Andersen wrote from Omaha that spring that one of the sisters had taken up Adventist teaching and lodged a Danish Adventist preacher (Guhl to Hendrikson, Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874, and O. P. Andersen to Hendrikson, Omaha, March 10, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878; translations from the Danish and Swedish generated by Claude). VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018

Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, built in 1878–79, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County; until 1901 this was Deer Lodge County, the county named in older records and in this guide’s photograph captions). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). In the 1870s the council also met in members’ houses on Dempsey Creek, near the site: in December 1876 it set its next meeting for Peter Jansen’s place on Dempsey Creek (council minutes, December 3, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). It was last photographed for this guide in August 2020. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. Everyone the sources place in the Montana church is listed in the register of Montana Morrisites on the People page. The Deer Lodge paper, the New North-West, spoke well of its Morrisite neighbors. In June 1878 it reported that the post office at Gwendale, Deer Lodge County, had been renamed Morristown, and that “as many of the people are Morrisites” they would likely take to the name. In 1883 it called the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River “largely composed” of Morrisites and praised them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding; in 1885 it noted “a large number of Morrisites in this valley” (New North-West, June 7, 1878, p. 3; April 13, 1883, p. 2; October 30, 1885, p. 3; see Newspapers). The paper’s notices place Gwendale in the upper Deer Lodge valley, near Warm Springs and Lost Creek. It was school district No. 6; in April 1875 “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” met at the Gwendale school house on the railroad question, with Morgan Evans in the chair and a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee; Gwendale primaries were held at Wier’s store; and a smelter there began work in August 1877 (New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2; June 18, 1875, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3). Morgan Evans, whose land later became Anaconda, gave Gwendale as his address. By 1883 the same school district, No. 6, was called Willow Glen, with Peter Jessen, a Gwendale man since the 1870s, as a trustee and J. I. Eardley as clerk (New North-West, May 4, 1883, p. 3). In March 1880 the land office listed Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims were held up while it decided whether the ground was mineral land; among them were Daniel James and William P. Thomas, on Warm Springs Creek east of where Anaconda was built (secs. 33 and 34, T5N R10W), and Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen, in sec. 9, T4N R10W, near today’s Opportunity (New North-West, April 30, 1880, p. 4); all four claims were patented as homesteads in 1880–81. In January 1882 the paper reported that John R. Eardley, formerly of San Francisco, had built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and that the neighborhood had petitioned for a post office there “to be called Willow Glen”; in March it reported his appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was” (New North-West, January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3). Gwendale, renamed Morristown in 1878, and Willow Glen were thus successive post offices for the same neighborhood, between Anaconda, Opportunity and Warm Springs. The exact site of the Gwendale school house is still not known. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property.

Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked.

Beyond the West Some places outside the American West appear in the sources but are not mapped here, since the movement did not settle there. Loughborough, Ashwicken and Walthamstow, England: George Williams led his followers from England by letter from 1869 until his death at Walthamstow on April 25, 1882 (see Chronology, 1869 and 1882–83). St. Ann’s Hill, Surrey: where Williams said the ancient records he translated came from (see Teachings). Copenhagen and Amager, Denmark: the Danish mission of S. P. Guhl and J. P. Lorentzen, 1869–71, and its break with Williams (see Chronology, 1870–71). Constantinople: where Almerin Grow carried Williams’s message to the Sultan (see Teachings).

Names and terms The names of the churches, places, offices and titles that readers meet across this guide, in brief. Each entry links to where the guide says more.

t: Church of the Firstborn The name by which Joseph Morris’s church, orga…
s: Church of the Firstborn The name by which Joseph Morris’s church, organized on April 6, 1861, at South Weber, Utah, is now usually known; its members are usually called Morrisites. It was not the church’s first name. Morris’s revelations call it simply “my Church,” and the revelation on baptism of April 3, 1861, speaks of members of “the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, under the fullness of the gospel” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 55, p. 78). Anderson, following Richard W. Young (1890), gives the name at the organization as the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High, and says it “later on” became known as the Church of the Firstborn. The Prophet Cainan declared that the church would “also be called The Church of the Firstborn,” and the Doves’ California congregation used the name from the 1870s (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 57, 66, 182). See more

t: Morrisites Followers of Joseph Morris, and members of the churches tha…
s: Morrisites Followers of Joseph Morris, and members of the churches that descended from his church. In South Weber the word lingered long enough to be used as a schoolyard taunt. During the siege Daniel H. Wells struck “Morrisite” and “Morrisitism” from Burton’s dispatches and told him to do the same, “as we do not wish to perpetuate them. When you speak, or write of the place, call it South Weber, or Kington’s Fort” (Wells to Burton, June 15, 1862, Daniel H. Wells, letterpress copy book, MS 1344, Church History Library, pp. 13–14). It was named for Bishop Thomas Kington; “Kington” is the correct spelling, but many accounts write “Kingston.” Search under both. See more

t: Prophet Cainan George Williams (born February 14, 1814, at Thorpe, Sur…
s: Prophet Cainan George Williams (born February 14, 1814, at Thorpe, Surrey), who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that gathered in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, from the late 1860s; he was writing to “Saints of the Most High in Montana” by December 1868. In a letter of January 6, 1879, he told the Montana Saints that the region where they lived was “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming; he set no date. He left America for England about January 1869. His letters from England are headed from Loughborough, London and Ashby by Brigg, Lincolnshire (1870–74), with a stay in the spring of 1873 at Stockport, Cheshire, at 23 Great Portwood Street, where John R. Eardley wrote on April 8, 1873, that “Bro Cainan is sitting by my side” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1872–1873), and Walthamstow, Essex, where he lived near and then with George Thompson (1875–80 and 1882), with a stay at Wrawby, near Brigg, Lincolnshire, in 1880–81, from where he wrote to Thompson (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1879–1882) (Church History Library, MS 31876); about 1870 he took his letters in care of Thompson at 336 Wellington Row, Hackney Road, London (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). On January 28, 1882, the Race Track council voted to “uphold Bro. George Thompson” as the one Williams had appointed “to write to the church in his place,” since he could no longer write himself (minutes, MS 31876, Minutes, 1882; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Thompson explained to the Montana church in 1882 that Williams “was not really Cainan the son of Enos, but that he represented him, & so with Joseph first and second” (MS 31876). He died in England on April 25, 1882, “being in his 68 year,” after two years of pain from a diseased shoulder (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1883, MS 31876). His birth date is given in FamilySearch Family Tree (KWJ8-P3L); the Race Track council kept February 14 as “Herrens Tjeners Fødselsdag,” the Lord’s Servant’s birthday (minutes, December 30, 1882, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude); Williams himself had asked in January 1877 that the day be “set apart by the faithful for a day of rejoicing … in all coming time” (Williams to Hendrikson, January 11, 1877, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877), and the council met to celebrate it in February 1882 (minutes, January 28, 1882, MS 31876, Minutes, 1882; translation from the Danish generated by Claude), and it was still one of the church’s two feast days in the twentieth century (Anderson, Revisited, p. 218). His wife Louisa and their children, six daughters and a son, stayed in Salt Lake City, in the 8th Ward by December 1869, when he gave “the address of my family” there (Williams to the Omaha church, December 24, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869), and in 1871, when the eldest, Adelaide Matilda, was thirteen. In 1870 the family wrote that grasshoppers had eaten their crops, and Williams asked the Omaha members to buy flour and send it by railroad, marked for “Mrs Susanna L. A. Williams” (Williams to Hendrikson, July 10, 1870, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870). Adelaide (born 1859 in Salt Lake City) was a schoolteacher in 1880; that year she went to Montana, where by September the Race Track council had helped with the cost of her journey (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1880; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). She never married, and died at Los Angeles on December 18, 1947 (1880 U.S. census, Salt Lake City, 8th Ward, ark:/61903/1:1:MNSV-RYF; California Death Index, ark:/61903/1:1:VPQR-KCV). About 1870 he wrote that he no longer had a home there, and from September 1871 he heard nothing from Louisa or from Susanna, his wife since 1846 (see Teachings); in 1872 and 1874 he asked Margaret Thomas in Montana to find out discreetly whether Louisa had married again. In July 1874 Margaret passed on Louisa’s charge that he “had another wife & two children” and money in the bank; he called it a seducer’s story, and Louisa still “my dearest Love, the mother of my children” (see Teachings). In 1871 the Omaha Saints sent the family flour, Eardley arranged goods for them and the Montana Saints sent help, which Williams said had “relieved me of dreadful thoughts for their safety this winter” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873). In December 1872 he had not yet had a carte de visite taken and was reluctant to, as “it would I know soon get in the public picture.” Five weeks before he died he called his illness “my martyrdom out of sight of my family” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). See more

t: Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High According to Anderso…
s: Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High According to Anderson, following Richard W. Young (1890), the name Morris’s church took at its organization on April 6, 1861 (Revisited, p. 66; see Church of the Firstborn). It was the name of the Montana church, used by its council by 1873 and kept after Williams’s death on April 25, 1882, when it was led in turn by William James, George Thompson, Andrew Hendrikson and George Johnson. By Anderson’s account it ended with Johnson’s death in 1954 (Revisited, pp. 212, 214); USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding. See more

t: Lord’s House The Montana Morrisites’ wood-frame church near Racetrack,…
s: Lord’s House The Montana Morrisites’ wood-frame church near Racetrack, built in 1878–79 on Andrew Hendrikson’s land and named for the panel over its doors. Williams first asked for it in October 1877, as a building that “when finished, will serve to carry out Temple ordinances,” left the choice of site to “the majority” in January 1878, and in August 1878 called it “a Temple in miniature and place of worship for the faithful,” and sent the words for its dedication in September 1878 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877, and Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1876–1878). It was dedicated on August 9, 1879 (Race Track council minutes, July 29, 1882, Church History Library, MS 31876), and the church kept the day as its anniversary and one of its two feast days, on which surviving Morrisites still gathered there in 1969 (Anderson, Revisited, p. 218); in 1884 John R. Eardley paid to have it painted (Church History Library, MS 32226). In 1887 three trustees were appointed so that it could be exempted from taxation. In November 1891 Eardley proposed moving it, because it stood out of the way across fields, tramps broke into it and sparks from passing locomotives had set the grass round it alight, to “the other end of Bro. Hendrickson’s field, adjoining the Public School House”; the matter was laid over (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1886–1887, and Minutes, 1891). It was still the church’s meeting place at the end of 1892, when Eardley urged the Saints to see that “the Lord’s House is none other than the very gate of Heaven to them” (Eardley to Hendrickson, December 25, 1892, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892); whether it was moved later is not yet known. The anniversary of its opening became a feast day at William James’s proposal, which Williams confirmed in September 1880 as “a perpetual day … like the 14 day of Feb.” (record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, Church History Library, MS 31876). It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive. See more
