t: Walla Walla Jesus The popular name for Arthur Davies (1868–1880), son …
s: Walla Walla Jesus The popular name for Arthur Davies (1868–1880), son of William W. Davies. Davies said that on the eighth day after the boy’s birth he proclaimed the Messiah come again in him and named him “Messiah Son of David”; the boy later took the name Arthur (1882 interview, Watson, p. 192). His younger brother David was held to carry the spirit of God the Father. Both died of diphtheria in February 1880 (Watson, pp. 191–93). The belief spread beyond Walla Walla: in 1877 the Carson Valley News reported that R. J. Livingstone had sold his property at Genoa, Nevada, to live near a child born at Walla Walla who was to be the Savior (May 29, 1877, p. 3). The name was current in his lifetime: at his death in February 1880 the Walla Walla Watchman called him “the Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called” (reprinted in the Seattle Daily Intelligencer, March 4, 1880, p. 3; see Questions). It is also the name is used in the Washington State Archives’ index to the 1880 lawsuit against Davies, in Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 paper and in the Fort Walla Walla Museum’s collection description. George Williams, writing from England in April 1877, counted “another with his come to Walla Walla and see my little Jesus” among “miserable speculators on your credulity” (Williams to William James, April 2, 1877, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1876–1878). See the question · See more

t: Seventh Angel A title Joseph Morris claimed, after the angel who sound…
s: Seventh Angel A title Joseph Morris claimed, after the angel who sounds the last trumpet in Revelation. For Morris it marked a stage in the soul’s ascent through the angelic ranks. He claimed it before the apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff at South Weber on February 11, 1861, saying also that he held “six times more keys of the Priesthood” than Joseph Smith (Wilford Woodruff journal, February 11, 1861, MS 1352, Church History Library). An informer heard him claim it again on May 12, 1861: “I say now I profess to be the Seventh Angel. The seventh thousand years is now ushered in” (“Doctrines of the Morrisites, May 12, 1861,” informer’s report, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). The phrase was already in Latter-day Saint use: Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 names “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel,” and in 1844 W. W. Phelps’s funeral sermon for Joseph Smith alluded to him as the seventh angel who pours out the last vial of wrath (Revelation 16). James Brighouse later used it for the title of his tracts. In Morris’s “Order of Sevens” the seven angels of the seven churches are Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah, and Seth, the seventh, presides (Gems of Inspiration, 1899); George Williams’s writings call Morris “Seth” (Watson, p. 90), and in 1873 Williams wrote of “the seventh Angel whom they wickedly slew” (Williams to Margaret Thomas, July 24, 1873, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). See more

t: Sides of the North George Williams’s name for the Montana Saints’ regi…
s: Sides of the North George Williams’s name for the Montana Saints’ region, from Psalm 48:2 (“the city of the great King” on “the sides of the north”). He wrote in 1879 to the “Saints of the Most High in Stake No. 1 on the Sides of the North in Montana” that the City of the great King would come down there before the Lord’s coming, and called the Lord’s House “my first House of Prayer on the Sides of the North” (MS 31876, Church History Library). See more

t: Reincarnation The teaching that spirits return to the earth in new bod…
s: Reincarnation The teaching that spirits return to the earth in new bodies. Morris dated it to a revelation of 1859; Forscutt called it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment.” Davies’s community taught it too. George Williams told the men he anointed at Council Bluffs and Omaha in 1869 who they had been: Carlton Fellows “was the Father to Simon Peter; Jonas was your name,” Hans Nielsen had been Eliab, David’s brother, and Jens Jensen had been Titus (record book, 1869, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Latter-day Saint writers called the belief by many names, among them re-embodiment, repeated embodiment, “baby resurrection,” plural or multiple mortal probations and “re-habiliment of spirits”; in this tradition, Kirk Watson notes, all of them meant a person reborn as a human of the same sex, never as an animal (Watson, Scriptural Mormonism, Ep. 113, November 14, 2026, at 6:16–7:04). See more

t: Consecration (law of consecration) Giving all one’s property to the ch…
s: Consecration (law of consecration) Giving all one’s property to the church. The phrase comes from Joseph Smith’s revelations (Doctrine and Covenants 42). Morris’s revelation of December 28, 1861, made laying all one possessed at the prophet’s feet the test of who could be delivered (The Spirit Prevails, No. 185), and the members consecrated their property on December 30, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Revelations of 1862 forbade giving consecrated property back to those who left, the dispute that led to the writs and the siege (Nos. 202 and 254). See more

t: Oath (1862) The oath every member of Morris’s church swore to the king…
s: Oath (1862) The oath every member of Morris’s church swore to the kingdom of God, to keep all the laws of God and the counsels of his prophet, given and to come. The revelation prescribing it is dated January 23, 1862 (The Spirit Prevails, No. 208); by Josiah D. Price’s account it was sworn on February 12, 1862, twelve people at a time, in the order of office set by No. 209. A separate soldier’s oath to defend the kingdom was sworn on May 26, 1862 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). See more

t: Foreshadowing Day May 30, 1862, at Kington Fort, when Morris’s church …
s: Foreshadowing Day May 30, 1862, at Kington Fort, when Morris’s church acted out the coming kingdom in a procession round the fort. Morris rode first, as the representative of Jesus, followed by the twelve generals on horseback, the first four on white, red, black and pale horses, and then seven companies of armed men; the leaders wore crowns on their hats, seven on Morris’s and fewer down the order of rank, and in the afternoon the lesser priesthood marched (The Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” pp. 6–7; Eli Smith to Christopher Layton, June 2, 1862, CR 1234 1, Church History Library; W. P. Thomas to his wife, May 30, 1862, MS 31876, folder 21, translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). It was the “foreshadow” of the coming kingdom that the revelations promised; two weeks later the posse arrived. See also Where did the rituals come from? See more

t: Seth The name George Williams and his followers used for Joseph Morris…
s: Seth The name George Williams and his followers used for Joseph Morris. In Morris’s “Order of Sevens” (below), Seth is the seventh and presiding angel, and Williams’s line of servants ran from Enos (Joseph Smith) to Seth (Morris) to Cainan (himself) (Gems of Inspiration, 1899; Watson, p. 90). Hence “Seth’s Diagram,” and S. P. Guhl’s letter of 1871 to “Seth’s disciples.” See also Prophet Cainan and Seventh Angel. See more

t: Order of Sevens Morris’s teaching of seven angels who preside over the…
s: Order of Sevens Morris’s teaching of seven angels who preside over the last dispensations of each earth: Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah, with Seth, the seventh, presiding (“The Order of Sevens,” in Gems of Inspiration, 1899). Williams kept it. See also Reincarnation. See more

t: Seth’s Diagram (the diagram) Morris’s chart of the worlds: a quorum of…
s: Seth’s Diagram (the diagram) Morris’s chart of the worlds: a quorum of 144,000 celestial globes, each governed by a god, all under the Most High God, with Enoch’s Zion, Adam’s world, the spirit world, Paradise, hell and outer darkness. Morris explained it at Weber in 1861; Eardley printed it in 1899 as “The Rounds of Eternity: Joseph Morris’ First Diagram”; a hand-coloured version with Swedish labels heads Williams’s record of letters of the 1870s; and missionaries were shown “the Eternal Rounds” near Warm Springs in 1899. In 1892 Eardley wrote that “Joseph’s mission was to reveal the diagram, and Foreshadow the coming kingdom.” See more

t: Birthright The teaching that each man’s place in the priesthood was fi…
s: Birthright The teaching that each man’s place in the priesthood was fixed by lineage from Adam through Seth and by his “first birthright in the spiritual state.” Williams kept it from Morris; the Montana court set it out as “the doctrines of Cainan” in May 1887 (High Court minutes, May 10, 1887, MS 31876, Church History Library); and an 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letter said men whose birthrights did not match their offices would be put in their right places “when a prophet comes having the Urim and Thummim.” William James claimed the Montana presidency for life “by birthright” in 1886. See more

t: Robe, crown and scepter The regalia of Morris’s church. Morris had a r…
s: Robe, crown and scepter The regalia of Morris’s church. Morris had a robe and crown, and he and his officers carried scepters; on Foreshadowing Day he rode in his robe with the rod in his left hand. The crown, as Wilford Woodruff saw it on June 16, 1862, was of tin painted yellow and lined with red cloth. Three painted wooden scepters survive in the Church History Museum: Morris’s, declaring him sent “to RULE over all ADAM’S posterity,” and those of Hugh Park (“number five”) and Daniel Smith (“number seven”) (LDS 65-3058 to 3060; Anderson, Revisited, pp. 116–17). Williams prescribed a linen robe for Montana’s president in 1874 and a fuller robe “in semblance to the Celestial attiring” in 1877, saying Morris had wanted every minister so clothed. See more

t: Soldiers of Israel The armed companies of Kington Fort. On May 16, 186…
s: Soldiers of Israel The armed companies of Kington Fort. On May 16, 1862, the “First Division of the Soldiers of Israel” was formed, with Morris as Captain at Arms, John Fred. Klingbeck as Lieutenant at Arms and seven captains, each over twelve men, and a second division of three companies followed; officers and men swore to defend “the Law of God.” Richard W. Young printed the oath and rosters, 142 men, in 1890 (The Contributor 11, no. 8, p. 284). See more

t: Stake No. 1 and Stake No. 2 The two divisions of the Montana church fr…
s: Stake No. 1 and Stake No. 2 The two divisions of the Montana church from 1874: William James’s Stake No. 1, at Warm Springs, and Andrew Hendrikson’s Danish-speaking Stake No. 2. Williams ruled in 1877 that each member might choose “the Stake convenient,” under “two distinct Presidencies”; that May the stakes agreed to keep out of each other’s ground. In 1886 James and the officers of Stake No. 1 broke with the church over George Thompson’s election. See more

t: Court of the Lord’s House The Montana church’s court of three officers…
s: Court of the Lord’s House The Montana church’s court of three officers, created by Williams in April 1877 to meet every May 10, and from August 1877 also every November 10, “that a portion of the weight of this infant Kingdom may not rest upon one” (Williams to James, April 2, 1877, and to Hendrikson, August 8, 1877, MS 31876, Church History Library). Hendrikson said it existed “to argue principles, doctrines or anything else,” since “Cainan is not with us.” See more

t: Elect lady, Lady Elect and High Priestess Women’s offices. A form “for…
s: Elect lady, Lady Elect and High Priestess Women’s offices. A form “for ordaining an elect lady,” signed by Morris in 1861, anointed the woman “that thou mayest be an heiress of the Priesthood of Melchisedec” (CR 1234 1, Church History Library). In Montana in 1872 Margaret Thomas was reordained “as the Lady elect to preside over the Female Order” (MS 32226). Williams called Marie Mortensen the Omaha congregation’s “High Priestess” in 1870 and had Sister Rasmussen ordained “High Priestess” for Stake No. 2 in 1877 (MS 31876). See more

t: Josephites The common nineteenth-century name for members of the Reorg…
s: Josephites The common nineteenth-century name for members of the Reorganized Church, after its leader Joseph Smith III. Danish “Josephites” were challenging S. P. Guhl to debate in Omaha by 1874. See Reorganized Church (RLDS). See more

t: Gems of Inspiration (1899) A collection compiled by John R. Eardley, a…
s: Gems of Inspiration (1899) A collection compiled by John R. Eardley, a former Morrisite, and printed in San Francisco by Joseph A. Dove: sayings and teachings of the movement, including “The Order of Sevens,” the “Rounds of Eternity” diagram and Eardley’s history of Kington Fort and the surrender. Public domain; at the Internet Archive. See more

t: Posse (posse comitatus) The force that besieged Kington Fort in June 1…
s: Posse (posse comitatus) The force that besieged Kington Fort in June 1862 was a posse comitatus, not an army: men of the territorial militia called out on Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, at the request of the territorial marshal, to help the deputy marshals Robert T. Burton and Theodore McKean serve the Third District Court’s writs for the arrest of Morris and others. See Morrisite War. See more

t: Adam–God teaching Brigham Young’s teaching, first preached in April 18…
s: Adam–God teaching Brigham Young’s teaching, first preached in April 1852, that Adam is “our Father and our God” (Journal of Discourses 1:50). The Latter-day Saint church later rejected it (Spencer W. Kimball, general conference, October 1976). Morris taught that the earth was organized by “Adam’s own Father” for Adam his firstborn, and Williams that Adam would head the planet’s government; see the At a glance table. See more

t: Reorganized Church (RLDS) The Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of La…
s: Reorganized Church (RLDS) The Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, now Community of Christ, which Forscutt and other former Morrisites joined in the 1860s and later. See more

t: “Probable” On this site, a mark that an identification is likely but n…
s: “Probable” On this site, a mark that an identification is likely but not proven: a FamilySearch match, or a person in the sources who may or may not be the one on the roll. See more
The Morrisite War

t: The siege of Kington Fort, June 13–15, 1862
s: The siege of Kington Fort, June 13–15, 1862 The “Morrisite War” is the common name for the three-day siege of Joseph Morris’s followers at Kington Fort, South Weber, Utah, by a territorial posse under Robert T. Burton (portrait). It ended with Morris dead, the men of the fort under arrest, and the movement scattered. This page gathers what the guide has on the siege, with its sources; the Chronology and the Kington Fort place page give more.

Why the posse came Morris organized his church at South Weber on April 6, 1861, and gathered his followers at Kington Fort, an abandoned settlers’ fort of 1853. On December 30, 1861, the members consecrated their property, and revelations of January and April 1862 forbade letting those who left take back what they had consecrated; the dispute over that property led to the writs (see Teachings). In the spring an armed party under Peter Klemgard brought three departing members, William Jones, John Jensen and Lars Gurtsen (both identifications probable), back to the fort and held them; Judge Kinney’s writ of habeas corpus of May 22, 1862, as printed by Richard W. Young, names “John Jensen, Louis Christian Jensen, [Lars Christian Gurtsen] and Wm. Jones,” the bracket apparently Young’s, and when Deputy Marshal Judson L. Stoddard tried to serve it, the copy he left was burned with live coals (Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 9 (July 1890): 349–50); their detention led to writs of the Third District Court for the arrest of Morris, John Banks, Richard Cook and others, which the fort refused to answer (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 99–108; “The Morrisite Movement,” letter 7 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 12, 1891, p. 3). On June 11, 1862, Acting Governor Frank Fuller ordered General Daniel H. Wells to furnish the territorial marshal, Henry W. Lawrence, and his deputies, Robert T. Burton and Theodore McKean, “a sufficient military force” to serve them (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, document 1,215, Utah State Archives). T. B. H. Stenhouse wrote in 1873 that Lawrence had warned Kinney and Fuller that a military posse “would certainly provoke armed resistance, and the innocent would suffer,” and had put off serving the writ; it was served while he was away in the East. He also wrote that the officers of the expedition consulted Brigham Young, who told them, “if fight it was to be, to ‘save the women and children, and be careful and not expose the boys’”—that is, the militia (T. B. H. Stenhouse, The Rocky Mountain Saints (New York, 1873), pp. 600–601). Orson F. Whitney, in his church-commissioned history of 1893, added that Brigham Young “was also very much averse to the execution of the process, fearing that it might result in bloodshed” (Orson F. Whitney, History of Utah, vol. 2 (Salt Lake City, 1893), p. 54 n.). Wilford Woodruff, who sat in the Historian’s Office next to Young’s, recorded both sides at the time. Before the hearing of June 18, Judge Kinney told him he had heard that Young blamed him for “all these things,” and answered, “I have not taken any step without counciling President Young”: the complainants, he said, had first been sent to Young, who told them to go to the judge and swear out their affidavits. On June 29 Young preached that “if he had had his own way he would have let them staid & rotted there,” but that Kinney “thought the Law must be honored” and called out a posse that “cost the lives of two innocent men” (Wilford Woodruff journal, January 1, 1860 – October 22, 1865, MS 1352, Church History Library, transcribed at the Wilford Woodruff Papers, June 18 and 29, 1862). The Morrisites had feared such an attack for months. Mark H. Forscutt later wrote that in December 1861, when reports came that men were being called out against the camp, it was spoken of as something to be done “Mountain Meadow fashion,” and that a band of Indians who passed through the fort were taken for “the allies in the Mountain Meadow Massacre” (Forscutt, Sketch, p. 40, MS 702, Church History Library).

The three days 13 Jun 1862The posse arrives about 10 a.m.; one of its members, John G. Chambers, puts it at “about 500 men,” with artillery. A notice is carried in by a boy herding the camp’s cows, giving the men named in the writs thirty minutes to give themselves up. While it is being read in the bowery, the first cannon ball “killed two women & wounded a third” (Chambers; Forscutt also saw two women dead). A Morrisite who was in the camp, whom Richard W. Young in 1890 believed to have been Mark H. Forscutt, told Stenhouse that Morris had gone to “inquire of the Lord” and come out with a written revelation promising that not one of the faithful would be destroyed; John Parsons was reading it in the bowery, and Richard Cook had risen to put the question to the people, when the ball struck. “There was not a Morrisite in the fort that was armed”; the men took up their arms about an hour and a half later. Burton held that the first two cannon were not loaded (T. B. H. Stenhouse, The Rocky Mountain Saints (New York, 1873), pp. 597–98). The posse’s side was told by Richard W. Young in 1890, from Burton’s and other posse members’ accounts: Burton, who had at first declined the duty, came with “about two hundred and fifty men,” a six-pound gun and a brass howitzer; Major Howard Egan, Judson L. Stoddard, Thomas Abbott and Wells Smith gave the proclamation to the herd boy at about 8 a.m.; and at 10 a.m., with no answer, two shots were fired over the fort, the second striking the ploughed ground in front and ricocheting into the bowery (Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 10 (August 1890): 370–72). Jared Smith of the posse is killed (John G. Chambers, “Siege of Morris fort, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; “The Morrisite Tragedy,” letter 8 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 19, 1891, p. 3). 14 Jun 1862Rain all day. That evening the posse fires the Ogden cannon and “the ‘Old Sow’” sent up from Salt Lake City (Chambers). That day “Messrs. Forscutt and Eardley, and several others, came out of the fort and surrendered to the deputy marshal” (Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 11 (September 1890): 429; Burton said the same at his trial in 1879). Fuller writes to Burton: “Let your acts still be tempered with mercy, but see that the Laws are vindicated” (copy, Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). 15 Jun 1862A Sunday. Posse men take a log cabin by the entrance, and Peter Wahler is killed. That morning Morris delivers a revelation promising deliverance “which ever way it comes” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 304). A white flag goes up. Morris is killed at the surrender, and John Banks, wounded, dies that evening or, by the posse’s account, early the next morning. The posse’s version, as Richard W. Young told it in 1890, differs from the Morrisite eyewitnesses’ (Alexander Dow’s affidavit is quoted under Who died): Burton rode in with Robert Golding, Judson Stoddard and the bugler Mark Croxall while the arms were being stacked; Parson asked what was wanted; Morris was allowed to speak and cried, “All who are willing to follow me, through life or death, come on!”; men started for the schoolhouse, where there were arms, and for the stacked guns; and Burton, unable to stop Morris, fired “his revolver twice at the retreating form of the prophet,” with “eight or ten shots in all” fired by him, Stoddard “and perhaps by one or two others.” Young names the dead as Morris, “Mrs. Bowman and Mrs. Swanee,” with Banks mortally wounded; of 140 men taken, 94, those “enrolled in the Morrisite army,” were taken to the city (Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 11 (September 1890): 429–31; no. 12 (October 1890): 466). Burton’s jury acquitted him in 1879 (see below). The men are listed as prisoners “Sunday, June 15, 1862 – 7 p.m.” (Chambers; “Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library).

The posse, June 12–18, 1862 Men, by unit, from the militia returns kept by Deputy Marshal Theodore McKean. About 520 in all. A summary report counts 244 men under arms and 29 teamsters from the Salt Lake County units and the Centerville company, with 21 wagons and about a hundred horses and mules; company rolls add about 245 men from Davis and Weber counties who joined at the fort. The total, about 520, is close to John G. Chambers’s “about 500” and to the Morrisite account that the 250 men Burton started with were “about doubled by the time he arrived,” against “only ninety men in our Camp” who carried arms (The Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” p. 7). The Weber figure is approximate, since two of its reports overlap, and some names on the rolls are hard to read. Among the posse men on the rolls are Judson L. Stoddard (Farmington cavalry), who served the writ, and Lieut. B. C. Critchlow (Weber), who later wrote reminiscences of the war. Not on the returns but named in Wells’s letter of June 15: Joseph A. Young, Brigham Young’s son, and Briant Stringham, both recalled to Salt Lake City by the President (Daniel H. Wells, letterpress copy book, MS 1344, Church History Library, p. 14). Source: “Militia companies’ reports” (dated 1866 in the catalog; the papers are from June 1862), Theodore McKean family collection, MS 33041, Church History Library, images 2–36 (view in the catalog). The names on the returns are in the posse file on the Data page. Other witnesses, both sides. At 3 a.m. on June 13, hours before the first shot, General Daniel H. Wells wrote to Burton from Salt Lake City sending musket cartridges, shells and fuses for the howitzer, shot for the twelve-pounder and powder: “Send us word every three or four hours how the work progresses,” and, in a postscript, “Guard against a sally from the enemy & take your time” (Wells to Burton, June 13, 1862, Theodore McKean family collection, MS 33041, Church History Library, images 40–42). His letters of the next three days survive in his copy book. On June 14 he sent tents, spades and picks for rifle pits, and advised Burton to fire as little as possible: “peradventure a little fasting will be good for their health.” On June 15 he warned of a sally “with bayonets, swords, pikes,” and told Burton to “be prepared to meet them with lead day or night at every point.” That evening, with the surrender at hand, he wrote: “We are pleased with the success of the shell, and with your gradual approach upon the enemy. Do not permit a rush upon their works, but continue to be careful of the lives of the men.” On June 16 he asked Burton to give provisions to the prisoners’ destitute families, advise them to disperse to the settlements, and “treat them kindly, and do not permit the boys to tantalize or otherwise mistreat them” (Wells to Burton, June 14–16, 1862, Daniel H. Wells, letterpress copy book, MS 1344, Church History Library, pp. 10–15). The June 15 letter also passes on that “the President desires the return of Joseph A. Young and Briant Stringham,” so Brigham Young’s son and Stringham were with the posse. Hans F. Hansen of the posse wrote in his diary eight days after the surrender that Morris’s people had crowned him “King of Kings and Lord of Lord’s,” that the judge had telegraphed President Lincoln for orders (a rumor; the order came from Acting Governor Fuller), and that when Morris and Banks would not give up, “we therefore had to kill them” (Hans F. Hansen, diary, June 23, 1862, English typescript, MS 14915, Church History Library). Lars C. Christensen, a Latter-day Saint whose family farmed two miles below the fort, saw a revelation read to the Danish members, “translated from the English by a man by the name of Lorensen”; he remembered the posse’s “rolling battery” of government wheels packed with willows, the women’s guns stacked in a pile apart from the men’s, and that he was paid to haul a load of prisoners to Salt Lake City (Lars C. Christensen, autobiography, 1892, MS 5831, Church History Library, pp. 12–13). Inside the fort, John L. Bear counted “20 rifles, a few shotguns and old Mexican firelocks”; at the surrender Morris and Banks “came arm in arm,” the people sang “Hail to the prophet,” and Morris asked, “Who will die with me?” before Burton fired (autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 26–27). Another Morrisite account was printed in 1891, when John Davis baptized “an aged man named Hastings,” very probably Winter Hastings of the roll, at Olney, Washington: he “was close by and heard the words of Col. Burton.” After the arms were stacked, Burton asked whether Morris had anything to say, and Morris answered, “All that are willing to follow me in life or death, come this way”; as they began to follow him to the schoolhouse, Burton said, “We have got enough of your d—— treason,” and “drew a revolver and fired at him until he fell” (Davis to the editors, Olney, Wash., February 9, 1891, Saints’ Herald 38, 1891, p. 134). It is Davis’s retelling, nearly thirty years after the event. New

The dead No list of the dead has been checked against all the sources, and the accounts disagree. Two posse men were killed, Jared Smith and Peter Wahler. On the Morrisite side, Morris was killed at the surrender and Banks died that evening; two women were killed by the first cannon shot on June 13; and two women were killed at the surrender, Isabella Bowman and a Danish woman called “Mrs. O’Hagg” or “Haag.” The Morrisite letters of 1891 count eleven Morrisites killed, and John L. Bear, who lost his wife and their sixteen-week-old baby to a cannon ball on the first day, ten (autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 25–27). See Who died at Kington Fort?

Prisoners and trials Of 149 men taken, 49, mostly older men and those who had surrendered during the siege, were discharged at the fort on June 16, and 98 were marched to Salt Lake City (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). Before Judge John F. Kinney, ninety-five were bound over on $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). In March 1863 seven were convicted of second-degree murder and the rest fined $100 each for resisting arrest (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); Governor Stephen S. Harding pardoned them all a few days later. Harding, who attended the trial, wrote nine years later that Burton “admitted his shooting the prisoners, and offered as an excuse that he did not think it safe to let Banks and Morris live.” The petitions for pardon were signed by the Gentiles, the federal officers and the officers at Camp Douglas; no Mormon signed them except Bill Hickman, who rode fourteen miles in the night to do it, though several came to Harding after dark to ask for mercy. “Scores of the wives and mothers of the condemned” begged him on their knees, and Bishop Woolley warned him that he “could not answer for my safety” if he pardoned them (Harding’s statement in Bill Hickman, Brigham’s Destroying Angel (New York, 1872), pp. 215–16). The pardons, dated March 31, name seven men for murder and sixty-nine for resisting an officer (Documents). The grand jury answered by presenting Harding to the court “as we would an unsafe bridge over a dangerous stream,” and Chief Justice Kinney left the responsibility “with the Governor” (Edward W. Tullidge, History of Salt Lake City (Salt Lake City, 1886), pp. 320–24). That May many left Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, for Soda Springs, Idaho, and Carson Valley, Nevada; others later gathered at Omaha and Council Bluffs and in Montana’s Deer Lodge Valley (see Chronology).

Burton’s trial, 1879 Robert T. Burton was indicted for the killing of Isabella Bowman in 1870 (an indictment voided in 1872) and again in 1877, and was tried and acquitted in 1879 (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 148–49). The second case began with his arrest on July 26, 1877, on a warrant sworn by the foreman of the grand jury (Salt Lake Herald, July 27, 1877, p. 3). The trial opened in the Third District Court before Judge Michael Schaeffer on February 18, 1879, with District Attorney Van Zile and James H. Beatty for the prosecution and Tilford, Sutherland, Hagan and Williams for the defence, and former Morrisites testified for both sides. The jurors were Ellsworth Daggett, Samuel H. Hill, James Crossly, Joseph Gorlinski (the foreman), David Rees, Ed. Butterfield, J. R. Bennion, Henry Wagener, Ralph Jenkins, T. C. Cutler, Patrick Phelan and John Cartwright, “one-half being non-Mormons” (Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 12 (October 1890): 470–71). The jury was out forty-six hours; the Deseret Evening News heard that three holdouts were “gradually reduced to one” (March 7, 1879, p. 2). The verdict, signed “Jury Room, March 7, 1879, 9.33 a.m.,” found “for the defendant of not guilty,” and the court room applauded. The Herald called it the strongest of three cases against Burton and expected the other two to be dropped (Salt Lake Herald, March 8, 1879, p. 3). Morris’s brother George, a Latter-day Saint high priest who had rejected Joseph’s claims, attended the trial and wrote that “there was no nesesity to shed one Drop of Blood” (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 198–99). Kenneth Godfrey wrote an article on the arrest and trial whose drafts are in his papers at Utah State University (see Repositories). The prosecution came out of the same federal effort that brought John D. Lee to trial for the Mountain Meadows Massacre: Sumner Howard, the United States attorney who prosecuted Lee in 1876, began the case against Burton that fall (Kenneth W. Godfrey, “Did the Bishop Murder the Morrisite Mrs. Bowman? The Arrest and Trial of Robert T. Burton,” unpublished typescript, citing Robert C. Freeman, “Judge Sumner Howard: Man With A Mission,” paper given at the Mormon History Association meeting, Snowbird, Utah, May 1996). The massacre was named at the trial. The Morrisite Philip Hewitt testified that as Morris fell, Mrs. Swanee (very probably Anna Hegg; see Who died at Kington Fort?) cried out, “is this going to be another Mountain Meadows Massacre,” before she too was shot, and that he had expected the same himself (Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, March 1, 1879, p. 1; the Deseret Evening News report of his testimony, February 24, p. 3, does not have these lines, and Hewitt said he did not see the women fall). A Morrisite account printed in 1879 gives the cry to another woman: at the March 1863 trial “the wife of John Parson,” called as a witness, held up the dress a cannon ball had torn and repeated what she had cried at Weber, “O God! is this another Mountain Meadow massacre?” (George S. and James Dove, A Voice from the West, San Francisco, 1879, p. 12). The two accounts cannot both be exact; the words may have been on more than one tongue. In his closing argument District Attorney P. T. Van Zile told the jury that he believed the Morrisites feared “another Mountain Meadow massacre,” and that “every man, woman and child expected to be killed” (Deseret Evening News, March 5, 1879, p. 1). Burton was acquitted. Writers hostile to the church had paired the two events since the 1870s (John Codman, The Mormon Country, 1874), and “The Elder” did so again in 1891, adding a claim, otherwise unsupported, that Joseph A. Young carried messages between Burton and Brigham Young during the siege (Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891, p. 3). No source shows any other connection between the two events.

Teachings

What the Morrisites taught A summary of the movement’s teachings, period by period, with the sources for each. It describes what the Morrisites and their successors believed; it does not argue for or against it. Where scholars disagree, both readings are given.

How we know The sources are uneven. Joseph Morris’s revelations were published only after his death, by a follower, as The Spirit Prevails (1886). His letters to Brigham Young survive in Young’s office files, and Kirk Watson’s The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026) prints them with other manuscripts of Morris, George Williams, William W. Davies and the Doves, many for the first time. Gems of Inspiration (1899) shows what the later church chose to keep. Mark H. Forscutt, an insider who later left, wrote a sketch of Morris; the newspapers of 1862 were hostile; and C. LeRoy Anderson’s history is the only book on the movement. For the later church there are Williams’s letters and the Montana minutes at the Church History Library (MS 31876 and MS 32226), and for Davies’s community the sworn testimony of 1880–81 (see Repositories). As Watson notes, almost everything written on the Morrisites has been about the siege, and almost nothing about their beliefs (Watson, p. 6). Teachings also changed over a century, so this page takes them period by period. Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

Joseph Morris (1857–1862) A prophet with a message for Brigham Young. Morris, an English convert, believed the Lord spoke through him, and he recorded more than 300 revelations. His letters to Young, from 1858 to 1860, show him first offering to work with Young and then, as no answer came, growing desperate; he believed he had been called to lead the church (Watson, pp. 5, 11–49). A revelation of January 1860 charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door; a clerk docketed it “Balderdash” (see Documents and Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris?). His followers later claimed that church leaders drew on the revelations he had sent and presented them as “new truths” (Watson, p. 11, citing Dove’s preface). Richard W. Young, summarizing what former Morrisites told him in 1890, says Morris taught that the world was “a great creature that has been growing for millions of years,” that Christ would come to establish the kingdom “with Adam as the second in authority,” “the principle of heirship,” that he was “the re-incarnate spirit of Moses,” and that Joseph Smith was the sixth angel of the Revelation and he the seventh (The Contributor 11, no. 8 (June 1890): 282). Moses, and Seth, the seventh angel. Morris claimed to be the reincarnation of Moses (Watson, p. 6); in a talk of 2026 Watson adds that Morris believed he had also been Seth, and that Joseph Smith had earlier been Enos and Elijah (Watson, Scriptural Mormonism, Ep. 113, November 14, 2026, at 21:47–22:26). He also taught an order of seven angels who preside over the last dispensations of each earth: Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah, with Seth, the seventh, presiding (“The Order of Sevens,” in Gems of Inspiration). Morris called himself the Seventh Angel; an informer heard him say so on May 12, 1861: “Moses could not reveal as much as I have … I say now I profess to be the Seventh Angel. The seventh thousand years is now ushered in” (“Doctrines of the Morrisites, May 12, 1861,” informer’s report, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library), and George Williams’s writings call the prophet of South Weber “Seth” (Watson, p. 90). Both identities appear in the sources. Two of his followers who later lived at Walla Walla, William W. Davies and R. J. Livingston, gave a fuller form in 1882: Morris declared himself “the spirit of Gabriel now occupying the body of Joseph Morris,” the same spirit that had been Seth, the son of Adam, and later Moses; and he said that John Banks, his strong right hand, carried the spirit of Hur, who with Aaron held up Moses’ hands in the battle with Amalek. Livingston added that Morris “never asserted that a spirit came the second time to complete an unfulfilled mission”; rather, that “the body could not be killed while its spirit mission was incomplete,” which, he said, was what caused such consternation when Morris was killed (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, Portland, 1882, pp. 371–73). These are recollections of twenty years later, from men who by then followed Davies’s own teaching of returning spirits. Young Joseph and the Reorganization. A revelation of May 4, 1861, answered whether the Lord had anything to do with the new sect of “True Latter Day Saints” headed by Joseph Smith’s son. It said he did: he was using them as a scourge to the “false shepherds” of his flock and would in the end bring many of them to Morris. Joseph Smith III had not yet been called as a prophet; if he were, the call would come through Morris, who alone held the keys of the dispensation (The Spirit Prevails, No. 64, pp. 90–91). The Reorganization was already noticed at Weber. In December 1860 its True Latter Day Saints’ Herald printed an unsigned letter from Weber County saying that many there acknowledged “Brother Joseph’s” right to lead the church; the letter does not mention Morris (True Latter Day Saints’ Herald 1, no. 12 [December 1860]: 292). By July 1861 the Herald was answering Morris directly, with “An Address to Joseph Morris, the Great False Prophet of Weber Co., Utah,” and an editorial, “Civil War in Utah,” that quotes his revelation of May 25, 1861 (The Spirit Prevails, No. 68), though it dates it May 15. This is the earliest known printing of one of Morris’s revelations (True Latter Day Saints’ Herald 2, no. 5 [July 1861]: 108–15, 116–19). Joseph Smith III read the same revelation to John Parson in January 1885, asking how he and others were to “become subject” to Morris’s organization if, as Parson said, Morris’s work was not to continue as a church; Smith wrote, “I urge nothing against Joseph Morris,” but “I neither attack his work nor accept it as binding on me” (Smith to Parson, January 25, 1885, Joseph Smith III Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, pp. 148–51, Community of Christ Library Archives). Several Morrisites later joined the Reorganized Church; see How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? Gods, angels and Holy Ghosts. In a revelation on the Holy Ghost, an early form of “Keys of the Priesthood” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 2), Morris taught that Holy Ghosts are men who once lived on a mortal earth, “millions” of them, made one as the Father and the Son are one, and that each god is subject to the one above him, up to “the first God of all” (Watson, pp. 50–53). Richard Cook explained it to six new members at their confirmation in May 1861: “The Holy Ghost is a redeemed being, one that existed in the world before this,” and such beings “are our guardian Angels,” so that each confirmed member was now “entitled to one of these redeemed beings a Holy Ghost” (“Doctrines of the Morrisites, May 12, 1861,” informer’s report, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library). Forscutt later remembered the theology as monotheistic at its root but wide enough to find a place for the faithful of every religion (Forscutt, Sketch, pp. 17–18). Who rules this world. Morris’

s: “The Rounds of Eternity: Joseph Morris’ First Diagram. Movements of the Planets from their Creation to their Exaltation.” The caption calls it a quorum of 144,000 celestial globes, each governed by a god, all governed by the Most High God (Psalm 82). From John R. Eardley, comp., Gems of Inspiration (San Francisco: Joseph A. Dove, 1899), p. 39; public domain. Scan at the Internet Archive. Its upper half is the cover design of Watson’s edition. The worlds. Eardley printed this diagram in 1899 as “Joseph Morris’ First Diagram” (above). A drawing in Josiah D. Price’s journal shows a central world ringed by smaller ones, with a column of worlds rising from it labeled with the patriarchs from Cainan upward (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). An undated essay among Alexander Dow’s papers explains such a figure, which it calls the Plummet (Zechariah 4:10), as the eternal progression of worlds: the first God’s world at the center, the others rising through their spiritual, temporal and celestial estates, and this earth, which has grown and moved 144,000 times since its creation, among them (Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f6, Community of Christ Library Archives). It may be “the diagram” that Eardley in 1892 said Morris had come to reveal (see the Montana church, below), and the drawing labeled “Seth’s Diagram” that opens Williams’s record of letters, 1873–1879 (see Repositories). All three share one design: a circle of worlds around a central globe, with a line of worlds running down from it toward this earth and outer darkness. A diagram was in use from the first months: on May 12, 1861, Cook gave the newly confirmed “an explanation of the diagram,” and in November 1861 Parson preached while “pointing at the diagram of the planets” (“Doctrines of the Morrisites, May 12, 1861,” informer’s report, “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862,” Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library; “Remarks of Mr. Parsons,” November 24, 1861, same file). A Swedish copy of “some explanations of the diagram given by Joseph Morris, Weber 1861,” made by Emanuel Strom in 1872, numbers the worlds by their estates: the first estate (1); this earth in its mortal estate (2); the celestial world, where “the eternal Father and his Son Jesus and the whole heavenly family” dwell (3); the spirit world, which receives the spirits from all worlds (4); and two worlds marked 5 and 6, which stand still as stations for the spirits of the dead. “Joseph Smith is now in the Terrestrial world, and presides over the two last-named worlds.” A thousand years make one “eternal day,” and a ring of worlds forms “a quorum of 144,000,” matching the 144,000 John saw on Mount Zion; each world moves 144,000 times before it is glorified, standing still 7,000 years after each move (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, pp. 55–57, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). The Eternal Rounds, 1899. In July 1899 two Latter-day Saint missionaries stayed with “Mr Petersons a Morisite” near Warm Springs, Montana, and “next morning they showed us through the Eternal Rounds” (John Welch, missionary journal, July 17–18, 1899, MS 29881, Church History Library, image 19). What they were shown is not described; being shown “through” it suggests a large chart or display of the diagram that Eardley printed the same year as “The Rounds of Eternity.” New

s: “Seth’s Diagram,” the first page of the record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, with Swedish labels: Enoch’s Zion (3), Adam’s world (2), the spirit world (4), Paradise (5), hell (6), the nine and a half lost tribes of Israel, outer darkness, and the line from Seth (1) through Enos and Cainan to Nachor beside “144,000” worlds (translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). Seth is Morris. Church History Library, MS 31876, Record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, image 4. Courtesy of the Church History Library, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. View in the catalog. Reincarnation. Morris taught that spirits return to the earth in new bodies; Joseph Dove dated the teaching to a revelation of 1859, and Forscutt called it Morris’s “strange theory of repeated embodiment.” Strom’s Swedish copy of “an article given by Joseph Morris concerning the resurrection of Jesus Christ” explains the resurrection itself in the same way: it “takes place by birth, just as they are born into the first or second estate,” the spirits being “brought forth by immortal parents”; Christ rose on the third day in the body that was crucified only because his mission was “altogether different from Adam’s offspring” (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, pp. 62–63, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). This is close to the “baby resurrection” that Brigham Young rejected. Where the teaching came from is disputed: see Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from? and the Glossary. The Doves’ first book, 1879. George S. and James Dove’s A Voice from the West records some Weber teachings not in The Spirit Prevails. The sacrament had not been taken at Weber; it would be “as soon as twelve individuals can meet together under the covenant.” The half hour of silence in heaven (Revelation 8:1) meant twenty years, so that if Morris’s preparation began in 1859, a new one would begin in 1879. The apostles had tried in quorum to unfold the principle of the first- and second-born sons, and Abraham Taylor “sent down to Salt Lake City for some buttons to make a diagram on the table,” but it could not be unfolded then. Asked whether Morris ever ordained anyone to the Melchizedek priesthood, the Doves answer no: “He always said, ‘You are an heir with me, to the High Priesthood.’” On reincarnation they make Seth, in turn, Shem, Moses, Samuel and Zerubbabel, “Lastly He comes as Joseph Morris” (pp. 17–20, 39). The book ends with Joseph Taylor’s hymn “Thoughts of the Past,” on the baptisms in the Weber, the bowery, Foreshadowing Day and the June battle (p. [42]). The coming of Christ, and consecration. Morris taught that Christ would come soon to deliver his people, and he tied the coming to the consecration of their property. On December 28, 1861, a revelation promised that the Lord would not delay once the people were prepared; on December 30 another promised that he would come “to-morrow morning” if those present consecrated all their property in the way appointed (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 186 and 188–189, pp. 336–39). When the morning passed, a revelation of January 6, 1862, blamed those who had consecrated unwillingly, and one of January 11 refused to set another time (Nos. 195 and 199, pp. 350, 359); in February deliverance was promised after the people had taken an oath (No. 224, p. 419). Josiah D. Price recorded that the saints consecrated their property on December 30, 1861, and swore the oath to the kingdom on February 12, 1862, twelve at a time: the apostles, the high priests and the priests of Aaron, then their wives in the same order, and last the boys and girls, the order set by the revelation of January 25, 1862 (No. 209) (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Price also copied Welsh translations of the consecration revelation and the oath. Revelations of January and April 1862 forbade using the property of “the rebellious” and forbade letting those who left take back what they had consecrated (Nos. 202 and 254, pp. 368, 490), the dispute that led to the writs and the siege. John Parson, speaking at South Weber in September 1861, set consecration against Brigham Young’s church, whose apostles, he said, had promised that land would not be monopolized and that all would have equal rights, and had not kept the promise (Watson, pp. 64–67). See How did believers survive failed prophecy? Judgment. The revelations of 1861–62 also foretell judgment on the wicked. A revelation read at South Weber on September 29, 1861, says Christ will come “as a thief in the night” and as a refiner, and will destroy his enemies, among them the leaders of his former church (Watson, pp. 60–64; The Spirit Prevails, No. 104). In a tongue of June 8, 1862, the “3rd Captain of the Lord’s Host,” an angel from an earlier earth, told of a camp like Kington Fort whose faithful, at “the test,” killed the hypocrites among them, and whose prophet then enforced the law of God on pain of death (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 638–42; Watson, pp. 72–79). Watson reads such passages as showing that Morris expected human as well as divine agents of judgment, including against dissenters in his own community (Watson, p. 8); Anderson held that the judgment Morris foretold was God’s alone (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 108, 111). Spiritual gifts. Speaking in tongues and their interpretation, and messages from angels, were part of worship at Kington Fort. An interpretation of June 7, 1862, taught that the gifts are given to mortals and cease only at the resurrection, when the faithful become angels who give them to others, and that they had left the older church because a council in Brigham Young’s house decided to put them down (Watson, pp. 70–72). See What became of the spiritual gifts? Church order and ritual. Morris organized his church on April 6, 1861, at South Weber, with a First Council and apostles (Glossary). Scepters, a robe and cr

George Williams, the Prophet Cainan (1863–1882) What Williams kept and changed. Williams built on Morris’s teaching and also altered it. He kept the order of sevens and birthrights, the diagram of worlds, Cain’s line, the robe (which he said Morris had wanted every minister to wear) and the condemnation of Brigham Young. His line of servants, from Enos (Joseph Smith) to Seth (Morris) to Cainan, follows a sequence Morris had already given in 1860, telling Young that “Joseph Smith was my forerunner and I was the forerunner to Adam” (address to Brigham Young, September 22, 1860, Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f5, Community of Christ Library Archives). Other things changed. Morris had looked for a temple in “the land of promise” and given no endowments “in this place” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 30); Williams said Jackson County had “left the paths of virtue,” placed the gathering on “the Sides of the North” in Montana, and brought robes and “Temple ordinances” into the Lord’s House there. Morris set days for Christ’s coming; Williams wrote that “it is not for us to set the times.” Morris foretold the destruction of the wicked; Williams taught that nearly all would be saved, by grades. Tongues, central at Kington Fort, were ruled out of public meetings in Montana in 1881; the “elect lady” of 1861 grew into the office of High Priestess; and Williams departed from Morris’s rule of one wife for eternity. In 1881 he also read Morris’s claim to be Moses as a manner of speaking: Morris “meant he represented Moses.” Each point is documented in the paragraphs that follow and under Joseph Morris above. His calling. Williams, the Prophet Cainan, told of visions in 1862. On April 15, near a canyon in Salt Lake Valley, he saw the armies of heaven and the Father and the Son; from August 25 to 27, on a mountain east of the valley, John the Revelator baptized him, and Seth and Enos, who had “sealed our testimony with our blood,” declared him “Cainan, then Melchisedec, now George Williams” and gave him the keys of the priesthood, among them the keys of birthright and of sealing (“Interviews with Celestial Beings,” Watson, pp. 81–90; Gems of Inspiration). Seth is Morris. Enos was long taken in this guide to be John Banks, killed with him, but Williams himself wrote in December 1881 that “Joseph Morris said Joseph Smith was Enos, but meant he represented Enos; he also said he was Moses, but meant to say he represented Moses,” and that he, Williams, had used the same “mode of expression” in calling himself Cainan; omitting the word “represent,” he wrote, “may have caused wrong impression” (Williams to Andrew Hendrikson, December 29, 1881, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881). George Thompson had used the same reading in 1869: “The Ministers of Enos — or J. S. — brought something like the little Book. Seth — or J. Morris — brought something very much resembling the little Book” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874, July 29, 1869). An earlier witness is the Danish record of a meeting at Omaha on January 26, 1869, with Williams present: Hans Knudsen testified to “the three prophets Enos, Seth and Cainan,” and Cainan said that “40 years back in time Enos came forth with a revelation and organized a church,” and that Joseph Smith had died twenty-five years before, leaving a church without prophet, seer and revelator (“Cainans Diverse Skrivelser,” January 26, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Williams himself wrote that autumn of “our Lord and his apostles, Joseph the first, Joseph the second and the Lord’s Servant,” and that “the Josephs, Seth & Enos leaveth me not comfortless” (Williams to the Omaha church, September 16 and October 13, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869). In 1872 he listed those whose birthright entitled them “to be visited by these immortals”: “Adam with Jehovah, Moses with Jehovah, Abraham with Jehovah, Jesus with Moses & Elijah, Paul with Jesus, Joseph with Moroni, with Peter, James & John, Joseph the second with the Lord of Hosts, Cainan with John the Revelator, Seth & Enos” (Williams to the Saints in Montana, August 1872, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1872–1873). The line of servants in his letters runs from Enos to Seth to Cainan, that is, from Joseph Smith to Morris to Williams; Smith and Morris had both “sealed” their testimony with their blood. Williams also claimed the use of the Urim and Thummim and said he had met Muhammad, Joseph Smith and Morris (Watson, pp. 80, 92–96). From 1869 he led from England, by letter (see Chronology). In May 1875 he wrote that God would lay no other foundation in this generation than “Seth, Enos & Cainan the first Born Sons of the first Presidency in the last quorum of Heavens,” and that “I could not avoid being Cainan, and whosoever is offended with me is offended with the Eternal Father that have chosen me” (Williams to Margaret Thomas, May 10, 1875, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). Mahomet. In August 1877, with Russia and Turkey at war, Williams told the Montana Saints of an earlier “Interview with Mahomet.” His own copy of it, headed “Copied from my Journal in the year 1867,” places it in Utah: “While on a visit with a friend called the Stranger under the Mountains by the Mouth of Little Cottonwood Kanyon,” a voice told him to send the friend away, and in “a wood of cottonwood trees” a figure in green appeared and said, “I am Mahomet, and before I was Mahomet I was Ishmael the Son of Abraham and Hagar” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Writings of Cainan, circa 1867–1872). The Montana church (1882–1954) Continuity with Weber. Writing for the dying Williams in March 1882, George Thompson told the Montana church that “those who have been baptized by Joseph or under his ministry at Weber are members of the fullness under Cainan without being rebaptized,” while others must be baptized “into the fullness” before they could become members, and that Cainan’s church was “a continuation of the Church formed by Joseph at Weber” (Thompson to the Montana church, March 23, 1882, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1879–1882). From prophet to vote. Before he died in 1882 Williams wrote that the organization should stay as it was for twelve months and that William James should then be put before the whole church and, if sustained “by uplifted hand,” remain from year to year. After him the church chose its presidents at general assemblies (1883, 1886); Andrew Hendrikson presided from 1886 to 1921 and George Johnson until shortly before his death in 1954, with which, Anderson writes, the church came to an end; USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding (see How did a prophet’s movement become a church run by vote?). The Son and the Father. In October 1897 Andrew Hendrickson drafted an answer to a reader’s question in the Christian Herald of New York about “who our dear Lord are, and his true position.” From the Gospel of John and 1 Corinthians 15 he argued that the Son is subject to the Father, that “the greater always send the lesser,” and that there is “no room for equality” (Hendrickson to the Christian Herald, Race Track, October 20, 1897, draft, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1893–1901). Worship and neighbors. The Lord’s House near Racetrack, built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879, held Sunday meetings. The council kept the sacrament open to non-members who came as “friends for the gospel’s sake,” and in 1886 it accepted an invitation to use the Reorganized Church’s meeting house in Deer Lodge City (see How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another?). What the later church kept. Gems of Inspiration, compiled by John R. Eardley and printed by Joseph A. Dove in 1899, is the movement’s own selection a generation after Morris. About a third of it is a history of the Morrisites, written against the Mormon church; the rest is Morris’s articles, among them “Keys of the Priesthood” and “The Order of Sevens,” and Williams’s visions, letters and records, including two letters to the Saints in Montana. It keeps the order of gods, angels and birthrights and the line from Morris to Williams, condemns polygamy, and does not use the word reincarnation. What was taught in the church’s last decades is not yet known. Doctrine and disappointment, 1887–91. The church’s court, which Hendrikson said existed “to argue principles, doctrines or anything else, and as Cainan is not with us there is no other place to appeal,” set out “the doctrines of Cainan” in May 1887: a high priest’s “first birthright in the spiritual state” placed him in his father’s priesthood, and his birthrights in mortality gave him experience of everything, “so that when he becomes a God he then can judge and rule in righteousness from his own experience,” while some of the heirs of salvation “merely pass thro a mortal womb so as to go across over to Paradise,” according to their behavior “in their spiritual estate” (High Court minutes, May 10, 1887, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1886–1887). In November 1874 George Thompson had looked further off, to “about the year 1902,” “the day when Joseph will return & be introduced to us by his 1st & 2nd Councilors … in fulfillment of what was foreshadowed at Weber”; until then “our Weber family” were consigned to darkness “to atone for their misstep in giving up the Prophet to the Mormons” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874, November 2, 1874). In 1880 William James had looked for the coming of Christ in 1891. On November 10, 1891, Hendrikson told the court that they had been “led for many years past to expect that in the present year the ‘winding up scene’ would take place,” but that he still believed “he should live to behold the coming of the Son of Man, as he had been promised by the Lord’s servant Cainan.” Eardley looked instead to a coming “war of the nations,” which Williams had once foretold to him, and to “the coming forth of the next servant according to birthright, even Mahalaleel”; he likened the Saints to the wise and foolish virgins, “drowsy and sleepy,” though some “have retained their faith.” He also urged prayer standing with hands raised, as Williams prayed, “with body erect, and hands uplifted to heaven,” and called kneeling “the Sectarian method” (court minutes, November 10, 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1891). Eardley had already conceded a point a year earlier. The church, he wrote in March 1890, was shrinking toward Daniel’s stone “cut out of the mountain without hands,” and “Bro Cainan represented himself as that stone, he was mistaken as all other prophets have been in some things” (Eardley to Hendrickson, March 20, 1890, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1890). The hope outlived 1891. In June 1892 George Thompson asked how the churches would receive “our Joseph with his two Councelers — Enoc and Cainan —” if they appeared to gather “the scattered sheep of Weber,” purge the church in Utah and make headquarters in Jackson County (the spelling “Enoc” is Thompson’s). After Parson’s death that month Eardley concluded that “Joseph’s mission was to reveal the diagram, and Foreshadow the coming kingdom. All other things which transpired were of a secondary consideration” (Thompson to Eardley, June 26, 1892; Eardley to James Dove, June 18, 189

t: William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven (1866–1881)
s: William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven (1866–1881) Davies, who had been with Morris, began his own community in Montana in 1866 and led it near Walla Walla, Washington, from 1867; many of its members were converts from San Francisco and Portland who had never been Morrisites. Watson calls it “a novel and mystical Christian sect” with roots in Morris and Joseph Smith (Watson, p. 111). Davies declared in 1867 that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, in which baptism was set aside for “the Holy Vow of THE COVENANT”; members gave their labor and property to a common fund, and he signed himself the Standard of Israel and dated his papers by the Millennial Era (Watson, pp. 124, 128, 184). He testified in 1881 that reincarnation was “taught & believed” (Watson, p. 186), and he taught that his sons Arthur, later called the “Walla Walla Jesus,” and David carried the spirits of the Son of God and of God the Father; both died of diphtheria in February 1880 (Watson, pp. 191–93). Former members testifying against him in 1880–81 described more: Davies as the third person of the trinity, the Holy Spirit, standing at services “with a child on each side, representing the trinity on earth”; Davies as the reincarnation of Adam, Abraham, Noah and David, with four “sons” as “the four corner stones” of the kingdom, one of them Joseph Bowman as Elias; a Messiah who “at 15 would go out with a sword”; circles of seven, and of seven times seven, around the trinity; and horses as symbols of the divine attributes, “the White Horse represents Peace; the Black Horse, Justice; the Bay Horse, Judgment, and the Pale Horse, Death,” an echo of the Morrisites’ Foreshadowing of 1862 (testimony of George Lee, D. V. Lambert and Peter C. Klemgard, Walla Walla Statesman, January 1, 1881, p. 2, and February 5, 1881, pp. 3–4). In 1878 his missionary S. W. Wood told the New York Sun that there was “no marrying” in the community: couples who joined married were left as they were, but every soul was created mated with another, and when the two met they were one (“Mr. Wood of Walla-Walla,” The Sun, November 14, 1878, p. 1). His own pamphlets, hymns and interviews, which give his side, are in Watson, pp. 111–97. See William W. Davies and the Kingdom of Heaven. Some of Williams’s own followers counted Davies among the fallen. In a notebook of questions for Williams from the Council Bluffs years (about 1869–72), Andrew Henriksen reported that one “Ole” had taught at meetings there that “William Davis, the firstborn son of the seventh of Adam’s wives, is a fallen spirit”; that the firstborn of each of Adam’s wives would be “kings and priests and rulers on this earth after their father Adam through all eternity”; and that a person born crippled was a fallen spirit, which Henriksen doubted, since a born-crippled man in his own family had three well-formed children. He asked how these teachings were to be understood, “since they contradict each other” (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library, “Miscellany, 1886,” images 1–2; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

Other branches The Doves. James Dove and his son George followed Morris, then Williams, then Davies; in 1873 George began receiving communications and organized a Church of the Firstborn in California of about thirty people, seeing himself as the publisher and organizer of Morris’s revelations rather than a prophet (Watson, pp. 198–99). The Doves published The Spirit Prevails and the roll of membership in 1886, and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation (1892), which Watson calls the earliest book on the subject in the wider Mormon tradition (Watson, pp. 199, 208–64). The Montana council disowned them as “pretenders” in 1885. James Brighouse. His Order of Enoch in Independence, Missouri (1884), taught celibacy; no Morrisite source for its ideas has been traced (see the lineage chart under History).
Looking for the coming, 1861–1891

t: Every moment the sources record when the time of Christ’s coming was s…
s: Every moment the sources record when the time of Christ’s coming was set, tied to a condition, refused, or explained after it passed. The chart has two stretches of time, Kington Fort in 1861–63 and the years from 1866, with the gap between them left out; each lane is a branch of the movement, and each shape a kind of claim. Select a mark to read the entry, with its source; the same entries are listed in full below. Background. At Kirtland on February 14, 1835, Joseph Smith said that “the coming of the Lord, which was nigh” would come within “fifty six years”: in 1891 (Minutes, Discourse, and Blessings, 14–15 February 1835, The Joseph Smith Papers). Orson Pratt later printed the statement in a note to the Doctrine and Covenants, and it is probably the source of the 1891 that William James gave in 1880 (entry 28). Day set. A day named for the coming or the deliverance Year set. A year looked for, by a leader or member Condition attached. A promise that waits on what the people do Imminent, no date. The coming foretold as near, with no day named Kingdom date. A day set for a kingdom, not for the coming Messiah claimed present. A claim that Christ had already come again in someone Refusal to set a date. A leader declines to name a time Response after a date passed. What was said once a day or year went by
The 34 entries, with sources

W. Burton, sent these revelations to Salt Lake City within the week. Source: The Spirit Prevails, No. 154, pp. 267–68; W. W. Burton to C. W. West, December 12, 1861, Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library.

s: 5 Dec 8, 1861 Response after a date passed Revelation through Joseph Morris, headed “The Enemies Disappointed” The posse had not come because the resistance had struck its leaders with fear; they were “not in such a hurry as they were before,” but must come now or give up. What followed: The people consecrated their property that day, by Josiah D. Price’s account. The morning passed. Source: The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 188–189, pp. 338–39; Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives. See: Teachings: Joseph Morris · How did believers survive failed prophecy?

s: 8a Jan 1, 1862 Response after a date passed Revelation through Joseph Morris, the day after the coming promised for the morning Answers Morris’s fear that Christ was “a traitor to you because of the many disappointments”: the promises about the time of the deliverance “have failed, because they were intended to fail.” “If I had told them the naked truth, I could not have led them on at all … I had to mention dates.” No more dates would be given until the deliverance. Source: Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 250–55, Community of Christ Library Archives; not in The Spirit Prevails. See: How did believers survive failed prophecy?

s: 8c Jan 6, 1862 Imminent, no date Revelation through Joseph Morris “You insult me beyond all manner of reason!” With wood for two or three days and snow falling, Morris is told: “In the course of a few more days, you will witness many thousands of the inhabitants of this territory lying dead upon the ground,” nearly half of them at the first move. Source: Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f2 (loose sheets, Nos. 177 and 178), Community of Christ Library Archives; not in The Spirit Prevails.

s: 9 Jan 6, 1862 Response after a date passed Revelation through Joseph Morris Blames those who had “consecrated property unwillingly.” Source: The Spirit Prevails, No. 195, p. 350. See: Teachings: Joseph Morris

s: 11 Jan 11–12, 1862 Response after a date passed Revelation through Joseph Morris, and an informer’s report of the next day “The reason why I delay so long the deliverance of my people”: some who had voted and deeded their property would not give it up when the steward called. An informer heard it preached the next Sunday that the Lord could do nothing until they brought all their substance to the prophet’s feet. On condition: Full consecration. Source: The Spirit Prevails, No. 200, pp. 361–62; Wm. W. Burton, Ogden, January 14, 1862, Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, Church History Library.

What followed: Price dates the swearing, twelve at a time, from February 12; on February 15 a revelation found it nearly done (No. 223). Source: The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 213, 216 and 224, pp. 397–98, 403–4, 419–22; Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives. See: Glossary: Oath

s: 13 Feb 20–21, 1862 Response after a date passed Revelation through Joseph Morris, headed “Revelation Showing the Reason Why the Lord Has Disappointed His People” The disappointments had been sent on purpose: “blank disappointments, time after time,” to show the people they were not prepared. See: How did believers survive failed prophecy?

s: 14 Mar 29, 1862 Imminent, no date Revelation through Joseph Morris “My people may judge by the movements of mine enemies that my coming will take place in a very few days.” Source: The Spirit Prevails, No. 252, pp. 484–86.

See: Chronology, 30 May 1862

s: 16 Jun 8, 1862 Response after a date passed A tongue through Morris, interpreted by David Richards: the “3rd Captain of the Lord’s Host” On the angel’s own earth the faithful had also set dates and been disappointed; the error lay not in setting them but in refusing to give them up. Source: The Spirit Prevails, pp. 638–42; Watson, pp. 72–79, at 76–77. See: How did believers survive failed prophecy?

Source: Andrew Hendrickson’s copy of 1883, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881. See: Teachings: Cainan · Glossary: Sides of the North

s: 28 May 10, 1880 Year set William James, president of the Montana church, in the Lord’s House “Orson Pratt made it out that 61 years after the organisation of Church of J Smith will be the coming of Christ … if we have but 11 years more then it will be a short work to be done”: that is, 1891. Eardley Parson wrote to Eardley that the work under his charge would be “established this year,” and a Tribune letter of his called 1891 “a year of expectancy of great things”; Eardley called it “the year in which we have been led to expect so much.” Source: Parson to Eardley, 1891; “The Elder,” Sunday Salt Lake Tribune, May 31, 1891; Eardley to the court, 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1891. Eardley, to the same court Looked instead to a coming “war of the nations” and to “the next servant according to birthright, even Mahalaleel,” and likened the Saints to the wise and foolish virgins. Source: Court minutes, November 10, 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1891. See: Teachings: the Montana church Not drawn: James Brighouse, who from 1885 proclaimed himself the embodiment of the Second Coming, has no traced Morrisite link. Entry 1 is an informer’s report, and entry 11 draws partly on one; the rest of the Kington Fort entries are the revelations as printed in The Spirit Prevails (1886) or in manuscript copies. Corrections and additions are welcome.

Later echoes What follows shows how Morrisite teaching has been read and borrowed since, not that it was carried on. Leland Jensen’s Missoula sect already held that the Montana State Prison at Deer Lodge was Ezekiel’s temple; after its members came on the Morrisites in 1990 through Anderson’s history, they took Williams’s 1879 letter as confirmation, and Neal Chase set out the connection in Ezekiel’s Temple in Montana (1990). Anderson finds that the book credits Williams with far more prophetic ability than he had (Revisited, pp. 216–18). Chad Daybell’s assignment of past lives and talk of marriages across lives have invited comparison with Williams’s practice, but no line of descent has been shown, and both draw on older Latter-day Saint ideas; Israel A. J. Dennis’s Church of the First Born (1889) shows how readily the name and the doctrine could arise on their own. See Is there a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s?

Common misreadings “Morris opposed polygamy.” His own article treats plural marriage as a law for this life, at God’s time, with one wife sealed for eternity; it was not practiced at the fort (see Marriage, above). “Reincarnation came from Charles B. Thompson.” Anderson proposed it; Watson disputes it (see the question). “Church of the Firstborn” as Morris’s own name for his church. It is later usage (Glossary). “Williams prophesied that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming.” His letter names the region where the Saints lived, “the Sides of the North,” and sets no date. Davies’s community as a Morrisite congregation. It was a new movement led by a former Morrisite, made up largely of new converts.

Read the teachings yourself The Spirit Prevails (1886): Morris’s revelations. Free online; see Start here. Gems of Inspiration (1899): what the later church kept. Free online; see Start here. Kirk Watson, ed., The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026): Morris, Williams, Davies and the Doves in one volume, with an introduction; the place to start for most readers. C. LeRoy Anderson, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited) (2010): the standard history.
