Burton” (box 46); “Did the Bishop Murder the Morrisite Mrs. Bowman?: The Arrest” (box 39, book 24); “Remembering Cache Valley: Did Bishop Burton Murder Mrs. Bowman?” (1998; box 39, book 26); “The Morrisites” (box 34, book 6, 1989–90) and “The Morrisite War” (box 38, book 22); and a Robert T. Burton (Morrisites) file among his Church history research files (box 64). Not yet seen for this guide. Access Finding aid New

Willow Glen photographs Anaconda, Montana Held by Marcus Daly Historical Society Museum and Archives, Anaconda, Montana, in the basement of the Copper Village Museum and Art Center (the original city hall); kept by volunteers Contents Photographs of Willow Glen, east of Anaconda, among them two 1915 groups of the Rasmus Rasmussen family captioned “Morrisites” (010-10-000332 and 010-10-000333), a view of the Willow Glen Stock Farm, and fire damage at Willow Glen (print P-003605, negative N401139). In the museum’s numbers P marks a print, N a negative and G a glass negative. A fire caused by lightning destroyed barns at Willow Glen, then a ranch of the Mt. Haggin Livestock Company, on August 6, 1963 (Anaconda Standard, August 7, 1963, p. 1); the photographs are dated “1970’s.” The museum also holds the Mason & Hamlin organ said to have come from the Morrisites (see Open questions and Images, MO-IMG-102 to 104) and two dolls that belonged to Myrtle and Evelyn Staffanson, labeled as Morrisite children’s dolls (MO-IMG-105 and 106). The photographs, the 1963 report and the organ were brought to this guide’s attention by Jim Furshong, a volunteer at the museum. Access Through the director of the Copper Village Museum and Art Center. The photographs are not reproduced in this guide. New

Eliza Eardley Hardin reminiscence MTHS SC 788 Held by Montana Historical Society Library & Archives, Helena, Montana Extent 11 pages, typescript, signed; undated (received by the Society in 1952) Contents Hardin (born 1873) recalls her family’s journey by covered wagon from Salinas, California, in 1881 and their arrival that August at a crossroads east of the later Anaconda, where her father, “Mr. Eardley,” built a log store he named Willow Glen, which became a post office. The New North-West credits the Willow Glen store and post office to John R. Eardley (January–March 1882), so she was evidently his daughter. Family Tree agrees: it identifies her as Eliza Fitchford Eardley, born at Stockport, England, on February 25, 1873, a daughter of John Rowley Eardley and Sarah Jane Jackson of the 1861–62 roll, who married Andrew Evan Hardin at Santa Rosa, California, in 1899. It gives her death as September 21, 1969, at San Diego; the Society’s catalog has 1967 (FamilySearch K2TC-7BS). She describes “an old log church” near the crossroads and a William James living next to it, very probably the Morrisite leader of that name, though she never calls the people Morrisites. The church’s own minutes bear her out: the Montana council met at the Willow Glen meeting house in 1882, 1884 and 1885, the meeting place of the Warm Spring Creek stake under William James, and an Eliza F. Eardley voted at the general assembly of April 25, 1886 (Church History Library, MS 32226). See Deer Lodge Valley. Access Open. The Society scanned it for this guide in November 2026; small scans are provided on request. Cite as: Eliza Eardley Hardin, reminiscence, undated (received 1952). Eliza Eardley Hardin Reminiscence. SC 788. Montana Historical Society Library & Archives, Helena, Montana. New

t: Montana Homesteading Project records: the Eliason form
s: Montana Homesteading Project records: the Eliason form MTHS MC 340, box 2, folder 21 Held by Montana Historical Society Library & Archives, Helena, Montana Contents A Historical Information Submission Form, “Eliason, Elias [homesteaded c. 1900 Deer Lodge–Powell Co.],” with supplemental family material. It records the Eliason family’s move from Soda Springs, Idaho, to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1871. See Erik Eliasson. Access Open. The Society does not hold copyright in the supplemental material, which was submitted by the family; this guide summarizes it but does not quote or reproduce it. New

Deer Lodge, Montana genealogy papers, 1860–1990 USU COLL MSS 157 Held by Special Collections & Archives, Utah State University Extent 2 boxes (1 linear foot) Contents Family genealogies from the Deer Lodge Valley, compiled by Joan Crum, with particular attention to Morrisite families. Access Open to research. Finding aid

Henry Hendrickson interview, April 19, 1962 UM OH 018-001 Held by Archives and Special Collections, Mansfield Library, University of Montana, Missoula; Religion in Montana Oral History Collection Extent One audio recording (36 minutes) and a 28-page transcript Contents Henry Hendrickson, interviewed by Don Cornelius for his 1962 thesis on Mormonism in Montana (listed under Theses), describes the families, his own among them, who settled in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s, and the Church of the Firstborn, or Morrisites. Hendrickson, born in the valley in 1877, was the son of Andrew Hendrikson, who led the Montana church until his death in 1921. He recalls that his father was never a Latter-day Saint, joined the group around Council Bluffs and Omaha, and came with it in 1872 by rail to Corinne and then by wagon, a party he put at seventy-five or eighty people (pp. 10–13, 19); that besides the church at Race Track there was another “up around Lost Creek,” near Anaconda, with settlers also around Warm Springs (pp. 1–2); that most were Scandinavians, Danes above all around Race Track (p. 3); that the Eliasons came from Soda Springs (p. 11); that John Eardley had gone with the California group and came back to Montana (pp. 4–5); that preaching was mostly from the Bible, sometimes from the Book of Mormon and the Doctrine and Covenants (pp. 20–21); that Latter-day Saint missionaries were sometimes allowed to speak in the Race Track church (p. 20); and that the church faded around 1919–20, the young people joining the Reorganized Church, with George Johnson, who lived to be 98, the last preacher (pp. 8–9, 18). He left the valley in 1908. The catalog spells the name Hendrickson; Anderson spells Andrew Hendrikson’s name without the c. Access The transcript is online; the library holds copyright, and permission may be needed to quote it. Catalog record and transcript New

Morrisite manuscripts, University of Utah U of U MS 0111 · 0260 · 0261 · 0263 · 0365 Held by J. Willard Marriott Library Special Collections, University of Utah, Salt Lake City Contents Mark H. Forscutt’s partial history of the Morrisite church (MS 0261), which may be a photostat of his “Sketch” (see Documents); Danel W. Bachman's 1970 BYU paper “Joseph Morris and the Morrisites” (MS 0260); Jacob Miller papers (MS 0111); Karl Banks's essay “A Brief History of John Banks and the Morrisite Movement” (MS 0263; 12 pp.), on his grandfather, of which Johnny Wade Hansen’s BYU paper of 1969 cites another copy at Brigham Young University (Hansen, pp. 2, 6); and the Agnes Just Reid papers, 1850–2004 (MS 0365; 1 box), whose first folders hold biographical sketches of Emma Thompson Bennett Just by her daughter Agnes and others and an oral history, with correspondence about the publication of Letters of Long Ago (see the Bibliography). Access On-site use only, at the library. Neither the Banks essay nor the Reid papers has yet been read for this guide. Reid papers finding aid New

Gordon M. Howard papers, 1716–1977 USHS Mss B 279 Held by Utah State Historical Society, Salt Lake City Extent 3 boxes Contents Howard's research notes, correspondence, and draft chapters on Joseph Morris and the Morrisite War. Box 2 holds copies of court papers: People v. Peter Klingard, Third Judicial District, 1863 (folder 5), and a register of arrests of Morrisites, 1863 (folder 6). Access Finding aid

William W. Davies collection, 1929–1976 WCMss124 Held by Whitman College and Northwest Archives, Walla Walla, Washington Contents Clippings, copies of depositions, court testimony, and judgments, letters and articles by Davies, and an academic paper on the Kingdom of Heaven. Access Open. Finding aid · catalog record Also at Whitman “Davies family and home, ‘Walla Walla Jesus’,” 1882, one photograph and two negatives, in the Walla Walla photographs collection (WCMss-066, box 39, folder 72; catalog record). A subject file on Davies, 1992, in the Vance Orchard Papers, the research files of the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin columnist (WCMss-118, box 4, folder 20; catalog record).

t: Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880
s: Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880 Frontier Justice WAL-3153 Held by Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, Cheney, Washington Contents Case file of the Washington Territorial District Court for Walla Walla County, original case no. 2373, 1880: a civil suit to collect wages and debts brought by Asa B. Cilley, Thomas W. Evans and A. J. Courtney against William W. Davies, Alfred Davies and W. Wood. The archives’ index calls it the “Walla Walla Jesus” case. The file runs to 292 pages. It holds depositions taken before a referee in 1880–81 by members and former members, among them Peter C. Klemgard, Swen O. Hagg and Broer Sorenson of the 1861–62 roll, and Davies himself; a list of the forty-three members in March 1881, with their ages; printed tracts, hymns and letters by Davies filed as exhibits, among them his printed “Synopsis of Remarks” at a meeting of January 2, 1876; lists of donations to the community from 1866 to 1878; the referee’s report; the judgment of May 25, 1881, for $3,225 (Evans $2,700, Courtney $400, Cilley $125), with interest and costs; and the sheriff’s returns: Davies’s livestock and equipment were sold on June 11, 1881, and the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east, on July 16, 1881. Related case First National Bank of Walla Walla v. William A. Davies, William W. Davies and Lewis H. Bowman, 1885 (WAL-4626, original no. 4262; 28 pages): nine promissory notes of November 14, 1879, totaling $1,770, made by William W. Davies and his son William A. Davies to Lewis H. Bowman, who sold them to the bank the same day. The bank sued in February 1885 and took judgment by default on May 21, 1885, for $4,141.60 with attorney’s fees. The son was served in Lincoln County, near Sprague. Zbaraschuk (1989) lists two more suits by the same bank in the territorial district court: case 3093 (1882), against William A. and William W. Davies, on promissory notes, ending in judgment for $4,259 with costs and interest; and case 3260 (1883), against William A. and William W. Davies, Grosvenor S. Andrus, D. S. Baker and John F. Boyer, which he says holds 188 pages of testimony, including Andrus’s and both Davieses’. Neither has been ordered for this guide. New Access Indexed in “Frontier Justice,” the Washington State Archives’ guide to the territorial court case files, 1853–1889 (index record, 1880; 1885). The papers are not online; copies may be ordered from the Eastern Region Branch, which scanned both files for this guide in November 2026. Pages 158–195, the depositions of five defense witnesses, were missing when the county microfilmed the file; Whitman College Library later found them among its own holdings and returned them, and they are now with the case file (notes by the Walla Walla County clerk and by the archivist, 2002, filed with the case). Pages 133–157 are not in the file. The archivist who scanned it for this guide confirms that the whole file, several folders, was scanned and sent, and that these pages were evidently already missing when it came to the archives; he suspects they left the courthouse the same way pages 158–195 reached Whitman, perhaps when the clerk’s office reported the records “checked out” (Lee Pierce, Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, email to the editor, November 9, 2026). Kirk Watson reports that they are not in FamilySearch’s images of the county microfilm either (FamilySearch, sign-in required). Zbaraschuk (1989), working from that microfilm, already noted “major gaps” in the pagination. New Kirk Watson’s edition prints Davies’s own deposition in the 1880 case.

Diaries, letters, and federal records Several repositories Church History Library Brigham Young correspondence; Journal of Wilford Woodruff; Journal History of the Church; “Niels Anderson matter, 1903” (Joseph F. Smith stake correspondence, CR 1 191; digitized), letters of January–March 1903 from Niels Anderson, one also signed by Mary Christoffersen Anderson, asking the church’s help for the injury Mary received in 1862, with a clerk’s draft for the reply and the Bannock Stake president’s report of May 19, 1903, on the First Presidency’s inquiry; George Morris reminiscences, circa 1867–1886 (MS 1614; catalog record), by Joseph Morris’s brother, with a family genealogy and incidents about Joseph. The manuscript opens “A Short sketch of the Geneoligy and History of George Morris” (p. 1). Two accounts by men called out against the Morrisites: Newton Tuttle’s diary, January 1859–June 1862, kept at Bountiful, which includes his service in the territorial militia during the Morrisite War (MS 4299 1; catalog record), and Benjamin C. Critchlow’s reminiscences, circa 1865, of Weber County, the Utah War and the Morrisite War (MS 1662, carbon copy of a typescript; catalog record). Neither is digitized, and neither has yet been read for this guide. New Church History Library: diaries, reminiscences and militia returns read in November 2026 Theodore McKean family collection, MS 33041, “Militia companies’ reports” (catalog date 1866; open to research; 42 images): the posse’s summary report and company rolls, June 12–18, 1862, and Daniel H. Wells’s letter to Burton of June 13 (see the posse chart). Johann L. Baer [John L. Bear] autobiography, circa 1908, MS 10240 (typescript, 89 leaves; open), very probably the text behind the Journal of History serial of 1911–12: Weber, the siege, Camp Douglas, Soda Springs and the Reorganized Church. Daniel H. Wells papers, MS 1344, letterpress copy book (open): Wells’s letters to Burton during and after the siege, June 14–16, 1862 (pp. 10–15). George A. Smith papers, MS 1322, incoming letters, L–Y, 1868 (open): Jesse N. Smith’s letter from Copenhagen of November 3, 1868 (images 39–41). Joseph F. Smith papers, MS 1325, General correspondence, “A–Cl, 1862” (open): Jacob G. Bigler’s letter of July 5, 1862, with pre-siege rumors of Morris and a story of his meeting Brigham Young (images 56–57). Hans F. Hansen reminiscence and diary, MS 14915 (Danish, with an English typescript; open): a posse member’s entries of 1861–62. Lars C. Christensen autobiography, 1892, MS 5831 (typescript; open): a Latter-day Saint neighbor of the fort. John Welch missionary journal, 1899–1900, MS 29881 (open): Race Track and Warm Springs, July 1899. Digitized but restricted (they do not open online, even with a Church Account): Woolley family collection, MS 32665 (letters of 1856–65 referring to Governor Harding, the Morrisite war and Connor); Johan F. F. Klingbaek journal, circa 1857–1877, MS 8268 (Danish: emigration, the Morrisites and the Reorganized Church; read for this guide under a digital-access grant in November 2026, from the Church Historian’s Office microfilm of 1963; parts of the 1859–62 pages, including the voyage and the siege, are covered by later pasted newspaper clippings and cannot be read on the microfilm); and Benjamin C. Critchlow’s diaries, MS 22600 (see above). Henry Holmes journals, 1856–1874, MS 426: volumes 1–3, in Pitman shorthand, are digitized; the typed transcriptions are digitized but restricted. “History of the ‘Morrisites,’ Hugh F. O’Neil and others,” MS 8305: listed as open to research, but the digital copy asks for a sign-in even with a Church Account; ask the library. Closed to research: “Morrisite Staff,” CR 100 708, a 2024 Church History Museum research report by Dennis Wright on the three staffs (LDS 65-3058). Not digitized; to be seen at the library: Lars C. Larsen notebook, MS 21929 (Danish; questions and answers on Morris’s teachings, with a family genealogy; possibly the L. C. Larsen of Deer Lodge); Lars C. Christensen autobiography, MS 844 (another copy of MS 5831, probably); Louis Garff, MS 1754; Christian F. Twede, MS 11239; Byron L. Bybee interview, 1961, MS 6230 12 (Uintah, with the interviewer’s comments on the Morrisites); Agnes J. Reid interview, July 5, 1970, MS 21605 (Harold S. Forbush, Ricks College oral history; brief references to the Morrisites and Soda Springs); and, catalogued as bearing on the Morrisites (checked November 21, 2026): Joseph Wild statement, 1884, MS 5852 (on John Banks and the Church of the Firstborn); John Jenkins journal, MS 7257 (Cache Valley); Sketch of Mary L. Morris, MS 6594; Joseph J. Taylor papers, MS 10413; William Butler, MS 17145; George R. Hill, MS 16123; James Cowper correspondence, 1861–69, MS 24755; and Ezra T. Benson letter, 1863, MS 17517. New University of Utah Diary of Hans Olsen Magleby; journal of John L. Blyth, 1858–1863; pioneer journal of Jacob Miller; Timothy Kendell autobiography (MS 0041), recalling South Weber as briefly called Morristown. Utah State Archives Territorial militia records (series 2210; images and a name index on FamilySearch, collection 1462415): Acting Governor Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, calling out the posse (copied in document 1,215); a list of the South Weber company’s officers, April 22, 1859; Weber District muster rolls of the 1857 call-up, which include Robert Farley and John Parson. National Archives Record Group 60, Department of Justice chronological files, Utah, box 683: Sumner Howard to Attorney General Charles Devens, July 28, 1877. Record Group 49, General Land Office land entry case files: the papers behind the federal land patents of Morrisite settlers, among them Erik Eliasson’s homestead (Helena land office, Homestead Certificate 560, patented 1888) and Niels R. Beck’s preemption entry (Helena, certificate 230, patented 1871), whose proofs should give the date each man settled on his land. Copies are ordered on NATF Form 84 (online ordering). Bureau of

t: Joseph Morris letters and revelation manuscripts
s: Joseph Morris letters and revelation manuscripts CR 1234 1 · digitized Held by Church History Library, Salt Lake City Contents Morris’s letters to Brigham Young (1857–1860), the originals of the copies in the USU collection, and manuscript revelations from 1859–1862, in Brigham Young’s office files (President’s Office Files, General Office Files: folders “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” and “1861–1862”). No letter from Young to Morris has been found. Kirk Watson’s edition transcribes twelve letters of 1858–1860 with item-by-item links (see Bibliography); a dated list is on the Documents page.

Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901 CHL MS 31876 · MS 32226 · digitized Held by Church History Library, Salt Lake City Extent MS 31876: 3 boxes, 54 items, available only as digital images. MS 32226, 1869–1890: 1 box, 9 folders. Contents The records of the followers of George Williams, the Prophet Cainan, in Council Bluffs, Omaha and the Deer Lodge Valley. MS 31876 holds Cainan’s epistles and letters to William James, John R. Eardley and the Montana followers, written from Salt Lake City and then from England (1864–1878); record books of his writings, among them Swedish translations by Emanuel Strom (1872; his “Record of epistles” also copies Morris’s “Keys of the Priesthood,” headed “Syd Wiber Dec 12te 1860,” and his article of June 4, 1861, on polygamy) and a Niels Jensen record (1870–1879; Danish copies of Williams’s letters of 1870, an English copy of a revelation on trials, and a letter of 1875 from Barnet Moses Giles); copies of records from St. Ann’s Hill in Surrey, England (in the folder “Writings of Cainan, circa 1867–1872,” with Williams’s 1867 “Interview with Mahomet,” three chapters of the records, a Danish translation, and “The Lord’s Supper,” Williams’s answer to the council’s meeting of November 10, 1881, in a copy made by John R. Eardley); council minutes, 1869–1891; letters of Andrew Hendrikson, William James, George Thompson, John R. Eardley, Almerin Grow and William P. and Margaret Evans Thomas, with letters in Welsh to the Thomases from John D. Bowen at Austin, Nevada, 1872–74; a folder of miscellany (catalogued as 1886, but running from about 1869 to the 1890s) with Andrew Henriksen’s Danish notebook of questions from Council Bluffs, which also gives the address of Isaac Sheen, editor of the Reorganized Church’s Herald at Plano, and a fair copy of Morris’s revelation on young Joseph Smith numbered 67 and dated May 9, 1861 (The Spirit Prevails prints it as No. 64, May 4); and a photograph of the Deer Lodge church building. MS 32226 holds two minutebooks (1872–1874, and the Montana council minutes, 1881–1890) with loose minutes, 1869–1874; Danish membership records for Council Bluffs and Omaha, circa 1869–1872, among them the Council Bluffs register of twenty-seven members, with eight baptized at South Weber in 1861, and the Omaha congregation’s register of forty-two members with their birthplaces and baptisms at South Weber (1861), Omaha (from January 1869), Fremont and Crescent City, Iowa (1871), read in November 2026; a record of members of stake number 2 in Montana, 1874–1887; and two letter copy books of Cainan’s letters and instructions, circa 1866–1882 (the first, circa 1866–1877, read in November 2026, is a fair copy made in or after 1893, since a note in it cites the Saints’ Herald of that year, of Williams’s letters to John R. Eardley, 1866–1878, and to Robert Ford, 1871, with pages of proof texts). Most of the minutes and many of the letters are in Danish, with some items in Welsh. The membership record of Stake No. 2 and the Montana council minutebook for 1881–1890 (MS 32226, folders 7 and 3) were read for this guide in November 2026, and in MS 31876 the letters of 1879–1882 in part, the letters to William James of 1874–1875 and the membership slips. Among them are Williams’s own note of January 29, 1882, naming James to be put before the church after his death; an envelope to James inscribed “I leave you in charge after my decease”; Williams’s letters of 1880 and 1882 about his eldest daughter Adelaide (Adelaide Matilda, thirteen in April 1871, as he named her to the Thomases; about 1870 he gave her address as “Miss Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams,” writing out “all the Christian names because there is many Williams’”; the longer form named the household’s three women, Susanna, Louisa and Adelaide, who appear together in the 1880 census, and she died at Los Angeles in 1947 as Adelaide M. Williams, California Death Index, ark:/61903/1:1:VPQR-KCV), a teacher at the Episcopal school in Salt Lake City who came to Deer Lodge; S. P. Guhl’s letter from Omaha of November 1874 disputing James’s authority; John R. Eardley’s letter from Hollister, California, of November 1875; and, among the letters to Eardley (read in part), his own letter of February 1880 planning a store in Montana; George Thompson’s letter from Essex of December 1886 and his letters to William P. Thomas, 1869–83; Thompson’s letter of March 23, 1882, written for the dying Williams; Williams’s letters of 1868–1873 and 1876–78 in part; his letters to Andrew Hendrikson at Council Bluffs and Omaha, 1869–73, surveyed; and the Danish council minutes of the Race Track stake for 1882–83; the Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871; the 1869 record book; the council minutes for 1873–74 and 1879, with those for 1875, 1877 and 1878 in part; Sven Olson Hagg’s letters of 1866 and 1869; the first of the letters to Andrew Hendrikson, 1869; and, among the letters to the Montana followers of 1878–1881, Andrew Hendrickson’s 1883 copy of Williams’s letter of January 6, 1879, on “the Sides of the North” (see Teachings). The record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, mostly in Swedish and Danish copies, opens with a drawing labeled “Seth’s Diagram” and was surveyed only. The rest has not yet been read. The Danish passages quoted in this guide were transcribed and translated by Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, from the catalog’s page images. No Danish reader has checked them yet, so treat them as provisional and check the originals before relying on a reading. Access Open to research; the library lists no known copyright. Both collections can be viewed page by page in the library’s online catalog without signing in. MS 31876 · MS 32226 New

t: Church files on the Morrisites and the siege, 1861–1862
s: Church files on the Morrisites and the siege, 1861–1862 CHL CR 100 397 · CR 1234 1 · digitized Held by Church History Library, Salt Lake City Contents In the Historian’s Office collected historical documents (CR 100 397), open to research: “Siege of Morris fort, 1862 June,” John G. Chambers’s account as a member of the posse (22 pages), with copies of a rod inscription and of a letter found in the willows near the fort; and “Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” the lists of the 149 men taken (100 brought to Salt Lake City, 49 discharged at the fort, with birthplaces and ages), Thomas Bullock’s minutes of their examination before Judge Kinney, and copies of the inscriptions on three rods of office, taken from the originals on June 19, 1862. In the Brigham Young office files (CR 1234 1), “Morrisite papers, 1861–1862”: reports of Morrisite meetings and sermons sent to Brigham Young, many through Chauncey W. West of Ogden, among them an eyewitness description of the procession of May 30, 1862, and a second copy of the prisoner lists. Read for this guide in November 2026. Not online Two posse-side accounts named in the catalog are not digitized and must be seen at the library: the Newton Tuttle diary, 1859–1862 (MS 4299 1), and Benjamin C. Critchlow’s reminiscences, circa 1865 (MS 1662). Critchlow’s diaries (MS 22600), whose 1887 volume includes his recollections of the siege, are digitized but restricted.

Books of Joseph Morris’s revelations CHL MS 1266 · MS 5576 Held by Church History Library, Salt Lake City Contents Joseph Morris revelations, 1859–1862 (MS 1266; 2 folders): a volume in which his revelations were logged, with papers of extracts from them. Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1863 (MS 5576; 1 folder, 58 leaves), catalogued under Robert Henry Ford: a record of revelations given to Morris and of exhortations by his successor, George Williams, to the remaining Morrisites. Williams addressed his “First Epistle of Cainan to Robert Ford” (Loughborough, February 7, 1871) to a Robert Ford, probably the same man (letter copy book, circa 1866–1877, MS 32226). Neither has yet been seen for this guide. Access Open to research. Neither is digitized; both are on microfilm and can be requested at the library. MS 1266 · MS 5576 New

Morrisite scepters LDS 65-3058 · 3059 · 3060 Held by Church History Museum collection, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Salt Lake City Description Three painted wooden staffs, each with a printed inscription mounted on the shaft. The editor saw them in the museum vault and transcribed the inscriptions. Photographs courtesy of the Church History Museum, of the three scepters together (p. 116) and of an inscription band close up (p. 117), were published with the editor’s transcription of the inscriptions in Anderson, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited) (2010), 116–17. They are not reproduced here. Inscriptions Joseph Morris’s scepter declares him sent “to RULE over all ADAM’S posterity” and is signed “Joseph Morris, PRESIDENT of the Melchisidec Priesthood.” The other two belonged to Hugh Park (“number five,” his name written over an earlier one) and Daniel Smith (“number seven”), each presenting himself as a ruler “over all Abraham’s seed.”

t: South Weber Pioneer Cemetery records and local history files
s: South Weber Pioneer Cemetery records and local history files South Weber City · not online Held by South Weber City, South Weber, Utah Contents The Pioneer Cemetery’s burial records, Mattie G. Ray’s compiled list (1998) and a plot map, with the city’s notes on the cemetery (deeded to the city by Brent Winchester in 1981; restored by an Army Reserve unit in 1973–75); handwritten notes for a talk on the Morrisite War, 1963; Johnny Wade Hansen’s BYU seminar paper of 1969; two undated papers of local tradition about the siege; Norma Earl Allred’s compilation of South Weber families; and newspaper clippings, about 1975–2006. They place Joseph Warner, Isabella Bowman and Charles Patton Bowman in or by the cemetery (see Kington Fort). Access Ask the city offices. Copies were sent to the editor by Lisa Smith in November 2026; they are cited here, not reproduced.

t: Joseph Morris Papers, Josiah D. Price journal, copies of the roll, Wandell and Warner letters, and the Deer Lodge Branch register
s: Joseph Morris Papers, Josiah D. Price journal, copies of the roll, Wandell and Warner letters, and the Deer Lodge Branch register CofC P6 · P11-1 · P24 · P26-22 · P39-8 · P101 · #228 Held by Community of Christ Library Archives, Independence, Missouri Contents P11-1, Joseph Morris Papers (folders 1–6), which appear to be Alexander Dow’s papers: in f1 and f2, a later fair copy in a ledger (pp. 149–263, in five booklets, with a few pages missing) of selected revelations with their own numbering, which runs with that of The Spirit Prevails to about June 1861 and then falls behind, and a later reader’s pencil numbers keyed to the book; in f2, an earlier copy on loose folded sheets, numbered and dated, of revelations of December 11, 1861 to January 6, 1862, a later copy of the revelation of April 21, 1862, and the start of a Danish translation of the revelation of November 8, 1860. The copies hold four texts not in The Spirit Prevails (an address to Young of December 11, 1860; revelations of January 1, 5 and 6, 1862; and one copied as “June 13, 1862,” on Adam as the “Loyal President” of this earth), and several dates that differ from the book (the “Rod of Moses” revelation is dated April 24, 1860, against the book’s September 24; two others differ by a day or two); manuscripts of revelations of 1860–62, among them the oath of the high priesthood, “Keys of the Holy Priesthood,” the revelation of April 4, 1861 (The Spirit Prevails, No. 56) with signatures on the back, and the revelation of June 15, 1862, the third day of the siege (The Spirit Prevails, No. 304); an address to Brigham Young dated September 22, 1860, which is not in The Spirit Prevails; a prophecy dated at Great Salt Lake City, March 8, 1863; a catechism on the first chapter of Genesis and an essay on the Plummet; a folder of undated instructions (f6) with copies of the rite for administering to the sick, the revelation advising slowness of speech in ordinations (No. 57), the bride’s part of the marriage covenant (No. 89), part of the prophecy of December 21, 1860 (No. 30), and an “Inscription upon the Prophet’s sceptre,” the text on Morris’s own rod (see Teachings); a letter on the tides written from Camp Douglas in 1869 in answer to an article in the Alameda County Gazette (another copy in f5); and, in f5, a prophecy given in tongues at Great Salt Lake City on March 8 and 24, 1863; Dow’s own account of the siege; a letter of Joseph Smith III about Dow (Plano, 1870) and Dow’s letter to Smith (St. Louis, 1873); and Dow’s business papers, 1854–64. P26-22 f1, a photocopy of the journal of Josiah D. Price, 1858–1873, in English and Welsh: his own baptism on December 3, 1861, as the “431st person” in the church; the six baptized on April 6, 1861; the consecration of December 30, 1861, and the oath of February 12, 1862; Welsh translations of the consecration and oath revelations and of ordinances, and a Welsh prophecy of a new priest (Testament of Levi 18) apparently copied from a Welsh Latter-day Saint periodical; the drill, oath and Foreshadowing of May 1862, copies of ordinances and of the scepter inscription, a drawing of the worlds, and Price’s accounts. P101 f3 and f32 (Miscellaneous Collection): copies of the 1886 Roll of Membership, one with tally marks, and a transcript of the headstone of Niels and Mary Anderson at Soda Springs. P24, Henry A. Stebbins Papers: Charles W. Wandell’s letters to Alexander H. Smith and Joseph Smith III from San Juan, California, July–August 1873, on the Morrisites there, with his partial copy of the first two chapters of the St. Ann’s Hill records (f26–f28), and Joseph Warner’s letter to the Saints’ Herald, August 1, 1877 (f5 item 18). The Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), the RLDS membership register from about 1881, with marriages to 1919 (entries to about 1900 read for this guide); and reports of the Deer Lodge branch historians and Saints’ Herald notices of the branch, 1920s–1980s. Among the historians’ reports is a typed “History of Deer Lodge, Montana Branch” of about 1960–62, compiled by three members partly from a Christoffersen descendant’s memories: the Eliasson and Christoffersen families, the branch’s two church buildings (the second begun about 1892 and dedicated in 1901), its pastors, the Warm Springs branch of 1911–17, and the Lord’s House at Racetrack. P6, Joseph Smith III Letter Press Books (JSLB4): his letter to Kate Field of September 1, 1884, on Forscutt’s “sketch of the Morrisite persecution”; to John Parson, January 25, 1885, on Morris’s revelation No. 64; and to H. P. Brown, Parson and Heman C. Smith, June–July 1888, on Parson and Dr. P. W. Poulson’s “Order of Messiah.” Henry A. Stebbins’s letterbook (HASLB7, pp. 236–37): Parson’s RLDS baptism and expulsion dates. John L. Bear Papers (P39-8 f1): his mission diary, 1881–82. These were found through the Archives’ Archival Document Data Base (2004), a set of searchable transcripts. How it was searched In November 2026 the editor downloaded the posted volumes and searched their text for Morrisite terms and for every name on the roll and the people pages, with spelling variants; each item used here was then read on the page image. The text layer misreads many words, splits names across lines and gives married women under their husbands’ names, so a search that finds nothing is not proof that a person is absent. The volumes for 1862–65 had no hits for Morrisite terms and should be read by hand. Access Free to read and download.

Using the secondary literature Most of what has been written about the Morrisites rests on a small number of earlier works. Later histories, theses and articles often take their account of 1862 from Anderson, from the 1880s and 1890s retellings in the Salt Lake Tribune and the Contributor, or from one another, so an error made early can travel a long way. The theses listed below are valuable for what their authors saw or heard themselves, such as Don Cornelius’s 1962 interviews in Montana and Julie A. Wright’s use of mission records, and weaker where they summarize events at second hand. Where a fact matters, follow it back to a record made at the time: the court records, the cemetery sexton’s book, the 1886 roll, land and census records, and the newspapers, read in the original rather than in reprints. This guide is held to the same rule; it has its own unsettled points, which are listed on the Questions page, and corrections are welcome.

Common errors in print Claims that recur in published and unpublished accounts, and now in online videos, with what the records show and where to check. They are listed to help readers, not to fault the authors, most of whom were relying on what they had been told. The siege at “Manti” or “Knight Fort.” The siege of June 13–15, 1862, took place at Kington Fort, the Morrisites’ settlement on the Weber River at South Weber, Weber County, Utah. “Kingston Fort” is a common spelling of the same place. See Kington Fort. Kington Fort as a military post. It was a settlers’ fort, built in 1853 and abandoned about 1858, not an army post. See Glossary. Morris excommunicated by Taylor and Woodruff in February 1861. At South Weber on February 11, 1861, the apostles John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff cut off sixteen of Morris’s followers, among them Bishop Richard Cook; Morris’s name is not on the list Woodruff recorded (Woodruff’s journal, February 11, 1861). See Chronology. A skirmish with the militia. It was a three-day siege, June 13–15, 1862. The force was a posse comitatus under the deputy U.S. marshal Robert T. Burton, raised from the territorial militia on Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11 to serve the court’s writs for the arrest of Morris and others. See Morrisite War. Acting Governor Frank Fuller as a Latter-day Saint. Fuller, who called out the posse, was born in Boston, trained as a physician and dentist, and worked as a newspaperman in New Hampshire before President Lincoln appointed him secretary of Utah Territory in 1861; no record found makes him a member of the Church (Mark Twain Project, biography of Frank Fuller; University of Utah, Marriott Library, Frank Fuller papers, finding aid). In March 1863 a report from Camp Douglas named him with ex-Governor Alfred Cumming and Chief Justice John F. Kinney, both non-Mormons, as officials who had followed Brigham Young’s lead (The War of the Rebellion: Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 2, p. 370). See Morrisite War. A single, settled death toll. Accounts differ on how many died and on some of their names and dates; no list has yet been checked against all the sources. See Who died at Kington Fort? One posse man killed. The posse lost two: Jared Smith on June 13 and Peter Wahler, a German-born single man of about twenty-five, on June 15 (Woodruff’s journal, June 16, 1862). The sexton’s record lists Wahler, as “Walden,” next to Morris, and so does the city’s register of deaths; the name “John Peter Wahlin,” found in print, is not in either record. One account of how Morris died. Morris was killed at the surrender on June 15, but the Morrisite and posse accounts of the moment differ. Read them side by side rather than taking one as fact. A posse of a thousand men. The figure comes from Morrisite accounts. The militia returns kept by Deputy Marshal Theodore McKean list about 520 men, from Salt Lake County, Davis and Weber; estimates of “perhaps 500” were closer. See the posse chart. The infants held by the women killed on June 13 were unhurt. John L. Bear wrote that a cannon ball struck his shelter about two hours after the first shot and killed his wife and their sixteen-week-old baby, who were buried together that night (autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 25–26). See Who died at Kington Fort? Morris’s wives turned against him by church leaders. This is the Morrisite history’s account of his first marriage. The records show that Morris himself petitioned the Sanpete probate court for a divorce from Mary on April 6, 1854, and that she married Henry Beal at Ephraim on July 4, 1854, and lived there for the rest of her life, raising Morris’s daughter in the Beal household. See the Chronology, March–April 1854. Morris born on December 15, 1824 (or 1822). The day is the same in every source; the year is not. The ages given at his marriage in 1847 and in the 1850 census point to 1823. See the Chronology. Morris burned twice in the mines, and speaking seven languages. His brother George mentions one severe burn by fire damp, the explosive gas that collects in coal mines, and the Morrisites’ own history also gives one mine explosion, which disabled him for a year (The Spirit Prevails, 1886, p. 2). The seven languages come from a letter of their father’s, as George reports it: Joseph “Could Speak 7 different Languages in perfection” through the gift of tongues (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 115, 179). See Documents. Morris buried beneath a street. The Salt Lake City Cemetery sexton’s record lists him as no. 1469, June 15, 1862, in the pauper ground; the street story has no published source yet. See Where is Joseph Morris buried? Mark H. Forscutt as an RLDS apostle. Forscutt was an apostle in Morris’s church and clerk of its First Council; in the Reorganized Church he was a minister. Dates and names taken from reprints. The first dispatch from Salt Lake City, of June 16, 1862, was reprinted across the country, and its wording drifted as it was copied: “the prophet Moses” became “Prophet Morris,” and “the 15th” became “the 5th.” Cite the earliest printing. See Newspapers. The Montana church ending with George Williams, or with no leaders after him. It was led by William James, George Thompson (from 1886), Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954), until his death in 1954, with which, by Anderson’s account, the church came to an end (Revisited, pp. 212, 214); USU’s finding aid gives 1969 for its formal disbanding. See How and when did the Montana church end? John R. Eardley, called an apostle in 1861, was still called “Apostle Eardly” by Latter-day Saint missionaries in 1896. The Lord’s House built in 1877. The council minutes show that the site on Andrew Hendrikson’s land at Race Track was chosen only on February 24, 1878; the House was built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879 (Church History Library, MS 31876). This guide gave 1877 until November 2026. See Lord’s House. Morris as a

Morris’s new church, 1861 Joseph Morris’s revelations reached the national press a year before the siege, through letters from Utah correspondents. Chicago Tribune, July 17, 1861, p. 3. In a column of Utah news. A correspondent’s account of Morris, “the new prophet,” and his revelations: war in the States, the fall of Brigham Young’s church, and the gathering of the Morrisites at Weber. The earliest page found on Newspapers.com; about seventy-five pages in the United States and Britain carried the story that summer and autumn. Newspapers.com subscription Wiltshire Independent (Devizes, England), September 12, 1861, p. 4. In “General Gleanings.” A paragraph beginning “Brigham Young has found a rival,” on Morris’s settlement near Zion. Newspapers.com subscription ↑ Back to the chart

The siege, 1862 The first reports went out by telegraph from Salt Lake City and were reprinted across the country and abroad within weeks. The Deseret News told the story its own way and never used the word “Morrisite”: in 1862 it wrote of a “band” and “the Davis County bandits.” Sacramento Bee, June 16, 1862, p. 3. “[Second Dispatch.] … Rebellion in Utah—The Prophet Moses, or ‘the Prophet Figgs.’” The original telegraphic dispatch from Salt Lake City, dated June 16. It is the source of most of the 1862 coverage elsewhere. As it was copied, the wording drifted: “the prophet Moses” became “Prophet Morris,” and “the 15th” became “the 5th.” Newspapers.com subscription Reprinted in Daily Alta California (San Francisco), June 17, 1862, p. 1, in the telegraphic column “Salt Lake, June 16th.” Newspapers.com subscription Oregonian (Portland), June 24, 1862, p. 2. “Disturbance at Salt Lake.” Credits “a dispatch to the Bee.” Newspapers.com subscription Chicago Tribune, June 25, 1862, p. 1. “Important from Utah. H. Wells.” A quarrel over the territorial militia. Governor Shaffer had banned musters and refused to recognize Wells as its lieutenant-general. To show that earlier governors had recognized him, Wells printed Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, requiring him to furnish Marshal Henry W. Lawrence and his deputies Burton and McKean with “a sufficient military force” to arrest Joseph Morris. That is the earliest printing of the order found for this guide. Burton’s arrest and trial, 1877–1879 Burton was arrested in July 1877 and tried in Salt Lake City in February and March 1879 for the killing of Isabella Bowman, one of the women shot at the surrender. The jury acquitted him. Carson Valley News (Genoa, NV), June 23, 1876, p. 3; May 29, 1877, p. 3; June 15, 1877, p. 3; June 22, 1877, p. 3; March 22, 1878, p. 3. The Morrisites of Carson Valley and William W. Davies. June 1876: “old man Robert Roberts,” who claims to be the Prophet Daniel, visits Genoa and says that the child “who is to ‘run’ the Kingdom of God on earth” is already born at Walla Walla; a small Morrisite meeting in the court house hears R. J. Livingston, then Roberts. May 1877: Livingston, “a long-time resident and rancher of Douglas County,” leaves on May 28 for “the Holy Land—Walla Walla.” June 1877: Livingston’s party passes Reno (from the Reno Gazette), and “Robert Roberts, the Morrisite Mormon who claims to be the Prophet Daniel,” is in town again. March 1878: Livingston’s letter from Mill Creek, Walla Walla, March 2, on the 440-acre farm he has bought. Roberts was Davies’s missionary (see People). The 1877 story was reprinted in the Salt Lake Herald, June 16, 1877, and other papers. Douglas County digital archive New North-West (Deer Lodge, MT), June 15, 1877, p. 2. “The Morrisites. A Good Immigration Story.” The Carson Valley News item on the “Prophet Daniel,” reprinted in Montana; it says the Morrisites “flourish largely in Carson Valley, Nevada.” Chronicling America New North-West, July 13, 1877, p. 4. “The Second Christ.” A description of Davies’s colony “between Mill creek and Russell creek,” about seventy people, “an off-shoot from the Mormon church” whose leader’s young son was claimed to be the second Christ. Chronicling America Salt Lake Herald, July 27, 1877, p. 3. “Arrest of Gen. Burton.” Burton’s arrest on July 26, on a warrant sworn by the foreman of the grand jury. Utah Digital Newspapers New York Herald, August 9, 1877, p. 2. “Murder Territory. Awful Revelations Made to the Utah Grand Jury.” A Salt Lake City letter of July 31 on the indictment of Burton and Dr. Jeter Clinton, naming the witness S. D. Sirrine. From the Sun the story passed to about twenty papers, most of them Kansas weeklies. Newspapers.com subscription Madisonian (Virginia City, MT), November 24, 1877. A Curious Person Who Wishes to See the Rev. Dr. Tyng.” Davies’s missionary S. W. Wood, on his way to England with a proclamation “that the Messiah had come,” tells the Sun that Davies learned in Montana in 1866 that he was the Standard of Israel and then the Comforter; that the society near Walla Walla is called by some the “Redemptionists,” has a tabernacle, a meeting house and a press, and has “no marrying”; and that the Messiah, “the Father’s Son,” was born in 1868 and is ten years old. The Rev. Stephen H. Tyng Jr. says he has had documents from the organization. Checked against the page image. Summarized in the Puget Sound Argus, December 12, 1878 (next entry). Argus, Dec. 12, 1878 · Argus, Aug. 28, 1879 · Spokan Times, Sept. 4, 1879 Salt Lake Herald, February 21 – March 6, 1879. “The Burton Trial,” daily reports of Burton’s trial for the murder of Isabella Bowman. The fullest account in the free archives. Former Morrisites testified for the prosecution and gave their homes in 1879. Among them were James Bowman (of Soda Springs since 1863), Mrs. Mary Anderson (of Soda Springs), Caroline Eliason, Mrs. Emma Just (of the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho), Jacob Johnson, Thomas Williams (of Ogden since 1865), Philip Hewitt (Salt Lake City) and a man from Hyrum whose name the scan garbles. Men of the posse also took the stand, among them Christopher Sproat, William H. Hunt and Dan Camomile. The defense called Thomas Abbott of Farmington, Robert W. Burton of Kaysville, John C. Thompson of Riverdale and Burton himself. Abraham Taylor, one of the seven convicted in 1863, testified near the close (reported March 4). The Ogden Junction of February 22 names another prosecution witness, Joseph Warner, born in Germany, who told the court of a vision of Joseph Smith at Providence that had got him cut off from the Latter-day Saint church, read a sermon of his own and recited a revelation. The text of these scans is poor, and the names are as read from it. 1880–1900 and the 1891 letters Thirty years on, the Salt Lake Tribune printed ten Sunday letters signed “The Elder,” under the running title “Charity for the Mormons” (May 31 to August 2, 1891). Three of them retold the Morrisite story from the inside. John R. Eardley wrote that the letters were John Parson’s, but they never name their writer and speak of Parson in the third person. They are partisan, written nearly thirty years after the events, and their numbers and quoted speech should be checked against the court records: the ninth letter’s list of the seven men convicted in 1863, and of their sentences, does not agree with the court report (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Daily Intelligencer (Seattle), March 4, 1880, p. 3, reprinting the Walla Walla Watchman. The death of William W. Davies’s elder son, “no other than the Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called,” the earliest use of the name yet found. Washington Digital Newspapers Walla Walla Statesman, January 1, 1881, p. 2, “The Trinity”; February 5, 1881, pp. 3–4, “A Fiery Furnace Fraud” and “A Tedious Trial.” Testimony against William W. Davies before Judge W. G. Langford, referee, in the claims of former members: George Lee, D. V. Lambert and Peter C. Klemgard (see the case file under Repositories). Jan. 1, 1881 · Feb. 5, 1881, p. 3 · p. 4 Salt Lake Democrat, November 24, 1885, p. 2. “Their Destiny.” An anecdote about an elderly man, once a Morrisite in Utah, meeting an old friend. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Herald, January 27, 1889, p. 7. “In Undimmed Glory,” with a letter from Boise headed “Morrisite Bugaboo.” The Herald’s Boise correspondent on the Morrisite affair being raised in Idaho’s territorial legislature. Utah Digital Newspapers Davis County Clipper, November 2, 1893, p. 1. “Farmington Fractions” (county court notes). The county had buried “the late Joseph Warner,” the Morrisite of South Weber, and sold his effects, “except some manuscript,” which its agent was told to dispose of if he could. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Herald, July 1, 1894, p. 14. “How to Spend Summer.” A resort piece on Soda Springs that recalls the Morrisites settled there by Connor. Utah Digital Newspapers New North-West (Deer Lodge), April 16, 1880, p. 3. “Distressing Accident. A Little Girl Burned to Death.” The original report of the death of the five-year-old daughter of Andrew Hendrickson, later president of the Montana Morrisites. The accident happened on the evening of Thursday, April 8, at the farm a few miles from Deer Lodge; the child lived twelve hours, and after a funeral on Saturday she was buried “in the silent village on the hill.” Her name is not given. Reprinted in the Helena Daily Independent, April 18, 1880, p. 3. See Andrew Hendrikson. Newspapers.com Helena Weekly Herald, April 22, 1880, p. 7. “A Little Girl Burned to Death.” Reprints the New North-West’s account of the death of the five-year-old daughter of Andrew Hendrickson, later president of the Montana Morrisites, at the family’s farm a few miles from Deer Lodge: her clothes caught fire from burning rubbish in the yard, and she lived twelve hours. A county obituary index gives the death as April 15, 1880, aged 5, and the child is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge, as Maggie Hendrickson (1875–1880). In England George Williams heard of it within weeks: on June 21, 1880, he wrote to William James of the “general mourning & sorrow” the news had cast and sent his sympathy to the Hendricksons (Church History Library, MS 31876). Chronicling America New North-West, April 13, 1883, p. 2. On the RLDS conference at Kirtland, taking that church to be of the same faith as the Morrisites; the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River are “largely composed of them,” and the editor praises them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding. Chronicling America New North-West, July 11, 1884, p. 3. “Reorganized Latter-day Saints.” Notice of W. W. Blair’s RLDS preaching at the Deer Lodge courthouse; the church, “like that of the Josephites and Morrisites,” is distinct from Brigham Young’s and opposed to polygamy. It names the church’s Montana congregations: at Rees Creek near Bozeman, at Willow Creek near Gallatin City, and “near Stuart, in upper Deer Lodge valley.” The Reese Creek branch in Gallatin County was the first in Montana, founded in 1868 by the missionary Joseph W. Morgan, who baptized John E. Reese there (Don Cornelius, “Mormonism in Montana, 1847–1898,” M.A. thesis, 1962, p. 56). Chronicling America New North-West, October 30, 1885, p. 3. “The preachers from California, to speak at the court house next Sunday afternoon, are Morrisites”: almost certainly James and George Dove, who visited the Morrisites at Deer Lodge, Race Track, Willow Glen and Anaconda that October and November (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 182, 207). “There are a large number of Morrisites in this valley.” Chronicling America New North-West, November 13, 1885, p. 3. “Notice. To all Whom It May Concern.” The Montana church disowns the Doves: two men “calling themselves ‘Doves,’” claiming to be Morrisites, are warned against as “pretenders” by the leaders of the church organized in the county “under the name of the ‘Church of the Saints of the Most High,’” who “utterly repudiate their claims, teachings and practices.” Signed William M. James, Andrew Hendrickson and John R. Eardley. The council had ordered the notice at its meeting of November 10 (Church History Library, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 25–27). Chronicling America New North-West, September 3, 1886, p. 3. Also February 19 and March 26, 1886, p. 3. “A Mormon Church, of the Morrisite branch, we are informed, is being constructed under the superintendence of Elder Clapp on the Cottonwood road about a half mile east of town.” An Elder J. C. Clapp had preached at the Deer Lodge court house in February and March 1886, once on the “Origin of the American Indians,” a Book of Mormon theme. The Morrisites’ own minutes settle the que

LatterDayTruth.org Salt Lake Herald (semi-weekly), Friday, March 11, 1904. “On Trial for His Reason.” Also Salt Lake Telegram, March 9, 1904, “Alleged to Be Insane.” William Jones of Blaine, Davis County, in his eightieth year, called the man “who caused the Morrisite War,” faces his daughters’ petition for a guardian (Second District Court, probate division, sitting at Ogden); the report recalls that he was held prisoner by the Morrisites, escaped and came back with the militia, and was a witness for the defense at Burton’s trial. The Telegram (p. 10) and the daily Herald (p. 1) carry the same report on March 9, 1904; the Telegram and gives his age as 80, which fits William J. Jones of the roll, born in 1825. The Herald clipping shows only “Friday, Mar[ch]” and the dateline “Ogden, March 8”; its date is the next Friday. Herald clipping at South Weber City. Henry Beal, mayor of Ephraim and president of the Snow Academy, married Mary Thorpe, Joseph Morris’s first wife, in July 1854, and had eight children with her (the count probably includes Morris’s daughter Ann Eliza, whom they raised). See the Chronology, March–April 1854. Salt Lake Tribune, February 18, 1907, p. 2. “Helped Establish Fort Douglas.” Interview with Presto Burrell, a sergeant in Connor’s command. He recalls the Morrisite men in the penitentiary in the winter of 1862–63 and their pardon, and says his company escorted the Morrisite colony to Soda Springs in the spring of 1863. He later took up a ranch on the Blackfoot River. Utah Digital Newspapers Salt Lake Tribune, November 13, 1907, p. 4. “Gen. Christofferson Dies at Farm Home”. Obituaries of Anders (Andrew) Christoffersen, on the 1861–62 roll as Andrus Christofferson, who died at his ranch north of Deer Lodge on October 20, aged 80. The Post gives his emigration in 1857, Burlington, Iowa, Utah in 1859 and Soda Springs, then Alder Gulch, Jefferson Island, Holt County, Missouri, and the Caribou district before he settled near Deer Lodge; a member of the Reorganized Church. t: The end of the Montana church, 1954–1962
s: The end of the Montana church, 1954–1962 The Deer Lodge Silver State Post records the last Morrisite minister’s death and, within a few years, speaks of the church in the past tense. See How and when did the Montana church end? Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), January 15, 1954, p. 2. A feature on George Johnson, then 97. Johnson’s own story as the paper told it: born near Copenhagen in 1856, he came to Council Bluffs at fifteen, became a Morrisite minister, crossed to Montana by wagon train with Andrew Hendrickson, reaching it “early in 1874,” and preached in family homes as Hendrickson’s assistant before he was ordained and the two led in building the church. His obituary and a 1956 article give 1873 for the journey. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), May 7, 1954, p. 7. “George Johnson Sr’s Last Rites Sunday, Burial in Hillcrest.” Johnson died on the morning of Thursday, April 29, 1954, at ninety-eight. An Episcopal priest conducted the funeral, quoting the words Johnson had used at funerals “as a minister of the Morrisite faith,” and he was buried in Hillcrest cemetery beside his wife, who died in 1907. The paper calls the Morrisite church “almost extinct these days.” Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), August 10, 1956, p. 7. An article on Johnson’s surrey and buggy, recalling him as a Morrisite minister who with Andrew Hendrickson built the little white church west of U.S. Highway 10. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), March 28, 1958, p. 12. Obituary of Mary Ann Goldie (1873–1958), daughter of Andrew Hendrickson. It describes the Hendricksons as members of the Morrisite denomination “known as the House of the Lord Church, which is no longer active here.” Newspapers.com subscription Also reported in Montana Standard (Butte), March 26, 1958, p. 7. “Mary Ann Goldie Called by Death.” The same obituary, two days earlier. Newspapers.com subscription Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), July 27, 1962, p. 7. “Early Day Records Sought By Valley Historical Society.” At the new Deer Lodge Valley Historical Society’s organizing meeting, interest focused on “the Morrisite church which was located at one time” in the south valley. Recent retellings, 1951 to the present Standard-Examiner (Ogden), June 12, 1955, p. 32. Howard S. Benedict (Associated Press), the Morrisite War, fourth in a series on tales of early Utah. A retelling of the siege, with photographs: the crossroads that marked the center of the fort, the place of one of the posse’s guns, and Vern Peek, son of Alford Peek of South Weber, holding the ten-pound shot that had come down from his great-great-grandmother, in whose lap it landed (see Kington Fort). UDN Sun Chronicle (Roy), June 7, 1956, p. 5. Bessie Bambrough, “Story of the Morrisite War,” series three, in the Hooper News column. A local retelling of the siege. The first cannon ball, it says, landed in the lap of William J. Jones’s mother, and the ball was kept by the family (see Kington Fort). UDN Sun Chronicle (Roy), July 5, 1956, p. 3. Hooper News column, sketches of South Weber settlers. Short lives of early settlers, among them William J. Jones (born in South Wales in 1825, a Morrisite from April 1861 who tried to leave and was held in a log cabin at the fort), William Parsons Jones of the militia, John Firth and John Bowman. UDN Pleasant Grove Review, January 30, 1958, p. 4. “Karl Banks Speaks to Mothers Study Club January 22.” Karl Banks of Pleasant Grove, grandson of John Banks, on Banks and Morris. He gave the talk again to other groups (the “Mormon Forum” at Gordon Howard’s home in Bountiful, with Juanita Brooks, Review, June 29, 1961; a DUP camp, April 20, 1972), and in 1968 read a manuscript of his on the siege to a Utah history study group at his home (Review, October 31, 1968). Its retelling has errors of date. UDN Salt Lake Tribune, March 3, 1974, p. 68. Review of Agnes Just Reid, Letters of Long Ago (Tanner Trust edition). Notes that Emma Thompson Just’s parents joined Morris, that as a girl she saw Morris shot, and that seventeen years later she testified against Burton. UDN Standard-Examiner (Ogden), May 30, 1974, p. 17. On Mark Stuart’s collection of Uintah artifacts. A student collector’s finds from the South Ogden–Uintah area include a cannonball from the Morrisite War. The article calls the leader “Samuel” Morris. UDN Ogden Standard-Examiner, June 29, 1975, p. 22B. “Morrisite War Touche[d] …” (headline only partly read). An anniversary retelling. Newspapers.com subscription Davis County Clipper, October 22, 1976, p. 34. “Historians Honor Dr. Howard.” Gordon M. Howard of Bountiful receives the Utah State Historical Society’s Dale L. Morgan award for “Men, Motives and Misunderstandings,” his 1976 Utah Historical Quarterly article on the war. He illustrated it with his photograph of the cannon at the DUP monument in Farmington as a Nauvoo Legion gun used in 1862 (but see 1989 below). UDN Standard-Examiner (Ogden), May 9, 1979, p. 75. Debbie Boothe, on the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery. Says Joseph Werner lay in an unmarked pauper’s grave. UDN Davis News Journal, April 3, 1980, p. 9. Doneta Gatherum, South Weber column. After the war the fort’s land was taken up by neighbors: a school on the southwest, John Firth on the northeast, John Bowman’s rock house (1875) on the southeast, Parley Prophet on the northwest, and the center (about 475 East 6650 South) a town square and ball field. Its dates for the siege are wrong. UDN Davis News Journal, May 29, 1980, p. 15. Doneta Gatherum, on the Parley Prophet home. Parley Prophet’s first log house stood just west of the old Morrisite fort; his grandson Glen Ray recalls the fort area as the town park, with home plate near the house’s east windows, which had to be shuttered. UDN Davis News Journal, October 16, 1980, p. 25. Doneta Gatherum, “South Weber School.” The South Weber schoolhouses of 1859 (adobe), the second and the 1888 frame school stood just inside the old fort, about 440 East 6650 South; with Glen Ray’s and Leonard Bowman’s recollections and a drawing of the 1888 school by Charles Lunn. UDN Salt Lake Tribune, February 26, 1981, pp. D-1–D-2. “‘Morrisite War’ Disappears in H[istory] …” (headline only partly read). Local memory of the siege at South Weber, with the foundation of the fort’s schoolhouse on Brent Winchester’s land and the recollections of Mattie Ray. South Weber City holds a clipping. Newspapers.com subscription Davis News Journal, June 3, 1981, p. 17. On Mr. Craig of Layton. Craig still owned a cannonball from the Morrisite War that his grandfather Harris had found while farming in the hills where Hill Air Force Base’s main runway now is. UDN Daily Herald (Provo), July 19, 1981, p. 50. Theron H. Luke, “Prime Time” column. On Connor’s escort of the Morrisites to Soda Springs and Morristown; counts at least six Morrisites killed, four of them women, and two militiamen; describes the Anderson monument in the Soda Springs cemetery. Luke also spoke and taught on the war from the 1950s to the 1970s. UDN Missoulian, May 8, 1982, p. A-8. Bryan Di Salvatore, “Morrisite Saga Transcends Its Subject.” Review of C. LeRoy Anderson’s For Christ Will Come Tomorrow. Newspapers.com subscription Herald Journal (Logan), April 19, 1982, p. 17. On B. F. White and Oneida County politics. Notes significant numbers of Morrisite and RLDS dissenters at Malad and Soda Springs, and White’s balanced county slate of “Gentiles, Josephites, Apostates and Mormons.” UDN Davis News Journal, May 27, 1982, p. 24. Doneta Gatherum, South Weber column, on the pioneer graves. Also in the Kaysville Weekly Reflex, same date. Werner is buried in the Pioneer Cemetery, among 68 burials; the first was Robert Cook, who died October 14, 1859. UDN Montana Standard (Butte), June 19, 1982, p. 5. “Deer Lodge Once Thought to Be Site of Second Coming.” With photographs, including the church. Brought to this guide’s attention by Kris Pozega, a great-great-niece of George Johnson. Not yet read for this guide. Salt Lake Tribune, April 28, 1983, p. 75. On Leonard Bowman and South Weber. Bowman says he learned about 1981 where Werner was buried and had a marker made for him,

Searching the newspapers The word “Morrisite” finds only part of the story. The Salt Lake papers of 1862 never use it. To find their reports, search a narrow range of dates for names and places: Morris, Kinney, Burton, Weber, Kington. Newspapers.com treats “Morrisite” and “Morrisites” as the same word, even in quotation marks. A search for either finds about 4,300 pages. Nearly a third of them come from 1871–1900, and more than half from after 1900. Many of the hits are about something else. In the 1850s, Illinois papers called the followers of a politician named Morris “Morrisites”; in 1920 a New Orleans baseball team had the same name. Common surnames (Morris, Fuller) bring in letter lists and war news. In Salt Lake papers of 1905–06, “Morrisites” are the supporters of Mayor Richard P. Morris. In 1908–19 they are the followers of Newfoundland’s premier, Edward Morris; from the 1880s on, papers in Morris, Illinois, Oklahoma and Minnesota use the word for their own townspeople. Adding Mormon, Utah or Brigham to a search screens out most of these. Utah Digital Newspapers has about fifty more pages from 1927 to 2024 that mention the Morrisites, mostly anniversary pieces and local history; they are not yet listed here. See them on Utah Digital Newspapers. Most reports from 1862, 1867 and 1877 are reprints. Find the earliest printing and note where later texts differ. The Deer Lodge New North-West (1869–97) is free on Chronicling America; a search for “morrisite” in it finds the seven pages listed here. Free sources for the West: Utah Digital Newspapers (the Deseret News, Salt Lake Herald, Tribune and others), Chronicling America, the California Digital Newspaper Collection, and, for Australia and New Zealand, Trove and Papers Past.

Short government records are transcribed here; the transcriptions are the editor’s, and corrections are welcome. Page images belong to their repositories, and some need a free account. Printed by the Morrisites The Spirit Prevails (1886) Joseph Morris What it is The revelations, articles and letters of Joseph Morris, printed in San Francisco by George S. Dove and Company. The fullest source for Morris’s teaching and for the community at Kington Fort. The manuscripts The book’s preface, “Concerning the Revelations,” says the revelations were read to the congregation and then kept in a locked chest. Right after Morris was shot, Hannah Banks and other women took it from the office and buried it after dark in the bowery where he had preached; three days later his widow took it. After her death her father sold it to Abraham Taylor, who kept it for more than twenty years and willed it to his son, Joseph Taylor of San Francisco (The Spirit Prevails, p. 3). J. H. Beadle wrote in 1870 that Morris “employed two scribes to take down his revealed gospel,” and that his followers then had “six volumes of them, each containing two or three hundred manuscript pages” (Life in Utah, p. 415); Stenhouse, in 1873, has “three English and three Danish clerks” at work daily writing them down (The Rocky Mountain Saints, p. 594). The account implies, without saying so, that Joseph Taylor’s chest supplied the text Dove printed in San Francisco: James Dove wrote that the brethren in Montana had George S. Dove pledge to publish the revelations “in their crude state,” and that the work took about seven months “as the revelations were in a very disordered condition” (A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, 1892, pp. 10–11, as quoted in Anderson, Revisited, p. 183), while the preface says only that a few brethren had kept copies. Other manuscript copies survive (see Repositories), so Dove may also have used them. Where the manuscripts went after 1886 is not known; for revelation manuscripts now in the Church History Library, see Repositories. Read it Internet Archive Roll of Membership (1886) Geo. S. Dove & Co. What it is Eight pages listing the people baptized at South Weber in 1861–62, printed in San Francisco in May 1886. Read it Transcribed on this site, with notes and links to FamilySearch Family Tree. Copy: Utah State Historical Society, PAM 9569c1.

A Voice from the West (1879) George S. and James Dove What it is A Voice from the West to the Scattered People of Weber and All the Seed of Abraham (San Francisco, February 1879; printed by Jos. A. Dove), 40 and [2] pages, signed by George S. Dove and James Dove, with Elizabeth Hughes as scribe. It calls itself “the first publication that has been issued pertaining to the principles … revealed to Joseph Morris in Weber” (p. 40). Its first chapter is the earliest printing of the “History of Events” that opens The Spirit Prevails (1886), in nearly the same words; the rest is the Doves’ own: the claimants after Morris, the founding of their Church of the Firstborn in San Francisco in 1876, and chapters on the priesthood, salvation and reincarnation, with a hymn by Joseph Taylor. Read it Digitized by the Church History Library (M294.7 D743v 1879; rights statement “No Known Copyright”): catalog record and page images. Read for this guide in November 2026. New Gems of Inspiration (1899) John R. Eardley What it is A collection by a former Morrisite of sayings and accounts from the movement, including Eardley’s history of Kington Fort and the surrender. Read it Internet Archive The Voice of the Seventh Angel! (1887–92) James Brighouse What it is Tracts of James Brighouse, whose title echoes Morris’s claim to be the Seventh Angel. Kirk Watson finds the two used the phrase differently, Brighouse drawing it from Revelation 11, and has found no other link between them. He also notes that the title was already in Latter-day Saint use, from Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 (“Michael, the seventh angel”) and W. W. Phelps’s 1844 funeral sermon for Joseph Smith, which alludes to Smith as the seventh angel of Revelation 16 (see the chronology under 1884). Read it HathiTrust · Google Books Not yet online Wanted Pamphlets Articles of Faith (San Francisco, 1887). A library or family that holds a copy could make it available to everyone; the editor will help arrange scanning and an Internet Archive copy.

t: Written by a Morrisite: Mark H. Forscutt
s: Written by a Morrisite: Mark H. Forscutt

“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” probably 1884–85 Mark H. Forscutt · CHL MS 702 Original Church History Library, Salt Lake City, MS 702. Manuscript, 54 leaves, in Forscutt’s hand. The Historian’s Office bought it from Forscutt in June 1902 and had it bound in 1903 (office label on the manuscript). Not digitized; the catalog offers it on request and on microfilm. Catalog record Copy Morrisite collection, Utah State University, USU CAINE COLL MSS 10, box 3, folder 1 Date Undated, but very probably written between September 1884 and the spring of 1885, for a book on Mormonism by the journalist Kate Field. Forscutt’s journal records that Joseph Smith III passed on her request for “an account of the Morrisite Schism” in September 1884; that on November 24 he “spent day preparing chapter (for Miss Field’s book) on ‘the Morrisites’”; and that in February and March 1885 he was “writing on Morrisite History,” once staying up all night at it (Forscutt, journals, September 23 and November 24, 1884, February 20–21 and March 23, 1885, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Smith’s side survives too: answering Field’s letter of August 27, he wrote on September 1, 1884, that Forscutt had passed through the week before and was then at Pittsfield, Illinois, and “I will write him what you state about his writing a sketch of the Morrisite persecution of himself” (Joseph Smith III Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, p. 123, Community of Christ Library Archives). The Sketch fits: it calls John Taylor (church president 1880–87) “the present head of the Utah Church,” and its text is broken into chapters “if desired.” Contents An insider’s history of the movement: the setting in Utah after Joseph Smith’s death, Morris’s call and claims, the organization of the church in April 1861, its theology and revelations, its relations with the Reorganized Church, the mounting conflict with the territorial authorities, and the opening of the siege of Kington Fort on June 13, 1862, which Forscutt witnessed. The manuscript breaks off at the foot of p. 54, just after the first cannon shot. On the last leaf Forscutt calls the Sketch “the basic material of an unfinished and therefore an unpublished work.” He writes that a committee in Salt Lake City had offered $10,000 for a completed history, of which forty-six chapters were written, and that he burned it before three witnesses. He adds that he would now leave out much of what the Sketch says, preferring to heal old wounds rather than reopen them. The Sketch copies Morris’s letter to George Leslie of July 9, 1861 (MS pp. 12–17), but leaves out its opening, which names Joseph Astel as the go-between, and its close, and adds remarks of Forscutt’s own; the letter is printed in full in The Spirit Prevails, pp. 670–74. Later use Forscutt’s daughter, Ruby Celeste (Forscutt) Faunce, published excerpts from his diaries, with her own commentary, as “Biography of Mark Hill Forscutt” in fifteen weekly installments of the Saints’ Herald, January 16 to May 1, 1934 (see Bibliography). The serial follows the Sketch closely: Morris’s letter to George Leslie, the Herald episode, the causes of the conflict, the training day and the siege. But she quotes Forscutt in the first person (“came into my hands … handed me a revelation”), so she seems to have worked from a first-person text other than MS 702, perhaps the diaries themselves or another draft. Her version of the revelation reads “declared to be a prophet of God and rightful heir” (Saints’ Herald 81, January 30, 1934, p. 143). Edition A documentary edition by the editor is in preparation; the text is not reproduced here. Short passages are quoted and cited elsewhere in this guide. About Forscutt Forscutt (1834–1903) was clerk of the Morrisite First Council and an apostle in Morris’s church, and later a minister in the Reorganized Church. Eric Paul Rogers, “Mark Hill Forscutt: Mormon Missionary, Morrisite Apostle, RLDS Minister,” John Whitmer Historical Association Journal 21 (2001): 69–100. Author’s copy (Zenodo)

t: Partial history of the Morrisite church, ca. 1862
s: Partial history of the Morrisite church, ca. 1862 Mark H. Forscutt · U of U MS 0261 Held by J. Willard Marriott Library Special Collections, University of Utah (photostat copy, 1 folder) Contents The finding aid dates it “circa 1862” and calls it a partial history, but gives no page count and does not say where the original is, and no copy is online. It may not be a separate work. A SNAC record describes a 54-page photocopy of Forscutt’s history that ends with his note on the larger work he burned, which matches the “Sketch” (CHL MS 702, 54 leaves, with that note on the last leaf); the repository of that photocopy is not given (SNAC resource 6731221). So MS 0261 may be a photostat of the Sketch rather than an earlier draft or a surviving part of the forty-six-chapter history. Not yet checked against the photostat. Access Finding aid

Government records Order calling out the posse, June 11, 1862 Utah State Archives, series 2210 What it is Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order to Gen. Daniel H. Wells to furnish the marshal a military force to arrest Joseph Morris. The original has not been found; this copy is in a letter from Nauvoo Legion headquarters of January 14, 1871 (document 1,215), which copies it among “communications … from predecessors of Governor Shaffer.” Text Executive Department Great Salt Lake City June 11th 1862 To Genl D H Wells Commanding Militia of Utah Territory: Sir— A requisition has been made upon me this day, by Henry W. Lawrence, Esqr.— Territorial Marshall for the Territory of Utah, through his deputies, R. T. Burton, Esqr. and Theodore McKean Esqr. for a military force to act as a posse comitatus in the service of certain writs issued from the Third Judicial District Court of said Territory, for the arrest of Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis County, in said district. It appears that said Joseph Morris and his associates have organized themselves into an armed force to resist the execution of said writs, and are setting at defiance the law and its officers. I therefore require you to furnish the said Henry W. Lawrence Esqr. or his Deputies aforesaid a sufficient military force for the arrest of the offenders, the vindication of justice and the enforcement of law. Frank Fuller Acting Governor and Commander-in-Chief. Newspapers “Fatal Resistance to the Laws,” June 18, 1862 Deseret News, p. 404 What it is The Salt Lake paper’s first account of the siege, written the day after the prisoners reached the city. It traces the writs from Enoch M. King’s complaint of May 22, served on the 24th by J. L. Stoddard, to the affidavits of H. O. Hanson and Philo Allen on June 10, and names Morris, Cook, Banks, Klemgaard and John Parsons as the men the writs were against. It reports two young men of the posse killed, “Smith and Wahler” (see Questions), and Cook, Parsons, Klemgaard and some ninety others brought in as prisoners on June 17. Read it Utah Digital Newspapers (search the Deseret News for June 18, 1862)

“The Davis County Bandits,” June 25, 1862 Deseret News, p. 412 What it is The result of the hearing before Judge Kinney in chambers, June 18–19, 1862. Richard Cook was fined fifty dollars and jailed thirty days for contempt and held to bail; Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson were remanded to prison; the other ninety-five men were held to bail of $1,500 each for the March 1863 term of the Third District Court, and stood surety for one another. It is the only list found so far of the men taken at Kington Fort, and a check on the roll: 78 of the 95 match a man on the roll, 8 more probably do, and 9 are not on it (marked * below). On the roll Every man on this list who matches a name on the 1861–62 roll of membership is tagged 1862 prisoner there: the 78 held to bail, with Richard Cook, Peter Klemgaard and Christian Neilson. Hover over or tap a tag to see the name as the paper printed it and what happened to him. The 8 uncertain matches are not tagged. The men not on the roll are an open question (see Questions); for the trials of March 1863, see the next entry.
