“Third District Territorial Court,” April 1, 1863 Deseret News, p. 4 What it is The court’s own report of the March 1863 term at Salt Lake City, Chief Justice Kinney presiding, in which the Morrisites taken at Kington Fort were tried. It names the seven convicted of murder, whom the Morrisites’ own histories name differently, and the eighty-five men tried for resisting an officer. Earlier in the term The weekly reports before the verdict fill in the term. On March 9 Kinney charged the grand jury on “the unfortunate circumstance which transpired in Davis county last summer,” an armed resistance to the court’s writs “by a company of men at the head of which was one Joseph Morris,” and read them the affidavits on which the writs had issued (Deseret News, March 11, 1863, p. 5). On March 13 the names of those bound over for resisting process “last June, at South Weber” were called, and twenty were absent and their recognizances forfeited: Peter L. McCue, James Richardson, Josiah D. Price, John A. Merrick, Peter McCue jr., David Park, William F. Rogers, Wm. Hill, John Eames, Wm. Chamberlain, John Winn (“reported dead”), Hugh Davies, James Laird, Hugh Park, John Petrie, Peter Moffat, Alexander Richardson, James Dove, George Dove, Andres Anderson and Wm. Adams (Deseret News, March 18, 1863, p. 8). On March 19 the grand jury indicted ten for murder, Peter Klimgard, Christian Neilsen, Richard Cook, John Parsons, Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jans Christiansen, Andrew Lee, Andrew M. Mason and John E. Jones, and Peter L. McCue “and some ninety others” for resisting process. On March 23 the defendants pleaded not guilty, and their counsel, Charles J. Schultz and Appleby, moved to quash the indictments on the ground that the grand jury had not been lawfully chosen; Kinney overruled the motion as coming too late. The resisting-process case was tried first. Robert T. Burton, Judson L. Stoddard, Lot Smith, Robert Burton of Kaysville, Jeter Clinton, William Jones, John Jensen, James Hales, Andrew Cunningham and John Sorenson testified for the prosecution, and John Smith and Mark Forscutt for the defence (Deseret News, March 25, 1863, p. 5). The pardon On April 1 the paper printed Harding’s pardon of the seven “letter for letter,” received as it went to press, under the heading “A Contemptible Document”: the men had been released from the territorial prison that evening, and the editors called it a “flagrant outrage” and deferred comment “till our anger shall have abated” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863, p. 5). A week later it attacked the pardons of men found guilty “upon one of the most impartial trials ever witnessed” (“Executive Enormities,” Deseret News, April 8, 1863, p. 4). The murder trial In People v. Peter Klemgard and others, for the deaths of the two posse men, the prosecutor entered a nolle prosequi for Richard Cook. Robert T. Burton, Judson L. Stoddart, Theodore McKean, David J. Ross and James Hales testified for the prosecution; Margaret Cook, Jens Christian Sorensen, Mrs. Dove, James Bowman, Joseph Marsh, James Mather, Mrs. Banks, David Thomas, Mrs. Gray, John O. Mather, Mrs. Garrett, Philip Hewit, Peter Swenson and Lebrecht Bar for the defence. On Friday, March 27, the jury found Peter Klemgard, Christian Neilsen, Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason guilty of murder in the second degree, and John Parsons and John E. Jones not guilty. The sentences were fifteen years at hard labor for Klemgard, twelve for Neilsen and ten for each of the others. On Saturday Richard Cook, John Parsons and John E. Jones pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and were fined $100 each, and Cook’s $50 fine for contempt in June 1862 was remitted. Two lists of the seven The Spirit Prevails (p. 7) and Eardley’s Gems (p. 31) name the seven as Peter C. Klemgard, John Nielson, Abraham Taylor, George Lee, Christian Nelsen, Jens Christiansen and John E. Jones. The court report agrees on four, but has Kadrup Neilsen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason where they have John Nielson, George Lee and John E. Jones, and it records John E. Jones as acquitted. The report was printed within days of the verdict, and its sentences (fifteen, twelve and five of ten years) agree with Stenhouse; the Morrisite accounts were written decades later. Resisting an officer On Thursday, March 26, in the case of Peter L. McCue and others, the jury found the defendants guilty of resisting an officer and fined each $100. Chief Justice Kinney told them the court had been disposed to look with mercy on men who had acted under the direction of leaders they trusted. Of the eighty-five names called, sixty-eight match a man on the 1861–62 roll, nine more probably do, and eight are not on it (marked * below). The court found several defendants absent, so not all need have been fined; Stenhouse and Bancroft give sixty-six fined. Names called, March 26 Peter L. The Soldiers of Israel, May 16, 1862 The Contributor 11, no. 8, pp. 283–84 What it is The roster of the Morrisites’ armed companies, as printed by Richard W. Young, “The Morrisite War,” The Contributor 11, no. 8 (June 1890): 283–84, with the soldiers’ oath. Young does not say where he found it; it was presumably among the papers taken at the fort or used at the 1863 trial, and the original has not been seen for this guide. “On the sixteenth of May, the First Division of the Soldiers of Israel was formed. Joseph Morris was Captain at Arms; John Fred. Klingbeck was Lieutenant at Arms, and John Nielson, Andrew Lee, John E. Jones, Christian Nielsen, Andrew M. Mason, Niels Peterson and P. C. Klemgaard were named as the seven captains of companies. The companies contained twelve men each.” Each man swore “that I will both faithfully abide the Law of God, and defend it unto death at the peril of my life … and that, as a soldier, I will obey my commander.” Young counts “one hundred and forty-two men enrolled in the army,” besides others not enrolled. The names have been checked against the page images and are spelled as printed; the third company of the First Division is misprinted “No. 2.” No. 7 Company is made up of the apostles, Mark H. Forscutt among them. The Lieutenant at Arms was Johan Frederik Fransen Klingbaek (1815–1885), brother of Jacob Carl Klingbech and probably the roll’s “Solsan F.” Klingbeck; his journal, in Danish, is at the Church History Library (MS 8268). Governor Harding’s pardons, March 31, 1863 Tullidge, History of Salt Lake City, pp. 319–20 What it is The two pardons that Governor Stephen S. Harding signed at Great Salt Lake City on March 31, 1863, countersigned by Secretary Frank Fuller, as printed by Edward W. Tullidge, History of Salt Lake City (Salt Lake City, 1886), pp. 319–20. The originals, in the territorial executive records, have not been seen for this guide. The first pardons the seven convicted of murder in the second degree; the second pardons sixty-nine men “convicted of the charge of resisting an officer in the service of process,” and absolves them from “the fine, costs and charges.” The names below have been checked against the page images and are spelled as printed. Orson F. Whitney gives the same total: Harding “extended executive clemency to the whole seventy-six in two proclamations bearing date of March 31st, 1863” (History of Utah, vol. 2, p. 100). The murder pardon Peter Klemgard, Christen Nielsen, Gens Christensen, Kadrup Nielsen, Abraham Taylor, Andrew Lee, Andrew M. Mason. These are the seven of the court’s own report (see the Deseret News, April 1, 1863), not the seven of the Morrisite histories. The resisting pardon Richard Cook, John Parson, Edward Moss, Daniel Smith, John B. Ledgeway, John O. Mather, James Mather, Richard D. Aloey, Alexander Warrender, William McGhie, Elijah L. Chappel, John E. Jones, John Cook, David Thomas, Peter John Moss, Joseph Taylor, Mathew Mudd, James Bowman, Robert E. Farley, William W. Thomas, Alexander Dow, John Keehorn, John C. Edwards, John Gray, Joseph Dove, Thomas L. Williams, William Davis, Alonzo Brown, Edward Lloyd, Samuel Halse, Elijah Clitford, George Thompson, Goodman Goodmunsen, Charles Higham, John E. Reese, Soren Peter Gould, Jorjen Jensen, Soren Willissen, Lars Christen Hanson, Andres Jensen, Swen Hagg, Soren Peter Rasmussen, Hans Peterson, Peter Peterson, John Peter Sorensen, Neils Larsen, Neils Andersen, Michael Christen Christiansen, Gens Paulsen, Neils Peterson, Lars Christen Larsen, Hans Aggerson, John G. Looselary, Lebrecht Barr, John Neilsen, Nels Rasmussen Beck, Christen Jensen, Peter Swenson, Neils Magnus Jorensen, Rasmus Rasmussen, James Peterson, Lars Olsen, Gens Christian Senensen, Hans Peter Smith, Andres Anderson, Andres Christopherson, Hans Hanson, Ole Rosenblade, Peter Sorenson. Compared with the court report The sixty-nine are the sixty-six fined on March 26, the number Stenhouse and Bancroft give, with Richard Cook, John Parson and John E. Jones, who pleaded guilty on March 28. Six names in the pardon are not among those the Deseret News printed for March 26: John Keehorn, Soren Peter Gould, Jorjen Jensen, Soren Willissen, Peter Swenson and Neils Magnus Jorensen; and the pardon’s George Thompson is probably the paper’s “Geo. Thomas.” Twenty-three men called on March 26 are in neither pardon and were presumably absent: Peter L. McCue and Peter McCue Jr., James Richardson, Josiah D. Price, Richard John Livingston, William White, John A. Merrick, David Park, William F. Rogers, William Hill, John Eames, William Chamberlain, John Winn, John Trehaird, James Laird, William Adams, Hugh Davis, Hugh Park, John Petrie, Peter Moffat, Alexander Richardson, James Dove and George Dove. The grand jury said that sixty-six appeared and were tried, “the others having left the country.” Tullidge prints “Aloey” (the Deseret News has Alvey) and “Clitford” (Clifford). The men on the roll are linked from the Name index. The grand jury’s answer The grand jury of the same term, twenty-three men headed by George A. Smith and Franklin D. Richards, presented Harding to the court “as we would an unsafe bridge over a dangerous stream,” for “turning loose upon the community a large number of convicted criminals” less than three days after the sentences. Its presentment gives the court’s own count: “some ninety or more” indicted for resisting an officer, sixty-six tried, and ten indicted “for the murder of Jared Smith.” Chief Justice Kinney had it entered in the record and left the responsibility “with the Governor, who, in the exercise of a naked power, has seen proper to grant executive clemency” (Tullidge, pp. 320–24). Stenhouse adds that the same grand jury voted Camp Douglas “a nuisance” (T. B. H. Stenhouse, The Rocky Mountain Saints (New York, 1873), p. 605). Read it Internet Archive

The Wells–Shaffer correspondence, October 29, 1870 Deseret Evening News, p. 2 What it is A quarrel over the territorial militia. Governor J. W. Shaffer had banned musters by proclamation on September 15, 1870. When Daniel H. Wells, signing as lieutenant-general of the militia, asked him to suspend the ban, Shaffer refused to recognize the rank and called the militia “an unlawful military system.” Wells answered in a letter to the editor and, to show that earlier governors had recognized him, printed two letters from 1862. The first is Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order for the posse sent to Kington Fort, the earliest printing of it found for this guide. Fuller’s order, June 11, 1862 EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT, Great Salt Lake City, June 11, 1862. TO GEN. D. H. WELLS, Commanding Militia of Utah Territory: Sir:—A requisition has been made upon me this day, by Henry W. Lawrence, Esq., Territorial Marshal for the Territory of Utah, through his Deputies, R. T. Burton, Esq., and Theodore McKean, Esq., for a military force to act as a posse comitatus in the service of certain writs issued from the Third Judicial District Court of said Territory, for the arrest of Joseph Morris and others residing in the northern part of Davis county, in said District. It appears that said Joseph Morris and his associates have organized themselves into an armed force to resist the execution of said writs, and are setting at defiance the law and its officers. I therefore require you to furnish the said Henry W. Lawrence, Esq., or his Deputies aforesaid, a sufficient military force for the arrest of the offenders, the vindication of justice and the enforcement of law. FRANK FULLER, Acting Governor and Commander-in-Chief. The rest of the page Wells’s request of October 25 (signed with H. B. Clawson, adjutant-general), Shaffer’s refusal of October 27, and Wells’s letter to the editor, which also encloses Governor Stephen S. Harding’s letter of November 26, 1862, about arms furnished to the territory since 1861. An editorial in the same issue, “An Extraordinary Letter,” introduces the correspondence. A week later Henry W. Lawrence answered Wells in the Salt Lake Weekly Tribune (November 5, 1870) on who directed the force at Kington Fort; see Newspapers. Transcription Transcribed for this guide from the page image, November 2026; the full text of the correspondence (about 2,700 words) is available on request (Share records). The page is in the public domain. Read it Utah Digital Newspapers (the page image; the text the site provides with it is too garbled to use)

Church records “Niels Anderson matter, 1903” Church History Library, CR 1 191 What it is Letters of Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson to President Joseph F. Smith, January–March 1903, asking help for Mary, wounded at Kington Fort in 1862, with the office’s draft reply and related correspondence. Read it Church History Catalog (24 images)

Joseph Morris’s letters and revelations Church History Library, CR 1234 1 What it is Morris’s letters to Brigham Young and manuscript revelations, 1858–1862, in the folders “Revelations of Joseph Morris” in Brigham Young’s office files. Kirk Watson’s edition, The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026), transcribes twelve of them, from October 11, 1858, to November 26, 1860, in its section “Joseph Morris, Letters to Brigham Young,” and gives the catalog link for each. Watson notes that the revelation headed February 18, [1859], is No. 6 of The Spirit Prevails, dated there September 6, 1860. The letters, by date October 11, 1858 · January 1, 1859 · revelation of January 26, 1859 · revelation of February 18, [1859] · February 24, 1859 · April 21, 1859 · June 15, 1859 · September 1, 1859 · April 20, 1860 · June 24, 1860 · November 21, 1860 · November 26, 1860. Dates as Watson gives them, from the manuscripts; links from his notes. Church History Catalog; a free Church Account may be required. Find more Search the Church History Catalog for CR 1234 1. Two more revelations, of January 14 and 16, 1860, are filed elsewhere in the same papers (see below).

George Morris reminiscences, circa 1867–1886 Church History Library, MS 1614 What it is The reminiscences of Joseph Morris’s elder brother George Morris (1816–1897), written from about 1867 to 1886: his life in England, his conversion and emigration in 1842, Nauvoo, the crossing, and his life in Salt Lake City, with a family genealogy and his own photograph (taken January 1, 1877). The bound manuscript runs to 234 pages in George’s hand (321 images, the rest blank). George was born on August 23, 1816, at Handley, Cheshire, the eldest of six children: George, Mary Ann, William, Joseph, Fanny and Mathew; their mother also had a son by an earlier marriage, James Silverthorn. Brought to this guide’s attention by Kirk Watson, who finds in it valuable evidence of Morris’s personality, theology and life. On Joseph Read for this guide in November 2026. The passages about Joseph are: p. 80, 1853–54. In the running story of George’s own life: Joseph came in the fall of 1853 with a wife and one child and lived with George through the winter; in the spring he went south “to his wifes Brother where she left him,” and he came back alone in the summer of 1854. pp. 115–22, his life and death. Baptism and the gift of tongues, a suspension, a coal-mine burn; marriage to Mary Thorp; St. Louis and a steamboat; a branch presidency at Pittsburgh; arrival in Utah in the fall of 1853; his claim to stand “at the head of his Fathers Famaly”; his marriages to the widow Elizabeth Mills and, at Provo, to “Elize Jones”; a private revelation offering George “the Apostleship”; the gathering, the prisoners, Judge Kinney’s writs and the posse. George gives Joseph’s age at death as “the 38th year of his Age” and names the two posse men killed as “Peter Waldin and Jarad Smith.” He judges Joseph “A Poor weak Deluded Mortall” but rejects stories that he was immoral with women. pp. 178–81 (March 1876). George’s copy of Brigham Young’s note permitting him to do proxy ordinances for Joseph (“it can do you no harm to act for him”); the father’s report that Joseph “Could Speak 7 different Languages in perfection”; Joseph’s piety, poverty and memory; and George’s view that without John Banks, the Cooks and others he “might have Charged around untill today without affecting anything.” pp. 186–87 (September 6, 1876). The proxy ordinances at the Endowment House, among them “Joseph Morris Jr and Mary his wife”; which Mary is not said. pp. 198–99 (February 1879). George attended Burton’s trial and judged that “there was no nesesity to shed one Drop of Blood.” George gives three dates for Joseph’s death (June 15, 22 and 28, 1862); the first is correct. On p. 24 he baptized “one of my Brothers and my Sister” in a river as he left home for Liverpool in February 1842; the brother is not named. George was hostile to Joseph’s claims, and his figures for the gathering (“about eight hundrad,” no crops for two years) are larger than other sources give. Records found since bear out his outline of Joseph’s early life: the 1841 census at Dukinfield (Joseph, fifteen, a coal miner in their father’s household), the 1847 marriage to Mary Thorp at Mottram in Longdendale, and the 1850 census at St. Louis; they differ from him on the year of Joseph’s baptism, which is still unsettled (see the Chronology). t: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860
s: Two revelations to the First Presidency, January 14 and 16, 1860 Church History Library, CR 1234 1 What it is Two manuscript revelations, signed “Jesus Christ” and addressed to “the first presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Later day saints and all so to the twelve apostles.” Both demand that the leaders receive “my servant Joseph.” They are filed as anonymous letters among Brigham Young’s incoming correspondence for 1860, outside the folders of Morris’s revelations, and were identified by Kirk Watson in November 2026, after his edition of Morris’s letters was published, so they are not in it. Why they matter They are among the earliest dated revelations of Morris to survive in manuscript. The Spirit Prevails has only No. 2 (“Winter of 1859”) before them; its No. 3 is dated March 1860. Neither is printed there, but both are early forms of later texts. The January 14 revelation opens “when you whas small in your own eyes i took you and i rose you to the apostle ship,” the same opening as No. 18, “Revelation to President Brigham Young” (October 2, 1860). Like No. 18, it charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door and speaks of “the throne of isreal.” But it is addressed to the Twelve as well as to Young, and its warnings to them, which name Jeroboam, promise “fresh apostles” in their place and threaten to cut them off root and branch, are not in No. 18, which is addressed to Young alone. The January 16 revelation requires anyone with “gould and silver and houses and lands and whives” to “lay them at the feet of my servant Joseph,” the test Morris set out again in No. 185 (December 28, 1861). How they were received The office docket on the January 14 letter reads “Jan 14 1860 / Balderdash / About revelations / Rec Jan 20 1860,” and the same clerk wrote “Balderdash” above the heading of each revelation. The letter is addressed “To president Brigham Young grait Sault Lake City.” The hand Kirk Watson, who has transcribed many of Morris’s writings, identifies the hand and spelling as Morris’s. He compared the January 14 revelation with a revelation “to president young” dated October 11, 1858, catalogued as a “Joseph Morris letter” in the folder “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” of the same office files. The two share the same dating formula (“October the 11 1858,” “January the 14 1860”), the same letter forms and the same phonetic spelling (“speckelating,” “whas”). Read it January 14, 1860 (5 images) · January 16, 1860 (2 images). Church History Catalog; Brigham Young office files, General Correspondence, Incoming, General Letters, A–Bi, 1860, “Anonymous letter.” For comparison, the revelation of October 11, 1858 (9 images; President’s Office Files, General Office Files, “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860”). A free Church Account may be required. Transcription by Kirk Watson: “Missing revelation Joseph Morris to BY 1860” (Google Docs), linked with his permission.

t: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber…
s: MO-IMG-032The slough below the bluffs. Kington Fort stood on the Weber River flood plain, in a bowl ringed on the south and west by sandy bluffs about half a mile off and some two hundred feet high. On June 13, 1862, the posse took its position on the bluffs south of the fort, from which it could see into the fort (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 64, 112, 128). The plan of the fort drawn by G. Q. Jones for the Sons of Utah Pioneers (1996) marks a slough just outside the south gate, and its notes say that on June 15 an armored battery made from the rear of a wagon was rolled toward the fort, caught a wheel in the mud and tipped over, and that its crew retreated under musket fire. Jones does not give his source, and Anderson describes the rolling battery as pushed up to the fort wall (p. 135). A posse member, John G. Chambers, describes it as “of willows placed lengthwise through three hind wheels of a wagon,” brought forward after the posse took a cabin near the entrance, and says the Morrisites’ fear of it hastened the white flag (John G. Chambers, “Siege of Morris fort, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). The editor, from Jones’s plan and the comments of the South Weber historian Ed Cooper on a visit to the site, takes this to be the slough where the battery mired. See the map on the Kington Fort page.South Weber, Utah · before February 2004 (scanned print)

Transcription of the Anderson plaque (MO-IMG-061) NIELS ANDERSON · OCTOBER 3 [?], 1835 – MARCH 4 [?], 1926 MARY CHRISTOFFERSEN ANDERSON · JULY 26, 1847 – JULY 13 [?], 1928 THEY WERE BORN IN DENMARK; JOINED THE MORMONS THERE. IN 1857 MRS. ANDERSON ARRIVED AT BURLINGTON, IOWA; DETAINED THERE UNTIL 1859 ON ACCOUNT OF JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAVING TO BE SENT TO UTAH. THAT YEAR SHE WALKED NEARLY ALL THE WAY TO SALT LAKE CITY. IN 1860 MR. ANDERSON CAME; HE PULLED A HAND-CART FROM FLORENCE, NEBRASKA. THEY SOON SAW THE DECEPTION IN “BRIGHAMISM,” JOINED MORRIS A SECEDER FROM BRIGHAM. MAY 22 [?], 1863, THEY CAME TO SODA SPRINGS WITH THE FIRST SETTLERS; THEY WERE ESCORTED AND PROTECTED BY GEN. CONNOR AND CALIFORNIA VOLUNTEERS. JULY 20, 1863, THEY WERE MARRIED HERE; THEIR MARRIAGE WAS THE FIRST IN IDAHO TERRITORY AS FAR AS THEY KNEW. LATER MR. ANDERSON BECAME “THE FATHER OF THE ANTI-MORMON PARTY” IN IDAHO. AT SOUTH WEBER, UTAH, JUNE 13–15, 1862, MR. AND MRS. ANDERSON WERE IN “THE MORRISITE MASSACRE.” MRS. ANDERSON’S CHIN WAS SHOT AWAY WITH A CANNON BALL, THAT KILLED MRS. BARBARA DE[…]THELM [?] AND MRS. JOSEPH (?) MARSH, FIRED BY GEN. ROBERT T. BURTON’S MORMON MILITIA INTO A BOWERY OF UNARMED “MORRISITES,” JUNE 13, BECAUSE THEY REFUSED TO OBEY “BRIGHAM’S” DECREES, AFTER JOHNSTON’S ARMY HAD LEFT UTAH ON ACCOUNT OF THE CIVIL WAR. MRS. J. L. BEAR AND HER BABY WERE KILLED WITH ANOTHER CANNON BALL. THEN MANY MORRISITES WITH THEIR OLD GUNS TRIED RESISTANCE. ON THE THIRD DAY ALL SURRENDERED UNDER A WHITE FLAG. MRS. ANDERSON SAYS: “WHEN MORRIS CAME BEFORE GEN. BURTON, THE LATTER USED ABUSIVE LANGUAGE AND TRIED TO RIDE OVER MORRIS ON HIS HORSE. THIS ABUSE WAS ON ACCOUNT OF HIS RELIGIOUS TEACHING. I SAW HIM … SHOOT MORRIS.” DOW’S AFFIDAVIT SAYS: BURTON SHOT MORRIS, BANKS, MRS. JAMES BOWMAN AND ANOTHER WOMAN, AFTER THEY SURRENDERED. TEN “MORRISITES” WERE KILLED, AND ONE “MORMON.” THE PRISONERS WERE TO BE TRIED AT THE NEXT TERM OF COURT HELD BY CHIEF JUSTICE KINNEY, A MORMON. IN THE MEANTIME GOV. HARDING, ASSOCIATE JUSTICES WAITE, DRAKE, COL. CONNOR AND VOLUNTEERS ARRIVED. “SEVEN MORRISITES” WERE SENTENCED TO IMPRISONMENT FROM “TEN TO FIFTEEN YEARS.” “SIXTY-SIX” HEAVILY FINED. “WE,” WROTE GOV. HARDING IN 1874, “ATTENDED THROUGH THE TRIAL, WHICH WAS NOTHING BUT A MOCKERY. BURTON ADMITTED HIS SHOOTING THE PRISONERS. … HAD I BEEN ON THE BENCH I SHOULD HAVE HAD HIM ARRESTED … ; BUT IT WOULD HAVE BEEN USELESS. THE JURORS WOULD ALL BE MORMONS, AND RECOGNIZE NO LAW BUT ‘THE COMMANDS OF AUTHORITY.’ “PETITIONS WERE GOTTEN UP FOR THE UNCONDITIONAL PARDON OF THE MORRISITES, WHICH WERE SIGNED BY ALL THE GENTILES, … NOT A MORMON SIGNED THEM. … “I ISSUED THE PARDON; … SOME MOUNTED MORTARS … COMMANDING THE BEE-HIVE HOUSE AND LION HOUSE, MADE THINGS TOLERABLY SMOOTH ON THE SURFACE.” BRIGHAM YOUNG JUNE 15, AS BY H. P. McLANE, SAID, “THAT MORRIS AND BANKS WILL BE TAKEN I HAVE NO DOUBT. … BUT IF I HAD MY OWN WAY ABOUT IT, I WOULD NOT SPARE NEITHER MAN, WOMAN NOR CHILD; BUT AS IT IS A UNITED STATES AFFAIR, THEY CAN HAVE IT AS THEY PLEASE. BUT AS REGARDS THIS YOUNG MAN, HE HAS DIED A MARTYR TO THE CAUSE AND KINGDOM OF OUR GOD. … THIS WAS A MATTER OF NECESSITY. … THE WORST … I [?] DISLIKE … , IS THAT AFTER THEY ARE ROUTED, THE … ACCURSED DEVILS … WILL BE TRYING TO SNEAK BACK INTO THE CHURCH AGAIN. …” R. W. YOUNG WRITING FOR THE “CONTRIBUTOR,” OF 1890, FOR THE MORMON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION SAYS: “THE … ACTION OF THE GOVERNOR WAS FOLLOWED … IN COURSE OF TIME, BY PERSECUTION OF GEN. BURTON. … A GRAND JURY WAS LED IN … 1870, TO BRING IN AN INDICTMENT FOR MURDER … , AND … (HE) THOUGHT HIMSELF COMPELLED BY CIRCUMSTANCES TO EVADE ARREST … LATER, ANOTHER INDICTMENT WAS FOUND AGAINST GEN. BURTON … , HE MADE NO ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE. …” BETWEEN THESE TWO INDICTMENTS A RULING HAD “PROVIDED IN SUBSTANCE FOR JURIES HALF MORMON, AND HALF GENTILE.” THIS YOUNG SAYS, “THE PROSECUTION LABORED LONG, AND,” “CLOUDS OF WITNESSES WERE BROUGHT FORTH,” “TO PERSUADE THE JURY,” “ONE-HALF BEING NON-MORMONS,” THAT BURTON KILLED MRS. BOWMAN. THIS CASE WAS NO. 3109, U.S. VS. BURTON FOR “MURDER 1ST DEGREE,” SET FOR TRIAL 1ST DAY OF FEB. TERM 1879, MARCH 8 — INDICTMENT DISMISSED. THIS WAS ONE OF THE THREE INDICTMENTS AGAINST HIM. IT WAS ASKED: WHAT ABOUT THE CASE FOR KILLING MORRIS? U.S. DISTRICT ATTORNEY VANZILE ANSWERED “WHAT IS THE USE, IF THEY WILL NOT CONVICT FOR KILLING AN INNOCENT WOMAN?” TO FATHER AND MOTHER, AND HISTORIC TO MAN, WE DEDICATE THIS MEMORIAL. ABRAHAM CHRISTOPHER ANDERSON, I[D]A COLLETT, ANNA CHRISTINA ROGERS, DAVID ANDREW ANDERSON, ABELONE LARSEN, PETER WILLIAM ANDERSON, NIELS CHRISTIAN ANDERSON, MARY AMELIA VERHAM. Transcribed by the editor from MO-IMG-061 (October 2018), keeping the plaque’s capitals and punctuation; paragraphs follow its indentations. Ellipses and the “(?)” after “Joseph” are on the plaque. Bracketed readings are the editor’s and are uncertain where the bronze is worn: the dates marked [?], the first victim’s surname (perhaps the Swiss name Diethelm), and Ida Collett’s first name. The plaque is the Anderson children’s account and quotes its sources selectively; compare the trial record and the histories in the Bibliography. Corrections from a clearer reading are welcome. t: At the Copper Village museum: the organ and the Staffanson dolls, November 18, 2026
s: MO-IMG-099Looking out from the ranch toward the Anaconda smelter stack.Deer Lodge County, Montana · July 8, 2013 At the Copper Village museum: the organ and the Staffanson dolls, November 18, 2026 Photographs by the editor at the Copper Village Museum and Art Center, Anaconda, with the museum’s permission; Jim Furshong, a volunteer at the museum, showed them. The organ by local tradition came from the Lord’s House at Racetrack; on its date and history, see Where did the Copper Village organ come from? The two dolls, by the museum’s label, belonged to Myrtle and Evelyn Staffanson; they were donated to the museum by Claudia Eastmark of Anaconda. The sisters were Myrtle D. Staffanson (1898–1977) and Vera Evelyn Staffanson (1912–1989), daughters of Jacob Malvinus Staffanson (1863–1921) and Glendora Gould, who married at Anaconda in 1889, and granddaughters of Peter Staffanson (1823–1913) and Cecilia Nilsson. In 1910 the family was living in the Lost Creek school district, one of the old Morrisite neighborhoods near Anaconda: Jacob, 47; his wife, 35; their children Beulah, Myrtle (11), Ida, Ernest and Clifford; and Peter, 86, listed as grandfather (1910 U.S. census, Lost Creek School District, Deer Lodge County, Montana, sheet 1A, household of Jacob M. Staffanson, NARA T624; FamilySearch). In 1920 Jacob and Glendora were still in the Lost Creek district with Clifford, 10, and Evelyn, 7 (1920 U.S. census, School District 5, Lost Creek, enumeration district 19, Deer Lodge County, Montana, sheet 2A, household of Jacob M. Staffanson, NARA T625; FamilySearch). Peter (the name is also spelled Staffenson) was named to preside over the second quorum of Seventies when the church in Montana was organized in 1872 (see Chronology, 22 Sep 1872), and in 1879 Williams heard that he had a wagon and wished to drive him round when he came (Chronology, 6 Jan 1879). Don Cornelius interviewed Agnes Staffanson about the Montana Morrisites in 1962 (see Bibliography).

MO-IMG-106The museum’s label: the dolls “belonged to the Morrisite children,” and to Myrtle and Evelyn Staffanson. It says the Morrisites came to the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1860s and “disbanded in 1920”; the church’s own records show the Race Track congregation meeting at the Lord’s House until the 1950s (see How and when did the Montana church end?).Anaconda, Montana · November 18, 2026 People and portraits Historical portraits from the editor’s files; their original sources were not recorded. Portraits published in Anderson, Joseph Morris and the Saga of the Morrisites (Revisited) (2010), not reproduced here: Joseph Morris, with a man captioned as his older brother William, dated about 1841, England (p. 118). The only photograph identified as Morris; on its date and identification, see Open questions. A later portrait captioned as Mary Christoffersen Anderson, different from MO-IMG-062 (p. 119). The caption makes her seventeen when she was wounded; the birth date on her gravestone, July 26, 1847, makes her fourteen. George Thompson, with two unidentified women, in a pony cart (p. 120). The caption calls him one of the first to join the Morrisite army and a later successor to George Williams, the Prophet Cainan; Anderson’s text dates his election as president of the church to May 1886. John R. Eardley, George Williams (the Prophet Cainan), and George Thompson, England, about 1873, during a Morrisite mission there under Williams (p. 121). George Johnson and Andrew Hendrikson (spelled Henrikson in the caption), Danish immigrants who led the Montana church (p. 124). The caption’s “from 1866” for Hendrikson’s presidency is a misprint; Anderson’s text gives 1886 to 1921. See Chronology.

Membership

The 1861–62 Roll of Membership The men and women baptized into Joseph Morris’s church at South Weber, Utah Territory, in 1861–62, as printed in San Francisco in 1886. A work in progress. The names are checked against the printed pamphlet (a photocopy, November 2, 2026). FamilySearch links, notes and later paths are added as sources turn up, so the counts below will grow. Last updated November 23, 2026. Know something about someone on the roll? Write to contact@morrisite.org. 180 names link to FamilySearch (115 probable). Tap or hover over a link, dot or bar for the evidence; 154 names have a notes button with what the sources say about them. 81 men are marked 1862 prisoner: they are on the list of men taken at Kington Fort and brought before Judge Kinney (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). 2 are marked held at the fort: men the Morrisites themselves had captured and held in a log house that spring, whose detention brought the posse. 43 names have a full page with sources. s: Rosser, Jenkins: Printed so, among the R’s; probably Rosser James Jenkins (1834–1903), a Welsh convert who lived at Ogden from 1856 to 1863 and later in Deer Lodge County, Montana, where he was an elder of the Reorganized Church. His wife, Ann Price, was a sister of Josiah D. Price, who is on the roll (FamilySearch K2YV-W6G, LZ2V-K7F; Find a Grave 65300911, 65300933). Ann is not on the roll. He crossed the plains in the John A. Hunt wagon company of 1856. His obituary in the Reorganized Church’s Zion’s Ensign says he “united with the Reorganization in 1861”; the Reorganized Church had no missionaries in Utah until 1863, so the date fits a Morrisite baptism (“Died,” Zion’s Ensign, July 16, 1903, p. 8; Church History Biographical Database). ↩

About this roll Roll of Membership: Names of Persons Baptized into the Fulness of the Gospel USHS PAM 9569c1 Published San Francisco: Geo. S. Dove & Co., May 1886. 8 pp. Subtitle: “Names of persons baptized during the administration of Joseph Morris, at South Weber, Utah Territory, in the years of 1861 and 1862.” Copy Utah History Information Center (Utah State Historical Society), Salt Lake City, PAM 9569c1; gift of William Mulder. Larson’s transcription also records the words “Reorganized Church Library,” probably a library mark on the copy. Compiler’s note “All the names that we found in the record book are in this list. We feel assured that there were many persons baptized whose names were not recorded.” Absence from the roll does not show that someone was not a member. Pencil notes In the copy Larson transcribed, someone has totaled the names in pencil at 430 and marked the church’s officers (listed above); a further pencil note reads “174 Scan names,” apparently a count of Scandinavian names. The roll has 430 names, matching that total; Larson’s transcription had left out David Thomas (note 10). This transcription Made from David A. Larson’s transcription of the Utah State Historical Society copy (MORRISITES-L mailing list, RootsWeb, March 25, 2007), then checked name by name on November 2, 2026, against a photocopy of the printed pamphlet in the editor’s files. The check restored one name (David Thomas) and corrected fourteen spellings to match the print. Names follow the order and spelling of the roll; where a name repeats, the roll adds “2.” Notes on doubtful readings are numbered. Links to FamilySearch Family Tree 180 linked, 115 probable What they are Where a person on the roll has been identified with confidence in FamilySearch’s Family Tree, the name carries a link to that record. Hover over a link to see the basis for the identification and who supplied it. Links open FamilySearch’s public page for the person, which needs no sign-in; a free account shows the full record and its sources. Family Tree is open to editing by anyone, so check those sources before relying on it. What counts A shared name is not enough. A match needs something tying the person to the Morrisites or to South Weber in 1861–62, or a name rare enough in Utah Territory then to leave no other candidate. Matches that rest on circumstantial evidence, such as a husband and wife both on the roll and a likely place, or a family whose members on the roll all match one family in Family Tree, are linked but marked “probable”; corrections are welcome. Cases with more than one candidate are explained in the notes instead. Contribute If you can identify someone, send the FamilySearch ID and your evidence to contact@morrisite.org. Contributions are credited. Families on the roll Updated as evidence is added What it shows People on the roll who were related by birth or marriage, grouped by family, with the places they lived after 1862. The groups come from Family Tree, membership records and published histories; a relationship that rests only on a likely guess is left out until it is checked. Many Morrisite families stayed together after the siege and married into one another at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge and in the Carson Valley, so a descendant of one family may find related families in the same group. Contribute If you know of a connection that is not shown, write to contact@morrisite.org. What became of them Updated as evidence is added How it is counted Each person counts as “not yet known” until a source shows where he or she went: the RLDS Church (Reorganized Church, now Community of Christ), back to the LDS Church, one of the later Morrisite groups in Idaho, Montana, Nevada, California, Washington Territory or Iowa, or death at Kington Fort during the siege of June 13–15, 1862. Many Morrisites joined the RLDS Church only after years in the groups at Soda Springs, Deer Lodge, Carson Valley or Walla Walla; when a source shows both stages, the person is counted as “stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church,” with a half-green, half-blue dot. The sources are RLDS and LDS membership records, FamilySearch, and published histories. Where the source names someone who is probably, but not certainly, the person on the roll, the evidence begins “Probable identification.” A colored dot beside a name shows the category; hover over it, or tap it on a phone, for the evidence. Send additions or corrections to contact@morrisite.org. Reading the roll Spellings vary, especially for Danish and Swedish names: search under Hanson and Hansen, Peterson and Petersen, Christiansen and Christensen, Sorenson and Sorensen. The roll itself spells some families two ways (Peterson and Petersen; Lorensen and Lorentzen). In its own text this guide names people as the roll spells them, or by the fuller name on their person page (Peter C. Klemgard; Sven Olasson Hägg, the roll’s Svend Hegg). Where it quotes or summarizes a document, it keeps the document’s spelling, so the same man may appear as Klemgaard in the Deseret News or Swen O. Hagg in a court file. The roll records baptisms in 1861–62. It does not show who remained in the church, who left before the siege of June 1862, or who later joined the Soda Springs, Carson Valley, Walla Walla, or Montana groups. Later rolls, including those of the Montana church, which lasted until 1954 or, formally, 1969, are cited in Repositories but not published here.
Who they were

The people on the roll Who joined Joseph Morris? This page counts what can be said of the 430 people on the 1861–62 roll of membership. Some figures cover everyone on the roll, judged from their names. The rest come from the people identified so far in FamilySearch Family Tree, and hold only for them. The roll is not a full list of members. Its compiler wrote that “many persons baptized” were never recorded. The lists behind these figures can be downloaded, and counted in other ways, on the Data page. Corrections and new identifications are welcome at contact@morrisite.org.

Paths into the movement What brought Latter-day Saints to Joseph Morris? The members left few accounts of their reasons, so this section tests what the records can show: when people reached Utah, whom they crossed the plains with, where they came from, and whether they joined as families. Companies are known for 98 of the 178 people linked to Family Tree, from the Mormon Pioneer Overland Travel records attached there and from the rosters of the Church History Biographical Database (CHD). These are associations in the records, not reasons the members gave. When they came, against everyone who came 1847–51 0.5 1852 0.5 1853 3.9 1854 3.3 1855 5.3 1856 4.5 1857–58 1.1 1859 11.2 1860 7.3 1861 0.0 Roll members per 1,000 people in the CHD’s pioneer companies of each year. The highest rate is 1859 (18 of 1,606). People who had arrived in 1859 and 1860, a year or two before Morris began baptizing, joined about twice as often as those who came in 1853–56, and far more often than those who came before 1853. Those who arrived in 1861 had little time to join before the roll closed. CHD counts are the names it holds, not every emigrant; the roll members identified so far are not a random sample, and some were found by searching these same rosters. Crossing together Robert F. Weighing the factors Factor What the records show How far it goes Recent arrival 63 of 117 identified people with a year of arrival reached Utah in 1856 or later; the rate per 1,000 emigrants peaks in 1859. Strong pattern, the clearest in the records. Why newcomers joined more often (fewer ties to their wards, less property, hardship on arrival) is not yet measured. Crossing together 65 of 98 with a known company shared it with another roll family. Moderate. It overlaps with origin and with how the names were found. Language and origin 168 of 430 names on the roll are Scandinavian. Strong for the roll as a whole, but it overlaps with arrival year; how it compares with the population of Utah in 1861 has not been measured. Family 131 roll names belong to the 31 family groups found so far (see the roll). Strong where known: families often joined together, so one household’s decision accounts for several names. Many relationships on the roll are still unfound. Place 57 of the 91 roll members found in the 1860 census lived in Davis or Weber County, near South Weber. Strong but expected: Morris preached and baptized there. Leaders and wards The South Weber bishop, Richard Cook, and his brother John joined; sixteen were cut off together on February 11, 1861. Not counted. Followed through the roll notes and person pages. The factors overlap: a Danish family who crossed in 1859 and settled near South Weber counts under four of them at once, so they cannot be added up. A fair reading is that Morris drew most on recent emigrants, Danish and British, who came as families and lived near him, and least on Saints settled since the early 1850s.

Others named in the sources People whom the sources name as Morrisites, or as followers of a later offshoot, but who are not on the printed roll of 1861–62. Each entry rests on a source that names the person as a member, officer, missionary, donor or prisoner; family tradition alone is not enough, and only people who have died are listed. “Probable” marks an identification or a membership that is not certain. Morris, Joseph (born December 15, 1823; died June 15, 1862) Morrisite The prophet himself. The printed roll lists his followers, not Morris. His wife Mary Olsen, a Danish convert he married soon after a revelation of August 23, 1861, is probably the roll’s “Mary Morris”; she was probably Karen Marie Olsen (born 1843), daughter of Ole and Anne Olsen, and so probably also the roll’s “Karen Morris” (see the roll notes for Karen Morris and Mary Morris). In 1878 James Bowman, at Soda Springs, mentions a debt of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law,” apparently living nearby; he is not named (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). Born at Burwardsley, Cheshire, he was a coal miner as a boy at Dukinfield and married Mary Thorp, a weaver, at Mottram in Longdendale in February 1847; three of their children died in infancy, in Cheshire and at St. Louis, and a daughter, Ann Eliza, was born on the trail in September 1853. In April 1854 Morris petitioned the Sanpete probate court for a divorce; Mary married Henry Beal at Ephraim in July and raised Ann Eliza (later Mrs. Alfred Pehrson, 1853–1939) in the Beal household. Mary Thorpe Beal died at Ephraim in 1905; she was the grandmother of Thorpe B. Isaacson, a counselor in the First Presidency. Morris’s second and third marriages, to the widow Elizabeth Mills (1855) and to Elizabeth Jones at Provo (1857), were short. His elder brother George’s reminiscences give his life before Utah (see Documents), and the Chronology gives the records. (Anderson, Revisited, 87, 104–5; The Spirit Prevails, 149–51; George Morris reminiscences, CHL MS 1614, 115–22; Mottram in Longdendale marriage register, 1847; 1841 and 1850 censuses; Merrill D. Beal, 1971, 35; Utah death certificates, 1905, 1939)

Bowman, Isabella (died June 15, 1862) Morrisite Killed at Kington Fort during the surrender, one of the two women shot by Robert T. Burton’s party. Burton was indicted for her killing in 1870 (the indictment was voided in 1872) and again in 1877, tried from February 18, 1879, and acquitted. Alexander Dow’s affidavit of April 1863 calls her “Mrs. Bowman, wife of James Bowman.” The 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letter says she was holding Joseph March’s baby, whom she had taken in after its mother was killed. Wife of James Bowman (below), who was still a believer at Soda Springs in 1878. Not on the printed roll; she may have joined after it was made. South Weber City’s cemetery records say that “Bella Bowman” was buried outside the Pioneer Cemetery fence near its northeast corner. (Salt Lake Herald and Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, Feb.–Mar. 1879 (Burton trial); Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Anderson, Revisited, 148–49; South Weber City cemetery records)

Søndermark, Anders (born 1821) Morrisite Born at Vrensted, Jylland, Denmark, January 9, 1821; entered in the draft register as Anders Sørensen, an Aaronic priest. Baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, “by Morrisen og Mikkelsen,” very probably Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen (a Niels Morrison was among Morris’s followers at South Weber in February 1861), and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869, and probably the “Bro. Søndermark” of the Fremont council of November 30, 1871, who said he believed “J. Morris was a Prophet.” Excluded from the Omaha congregation on November 30, 1871. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude; Fremont council minutes, November 30, 1871, MS 31876; Wilford Woodruff journal, February 11, 1861, MS 1352)

Søndermark, Karen Sørensen (1861–71) Morrisite Born at Vrensted, Jylland, Denmark, October 9, 1822; entered in the draft register as Karen Maria Sørensen; wife of Anders Søndermark. Baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, “by Morrisen og Mikkelsen” (very probably Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen), and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869; excluded on November 30, 1871. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude)

Knudsen, Hans (1861–71) Morrisite Born on Fyn, Denmark. Baptized at South Weber on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelsen and confirmed by Joseph Morris; a leading member of the Council Bluffs congregation from 1869, baptizing and confirming others there and at Omaha and Crescent City. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude)

Fellows, Carleton (born 1809) Morrisite Born at Buffalo, New York, August 15, 1809. Baptized at Omaha in 1869 by S. P. Guhl and Hans Knudsen; husband of “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” who had been baptized at South Weber. In 1869 Williams told him he had been Jonas, the father of Simon Peter. Both were excluded from the Council Bluffs congregation on February 5, 1871. (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude; record book, 1869, MS 31876) Taken at Kington Fort, June 1862 (14) Men held to bail after the surrender or tried in March 1863 whose names do not match anyone on the roll. Being taken prisoner does not by itself show membership: Val Holley names eleven Slaterville and Marriott men among the prisoners. See the June 1862 list and the Questions page.

Bowman, James (1816–1903) Kington Fort Husband of Isabella Bowman, who was killed at the surrender. Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863; moved to Idaho in the spring of 1863. In 1879 he testified at Burton’s trial that he had lived at Soda Springs since 1863. In August 1878 he wrote from Soda Springs to Erick Eliason in Montana, signing himself “yours truly in the New Covenant”; he had received “the Epistle so kindly sent me by the friends in Deer Lodge” and passed it on to “Father Christofferson,” and among debts owed him he lists one of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). Not the John Bowman of the roll, who was at Kaysville in 1870 and South Weber in 1880; Anderson also treats them as two men. Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households lists “James & Sarah A.” Bowman in a log house there in 1860 and says that Sarah died in the cannon attack of June 13, 1862 (Norma Earl Allred, comp., South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952 (2004), no. 44); the name and the manner of death differ from the contemporary accounts of Isabella Bowman, and the compilation gives no source for them. He died at Soda Springs on June 7, 1903. The RLDS Saints’ Herald printed his death as that of “Elder James Bowman,” born February 19, 1816, at Manchester, England, with a tribute from the Soda Springs Idanha Chieftain: “No man in need who asked of him but received assistance.” The title suggests that he had joined the Reorganized Church, but no record of his baptism has been found (Saints’ Herald 51, 1904, p. 213). (Deseret News, June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863; Salt Lake Herald, Feb. 21, 1879; Anderson, Revisited, 148, 162; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Saints’ Herald 51 (1904): 213) The Montana church (12) Leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High in the Deer Lodge Valley, 1870s–1969, who are not on the roll.

Williams, George (died 1882) Montana church The “Prophet Cainan,” who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s; in January 1879 he wrote that the Montana Saints lived on “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming (see the Chronology). (Anderson, Revisited; Watson)

Hendrikson, Andrew (died July 3, 1921) Montana church page A Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, born at Ondrup, Jutland, on July 29, 1843, and baptized into the Morrisite church in the Missouri River at Omaha on January 22, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871,” Council Bluffs, MS 32226; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In October 1869 Williams named him “the Keeper of the Book” for the Omaha and Council Bluffs fund of free-will offerings (Williams to the Omaha church, October 13, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869). He baptized converts at Omaha, Council Bluffs, Crescent City and Fremont in 1870–71, among them Carie (Carrie) Hendrikson, born at Asted near Frederikshavn on April 6, 1853, whom he and Peter Staffenson baptized at Crescent City, Iowa, on October 16, 1871 (Montana membership record, 1874–1887, Church of the Firstborn records, MS 32226, Church History Library). She was Carrie Jensen before her marriage; her obituary says she came from Council Bluffs to Corinne, Utah, and from there to the Deer Lodge Valley by covered wagon in 1872, the year of her marriage (Independent-Record [Helena], January 11, 1936, p. 2). Her grandson Robert Staffanson wrote that she left Denmark alone at eighteen, knowing no English, to join an aunt living near Deer Lodge (Robert Staffanson, Witness to Spirit: My Life with Cowboys, Mozart & Indians [Deadwood, Ore.: Wyatt-MacKenzie, 2015], ch. “First Movement: Cowboys”). In April 1872 Williams sent the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs “instructions for gathering up to Montana”; by September Hendrikson was in the Deer Lodge Valley, where he was made second counselor to William James (see Chronology, 22 Sep 1872), and in December Williams wrote to him at Warm Spring Creek, congratulating him on his marriage (Williams to Henrickson, April 7 and December 18, 1872, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1872–1873). On February 24, 1878, the council chose his land at Race Track for the Lord’s House (see Lord’s House). The church’s record of members lists children born in the valley: Maryann at Warm Springs in 1873, and Henry (1877) and James (1878) at Race Track (same record, where the last name was read as “Jeny”; his birth date, December 28, 1878, is that of James, or Jim, Hendrickson). On the evening of Thursday, April 8, 1880, a daughter of five was badly burned when her clothes caught fire at a rubbish fire in the yard of the farm; her father put out the flames in a watering trough, but she lived only about twelve hours, and she was buried after a funeral on Saturday “in the silent village on the hill” (New North-West [Deer Lodge], April 16, 1880, p. 3; reprinted in the Helena Daily Independent, April 18, and the Helena Weekly Herald, April 22, 1880, p. 7). That June Williams wrote from England of “the terrible accident” that had killed “their dear girl” (Williams to William James, June 21, 1880, Church History Library, MS 31876). Her name was very probably Maggie: the City of Deer Lodge’s directory of Hillcrest Cemetery, in use since 1871, lists a Maggie Hendrickson in Protestant section 6, lot 138, grave 1, apart from her parents’ lot and from her sister Maggie Hare, and Find a Grave identifies that grave as hers (Hillcrest Cemetery directory, F–K, City of Deer Lodge; Find a Grave memorial 117354393). The next daughter, born that November, was also named Margaret (Maggie). She was not Maryann, who is listed, aged six, in the family’s household when the census was taken that June (1880 U.S. census, Deer Lodge Valley, Deer Lodge County, Montana, enumeration district 11, p. 4, household of A. Hendrickson, NARA T9). In 1900 Carrie was recorded as the mother of eleven children, ten of them living (1900 U.S. census, Cottonwood Township, Deer Lodge County, Montana, enumeration district 18, sheet 5A, household of Andrew Hendrickson, NARA T623). His daughter Julia (Mrs. George Staffanson) remembered him as a minister: her son recalled her singing at her work “the hymns she had learned in the church in which her father was a minister” (Staffanson, Witness to Spirit, same chapter). Counselor to William James from May 1882; presided over the Montana church from 1886 until his death. On January 27, 1904, he married his daughter Maggie to James B. Hare at Race Track, signing the certificate as “Minister in Church of Saints of the Most High” (Powell County, Montana, marriage records, vol. 1, p. 77; Montana Historical Society). Carrie died at the family ranch on January 10, 1936, aged 83, survived by ten children, among them Mrs. Agnes Olson of Deer Lodge (Independent-Record, January 11, 1936). His records, kept by his family, are a main source for Anderson’s book. (Anderson, Revisited)

Johnson, George (born in Denmark, 1856; died April 29, 1954) Montana church Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years, likewise never a Latter-day Saint; presided at the Lord’s House near Racetrack from 1921 until shortly before his death at ninety-eight, the last official leader of the Montana church. A county biography of about 1902 says he came to Montana in the summer of 1873, worked in Deer Lodge hotels, and then took up a stock ranch eight miles south of the town, and that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” On July 1, 1876, he married Josephine V. Oleson, a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. (Anderson, Revisited; Progressive Men of the State of Montana (Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902]), pp. 1092–93)

Beck, Lars P. (1844–1925) Montana church Lars Peter Beck. Born in Jylland (Jutland), Denmark; came to America in 1864 and married Maria Christensen at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, on March 7, 1869. Baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Andrew Henriksen and Niels Jensen, with his wife Maria; their eldest daughter had been born at Fremont in 1870. Ordained a Seventy in Montana on November 10, 1872, and a member of the council of the Danish-speaking stake from 1873 to 1883; the council met in his house near Deer Lodge on February 21, 1875, and their daughter Margaret was born at Deer Lodge that May. With his brother Nels J. Beck he met William P. Thomas at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1880. In February 1883 he said he could not see that choosing a president would do the church any good, and he was among the minority who would not accept William James’s election that April; his brother Nels voted for James. On May 26, 1883, the Race Track council released him as a teacher and, with his wife, from membership, saying that the dissenters “had separated themselves from us” (minutes, MS 31876, Minutes, 1883–1884; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Their children included Annie, Mary Ann, Margaret, Laura, Carl R., Harry H. and Joseph. He died at Deer Lodge on February 21, 1925, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery there. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), and minutebooks, 1872–1874, p. 3, and 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; council minutes, 1873–1883, MS 31876, Church History Library (translations from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303646; FamilySearch Family Tree, LK44-Y7K; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

Beck, Maria (1847–1938) Montana church Born in Slesvig (Schleswig), on January 7, 1847. Married Lars P. Beck (above) at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, in 1869, and was baptized with him at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Niels Jensen and Andrew Henriksen; the family settled near Deer Lodge, Montana, by 1875. Her maiden name was Christensen (Christiansen on her Find a Grave memorial). She died on May 13, 1938, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library (translation from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303647; FamilySearch Family Tree, L4QB-7GT; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

Beck, Nels J. (1847–1921) Montana church Nels Jensen Beck, brother of Lars P. Beck (above). Born at Jernved, near Ribe, Denmark, on May 6, 1847; came to America in 1872 and married Marie Helen Hansen at Deer Lodge that year; lived on Cottonwood Creek. The Montana council minutes of May 29, 1880, name “Lars Beck” and “his brother Niels Beck.” At the general assembly of April 25, 1883, “Nels Beck” and his wife voted to sustain William James, while Lars voted against. On April 25, 1887, “N. J. Beck” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House, with George Johnson and Emmanuel Strome, so that the building would not be taxed. Other “Niels Beck” entries in the minutes may be he or the roll’s Niels R. Beck. He died on October 4, 1921, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (Council minutes, May 29, 1880, MS 31876, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; minutebook, 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, GB7W-C7D; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

Strom, Emanuel (1846–1929) Montana church In a note in his record book he gives his birth year as 1846 and says he was received into “the church of the Saints of the Most High God” at Omaha, Nebraska, in 1872 (day and month uncertain; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). That year he copied Williams’s epistles and Morris’s revelations into Swedish. In March 1887, when Eardley went east, “Brother Strom” was to conduct the meetings, and on April 25, 1887, “Emmanuel Strome” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House. In 1924 he wrote, and signed “E Strom,” that a feeling had explained to him “the League of Nation, to be united and ready when the Lord want them,” and that a voice had said “1926 Salt Lake City shall be destroid and laid waist.” He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In January 1880, after a visiting preacher named Brand had spoken in the Lord’s House, he said that no “sectarian” preacher should speak there; in May he put to the council a question about Adam and Eve and the serpent, and was asked to bring his violin to the Fourth of July at Deer Lodge. In May 1881 he would not take the sacrament from Erik Eliason, who he said “had come forward and set himself in Cainan’s place and would not take counsel” (translations from the Danish generated by Claude). On February 20, 1880, at Lower Warm Spring Creek, he married Mary Josephine Hellstrom, daughter of Johan Helström (below). He died on January 2, 1929, and is buried at Anaconda. (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, and Record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; council minutes, 1876, 1880 and 1881, MS 31876, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrickson, March 11 and 18, 1887, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, K4YW-8YS)

Helström, Johan (1834–1913) Montana church Very probably the “Johan Helström,” born May 1, 1834, in “Dalene” [Dalarna?], Sweden, whom the Omaha register lists as baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on March 25, 1871, with Maria Helström. Family Tree has Johan Hellstrom born on April 29, 1834, at Gagnef, Dalarna; emigrated in 1864; died at Anaconda, Montana, on March 31, 1913. His daughter Mary Josephine married Emanuel Strom (above) in 1880. His son Peter Helstrom’s wife and children were to be baptized at Race Track on August 9, 1893. He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In 1876 the council heard a letter from Strom about his drinking, and in January 1880 it forgave him, after he had admitted being “under drink” and making threats over land, on condition that he give up strong drink “except the use of the wine at the Lord’s Supper” (translation from the Danish generated by Claude). A Peter E. Helstrom, very probably his son, was the elder in charge of the Reorganized Church’s Anaconda branch in 1926, when it had 42 members and no building (U.S. Census of Religious Bodies, 1926, schedule 489, American Religious Ecologies). (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), nos. 31–32, MS 32226, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrickson, July 27, 1893, and council minutes, 1876 and 1880, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KFR2-9KR)

Nielsen, Peter (born 1833) Montana church Born at Aalborg, Jutland, Denmark, on February 27, 1833. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on June 26, 1870, by Rasmus Rasmussen and Andrew Hendrikson. He went to Montana, and on July 27, 1887, Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Deer Lodge, as “Peter Neilson,” with members of his family; the branch register marks him as since deceased. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 27 and no. 25)

Thorkelsen, Niels (1823–1913) Montana church Born at Lyby [?], Skåne, Sweden, on March 3, 1823. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on July 22, 1871, by Andrew Hendrikson and Jens Jensen, with Pernelle Tyrkelsen; the draft register notes that he moved to Montana. In October 1890 he was baptized into the Reorganized Church in the Deer Lodge Valley, entered as “Neil Tarkelson.” Family Tree has Niels Torgelson, born March 4, 1823, at Lyby, Malmöhus, Sweden, husband of Pernilla Bengtsson (1824–1891), who died at Anaconda, Montana, on June 9, 1913. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 37 and no. 61; FamilySearch Family Tree, K2HT-982)

Jensen, Niels (1829–1914) Montana church Born in Jutland, Denmark, on March 12, 1829. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on March 12, 1869, by Jens Jensen, and confirmed by S. P. Guhl; in 1869 he led the district at Florence under the Omaha congregation, and at Fremont in 1871 he baptized new members with Hendrikson. He kept a record book of Williams’s letters in Danish copies, 1870–79, which also holds a letter of 1875 from the claimant Barnet Moses Giles (see Repositories). About March 1890 Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Willow Glen, Montana, with a Mary Jensen, born January 16, 1828, very probably his wife Maren, whom the Omaha register gives as born June 16, 1828. Family Tree has Niels Jensen, born March 12, 1829, at Smidstrup, Vejle, Denmark, married in 1851 to Maren Sørensdatter (1828–1914); he died at Deer Lodge, Montana, on November 22, 1914. The identification of the Montana Niels Jensen with the Omaha one rests on the matching birth date and wife. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 16 and nos. 59–60; Niels Jensen record, 1870–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KH45-1ZT)

Staffanson, Peter (1823–1913) Montana church page A Swedish shoemaker from Skåne, born November 22, 1823, who joined the Latter-day Saints at Copenhagen in 1852, crossed on the James Nesmith in 1855 and lived at Brigham City, Utah, until the later 1860s. He was baptized into the Morrisite church at Crescent City, Iowa, on February 2, 1869, and presided there from 1870; with Andrew Hendrikson he baptized Carrie, Hendrikson’s future wife, in 1871. In Montana he was named to preside over the second quorum of Seventies in 1872, went over to William James’s English-speaking Stake No. 1 in 1878, and was its bishop by 1883; in 1886 he held with James against George Thompson. He died at his ranch on Lost Creek near Anaconda on June 16, 1913, and is buried in the family cemetery there. Two of his sons married daughters of Daniel James, and two grandsons married daughters of Hendrikson. His son Jacob and Jacob’s wife Glendora were baptized into the Reorganized Church at Anaconda by A. B. Moore on October 23, 1897 (Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District, #228, Community of Christ Library Archives, nos. 119, 124). See his page. (Council Bluffs record of members, 1869–71, and minutebooks, Church History Library, MS 32226 and MS 31876; Eardley to Hendrickson, May 2, 1886, MS 31876; Butte Daily Post, June 16, 1913, p. 8) Followers of William W. Davies (24) Members, missionaries and donors of Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven near Walla Walla, 1867–81, as named in the 1880–81 lawsuit against him and the 1880 census. Many were converts made by his missionaries in San Francisco and Portland who had never been Morrisites; one former Morrisite testified that the Davies doctrine was “not like the Morrisite religion.” Those known or said to have been with the Morrisites before are also tagged Earlier a Morrisite. Davies testified that everyone on his list of donations except Niels R. Beck was a member.

Andrews Follower of Davies Foreman and agent of the community; Davies sent him east. A former member called him the “destroying angel”; another said he left of his own accord. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Bowman, Joseph Follower of Davies (probable) Called “the first born in the kingdom”; in Davies’s teaching he was counted among Davies’s sons, as Elias reincarnated. Compare Lewis H. Bowman, to whom Davies gave notes in 1879. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Cilley, Asa B. (at the camp 1871–79) Follower of Davies A blacksmith from Stockton, California, who learned the doctrine at Portland, Oregon, in the winter of 1870–71 and came to the camp in November 1871. He left in June 1879 and sued Davies with Evans and Courtney; the court awarded him $125. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Clore, Jesse Y. (born about 1823) Follower of Davies Born in Kentucky; first heard the doctrine at Gold Hill, Nevada, and took the vow at San Francisco about 1869. He lived at the camp, homesteaded four miles away, and testified for Davies in 1881 (“Jesse Y. Close” in the 1880 census). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census; The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878)
Corbett, Mrs. M. B. (born about 1834) Follower of Davies On Davies’s list of members in March 1881, aged 47; “Mary Corbet” in the 1880 census. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
Courtney, A. J. (at the camp 1876–77) Follower of Davies At the camp from about 1876 to July 1877; a plaintiff against Davies, awarded $400. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)
Degroot, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $218, 1869–78. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Evans, Thomas W. (at the camp 1870–78) Follower of Davies Earlier a Morrisite (probable) A plaintiff against Davies, awarded $2,700, the largest share. Davies said he came in 1870 and left in the spring of 1878. A Davies letter of March 1877 to a T. B. Evans, who was blind, looked for him “to come with Mr. Livingstone,” the roll’s R. J. Livingstone of Carson Valley. Emma Evans also testified. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Hagg, Ola (born about 1808) Follower of Davies Born in Sweden; at the camp from July 1868, and a witness for Davies in 1881. Probably the father of the roll’s Svend Hegg (Sven Olasson). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)
Hollenbeck, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $195, 1869–74. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Jones, Rachel D. (born about 1833) Follower of Davies Mrs. John E. Jones, born in Wales; a member from 1866, she came to Walla Walla with Davies in 1867. Her children were born in Utah and Montana. Her husband, sent out as a missionary in 1868 and later at Indian Valley, may be the roll’s apostle John E. Jones; that is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Kelley, Michael H. (born about 1843) Follower of Davies A sailor, born in Ireland; first came to the camp in November 1868, having learned the doctrine at San Francisco. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Lambert, V. D. (at the camp 1868–70) Follower of Davies A cooper and later a justice of the peace; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco in 1869–70. He left the community and testified against Davies. Sarah Lambert also testified. The Walla Walla Statesman printed his testimony as “D. V. Lambert”: fifty-two, a cooper and a justice of the peace, who had known Davies since 1868 through his missionaries Robert Roberts and Thomas Parker at San Francisco, and whom Davies ordained a preacher (February 5, 1881, p. 3). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Miller, Søren (born about 1817) Follower of Davies Earlier a Morrisite (probable) “Sorn Miller,” born in Denmark, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife and children Christian J., John M. and Christina, who are all on Davies’s 1881 list. Klemgard’s testimony implies that the elder Miller had been with him in Utah or at Soda Springs, that is, among the Morrisites. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Mortensen, James (born about 1825) Follower of Davies “J. Mortezen,” a shoemaker born in Sweden, at the camp from July 1868 with his wife Maria; their daughter Maria and Oscar Olsen are on the 1881 list. Whether the family connects to the Mortensens on the roll is not known. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Parker, Mrs. E. S. J. (born about 1824) Follower of Davies (probable) A widow, a member from 1868, at San Francisco. Probably the widow of Thomas Parker, Davies’s missionary there; whether he is the Thomas Parker on the roll is not settled. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)
Parker, Mary B. Follower of Davies “Mrs. Parker of San Francisco,” credited with gifts of $2,363.40, 1868–77. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)

Perkins, Cornelia S. (born about 1850) Follower of Davies Born in New Hampshire; a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from that fall. She took the minutes of meetings in shorthand, helped print the community’s tracts and taught the district school; later Davies’s second wife. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census; Find a Grave)
Perkins, M. A. C. (born about 1826) Follower of Davies Cornelia’s mother, a member from 1869 at San Francisco, at the camp from 1872. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Roberts, Jane S. (born about 1811) Follower of Davies Born in England; at the camp from 1868, with her daughter Emily J. Roberts. Testified for Davies in 1881. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Roberts, Robert (died January 1881) Follower of Davies Husband of Jane S. Roberts; Davies’s missionary at San Francisco and Portland, who preached the doctrine and administered the vow. Almost certainly the “old man Robert Roberts” who visited Genoa, Nevada, in June 1876 claiming to be the Prophet Daniel, told the town that the child who was to “run” the Kingdom of God was born at Walla Walla, and addressed a Morrisite meeting in the court house; the paper called him “the Morrisite Mormon who claims to be the Prophet Daniel” when he came again in June 1877. He was later expelled from the community and did not return. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; Carson Valley News, June 23, 1876, May 29 and June 22, 1877)
Smith, Mrs. Follower of Davies Credited with gifts of $122. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81, list of donations)
Turnbull Follower of Davies Named with Robert Roberts as administering the vow at San Francisco about 1869. Given name not recorded. (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81)

Wood, S. W. (born about 1823) Follower of Davies A photographer, born in England, who had an upholstery shop in Portland; he heard of Davies at San Francisco in 1868, came to the camp in the fall of 1869, served as a missionary and is credited with $5,921.65 on the list of donations. A defendant in the 1880 suit (“Samuel Woods” in the 1880 census). In November 1878 he passed through New York on his way to England to proclaim that the Messiah had come, and told the Sun of Davies’s revelation in Montana in 1866 and of the “Redemptionists” (The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878, p. 1). (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81; 1880 U.S. census)

Montana Morrisites: a register Everyone the sources so far place in the Morrisite church of the Deer Lodge Valley, from William W. Davies’s group of the mid-1860s to the Lord’s House at Racetrack, in one list: 96 people. Most joined after 1862 and are not on Morris’s roll. They came by way of the congregations at Omaha, Council Bluffs, Crescent City and Fremont, or were born in Montana. The main source is the church’s own record of members of 1874–87, with the minutes that record who voted in 1883 and 1886. Only people who have died are listed. See also the Deer Lodge Valley page and the Where they went map. Judgments made, and open questions. Spellings follow the sources, so one person may appear twice under different spellings where the record of members and the vote lists differ (for example Joni and John E. Johnson, Minie and Mamie Johnson). These are kept as separate rows and marked as questions, not merged. Where a person is listed only as “Sister” with a husband’s name, the given name is left blank unless another source supplies it. People on the 1861–62 roll who lived in the valley but whom no Montana church record yet names are listed separately, so that no one is counted a member on the strength of a census entry alone. Each open question is marked in its row and gathered at the end. Corrections are welcome at contact@morrisite.org. Member (53): Listed in the Montana record of members, 1874–87. Named in church records (25): Named as a member or officer in the minutes, but not in the record of members. President living in England (1): Elected president of the Montana church while living in England. On the 1861–62 roll; lived in the valley (15): On Morris’s roll and living in the valley, but no Montana church record yet names them. Davies’s group, 1864–67 (2): With William W. Davies in Montana before he led his followers to Walla Walla in 1867. Find a name or place
