Open questions

Questions for research Questions the guide has not been able to settle, for students, local historians, and other researchers. Questions of record can be advanced with records that are digitized or held in Utah, Idaho, Montana, or California. Questions of interpretation ask what the movement means for the history of religion; they suit theses and articles. If you take one up, or can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. Answers will be credited here. The edition of Forscutt’s “Sketch of Joseph Morris” is in progress by the editor. Questions of record

Where is Joseph Morris buried? Open Known The Salt Lake City Cemetery sexton’s record lists Morris under June 15, 1862, as no. 1469; the entry just before his, no. 1468, is Peter Wahler of the posse, written “Walden” (see “Did one posse member die, or two?” below). Morris lies in the pauper ground, in an unmarked grave. The city’s register of deaths enters “Walden,” “Morris Joseph” and “Banks John” together under June 15, with the cause “Resisting Federal Warrant” and burial in the strangers’ ground; two lines above them is Jared Smith of the 19th Ward, son of Arthur P. Smith, “killed at Weber” on June 13 (Salt Lake City “Record of the Dead,” 1862, p. 52, nos. 1469 and 1472–1474; the register’s numbers are not the sexton’s). New A tradition holds that he was buried beneath a street so that he would be trodden underfoot; no published source for it has been found. Where to look Salt Lake City Cemetery office (plat maps of the pauper sections); sexton’s records on FamilySearch; Salt Lake newspapers for June 1862 in Utah Digital Newspapers; where the tradition first appears in print or family accounts.

t: Where were the dead of Kington Fort buried?
s: Where were the dead of Kington Fort buried? Open Known The men are accounted for; most of the women are not. In the Salt Lake City Cemetery: Jared Smith of the posse (sexton’s record no. 1465, June 13, “Killed at Weber”); Peter Wahler of the posse (no. 1468, written “Walden”); Joseph Morris (no. 1469) and John Banks (no. 1470), in the pauper or strangers’ ground, unmarked (see Where is Joseph Morris buried?). Not in the Salt Lake City record: none of the Morrisite women killed at the fort appears in it between June 13 and mid-August 1862. Mrs. Bear and her baby, killed by a cannon ball on June 13: John L. Bear wrote that they were buried together that night, without saying where (autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 25–26). Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender: South Weber City’s cemetery records place a “Bella Bowman” outside the fence near the northeast corner of the Pioneer Cemetery, because residents did not want Morrisites inside; very probably she. Unknown: the two women killed by the first cannon shot on June 13 (one probably Mrs. Marsh, not yet checked against family records) and the Danish woman remembered as “Mrs. O’Hagg” or “Haag,” killed at the surrender. A local memory: in 1908 Henry Firth of South Weber showed John Ray Banks fifteen unmarked graves in the village cemetery that he said were those of Morrisites killed in the war (Banks, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” 1909, p. 2). That is more than the known dead; the Morrisite letters of 1891 count eleven Morrisites killed. Bendt Nielsen, buried in the Pioneer Cemetery after his death on July 15, 1862, was a Latter-day Saint settler, not a casualty. For the names and dates of the dead, see Who died at Kington Fort?; for the cemetery, the Kington Fort page. Where to look Davis County death and burial records for 1862; South Weber Ward and Weber Stake records; Thomas Peek’s South Weber diary (owned in 1969 by Richard O. Tucker); family records of the Bear, Bowman, Hegg and Marsh families; the Deseret News for June 1862; testimony at Robert T. Burton’s trial in 1879. If you know where any of the dead were laid, please write.

t: Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris?
s: Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris? Open Known About a dozen of Morris’s letters survive in Young’s office files (CR 1234 1). Anderson found no reply, and reports a penciled note on the first letter, “He’s weak minded.” Two more Morris texts, revelations dated January 14 and 16, 1860, were found in 2026 filed as anonymous letters; a clerk docketed them “Balderdash” and received them January 20, 1860, and the first charges Young with turning the Lord’s servant away from his door (Documents). That docket is so far the only recorded reaction from the office. Kirk Watson’s edition transcribes twelve of the letters, October 11, 1858, to November 26, 1860, with catalog links (dated list on the Documents page); others may be catalogued as anonymous. A story that Young did answer Morris face to face was going round among missionaries by July 1862: Jacob G. Bigler, writing from Liverpool on news brought by Chauncey W. West, who left Salt Lake City in mid-May, says Morris offered to make Young his counselor and Young dismissed him with an obscenity, which “Ended the interview.” The same letter has Morris’s horsemen to be met by “2,0000 of heavenly messengers to wipe out the Brighamites.” It is hearsay, with no date, place or witness, and it was written before news of the siege could reach England (Bigler to Joseph F. Smith, July 5, 1862, Joseph F. Smith papers, MS 1325, Church History Library, General correspondence, “A–Cl, 1862,” images 56–57). New Where to look Young’s letterpress copybooks and office journals, 1857–1861, in the same collection; the Journal of Wilford Woodruff for February 1861; the anonymous letters in the same files. What did Joseph F. Smith write to Niels Anderson? Open Known In 1903 Niels Anderson asked the church to help his wife, Mary Christoffersen Anderson, whose jaw was shot away in 1862. His letters survive (CR 1 191, digitized), and they answer a letter from Smith dated February 25, 1903, which is not in the file. Whether any help followed is unknown. Where to look Joseph F. Smith and First Presidency letterpress copybooks for 1903; Bannock Stake and Soda Springs ward records. Who were the Morrisites? In progress Known The roll of membership printed in 1886 lists 430 people baptized at South Weber in 1861–62. Since November 2026 this guide has linked 180 of them to FamilySearch Family Tree, marked 81 men named among the prisoners of June 1862, recorded the later path of 59, grouped families, and begun pages on individual members (for example John Parson and Erik Eliasson). Counts of sex, origin, age and birthplace are on Who they were. Most members are still known only by name, and the identifications marked probable need checking. For what they believed, see Teachings. Where to look The roll; Slaterville and other ward records; the 1860 and 1870 censuses; Soda Springs, Carson Valley, and Deer Lodge records; Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church; descendants’ family records. Findings are added to the roll and person pages with their sources; living people are excluded.

Who died at Kington Fort? Open Known Accounts differ on the number of dead and on some of their names and dates. The two posse deaths are now settled (Jared Smith and Peter Wahler; see below). On the Morrisite side, Morris was killed at the surrender and John Banks died in custody that evening; Forscutt saw two women dead from the first cannon shot on June 13, and the Anderson gravestone plaque says that Mrs. J. L. Bear (Anne Bar on the roll) and her baby were killed by another cannon ball, as does a 1988 article on John Lebrecht Bear that draws on his unpublished autobiography (Herald Journal, Logan, May 15, 1988, p. 47). Anderson, however, says that two women were killed while holding an infant and that in neither case was the child hurt (Revisited, p. 169 n. 6), but Bear’s own autobiography settles it for his family: about two hours after the first shot a cannon ball crashed into their shelter, killing his wife, and “all that was left of our 16 week old baby that she had in her lap was a handful of flesh.” He also says the first shot killed one woman outright and mortally wounded “a Swiss widow 65 years old,” and that that night “the Swiss brethern buried the widow woman and my wife with the remnants of the baby” in an old water ditch, wrapped in linen sheets (Johann L. Baer [John L. Bear], autobiography, circa 1908, typescript, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 25–26). Anderson’s note may refer to the first shot. Williams’s unfinished poem of 1865 on the siege tells of a babe “torn from the breast by a bombshell’s embrace” (see Nov 1865 in the chronology). At Burton’s trial in 1879 Mary Anderson, whose chin the first cannon ball took off, said it “killed a lady beside me,” and named among the dead “Morris and Banks and Mrs. Swanee and Mrs. Bowman” (Ogden Junction, February 22, 1879, p. 4); “Mrs. Swanee” was very probably Anna, wife of Swen O. Hegg (the roll’s Svend and Ann Hegg): two Morrisites who saw the shooting and later lived at Walla Walla, William W. Davies and R. J. Livingston, named the second woman killed at the surrender “Mrs. A. S. O. Hegg” and “Mrs. Anna Swen O. Hegg,” and “Swanee” sounds like “Swen’s”; she is The Spirit Prevails’s “Mrs. O’Hagg” and the “Haag” of the 1891 letters. Bear, who says he stood eight or ten feet from Burton, gives the same order: Mrs. Bowman called Burton “a blood thirsty hound” and was shot, “Then a Danish woman, Br. Sven Fleg’s wife, was shot” (“Fleg” is evidently a typing slip for Hegg); he counts ten killed on the Morrisite side (MS 10240, p. 27). Davies told the Walla Walla historian Frank T. Gilbert in 1882 that a shot fired at Banks missed him and killed Mrs. Hegg; Livingston, standing a few feet from Burton, thought Burton killed her by accident, “a ball intended for Morris,” and said that Banks was shot from behind by a posse man named Brown. Gilbert’s “List of the Killed,” from the two of them, has Morris, Banks, Mrs. Hegg and Mrs. Bowman killed after the surrender, and before it “Mrs. O. Olssen, Mrs. Labracht Bar and child, two females by the first cannon ball one of them an old lady from Germany, and one man a drum-maker”: in all, “one child, six women, and three men” (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, Whitman, Columbia and Garfield Counties (Portland, 1882), pp. 372–73). Emma Thompson Just, another witness at that trial, left recollections written down by her daughter in the 1920s, a late and family account: two killed by the first ball in the bowery; a babe in its mother’s arms that fell at the first shot and fell again when its “second protector” was killed; a woman who lost the lower part of her face; four killed under the white flag; her mother, hiding in a cellar, counting seventy-five cannon shots on the second day; and Mrs. Bowman shot after calling one of the leaders “a blood thirsty wretch.” She also says that on the stand in 1879 she confused Burton with Judson Stoddard, then dead, so that her evidence fell on the wrong man (Agnes Just Reid, Letters of Long Ago, 1923, pp. 59–64). The trial reports bear her out. On the stand she described the first shot killing two women and wounding a third; her family, with her aunt’s, sheltering in a cellar her father dug under their house; Mrs. Bowman as a small, dark woman who dropped the child and fell when she was shot; and her father, George Thompson, sitting down on Morris’s body and asking to be killed, since he had “nothing now to live for,” until a man snapped a gun at him and he was dragged away. She said the man on the dark horse shot both Morris and Mrs. Bowman, and admitted she might have things mixed because she had been so young (Salt Lake Weekly Tribune, March 1, 1879, p. 5). The defence answered that Stoddard rode the black horse and Burton a sorrel, and dismissed her, with Mary Anderson and a Johnson, as witnesses who had been children at the time (Deseret Evening News, March 5, 1879, pp. 1, 3; Ogden Semi-Weekly Junction, March 8, 1879, p. 2). In 1908 Henry Firth of South Weber pointed out fifteen unmarked graves in the village cemetery that he said were those of Morrisites killed in the war (Banks, “A Document History,” p. 2). Family Tree gives Ingry (Ingrid) Warner, born in Sweden in 1811, wife of Joseph Warner and probably the roll’s Ingray Werner, as dying on June 13, 1862, the day of the first cannon shot; the date has no source there and has not been checked (FamilySearch Family Tree, GK43-KYD). Isabella Bowman, wife of James Bowman, was one of two Morrisite women killed during the surrender (The Spirit Prevails names the other “Mrs. O’Hagg,” p. 8, and Dow’s affidavit calls her a Danish woman; she may be the roll’s Ann Hegg, wife of Svend Hegg, whom Family Tree gives as dying in 1862, but that is not checked); Robert T. Burton was indicted for her death in 1870 and again in 1877, tried in 1879 and acquitted (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 148–49). The Salt Lake City Cemetery interment register lists Morris (no. 1469, June 15, “Resisting Federal Wa

t: What do the Danish revelations say?
s: What do the Danish revelations say? Open Known The USU collection holds a bound volume of Morris’s revelations in Danish that does not seem to exist anywhere else. It has not been translated or compared with The Spirit Prevails. Where to look USU Special Collections, Caine MSS 10. A reader of nineteenth-century Danish handwriting is needed. Where are the records of the 1863 trials? In progress Known At the March 1863 term, ten Morrisites were indicted for killing the two posse men: seven were convicted of second-degree murder, two were acquitted, and one case was dropped (nolle prosequi). One man was sentenced to fifteen years, one to twelve, and five to ten. Sixty-six others were fined $100 for resisting the posse (Fanny Stenhouse, An Englishwoman in Utah, 1880; Bancroft, History of Utah, ch. 22). Governor Harding pardoned them all a few days later; Anderson (Revisited, p. 145) says the proclamation named the convicted men, and Eardley says John Parson carried the pardon to the penitentiary (Gems, p. 31). The Deseret News of June 25, 1862, names everyone brought before Judge Kinney after the siege: Richard Cook and Peter Klemgaard, Christian Neilson, and ninety-five others held to bail (Documents; the men are marked on the roll). The court’s own report, in the Deseret News of April 1, 1863, names them (Documents): Peter Klemgard (fifteen years), Christian Neilsen (twelve), and Abraham Taylor, Kadrup Neilsen, Jens Christiansen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason (ten each); John Parsons and John E. Jones were acquitted, and Richard Cook’s case was dropped. The Spirit Prevails and Gems give a different seven, with John Nielson, George Lee and John E. Jones in place of Kadrup Neilsen, Andrew Lee and Andrew M. Mason. The same report names eighty-five men tried for resisting an officer. Harding’s two pardons of March 31, 1863, are printed in full in Tullidge’s History of Salt Lake City (1886): the same seven for murder, and sixty-nine for resisting an officer, which fits the sixty-six fined with Cook, Parson and Jones (Documents). Still open: who “Kadrup Neilsen” was (he is not on the roll, though the pardon names him too), why the Morrisite accounts differ, and the court’s own case files. Where to look The Gordon M. Howard papers at the Utah State Historical Society (Mss B 279), box 2: People v. Peter Klingard, 1863 (folder 5), and a register of arrests of Morrisites, 1863 (folder 6). Utah territorial court case files at the Utah State Archives; the original pardons, in the territorial executive records (Utah State Archives).

t: Was Lot Smith at the siege?
s: Was Lot Smith at the siege? In progress The question Writing from Loughborough on April 12, 1873, George Williams warned the Montana church against spirits “more wicked than Burton and Lot Smith (the murderers at Weber)” (Church History Library, MS 31876). Robert T. Burton led the posse. Lot Smith (1830–1892), sheriff of Davis County and the militia officer famous among Latter-day Saints for burning the army’s supply trains in the Utah War of 1857, is not named in the accounts of the siege used by this guide. In 1857, the Utah History Encyclopedia says, he “outshone” Porter Rockwell and Burton himself in leading the militia against the army’s trains and livestock; Anderson calls him a “well-known guerrilla fighter and at times Young’s personal bodyguard,” and the most notable of the Mormons accused of harassing the Morrisites before the war (Revisited, pp. 227, 232). He later led Latter-day Saint settlers to northern Arizona, where he died in 1892. Probably not On April 28, 1862, the War Department asked Brigham Young for a cavalry company to guard the overland mail and telegraph; on April 30 Young told “Captain Lot Smith and Company” that they had been mustered into United States service for ninety days “to be employed in protecting the property of the Telegraph and Overland Mail companies in or about Independence Rock” (Brigham Young to Lot Smith and Company, April 30, 1862, Lot Smith papers, J. Willard Marriott Library, University of Utah). The company left Salt Lake City on May 1, spent June in camp at Independence Rock on the Sweetwater, in what is now Wyoming, returned on August 15 and was discharged on August 16 (Kenneth L. Alford and Joseph R. Stuart, “The Lot Smith Cavalry Company: Utah Goes to War,” in Civil War Saints, ed. Alford (2012), 127–41). The siege was June 13–15. Alford and Stuart say Smith sent Brigham Young several telegrams in June but not from where, and record no trip home that month; so he was very probably hundreds of miles away, which would also explain his absence from McKean’s posse returns. Anderson does not raise the question; he notes the call of April 28 (p. 110) but does not connect it with Smith. Sheriff in 1861 The Davis County Sheriff’s Office and Wikipedia list Smith as sheriff from 1854 to 1859, succeeded by Phelemon C. Merrill. Carmen R. Smith and Talana S. Hooper’s biography, working from the county court minutes, has Merrill in office only briefly in 1859, Smith reappointed that March and serving as sheriff under Judge Samuel Richards on March 11, 1861, and again after his cavalry service, in October and November 1862 and March 1863 (Lot Smith: Mormon Pioneer and American Frontiersman (2018), notes to the early chapters). So the Morrisite and posse-side accounts are right to call him sheriff in 1861–62. Anderson also has him acting as sheriff on December 8, 1861 (p. 82). Known Williams’s charge, made eleven years after the siege. The Morrisite letters printed in the Salt Lake Tribune in 1891 give Lot Smith a part before the siege, not in it: they say he came with about twenty armed men when Taylor and Woodruff met the South Weber branch on February 11, 1861, and that as sheriff at Farmington he collected the fines laid on the Morrisites for missing militia drill and attached their property, until he was “ashamed to take more” (letters 7–9 of “The Elder,” July 12, 19 and 26, 1891, p. 3; see Newspapers). Richard W. Young, writing in 1890 from the posse’s side, also says that “Lot Smith, sheriff of Davis County, while attempting to levy an execution, was met by armed men and ordered away from the place” before the siege, but does not name him among the posse (The Contributor 11, no. 9 (July 1890): 348–49). That may be why Williams named him with Burton. John L. Bear, in the fort, remembered Lot Smith trying to take the Parks family’s horse to cover the $25 drill fine (“And you want to take a $75.00 horse for $25.00”), again before the siege (autobiography, circa 1908, MS 10240, Church History Library, p. 24). He was a witness for the prosecution at the trial of the Morrisites for resisting process in March 1863, but the report does not record what he said (Deseret News, March 25, 1863, p. 5). Lot Smith does not appear on the posse returns kept by Deputy Marshal Theodore McKean (MS 33041, Church History Library; see the posse chart), though the returns may not be complete. The horse incident is in the Chronology (Dec 1861), with Eardley’s fuller account. To settle it Smith’s June 1862 telegrams to Brigham Young (Brigham Young office files, Church History Library, CR 1234 1), which should say where he was; the Lot Smith papers at the University of Utah (MS 0004); the company’s muster rolls; and Burton’s report of June 1862. Did one posse member die, or two? Answered Answer Two. Jared Smith, aged nineteen, was shot on June 13, 1862, the first day of the siege, “killed by a rifle ball from the fort” (Deseret Evening News, March 7, 1879, p. 2). Peter Wahler, about twenty-four, was shot through the head on June 15, the day of the surrender. Joseph J. Romney, captain of fifty, who went with the volunteers under James Lewis to take a house on the west side about half an hour before the surrender, testified at Burton’s trial: “as we entered one man was shot by a ball coming from the northwest part of the fort. He was a Danishman and fell and blocked the door” (Salt Lake Herald, March 1, 1879, p. 3). Wilford Woodruff’s journal for June 15 names him as “Peter Wahlen,” and the Deseret News of June 18 reports the deaths of “Smith and Wahler.” According to the transcription in his FamilySearch record, Robert T. Burton’s June 1862 report to Brigham Young (Brigham Young office files, Church History Library, CR 1234 1) sent home “the remains of Peter Wahler, 24 years old,” of the 1st Battalion, 3rd Regiment of Infantry, and said Burton could find no relatives of his in the territory. He was buried in the Salt Lake City Cemetery, where the sexton recorded the name a

t: Who were the men held after the siege who are not on the roll?
s: Who were the men held after the siege who are not on the roll? In progress Known Of the ninety-eight men the Deseret News of June 25, 1862, names as brought before Judge Kinney, eighty-one match names on the 1861–62 roll, eight are uncertain matches, and nine are not on the roll at all: L. Parr, S. Williamsen, J. P. Sorensen, H. Okensen, S. P. Rasmusson, J. E. Reese, J. C. Edwards, Saml. Hulse, and Peter Moffat. Three names first counted here turned out to be on the roll under other spellings, found through the emigrant company rosters of the Church History Biographical Database: J. G. Lousley is Loasle, John C. (Hans Kasper Loosli), John Trehan is Trahern, John, and Wm. Rogers is one of the roll’s two William Rodgers. Family Tree searches in November 2026 found no Morrisite tie for the other nine. They may have joined after the roll was drawn up, been in the fort without joining, or be misprinted. All nine are on the list of prisoners taken at the surrender on June 15, 1862, and brought to Salt Lake City, which gives each man’s birthplace and age (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; names as read from the manuscript): Labroch Par (Switzerland, 23), Soren Willison (Denmark, 46), Hans Okenson (Sweden, 23), Sorn P. Rasmerson (Denmark, 25), John E. Reese (South Wales, 44), John C. Edwards (South Wales, 38), Saml. Hulse (England, 30) and Peter Moffatt (Scotland, 22). In place of J. P. Sorensen the list has John Peter Lorenson (Denmark, 46); the roll’s John Peter Lorensen was born in Denmark in 1817, so “Sorensen” is very probably a misprint for him. Five of the nine were tried in March 1863: John Peter Sorenson, Soren Peter Rasmussen, John E. Reese, John C. Edwards and Peter Moffat are among the men found guilty of resisting an officer and fined $100 (Documents), and Harding’s pardon names all of them but Moffat, with Soren Willissen besides (Documents). Par, Okenson and Hulse appear in neither. So these men were taken in the fort and dealt with as Morrisites, which makes it likely that they joined after the roll was drawn up; who they were, and what became of them, is still open. Where to look The register of arrests of Morrisites, 1863, in the Gordon M. Howard papers (Mss B 279, box 2, folder 6), Utah State Historical Society; the 1860 census for Weber and Davis counties; ward records for South Weber and Slaterville; Val Holley, “Slouching Towards Slaterville” (2008), which names Slaterville and Marriott men among the prisoners. Are the January 1860 revelations in Morris’s hand? Answered (probably) Known The two revelations of January 14 and 16, 1860, are unsigned except as from “Jesus Christ,” name “my servant Joseph,” and share wording with Nos. 18 and 185 of The Spirit Prevails (Documents). Kirk Watson has compared the hand with a revelation of October 11, 1858, filed among the “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” in Brigham Young’s office files, and identifies it as Morris’s; the dating formula, letter forms and spelling agree (Documents). A comparison with a letter Morris signed in his own name would settle it. Where to look The folder “Revelations of Joseph Morris, 1858–1860” and Morris’s signed letters in the same files (CR 1234 1), viewable in the Church History Library catalog; other anonymous letters of 1858–61 in the same series. What happened at the Farmington court-martial of 1861? Open Known Forscutt’s “Sketch of Joseph Morris” says members of Morris’s First Council, among them John Parson, John and Richard Cook, and Forscutt himself, were summoned before a militia court-martial at Farmington in 1861 for refusing militia training, and that Forscutt was fined $56.80 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28–29, 34–35, 51). The 1861 territorial militia records checked so far (Utah State Archives, series 2210) contain no trace of it. A Morrisite letter of 1891 says that in September 1861 the square of the fort was named as a drill ground for the neighboring settlements, that the Morrisites stayed indoors, and that the fine for missing drill, three dollars at first, rose to thirty, forty, fifty or sixty dollars, collected by Lot Smith as sheriff, beginning with Morris (“The Morrisite Tragedy,” letter 8 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 19, 1891, p. 3). Forscutt’s diary, kept at the time, confirms the collector: on December 7, 1861, “Lot Smith came and read to the brethren” the fines, now $56.80, which they refused to pay (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62 (“Pettitt’s Pocket Diary for 1860”), Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Where to look Records of the Davis Military District of the Nauvoo Legion; Davis County court records; Woodruff’s journal and the Journal History for 1861; any later reference in the 1862 writs or the 1863 trials. When was the photograph of Morris taken, and who is with him? Open Known Anderson (Revisited, 118) dates the only known photograph of Morris to about 1841, in England, and identifies the man beside him as his older brother William, who came to America only after 1862. Commercial photography reached England only in 1841, and the second man looks much older than Morris, while family trees make William about two years his senior. Others date the picture about 1860. William, “next older then Joseph,” first came to Utah with his family in the fall of 1862, after Joseph’s death (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, p. 122), so a picture of the two together would have been taken in England, before Joseph emigrated. Where to look The original image and its owner; Anderson’s research files at USU (Caine MSS 10); Morris family descendants in England and Utah; the photographic process and studio, if a mount or case survives.
