t: How and when did the Montana church end?
s: How and when did the Montana church end? Open Known George Johnson presided at the Lord’s House until shortly before his death on April 29, 1954. Anderson calls him the last official Morrisite leader and dates the end to his death: by the 1940s fewer than a dozen members were active, and when Johnson died the church came to an end and the Lord’s House was boarded up (Revisited, pp. 212, 214). Surviving Morrisites, all of the second or third generation, still gathered at the Lord’s House on August 9, 1969, the anniversary of its dedication and one of the church’s two feast days, though by then the gatherings were more social than religious (p. 218). Anderson’s sources included his own interviews with Henry Hendrikson (1969) and Robert Johnson (1968). The finding aid for the Morrisite collection at Utah State University (Caine MSS 10) says the church officially disbanded in 1969, and the description of Anderson’s papers says that meetings were held irregularly until 1969, when it formally disbanded. In July 1899 the church was still meeting: a Latter-day Saint missionary held a meeting at Race Track, lodged with “Mr Hendrickson,” and was shown “the Eternal Rounds” by a Morrisite family, the Petersons, near Warm Springs (John Welch, missionary journal, July 15–18, 1899, MS 29881, Church History Library). Don Cornelius, interviewing in the valley in 1962, found a woman of one of the founding families acting as the “nominal leader” of the Morrisites’ descendants (“Mormonism in Montana,” 1962, p. 65). The local paper, at the time, supports Anderson’s date: Johnson’s obituary calls the church “almost extinct these days” (Silver State Post, May 7, 1954, p. 7); the 1958 obituary of Andrew Hendrickson’s daughter Mary Ann Goldie calls the “House of the Lord Church” no longer active (March 28, 1958, p. 12); and in 1962 the new valley historical society spoke of “the Morrisite church which was located at one time” in the south valley (July 27, 1962, p. 7). See Newspapers. Earlier, the church nearly broke up: after a division in 1891–92, Eardley in April 1901 called the members together “to prevent if possible the threatened collapse of God’s little church” (Eardley to Hendrickson, April 22, 1901, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1893–1901). What conflicts Small details differ even in the papers: a 1954 feature has Johnson reaching Montana “early in 1874,” his obituary and a 1956 article 1873. Henry Hendrickson, who had left the valley in 1908, told Cornelius in 1962 that the church faded about 1919–20 (interview, April 19, 1962, transcript pp. 8–10, 18; see Repositories), and Cornelius has the movement dying with Andrew Hendrikson and George Johnson, though he misdates Johnson’s death to the early 1930s. The two dates may describe different things: Anderson’s 1954 marks the end of the church as a led and worshipping body, while the 1969 of the USU descriptions may rest on the last of the feast-day gatherings, or on some formal act not yet found. No record made at the time has yet been seen for this guide: who, if anyone, presided after 1954, how often the survivors met, and what, if anything, formally ended the church are all unknown. Where to look The Morrisite collection at USU (Caine MSS 10), whose dates run to 1975, and Anderson’s papers there, including his 1968–69 interviews; the Deer Lodge Silver State Post (online for 1893–1963 through Newspapers.com), where Johnson’s obituary has now been found, for any report of meetings between 1954 and 1963; the Butte Montana Standard; local papers around August 1969, on microfilm at the Montana Historical Society; Powell County deed records for the Lord’s House land; and family memories, which descendants are invited to share.

t: What does Forscutt’s shorthand diary say about the spring of 1862?
s: What does Forscutt’s shorthand diary say about the spring of 1862? In progress Known Mark H. Forscutt, clerk of Morris’s First Council, kept a pocket diary at Kington Fort from December 1861. Its longhand entries run to April 1862 (see the Chronology); from April 24, 1862, he wrote in shorthand, and about twenty pages of the diary, covering the weeks before and during the siege, have never been transcribed. The shorthand is not Pitman’s or any other published system that has been identified, but an alphabetic system of his own, and Forscutt wrote out its alphabet on the inside back cover of his 1867 journal. Alan Bernthal-Hooker, an English mathematics teacher, worked out the system in 2026, beginning from shorthand passages beside longhand names, and the shorthand pages of the 1860–62 diary have been photographed for the editor’s edition of Forscutt’s writings. They may hold an eyewitness record of May and June 1862: the drill, the Foreshadowing, the writs and the siege itself. Where to look The original, in the Mark Hill Forscutt Collection (Vault MSS 811), L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University; a microfilm of the 1860–62 notebook at the Church History Library (MS 17393, “Journal, 1860–1862”). Help with the transcription is welcome; write to contact@morrisite.org. Questions of interpretation

t: Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from?
s: Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from? Open Why it matters Morris, Williams, Davies and the Doves all taught that spirits return to the earth in new bodies. The Latter-day Saint church never adopted the doctrine, but it was not unheard of among Latter-day Saints in the 1850s: Kirk Watson notes that the apostle Orson Hyde taught a form of it from 1846 to 1850, that Brigham Young and Wilford Woodruff later blamed Hyde when a belief called “baby resurrection” spread among church members in the 1850s, and that it was discussed in church meetings at Manti, in Sanpete County, in 1858–59 (there Bishop Warren S. Snow called the doctrine of “various ‘probations’” “not impossible but also not desirable” on December 5, 1858, and on July 3, 1859 said he “did not know how many Probations men had passed”; Manti Ward general minutes, Historical record, 1857–1859, Church History Library, LR 5253 11, images 130 and 222; passages located by Watson), and that it is arguably implicit in the Nauvoo teaching that people may become gods. A Swedish copy of an article attributed to Morris teaches that the resurrection “takes place by birth,” the spirits being “brought forth by immortal parents” (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, p. 62, Church History Library, MS 31876; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude), which is close to what Young rejected; see Teachings. Morris applied it to himself: in “The Order of Sevens” he taught that Seth had filled a second mission as Moses and was filling his third as Joseph Morris, and that Enos had returned as Elijah and then as Joseph Smith (The Spirit Prevails, p. 645; also pp. 665–66, and Morris to Brigham Young, November 21, 1860, Church History Library, CR 1234 1, in Watson, p. 47; references supplied by Kirk Watson). Where the Morrisites got it bears on how early Mormon ideas were carried and reshaped by dissenters. What has been proposed C. LeRoy Anderson suggested that Morris took the idea from Charles B. Thompson, leader of an earlier Latter Day Saint offshoot, reasoning that it had “no counterpart in orthodox Mormon theology.” Kirk Watson disputes this: the idea was circulating among Latter-day Saints in the 1850s; Anderson assumes Morris held it from the early 1850s, while the written record, including Joseph Dove’s understanding, says Morris “received it by revelation in 1859”; the two men’s theologies differ widely, Morris building on Nauvoo teaching about God that Thompson opposed, though both dwell on the patriarchs of Genesis; and no contact between them is known, as Anderson himself acknowledged, nor does either mention the other (Watson, correspondence with the editor, November 2026; he made the same case publicly in Watson, Scriptural Mormonism, Ep. 113, November 14, 2026, at 22:31–23:12). More generally, Watson finds that belief in reincarnation in Mormon history seldom passed from one person or book to another; far more often it came to someone by revelation and was then fitted into an existing Mormon theology (Watson, Ep. 113, at 35:36–36:06). Where Morris was when the idea reached him is still open. The records place him at Provo in 1857, where his ward disciplined him during the Reformation and where his first revelation is dated (see Chronology); Watson has found no record of him in the Sanpete minutes before he came forward as a prophet (correspondence with the editor, November 2026). In Davies’s community Watson summarizes Davies’s teaching as the incarnation of God the Father and Jesus Christ in two of Davies’s children, with Davies himself identified with the Holy Ghost (Watson, Ep. 113, at 24:21–24:38). Sworn testimony in the 1880 suit against William W. Davies shows how fully his branch held the doctrine. Witnesses on both sides described it: V. D. Lambert said Davies’s missionaries in San Francisco were teaching “the reincarnation of the souls” by 1868, that Davies was presented as Adam, Abraham, Noah and David returned, and that members who died would come back in new bodies and remain in the Kingdom; Christian Miller, still a member, said “the Spirit leaves the body at death & returns and is reincarnated”; and S. W. Wood listed reincarnation among the community’s principles. Davies himself testified that “the doctrine of reincarnation is taught and believed,” and five more members on his side, among them Broer Sorenson of the 1861–62 roll, described the same belief: that the soul lives on after death and returns to the earth in another body. Peter C. Klemgard, who had been at Kington Fort, told the court that the doctrine taught at the Davies camp was “not like the Morrisite religion” (Cilley, Evans and Courtney v. Davies, 1880–81, Washington State Archives; see Repositories). Other claimants Similar ideas appear in groups with no known Morrisite tie. James Brighouse seems to have taught reincarnation only after he left Missouri and returned to Utah (see the chronology under 1884). Israel A. J. Dennis (born 1852), a former Methodist holiness preacher and Seventh-day Adventist from Illinois, came to believe about 1881 that he was the reincarnation of the biblical Jacob, or Israel; he was briefly a member of the RLDS Church, organized a “Church of the First Born” in Kansas in 1889, joined the Latter-day Saints in Utah in 1890, and refounded his Church of the First Born in 1895. Watson finds several possible sources for that name, among them an Illinois sect that believed in reincarnation, a faith-healing church in New Jersey, and the Morrisites, but no evidence of contact with the Morrisites (Watson, “Newsie Messiah,” JWHA, 2024, and correspondence). In the later church In George Williams’s founding vision he learned, as Watson tells it, that he had been Cainan and then Melchizedek before he was George Williams: in his account of his second interview with celestial beings, Seth and Enos lay their hands on him and declare him “Cainan, then Melchisedec, now George Williams” (“A Description of Interviews with

t: Is there a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s?
s: Is there a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s? Open Why it matters Chad Daybell, an Idaho author of Latter-day Saint end-times novels, was convicted in 2024 of three murders committed in 2019 and sentenced to death. Prosecutors said he used apocalyptic prophecy and stories of possession by evil spirits to justify the killings (Associated Press, June 1, 2024). Some of what he taught resembles Morrisite teaching, and the two are now compared in print and online. Whether the likeness means descent or only a shared background bears on how ideas travel along the margins of the Latter-day Saint tradition. Likenesses Earlier lives revealed by a seer. In 1869 Williams told converts at Council Bluffs and Omaha who they had been. Carlton Fellows had been Jonas, father of Simon Peter, and Maren Fellows had been Abigail, who “after Nabal’s death was married to King David” (record book, 1869, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In January 2019 Daybell sent a document listing past lives for Lori Vallow, among them the wife of the prophet Moroni, and saying that he had been James the Just, married to her (FOX 10 Phoenix). Marriage across lives. A friend of Vallow’s testified that the two told her they had been married in a previous life (NPR, May 30, 2024). The name “Church of the Firstborn.” The Montana records are catalogued under it, and it was used in Daybell’s circle. Both took it from Latter-day Saint scripture (Doctrine and Covenants 76:54, 76:94, 93:22), and Israel A. J. Dennis’s Church of the First Born, above, shows how readily the name could arise on its own. An end close at hand. The Morrisites at Kington Fort awaited deliverance, and Sven Olson Hagg wrote in 1866 that their three and a half years of waiting were ending (see the chronology under 1865–66); Daybell, too, foretold an imminent end. Differences Daybell rated people on a scale of light and dark and taught that a person overcome by a dark spirit became a “zombie” whose body had to die (NPR, May 30, 2024). Christopher Blythe, who studies Latter-day Saint apocalypticism, has said he never saw that idea promoted in any Mormon group, nor “an LDS account that claimed someone’s identity was permanently taken over” (interview with Jana Riess, Religion News Service, August 18, 2020). Nothing of the kind appears in the Morrisite records read for this guide. In 1882 George Thompson, writing for the dying Williams, warned the Montana Saints not to “pray too much or they will invite foul spirits around them” (MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1879–1882), and the Montana councils met defiance with trials, exclusion and shunning (see the chronology under 1873). The violence in Morrisite history was done to the Morrisites, at Kington Fort. What has been proposed No source known to the editor shows Daybell drawing on Morris, Williams or Davies. Blythe traces his ideas to a modern prophecy subculture on the margins of the church, which grew out of nineteenth-century visionary culture and drew on visionaries such as Julie Rowe, Michael Stroud and Douglas Mendenhall (Blythe, “The Daybells and Latter-day Saint Apocalypticism,” Sightings, February 27, 2020, and the Riess interview). The phrase “multiple mortal probations,” used for past lives in Daybell’s circle, is current among some Mormon fundamentalist groups (Cristina Rosetti, quoted by FOX 10 Phoenix). Any common ground with the Morrisites probably lies further back, in the reincarnation ideas that circulated among Latter-day Saints in the 1840s and 1850s (see the question above). From there the paths divide: Williams’s teaching about earlier lives stayed doctrinal, while Daybell’s merged with a demonology of possession. Where to start Christopher James Blythe, Terrible Revolution: Latter-day Saints and the American Apocalypse (Oxford University Press, 2020); the 1869 record book in MS 31876 (see Repositories); reporting of the 2023 and 2024 trials in Boise; Rosetti’s work on Mormon fundamentalist theology.

t: Did the Prophet Cainan read birthrights by phrenology?
s: Did the Prophet Cainan read birthrights by phrenology? Open The page A typescript fragment in the Morrisite collection at Utah State University (Caine Coll. MSS 10, box 3, folder 7, p. 29) is filed after a general invitation dated at Soda Springs, August 12, 1863, to “the Scattered Sheep of Joseph to Come to Meet the Prophet of the Lord.” A note in the margin says it “does not follow logically” from that page, and its writer, date and recipient are lost. Kirk Watson prints both pages in The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026), pp. 90–91, and the quotations here follow his text. In substance, the fragment says that the Prophet, staying incognito at Cottonwood, told two visitors, a Brother Smith and Niel Beck, their priesthood by laying a hand on their heads (he “felt it Phrenologically”); that birthrights, known for now by inspiration, would in future be something “all will know by science”; that no descendant of Cain would be admitted to the Church; and that about twenty years of preaching would come before Moses and Christ. Kirk Watson brought the page to the guide’s attention. Who was the Prophet? The page does not name him. Watson identifies him as George Williams, the Prophet Cainan: the page was filed with the invitation, which USU’s indexes call “Cainan to Scattered Sheep of Joseph”; “Joseph” and the coming of Moses, whom the Morrisites identified with Morris, fit Cainan’s teaching rather than Joseph Smith’s; Cainan called himself a prophet; and Anderson describes him as living in secret. Cainan stayed in the Salt Lake area until 1869 (Anderson, Revisited, p. 168). Watson also notes a vision Cainan is said to have had in Little Cottonwood Canyon, which may or may not bear on the page’s “Cottonwood” (Watson, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). Who was meant by Cain? In Brigham Young’s Utah, “seed of Cain” usually meant people of African descent, and Williams had been a Latter-day Saint. But Morris taught that Cain was the son of the serpent, “Lucifer, the devil,” and a fallen angel, that a third of Adam’s children belong to Cain, and that Cain “claims the right to enter into the Church” (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 12–13, 448, 660–61, 664). The page’s promise reads like an answer to that claim, and its appeal to phrenology and “science” fits Morris’s meaning: if spirits return in new bodies, a birthright could be read from the body. Watson favors this reading. The Spirit Prevails also links the seed of Cain with “Gentile blood” (pp. 651–52), so a racial sense in how the teaching was heard cannot be ruled out. Why it matters Phrenology was widely popular in the 1840s, and Latter-day Saint leaders were divided over it, but Cainan may be the only Latter Day Saint leader known to have made it part of his religion. If Niel Beck is Niels R. Beck of Deer Lodge, the page is also the earliest known link between him and the Morrisite leadership, years before he sent money to William W. Davies, who testified in 1881 that “Mr. Beck is not a member.” Where to start The page and its neighbors in Caine MSS 10, box 3, folder 7 (the fragment and the 1863 invitation filed with it are printed in Kirk Watson’s edition, pp. 90–91), with the collection’s item indexes, which are available from USU Special Collections; Cainan’s letters and revelations in the same collection; Anderson’s chapters on Williams; The Spirit Prevails on Cain; the literature on phrenology among Latter Day Saints (a starting point is Wikipedia’s overview). Williams’s own words A letter in Williams’s hand supports the fragment on one point. On October 18, 1876, he wrote to William James that the “common Salvation” had “taken in negroes, Indians and every vile spirit that transgressed the righteous laws in their first estate,” that these “must be ruled over in this & every estate,” and that “our merciful God gave keys of detection, that if possible they may not press into our borders” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877). The letter does not say what the keys were. It does not mention phrenology. A letter of Williams’s of August 28, 1878, also supports the fragment’s setting: it recalls that Beck visited him “at Cottonwood” and left intending to follow him with “two wagons & much cattle” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881). The fragment says that “Niel Beck” visited the Prophet at Cottonwood, which agrees with Watson’s identification of the Prophet as Williams.

t: How did believers survive failed prophecy?
s: How did believers survive failed prophecy? Open Why it matters Morris set days for the Second Coming that passed; he was killed in the siege; Williams told the Montana Saints that the City of the great King would come down in their region, “the Sides of the North”; Davies proclaimed his infant son the Messiah. Yet the movement lasted more than ninety years. Who stayed, who left, and how they explained what happened are open questions. First findings The revelations show how the first disappointment was explained. On December 30, 1861, Christ promised to come “to-morrow morning” if those present consecrated all their property (The Spirit Prevails, Nos. 188–189, pp. 338–39). When the morning passed, a revelation of January 6, 1862, blamed those who had consecrated unwillingly; one of January 11 refused to make any further promise about the time; and in February deliverance was promised after the people had taken an oath (Nos. 195, 199 and 224, pp. 350, 359, 419). Three revelations of January 1, 5 and 6, 1862, left out of The Spirit Prevails but kept in manuscript copies, go further: the dated promises “have failed, because they were intended to fail,” for “if I had told them the naked truth, I could not have led them on at all”; Morris himself complains that the people will “deny everything,” and is answered with a threat that many thousands in the territory will die within days (Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f1, pp. 250–55, and f2, Nos. 177–178, Community of Christ Library Archives; see the Chronology, 1–6 Jan 1862). Josiah D. Price dates the consecration to December 30, 1861, and the swearing of the oath to February 12, 1862 (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). In June 1862 an angel speaking in tongues told the camp that on his own earth the faithful had also set dates and been disappointed, and that the error lay not in setting them but in refusing to give them up (Watson, pp. 76–77). Williams’s letter of January 6, 1879, set no date at all, but in Montana William James looked in 1880 for the coming of Christ in 1891, “11 years more” (minutes, May 10, 1880, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1880). When 1891 came, President Andrew Hendrikson told the church’s court that they had long been led to expect “that in the present year the ‘winding up scene’ would take place,” and that he still trusted Williams’s promise that he would live to see the Second Coming; John R. Eardley looked to a coming war of the nations and to a new prophet, Mahalaleel, and compared the waiting Saints to the wise and foolish virgins (court minutes, November 10, 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1891). See Teachings. Where to start The revelations and testimonies of 1862 in Kirk Watson’s edition; Williams’s letters at USU; the Davies material; the literature that began with Festinger, When Prophecy Fails; changes in membership over time (cited, not published as lists).

t: How did a prophet’s movement become a church run by vote?
s: How did a prophet’s movement become a church run by vote? Open Why it matters Authority passed from Morris’s revelations to Williams’s letters from afar, then to presidents elected at yearly general assemblies (1883, 1886) and to Danish lay leaders who had never been Latter-day Saints. Few movements of the period document that change so closely. Where to start Court and Council minutes and the Cainan letters in the Morrisite collection at USU (Caine MSS 10); the Montana minutebook, 1881–1890, and the Cainan letters at the Church History Library (MS 32226 and MS 31876, both online); Anderson’s chapters on the Montana church; the sociology of schism and of the routinization of charisma. First findings Williams himself began to spread authority. His letter of April 2, 1877, created “the Court of the Lord’s House,” three officers meeting every May 10, and later also every November 10, “that a portion of the weight of this infant Kingdom may not rest upon one,” with a report to go to him “for approval”; yet the same year he wrote that the next servant “will be chosen of God, not by man” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1876–1878, and Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877). After his death the court and the yearly assemblies chose the leaders; in 1887 Hendrikson reminded the church that it was “a trial to some” when Williams wrote that “the People should meet on the anniversary day and elect their President” (Minutes, 1886–1887). In July 1881 the dying Williams appointed George Thompson to act “in his stead,” but Thompson sent the appointment to Montana “for their approval or disapproval” (Thompson to the Montana brethren, August 21, 1881, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1878–1881).

t: Why were so many Morrisites Scandinavian?
s: Why were so many Morrisites Scandinavian? Open Why it matters Danish speakers were prominent from the start: Morris’s revelations circulated in Danish, the Omaha and Council Bluffs congregations kept Danish-language records in 1869, and the last Montana leaders were Danish immigrants. Judged by name alone, 168 of the 430 people on the roll have Scandinavian names (Who they were), and in 1889 Joseph Smith III found the old Morrisites at Soda Springs to be mainly Swedes, Norwegians, and Danes (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 437). Disappointment after emigration, language, poverty, and patterns of recruitment are all possible explanations. Where to start The 1886 roll of membership compared with Scandinavian Mission emigration records; the Danish-language material at USU; emigrant letters and Danish-language newspapers.

t: What became of the spiritual gifts?
s: What became of the spiritual gifts? Open Why it matters Speaking in tongues, interpreted tongues, and messages from angels were central at Kington Fort, as in the “3rd Captain of the Lord’s Host” testimony of June 1862. An interpretation of tongues of June 7, 1862, teaches that the gifts cease only at the resurrection and charges that a council in Brigham Young’s house decided to put them down (Watson, pp. 70–72). How Morrisite practice compares with the Latter-day Saint church in the 1850s has not been studied closely. First findings In Montana the gifts lasted at least into the 1880s, but they were brought under the council’s control. On March 26, 1881, the Race Track council examined a member who said that “spirits” influenced him and who had told his dreams in meeting. Rasmus Rasmussen cited Williams’s answer that the Evil One could give an influence that seemed good but was false, and a “key” of Joseph Morris’s for testing dreams. President Andrew Hendrikson ruled that anyone who would speak in tongues in a public meeting was led by the wrong influence, because God’s spirit would assist only in what the meeting was appointed for and would never lead anyone to overstep the order of the church (minutes, March 26, 1881, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1881; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Whether the gifts survived later in the century is not known. Where to start Kirk Watson’s edition; The Spirit Prevails; studies of spiritual gifts and the Reformation of 1856–57 in Utah.

t: Where did the rituals come from?
s: Where did the rituals come from? Open Why it matters The scepters, Morris’s robe and crown, the ceremony at Kington Fort in May 1862 that Anderson calls the Foreshadowing Ceremony, the holding of goods in common there, and later communal experiments at Walla Walla and in the Order of Enoch. Their relation to Latter-day Saint temple ritual and to the church’s own communal programs is unexplored. Where to start The scepters and their inscriptions (see Repositories); Anderson, Revisited, 116–17; The Spirit Prevails; Davies’s 1881 deposition in Kirk Watson’s edition. First findings Josiah D. Price’s journal describes the rites of May 1862 at Kington Fort: the four horsemen ridden by Morris, Cook, Banks and Parson on May 1, the soldier’s oath sworn by the companies on May 26, and the order of the Foreshadowing procession of May 30, with William Harris in the bishop’s robe; it also copies the inscription of Morris’s scepter and an oath sworn by members, who kissed “the written word of the Lord” (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives; see the Chronology). An onlooker’s letter of June 2, 1862, describes the procession of May 30 (Morris’s seven-crowned hat and seven-braided horse, Cook’s sword, Banks’s balances, Parson’s book); a form for ordaining an “elect lady” with consecrated oil survives from 1861; and copies made on June 19, 1862, of the inscriptions on three rods show them numbered five, six and seven, for Hugh Park, John Eames and Daniel Smith, beside Morris’s own (Brigham Young office files, CR 1234 1, and Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; see Teachings). In Montana the robe was prescribed by letter. Williams told William James in February 1874 to wear “a linen robe large and broad, reaching down to the feet,” saying that Morris had wanted his ministers so clothed, and in April 1877 sent a pattern for a fuller white robe with an embroidered sun, “in semblance to the Celestial attiring of the Celestial Priesthood.” James wore it to administer the sacrament in 1880 and to preside at the court in 1881. Williams also set out the dedication rite for the Lord’s House (1878) and the blessing of children (1879) (Church History Library, MS 31876, letters to Montana, 1874–1879; see Teachings).

t: What did Morris teach about marriage, and what did women do in the movement?
s: What did Morris teach about marriage, and what did women do in the movement? Open Why it matters Later writers often describe Morris as an opponent of plural marriage; Kirk Watson’s introduction argues that he accepted it as a celestial principle. Women’s part in the gifts, in testimony, and in the community has hardly been studied. First findings Morris’s own article on celestial marriage, dated June 4, 1861, falls between the two readings: the biblical law of many wives and concubines was given for this life, “not being a celestial law,” and kings and prophets who had many wives “can have but one sealed to them each for eternity” (The Spirit Prevails, pp. 651–52). An angel’s testimony through Morris in June 1862 calls polygamy true “in its proper time and place” (Watson, p. 78), and Morris did not authorize it at Kington Fort, treating it as belonging to a future time (Watson, p. 8 n. 8). Morris’s successor George Williams departed from his rule of one wife for eternity: while saying he had “never taught the doctrine or counselled the practice,” he kept the household he had formed as a Latter-day Saint, with Susannah and Louisa, and in 1871 taught that a high priest takes “one Daughter of each God” in the eternities (see George Williams). By 1899 the movement’s own history in Gems of Inspiration condemned polygamy outright, citing the Book of Mormon and the 1890 Manifesto, which may be where the later tradition began. Morris’s marriage rite of August 23, 1861, distinguishes two covenants. Ordinary couples, before a high priest, each give “my hand and heart in a marriage covenant for time”; the bride alone vows to keep herself “from all others,” while the groom pledges to be “a true and faithful husband” (The Spirit Prevails, No. 89, pp. 129–30; a manuscript copy of the bride’s part is in the Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f6). The prophet and prophetess alone were sealed “for time and all eternity” (No. 33, January 7, 1861, pp. 44–45). See Teachings. In Montana, Williams had a woman ordained to the priesthood. In January 1877 he wrote that “a Sister be ordained special for your Stake as High Priestess” to “minister to the Sisterhood in all things for their good, temporal & spiritual”; Sister Rasmussen was to take “a vow” and be ordained by Hendrikson and his counselor “in the pattern shown,” and Williams planned “a quorum of three” sisters (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877, and Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1876–1878). She had died by March 1881, when the Race Track council noted that “no one was appointed in her place” and Hendrikson said he had had no answer from Williams about it (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1881; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In 1882 Thompson asked the church to fill “the place of Sister Rasmuson”; women and girls voted in the election of 1886 (Minutes, 1886–1887). Where to start The Spirit Prevails; Kirk Watson’s introduction and sources; Emma Thompson Just’s letters in Agnes Just Reid, Letters of Long Ago; the Anderson plaque and other family accounts. How has the Morrisite War been remembered? Open Why it matters The descendants’ bronze plaque at Soda Springs, the 2006 monument at South Weber, folk traditions such as the street burial, and the church’s 1903 reply to the Andersons, which blamed the Morrisites, each tell a different story of the same three days. The 2006 monument The inscription on the Kington Fort–Morrisite War Site monument (Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128) is the version most visitors read. It calls the fort “a 645 foot by 645 foot enclosure,” puts the population at over 200, says that a cannon ball “killed two women and seriously wounded a teenage girl,” that “as the army assaulted the fort and breached the gates, two militiamen were killed,” and that “in the ensuing confusion, Morris, his second in command, John Banks and two more women were killed. In all, eleven people died” (inscription as photographed in December 2008, MO-IMG-001). The eyewitness accounts on the Morrisite War page tell it differently: the two posse men died during the siege, and Morris was shot after the surrender, not in confusion during an assault. The monument’s eleven includes the two posse men; the Morrisite letters of 1891 count eleven Morrisites. The 645-foot figure has not been found in an earlier source. New Where to start The plaque transcription (Images); the monument text; the 1903 file (CR 1 191); the Newspapers page, whose coverage chart shows when the press returned to the story: the 1877 national stories at Burton’s arrest, the 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letters retelling the siege from the Morrisite side, and the 1907 exchange in the Brisbane Truth; Daniel H. Wells’s 1870 letter in the militia dispute, which printed Acting Governor Fuller’s order for the posse (Documents); oral histories at USU and Weber State University.

t: How has the Morrisite story been passed down, and where do the common errors come from?
s: How has the Morrisite story been passed down, and where do the common errors come from? Open Why it matters The same errors turn up again and again (see Common errors in print), and tracing them shows how the story has moved. Some begin in the press of 1862, when one telegraphic dispatch was copied across the country and changed as it went. Some come from the partisan retellings of the 1880s and 1890s, on both sides. Some come from family memory, which is often right about people and places and less sure about dates: Eliza Eardley Hardin remembered Willow Glen’s founding in 1881, the newspapers first mention it in 1882. And some come from scholarship itself, as later works summarized earlier ones without returning to the records; even the federal gazetteer places the Willow Glen post office about a mile from where the 1882 paper put it. Today the story also travels by online video, where short pieces often borrow one another’s descriptions; their errors are those listed in Common errors, above all the claim that Morris broke away over polygamy. Who told the story, to whom, and why are questions for the history of memory as well as of the movement. Where to start The Newspapers page, which follows the 1862 dispatch through its reprints; the 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letters and Richard W. Young’s “The Morrisite War” in the Contributor (1889–90); the theses and their sources (Bibliography); oral histories such as the 1962 Hendrickson interview (Repositories); the Hardin reminiscence (SC 788, Montana Historical Society Library & Archives; see Repositories); C. LeRoy Anderson’s notes at USU, which show what he had in hand.

t: How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?
s: How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? In progress Why it matters Many Morrisites, and many of their children, ended in the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (RLDS, now Community of Christ). The move came not at once but in waves over sixty years, following the break-up of the movement itself: soon after the siege in Utah and Idaho, then among George Williams’s followers at Omaha, in Nevada and in California, then in Montana, and last among the young people of the Race Track church. Other Morrisites returned to the Latter-day Saint church. The Morrisites were not the first to bring reincarnation into the Reorganization: Kirk Watson notes that after Charles B. Thompson’s group broke up in the late 1850s, many of his followers joined the RLDS Church, some keeping the belief (Watson, Scriptural Mormonism, Ep. 113, November 14, 2026, at 16:07–16:58; see Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from?). First findings Soon after the siege (1863–1873). Mark H. Forscutt joined the Reorganization in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear also joined it, at Malad on November 29, 1869, and preached in the Cache and Bear Lake valleys; about 1870 a man at Bear Lake whom he had once seen at Weber ordering the Morrisites to drill told him that if the Josephites did not clear out, “we will serve you the same way as we did the Morrisites” (Baer, autobiography, MS 10240, pp. 42, 45). RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptized several people on the roll in 1865, and Robert Murdock baptized Josiah D. Price in Oneida County, Idaho, on February 3, 1867 (Price’s journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). Robert E. Farley joined in Nebraska in 1870, and Erick and Caroline Eliason were baptized together at Soda Springs, a Morrisite settlement, on June 9, 1870, which suggests the RLDS mission reached the community there directly. Not everyone was received: Alexander Dow sought fellowship at St. Louis and was refused over charges laid against him; Joseph Smith III advised in 1870 that he ask the St. Louis church’s forgiveness, and in 1873 Dow, still reading the Morrisite church as the woman of Revelation 12, asked Smith “upon what grounds could they refuse me into the church?” (P11-1 f4, Community of Christ Library Archives). Far from the settlements (1869–1891). Some who left the Morrisites joined the Reorganization wherever they had gone. At Mottsville, in Nevada’s Carson Valley, the RLDS branch organized in February 1869 won, by its president’s memory, only one of the Morrisite families who came from Utah in 1862, a Sister Cook (very probably Margaretta Cook), and in 1874 its members and about thirty Morrisites met together to hear a messenger with one of Morris’s revelations (Saints’ Herald 55, May 27, 1908, p. 524; see the chronology). Mark H. Forscutt baptized the Danish Soren Willadson and his family near Burlington, Iowa, in the spring of 1876; Willadson had “joined the Morrisites; became discouraged and went to California,” then back to Iowa (Saints’ Herald 38, 1891, p. 531, as “Soren Wilson”). And at Olney, Washington, in February 1891, John Davis baptized “an aged man named Hastings,” very probably Winter Hastings, who had been with Morris when he was shot (Saints’ Herald 38, 1891, p. 134). Not every death notice in the Herald means membership: it printed obituaries of Elizabeth Forscutt (1903), for whom no RLDS baptism has been found, and of “Elder James Bowman” of Soda Springs (1904). Among Williams’s followers (1871–1877). The first of Williams’s own followers known to have joined was Marie Mortensen, a leader of the Omaha sisters whom he had called “High Priestess,” in May 1871; Williams approved the council’s action and told it to let “her place & office be given to another” (Williams to Hendrikson, June 2, 1871, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1871). Margaretta Cook left the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and was baptized RLDS in 1873. That summer the RLDS missionary Charles W. Wandell, preaching at San Juan, Monterey County, California, on his way to Australia, counted “about twelve Morrisites” there; they showed him the first two chapters of Williams’s St. Ann’s Hill records, said to be “the sealed portion of the plates of the Book of Mormon,” and asked his opinion of their genuineness, and he sent a partial copy to Joseph Smith III (Wandell to Alexander H. Smith, July 31, 1873, and to Joseph Smith III, August 6, 1873, Henry A. Stebbins Papers, P24 f26–f28, Community of Christ Library Archives). By 1874 there were Danish “Josephites” at Omaha, and in 1877 Williams complained that S. P. Guhl and others were seeking the church’s records “to gain favor with young Joe” (Church History Library, MS 31876). Morrisites also read the Reorganization’s publications: on August 1, 1877, Joseph Warner, the “Brother Warner” of the 1876 Weber prophecy (see Who was “Brother Warner”?), wrote to the Saints’ Herald objecting to the Reorganization’s new translation of the Bible, which made the woman of Revelation 12 the Virgin Mary rather than the church (P24 f5 item 18, Community of Christ Library Archives). In Montana (1881–1900). The RLDS Deer Lodge Branch register opens with baptisms by W. W. Blair in the Deer Lodge Valley on August 21, 1881. In November 1886 Elder Joseph C. Clapp invited the Morrisites to use the Reorganized Church’s new meeting house in Deer Lodge City, and between 1886 and 1890 he baptized at Deer Lodge and Willow Glen. Among those he baptized were three men who had joined the Morrisite congregation at Omaha in 1869–71: Peter Nielsen (July 27, 1887), Niels Jensen, keeper of one of the record books of Williams’s letters (about March 1890), and Niels Thorkelsen (October 1890); the register also lists Christoffersen and Eliason children born at Soda Springs, baptized between 1879 and 1892, and Danish-born members baptized in 1886–96 (Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District, #228, C

t: How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another in the Deer Lodge Valley?
s: How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another in the Deer Lodge Valley? Open Why it matters For nearly a century three churches that traced themselves to Joseph Smith shared one valley. Latter-day Saint missionaries knew the Morrisite leaders well enough in 1896 to call John R. Eardley “Apostle Eardly” (Wright, 2004, drawing on the Butte District manuscript history). The Reorganized Church was active in Montana from 1868, and some Morrisites joined it, among them Lena Hanson at Deer Lodge in 1895. Hymnals and a 1931 Reorganized Church lesson quarterly were still in the Lord’s House in 2020 (see Images). Whether the three groups competed for members, shared buildings, preachers or burial grounds, married into one another’s families, or simply kept apart, and how that changed as the Morrisite church dwindled toward 1969, has not been studied. First findings The Montana council’s minutes for 1881–1890 (Church History Library, MS 32226) give some early answers. In November 1886 an “Elder Clapp of the Reorganized Church” invited the Morrisites to use the Reorganized Church’s meeting house in Deer Lodge City while he was away preaching in Utah, and the council agreed to accept and to announce the meeting “among the Josephites and Morrisites.” This was the church the New North-West had reported in September 1886 as going up under Clapp’s direction on the Cottonwood road east of town (see Newspapers). The Reorganized Church branch remembered that building as its first church, “on Cottonwood Creek,” built under John Eliasson of a Morrisite family and later used as his blacksmith shop; its second church, begun about 1892 with Andrew Christofferson, another Morrisite son, on the building committee, was dedicated in 1901 and still stands (Places). A year earlier the council had placed a notice in the same paper disowning George and James Dove of the California congregation as “pretenders” (November 13, 1885). In 1888 and 1889 the council discussed John Parson, the former Morrisite apostle, who still held Reorganized Church membership while following a self-styled prophet in Oakland, California, and took it as a sign of waning confidence in “Young Joseph’s prophetic office.” Speakers cited Brigham Young both as a cautionary example and as an authority on running a branch, and in 1889 said Williams’s predictions about “the Utah people” were being fulfilled. The council also kept the sacrament open to non-members who came as “friends for the gospel’s sake.” Among Williams’s own followers, the earliest case found so far is fifteen years older and comes from the Omaha congregation: in May 1871 Sister Marie Mortensen, who had led its sisters’ meetings and whom Williams had called “High Priestess” in 1870, “had joined another church, the Josephites, and let herself be baptized by them.” She told the elders she was afraid “young Joseph was the man they said he was,” and chose to risk rejecting Cainan rather than rejecting young Joseph; she gave back her written appointment and was excluded (Omaha minutebook, May 7, 1871, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Williams approved: “you have done quite right, particularly in obtaining the papers; let her place & office be given to another” (Williams to Hendrikson, June 2, 1871, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1871). George Thompson, the newly elected president, wrote from England in December 1886 that Joseph Smith [III] “may be called through our Joseph,” and that John Parson “may be instrumental” in telling him of “the mission of the fullness,” but that he had “not yet called him” to be a prophet (Church History Library, MS 31876). In 1887–89 Eardley and Emmons were also in touch with David Whitmer and his followers, and read their papers, the Expositor and The Return (Eardley to Hendrickson, 1887–89, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1880–1889). In March 1890 John R. Eardley wrote that Brother Emmons of the Montana church had been baptized into the Reorganized Church and that Mrs. Emmons meant to follow at Elder Clapp’s next visit; “it was only a matter of time,” he wrote, and “our numbers are growing less” (Eardley to Hendrickson, March 20, 1890, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1890). Where to start The Butte District manuscript history of the Northwestern States Mission (Church History Library); Cornelius, “Mormonism in Montana” (1962), ch. 6, and his interviews; Wright, “Mormon Movement to Montana” (2004); RLDS branch records and Saints’ Herald reports from Montana (Community of Christ Library Archives); the New North-West and Silver State Post; the 1962 Hendrickson interview (Repositories); burials at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge; and family memories, which descendants are invited to share.

t: Where did the Copper Village organ come from?
s: Where did the Copper Village organ come from? Open Why it matters The Copper Village Museum and Art Center in Anaconda holds a Mason & Hamlin reed (pump) organ said to have come from the Morrisites, and by local tradition from the Lord’s House at Racetrack. If the tradition holds, it is one of the few furnishings of Morrisite worship to survive outside the church. Jim Furshong, a volunteer at the museum, brought the organ to this guide’s attention and showed it to the editor on November 18, 2026 (MO-IMG-102 to 104). It is a walnut parlor organ with a mirrored, spindled top, thirteen stops, two knee levers (a knee swell and a “full organ” lever) and two carpeted pedals. The nameboard prints Mason & Hamlin’s exhibition medals, the latest of them London, 1885, so the organ was made in 1885 or later; the knee lever marked “Patented Full Organ, June 25, 1878” gives the date of that device’s patent, not the year the organ was built. That fits a visiting organist’s description of it, when he played it at the museum on August 3, 2013, as a Mason & Hamlin parlor organ built in Boston about 1892 (“BIRD: Auf dem Lande, on Mason & Hamlin parlor organ,” YouTube, posted August 9, 2013). Either way, the organ did not come from Utah and was not bought when the Lord’s House was built and dedicated in 1878–79; it could still have been bought for the church, or by a Morrisite family, later, while the congregation met there into the 1950s. Museum volunteers say an accession sheet was probably made when the organ was donated but has not been found: for years donations to the museum and archives went undocumented, and volunteers are only now putting the collections in order. Where to start The museum’s accession files (Marcus Daly Historical Society Museum and Archives, through the director of the Copper Village Museum and Art Center; see Repositories); the organ’s serial number, which can date it from Mason & Hamlin’s production records; the Montana council’s minutes (Church History Library, MS 32226) and later church records, for any purchase or gift of an organ; and family memories, which descendants are invited to share.

t: Was Gwendale named for Gwenllian Evans?
s: Was Gwendale named for Gwenllian Evans? Open Why it matters Gwendale was the post office of the upper Deer Lodge Valley, near Warm Springs and Lost Creek, where Morrisite settlers such as W. P. Thomas lived; in 1878 it was renamed Morristown because, the New North-West said, many of its people were Morrisites (see Deer Lodge Valley). The Evans family called its homestead Gwendale Farm (In the Shadow of Mount Haggin, p. 134). The Montana Historical Society’s Women’s History Matters calls Gwenllian Evans, Morgan Evans’s mother, Montana’s first woman homesteader and “one of the territory’s first post mistresses” (“A Farm of Her Own,” May 20, 2014). The name looks like hers, and she may have kept the Gwendale office, but no record seen so far says either. Where to start The Post Office Department’s Record of Appointment of Postmasters, 1832–1971 (National Archives, Record Group 28; microfilm M841), for Deer Lodge County; the department’s site reports for Gwendale and Morristown; the New North-West; and the sources behind the Women’s History Matters essay.

t: Were the Evans and Thomas families of Gwendale connected to the Morrisites?
s: Were the Evans and Thomas families of Gwendale connected to the Morrisites? Open Why it matters Morgan Evans and William P. Thomas were Gwendale election judges together in 1876, and in 1880 their homestead claims were among the four held up by the land office (see the roll note for Thomas, W. P., probably the Morrisite of that name). The Evanses were Welsh, like William James, the Morrisites’ local president. The family account has them in Utah for about eight years before they came to the valley in 1865 (In the Shadow of Mount Haggin, p. 134), but Women’s History Matters says Gwenllian Evans emigrated to the United States in 1868, and her obituary, a clipping shared by Jim Furshong whose newspaper and date are not yet recorded here, says she came to Montana in 1869. Neither family history calls the Evanses Morrisites. The same obituary says “the late Mrs. E. P. Thomas” was her daughter. A family chart shared by a reader names her as Gwenllian Evans (1847–1891), born at Penderyn, Breconshire, Morgan Evans’s sister, and her husband as Evan Price Thomas (1845–1891), born in Carmarthenshire, a rancher on Lost Creek; the two were killed by lightning in July 1891 (Find a Grave memorial 106925533). The chart and Find a Grave both make him the son of William Price Thomas, and a 1945 account of the valley’s first settlers says that William Price Thomas was already settled on Warm Springs Creek when Morgan Evans’s party came in 1865 (Montana Standard, September 23, 1945). This is very probably the Morrisite W. P. Thomas, who was also born in Carmarthenshire (patriarchal blessing, MS 31876, Church History Library; see his note on the roll). The chart records a second marriage between the families: Morgan Evans’s daughter Rachel (1864–1951) married Joseph Henry Thomas (1863–1894), also a son of William Price Thomas, at Anaconda on September 18, 1890. Two of W. P. Thomas’s sons thus married into the Evans family. That ties the families closely, but it does not show that the Evanses were Morrisites. Where to start The Evans and Thomas homestead case files (National Archives, Record Group 49); the 1870 and 1880 censuses of Deer Lodge County; the Montana church’s Danish minutes and council minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876 and MS 32226), for the names Evans and Thomas; Latter-day Saint records of the Evanses in Utah before 1865; and family records, which descendants are invited to share.

Who was “Brother Warner”? Answered Why it matters In January 1875 George Thompson wrote from Walthamstow to William P. Thomas in Montana of a “Brother Warner” who claimed “to have seen Bro Joseph” [Morris] and to be sent to warn the brethren to gather to Weber, for “the Shepherds of Utah will be cut off in 1875 & the Saints be gathered to Weber in 1876”; Thompson was “looking for him & at Weber.” Williams had already warned the Race Track church in February 1875 against “one who is going round the Weber House saying he is commissioned by Seth to warn that people to gather back to Weber this year … I have not sent him” (Williams to Andrew Hendrickson, February 5, 1875, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1874–1875), and he rejected the prophecy in May 1875, and in June 1876 Thompson wrote that “some Jew or fanatic was bidding for your loyalty” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882). He would be a claimant who called the scattered Morrisites back to the site of the camp a dozen years after the siege. He was almost certainly Joseph Warner of South Weber. In November 1875 John R. Eardley wrote from Hollister, California, that “Bro. Warner—the German brother, has been through this country warning the Weber Saints to prepare for the coming of Bro. Joseph next June,” claiming “the Presidency of the Apostleship” and to be “President of Germany”; Eardley thought these “the aspirations of a diseased mind” and said Warner had “disgusted all whom I have conversed with” (John R. Eardley to William James, Hollister, California, November 9, 1875, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William James, 1874–1875). The roll lists a Joseph Warner and an Ingray Werner. A Joseph Warner, born in Germany, aged 45, was among the men discharged at the fort on June 16, 1862 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library); Anderson names a Joseph Warner among those who gained wider prominence in the scattered congregations (pp. 157, 181); Family Tree has a Joseph Warner, born in Hanover in 1816, in Cache County in 1860 (FamilySearch Family Tree, GK43-2XF); and in 1880 a Joseph Warner, sixty-two, born in Germany, widowed, a laborer, was living at South Weber (1880 U.S. census, South Weber, Davis County, ED 16). Testifying at Burton’s trial in February 1879, Joseph Warner said: “I was born in Germany; came here in ’56; came to Salt Lake first; I was in Providence and there I had a vision; Joseph Smith appeared to me; for which I was cut off of the Mormon church,” and “I joined Joseph Morris in May, 1861, at Weber.” He read the court a sermon “half in German and half in broken English” and recited a revelation in full, until, the reporter wrote, it proved “utterly impossible to obtain intelligent responses” and he was allowed to stop (Ogden Junction, February 22, 1879, p. 4). He died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September and before October 2 (the county court’s session of September 11 does not mention him), “an indigent person” who “left no relatives”; P. P. Prophet “and others” buried him at county expense and sold his effects, but “the manuscript he had not disposed of,” and on October 30 he was told to dispose of it “if he can” (Davis County Court minutes, October 2 and October 30, 1893, pp. 462, 470 (County court minutes, 1852–1893, FamilySearch film 484601, item 2, DGS 7579269); Davis County Clipper, November 2, 1893, p. 1). What became of the manuscript is not known. The marker in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021); the marker was probably set long after the burial (an Army Reserve unit restored the cemetery in 1973–75, according to the USGenWeb Archives page for it), and its date is an estimate; Find a Grave’s “1870” comes from a Utah State Historical Society listing of 2000 that most likely copied the marker (memorial 120420). A German-born Morrisite at Weber who had claimed a vision of Joseph Smith, still reading his own sermons and revelations in 1879, fits Thompson’s and Eardley’s words closely; what remains open is the fate of the manuscript he left in 1893. Where to start The Montana council minutes of 1874–76 and Williams’s letters of 1875 to William James and Andrew Hendrickson (Church History Library, MS 31876), for the name; Utah newspapers of 1874–76, for a prophet at Weber; the Davis County Court minutes from November 1893 on (County court minutes, 1893–1900, FamilySearch film 484602), for a later report on Warner’s manuscript, which may hold his revelations; who P. P. Prophet was, and his family’s papers; Thomas Peek’s manuscript “Early Settlement of South Weber” and his diary, owned in 1969 by Richard O. Tucker, which may mention him (the city’s cemetery records, read in November 2026, give no date for him; see Kington Fort); his excommunication at Providence, Cache County, in the ward records; and the 1870 census of Davis and Weber counties.

t: When was Arthur Davies first called the “Walla Walla Jesus”?
s: When was Arthur Davies first called the “Walla Walla Jesus”? Answered Answer In his lifetime, by his neighbours. When the boy died of diphtheria in February 1880, the Walla Walla Watchman wrote: “This boy, a little over twelve years of age, was no other than the Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called, and in whom the camp of Davies, at the foot of the Blue Mountains, had implicit faith. Great wonders were expected of this little Messiah, but alas! man proposes and God disposes” (Daily Intelligencer (Seattle), March 4, 1880, p. 3, reprinting the Walla Walla Watchman; Washington Digital Newspapers; checked against the page image). “So called” shows the name was already current. The Watchman itself, which is not digitized, may have used it earlier. Earlier mentions, without the name J. H. Beadle in 1870, of “another prophet named Davis” whose followers kept a child “dressed in white” as their future Christ (Life in Utah, pp. 427–28); the Carson Valley News in 1876 and 1877 (see Newspapers); the New York Sun of November 14, 1878, p. 1 (“Mr. Wood of Walla-Walla”; Chronicling America; checked against the page image), in which Davies’s missionary S. W. Wood called Davies “the Comforter” and his society the “Redemptionists,” and said the Messiah, “the Father’s Son,” “was born in 1868 in Walla Walla … He is now 10 years old” (consistent with his birth on February 11, 1868, given by Gilbert, and with the Watchman’s “a little over twelve” in February 1880; summarized in the Puget Sound Argus, December 12, 1878, p. 2); and the Watchman’s exposé of August 1879, as summarized in the Argus (August 28, 1879, p. 4: “a child that is the Savior of the world”) and the Spokan Times (September 4, 1879: “the father of Christ … the Savior of the world has made his second advent in the person of his twelve-year old son”). Davies himself called the boy “Messiah Son of David” (Watson, p. 192), as did Frank T. Gilbert’s county history of 1882 (Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, pp. 374–75). The 1879 summaries are quoted from the digitized text and have not been checked against the page images. Still open The Watchman’s own files for 1878–80.
What’s new
Recent and upcoming New work by contributors, coming programs, and the latest additions to this guide. To follow updates in a feed reader, subscribe to the RSS feed.

Contributor · new book Kirk Watson New book. The Morrisites: Writings and Revelations (2026), edited by Kirk Watson, collects writings of Joseph Morris, George Williams, William W. Davies, George S. Dove and James Dove, with his introduction. It is the most convenient way to read the movement’s own writings beyond The Spirit Prevails, and buying a copy supports this kind of independent work. Buy it on Amazon (paperback and Kindle). Now on YouTube. “Episode 113: Kirk Watson on Reincarnation in Early Mormonism,” on Robert Boylan’s Scriptural Mormonism podcast, premiered live on November 14, 2026; the conversation (44 minutes) includes the Morrisites. Watch on YouTube. For the guide’s account of the teaching, see Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from? New find. Kirk found two revelations of Morris, dated January 14 and 16, 1860, filed among anonymous letters in Brigham Young’s office papers, where a clerk docketed one “Balderdash.” He identified the hand as Morris’s and shared his transcription. They are early forms of revelations later printed in The Spirit Prevails. See Documents.

t: Lee Pierce and the Walla Walla court files
s: Archivist · Washington State Archives Lee Pierce and the Walla Walla court files For decades the story in Walla Walla was that the court records of the lawsuits against William W. Davies had gone missing. A researcher who asked for them at the county courthouse was told they had been checked out, and he never found them. They were safe all along in the Washington State Archives, whose Eastern Region Branch in Cheney holds the territorial court records for most of the state’s eleven eastern counties. Lee Pierce, an archivist at the branch, answered the editor’s request the next morning with page counts and costs for both files, and the same afternoon he scanned and sent the whole 1885 bank suit and most of the 292-page 1880 case. He also supplied the archives’ preferred citation, so the files can be cited properly. They hold sworn testimony from men and women who lived in Davies’s community, printed tracts filed as exhibits, the lists of what members gave, the 1881 judgment and the sheriff’s sales, much of it new to this guide. See Repositories. When the editor found a gap in the page numbers, Lee checked again: the whole file had been scanned and sent, and pages 133–157 seem to have been missing before it ever reached the archives. He suspects they went the way of pages 158–195, which turned up at Whitman College and were returned, and wonders whether this is what lay behind the clerk’s report that the records had been “checked out.” As he points out, territorial court files are permanent records that should never have left the clerk’s custody, so the missing pages may yet be found. Work like this rarely gets public credit, and guides like this one depend on it. Thank you, Lee.

t: How a descendant filled in the Eliason story
s: From the families How a descendant filled in the Eliason story Keith Chappelow, a descendant of Erik and Karin Eliasson, wrote to the editor with what his family knew. He sent the family’s account of the Eliasons at Soda Springs and Racetrack, pages from Joseph Smith III and the Restoration (1952), a family group sheet, and pages from a 1989 history of Powell County, Montana. That led to Family Tree links for Erik and Karin; their 1870 baptisms into the RLDS Church; their daughter Anna, whom an early county history calls the first white child born at Soda Springs; Erik’s brother Elias, who came to Soda Springs in 1863 but is not on the roll; and Joseph Smith III’s 1889 visit to the old camp at Weber with John Parson. See the pages on Erik and Karin. Is there a Morrisite in your family? Family accounts, letters, photographs, group sheets and local histories can answer questions no archive can. Share what you have; nothing is published without your permission.

From the community · local history groups What local history groups added In November the editor shared this guide in local history groups on Facebook in places where the Morrisites settled, beginning with Deer Lodge, Montana, and Walla Walla, Washington. Within a day the replies were changing the guide. Deer Lodge. A reader who once worked for a Soren Beck near Avon pointed the way to a 1902 biography of Soren R. Beck, who came to work on Niels R. Beck’s ranch in 1884 and was probably his nephew. A great-grandson of George Johnson, the last official leader of the Montana Morrisites, who preached at the Lord’s House near Racetrack until 1954, joined the conversation. So did descendants of families who built the church and worshiped there, neighbors who want to see it preserved, and a volunteer at the Deer Lodge County museum, which holds a pump organ said to have come from the Morrisites. Walla Walla. A reader asked whether the editor had checked Whitman College and recalled that the court records of the lawsuit against William W. Davies had gone missing from the county courthouse. Following up led to the case file in the Washington State Archives and to Whitman’s copies of depositions and an 1882 photograph of the Davies family and home. See Repositories. Since then. The Marcus Daly Historical Society Museum and Archives, in the Copper Village Museum and Art Center in Anaconda, shared ten photographs of the Lord’s House, inside and out, taken in 2020 and identified by Jim Furshong (see Images), and readers in Salmon, Idaho, told the story of Lars Christian Geertsen’s log house, a National Register landmark, damaged by fire and torn down in 2025. Thank you to everyone who has commented, shared and written. If your family or town has a Morrisite story, a photograph or an old record, share what you have. Nothing is published without your permission, and people are named only if they wish. Corrections Changes to a fact, date, name or identification that this guide stated earlier. Each links to the full entry.

s: 21 Nov 2026Woodruff’s journal for February 11, 1861 does record his exchange with Morris (the core of Whitney’s story); and the Søndermarks were very probably baptized by Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen, not Morris. Entry 21 Nov 2026Stenhouse’s “mother-in-law of the new prophet” is Mrs. O. Olssen (Anne Olsen) only if Morris’s wife was her daughter, not “very probably”. Entry 21 Nov 2026Morris’s birth is now given as December 15, 1823, not 1824. Entry 20 Nov 2026The Doves organized their Church of the Firstborn on July 2, 1876, not about 1874. Entry 19 Nov 2026The Agnes Just Reid papers are at the University of Utah’s Marriott Library, not Utah State University. Entry

Earlier corrections (21) 16 Nov 2026Corrections from local newspapers, 1956–1990. Entry 13 Nov 2026Page citations to Forscutt’s Sketch now follow his own numbering (p. 40, not pp. 40–41; pp. 7–11, not 8–12; pp. 28–29 and 34–35). Entry 13 Nov 2026The letter on the tides was written from Camp Douglas in 1869, and the “sceptre inscription” is the known text of Morris’s rod, not a new one. Entry 12 Nov 2026Williams’s 1881 sacrament ruling reads “outside the Church in fair standing,” not “but the Church,” as first quoted. Entry 12 Nov 2026Williams’s instructions for organizing in Montana date from August 2, 1871, not spring 1872. Entry 12 Nov 2026Mortensen’s 1870 title of High Priestess is four years earlier than Theodora’s (1874), not seven. Entry 12 Nov 2026Adelaide Williams was Adelaide M[atilda]; “Susanna Louisa Adelaide” named the household’s three women. Entry 12 Nov 2026Williams’s 1875 letter says Parson and others “attempted a business,” not “a Priesthood,” of their own. Entry 12 Nov 2026Adelaide’s full name: two letters of Williams disagree, so both forms are now given. Entry 12 Nov 2026“The Elder” letters began on May 31, 1891, and “established this year” comes from Parson’s private letter to Eardley. Entry 12 Nov 2026Omaha register details corrected from its draft: Rasmusson’s birthplace, Lundgreen’s baptism, the Søndermarks’ names, Hans Petersen’s exclusion. Entry 11 Nov 2026Williams’s 1879 prophecy named no county; his Who they were entry now follows his letter. Entry 11 Nov 2026Emanuel Strom’s 1872 copies of Williams’s epistles are in Swedish, not Danish. Entry 11 Nov 2026The Doves organized their Church of the Firstborn about 1874, not 1873, and it was still active in 1892 (since corrected to July 2, 1876; see 20 Nov). Entry 11 Nov 2026In Williams’s 1862 vision Enos stands for Joseph Smith, not John Banks. Entry 11 Nov 2026William P. Thomas was indicted in December 1876, not 1877, and found not guilty. Entry 11 Nov 2026MS 31876 citations now name folders by catalog title; some earlier folder numbers led to the wrong folder. Entry 11 Nov 2026The Montana church ended with George Johnson’s death in 1954 by Anderson’s account; the 1969 disbanding comes from USU’s finding aids. Entry 11 Nov 2026Williams’s January 1879 letter names no county and no date for the Second Coming. Entry 11 Nov 2026The Lord’s House site was chosen in February 1878; the House was not begun in 1877. t: 23 Nov 2026Niels R. Beck’s family history. The family life history of …
s: 23 Nov 2026Niels R. Beck’s family history. The family life history of Niels Rasmussen Beck at the Church History Library (MS 2735 275), until now known only from a summary, has been read. It adds his emigration in 1854–55 with two brothers, his son’s birth at St. Louis, the family’s memory of why he joined the Morrisites and why his wife stayed in Utah, a visit from his sons at Deer Lodge, and the bequests in his will.

t: 23 Nov 2026Johan Klingbaek’s journal. The Danish journal of Johan F. F…
s: 23 Nov 2026Johan Klingbaek’s journal. The Danish journal of Johan F. F. Klingbaek (Church History Library, MS 8268), read under a digital-access grant, identifies the Lieutenant at Arms of the Soldiers of Israel and, probably, two more names on the roll: Klingbaek himself (printed “Solsan F.”), who reached South Weber on July 13, 1861, and his wife Karen Andersen, who died there that October. It traces him afterward to Farmington, to the Reorganized Church in Nevada’s Carson Valley in 1869, and to the Payette Valley, Idaho, where he baptized his brother Jacob Carl in 1872. See the Klingbeck notes on the roll. Translation from the Danish generated by Claude.

t: 23 Nov 2026The Deer Lodge branch register, read in full. A complete re…
s: 23 Nov 2026The Deer Lodge branch register, read in full. A complete reading of the Reorganized Church’s Deer Lodge register (the Church History Library’s microfilm of the Community of Christ original) adds to Anders Christoffersen’s page his ordination as an elder in 1887, his children’s baptisms and marriages, and the death of his daughter Effie in February 1896, ten days after her grandmother Lena Hansen, whose register dates are now noted. It also places Hans Hanson at Deer Lodge in 1896, adds Andrew Hansen’s ordination and marriage, Peter Staffanson’s son Jacob joining at Anaconda in 1897, and, in the RLDS question, the 1926 census of the Deer Lodge and Anaconda branches.

t: 23 Nov 2026The Reorganized Church’s chapel at Deer Lodge. A history of…
s: 23 Nov 2026The Reorganized Church’s chapel at Deer Lodge. A history of the Deer Lodge branch written about 1960–62 credits John Eliasson and Andrew Christofferson, both of Morrisite families, with the branch’s two church buildings: a first church on Cottonwood Creek, later a blacksmith shop, and the present church, planned by Christofferson’s son-in-law Giles Wellington, begun about 1892 and dedicated in 1901. It still stands, and is now on the Places map. Added to Anders Christoffersen’s page, the two Montana questions and Repositories.

t: 23 Nov 2026The Willadsons of Burlington. Soren Willadson, who joined t…
s: 23 Nov 2026The Willadsons of Burlington. Soren Willadson, who joined the Morrisites, went to California and was baptized into the Reorganized Church by Mark H. Forscutt in Iowa in 1876, is now confirmed by the 1857 emigration register, and his grave as Soren Wilson is found in Shiloh Cemetery, west of Burlington. His wife, Anne M. (Ane Margrethe Jensdatter), has a new note from her 1898 obituary in the Saints’ Herald.

t: 23 Nov 2026Every name on the roll searched in the Saints’ Herald. The …
s: 23 Nov 2026Every name on the roll searched in the Saints’ Herald. The posted volumes of the Reorganized Church’s weekly, 1860–1958, were searched for every name on the roll and the people pages (see Repositories). New: the one printed report of John Parson’s death yet found (1892); the death notices of Mark and Elizabeth Forscutt (1903), James Bowman (1903) and James M. and Marie V. Emmons, whose dates are added to the Montana register; another Morrisite eyewitness of Morris’s death, Winter Hastings, baptized RLDS in Washington in 1891 (The siege); Soren Willadson’s baptism by Forscutt in Iowa in 1876; a joint meeting of Morrisites and the RLDS Mottsville branch in Carson Valley in 1874; and Montana notices of 1886–1925, among them a 1925 visit to the Lord’s House. See the chronology and How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?

t: 23 Nov 2026Obituaries of Rasmus and Lena Hansen, and the Deer Lodge ch…
s: 23 Nov 2026Obituaries of Rasmus and Lena Hansen, and the Deer Lodge chapel. Rasmus Hansen’s 1890 death notice and three notices of Lena Hansen’s death in 1896, among them her Saints’ Herald obituary, which says she and her husband “united with Joseph Morris,” are now on his and her pages and the Newspapers page. Anders Christoffersen’s page adds his children’s purchase of the Stuart ranches in 1891 and his place on the committee that built the Reorganized Church’s chapel at Deer Lodge in 1896, which is also noted under How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?

s: 23 Nov 2026Pages on the Christoffersen and Hansen parents. Peder Christoffersen (1810–1891) and his wife Abelone Maria (1816–1884), and Rasmus Hansen (1809–1890) and his wife Lena Dorthea (1809–1896), two Danish families on the roll whose children married one another four times, now have their own pages. They draw on the 1857 and 1859 passenger registers, the 1859 company reports, the oath roster and prisoner lists of 1862, censuses, the Reorganized Church register and the families’ gravestones at Soda Springs and Deer Lodge. The “Where they went” map now shows where each of the four died.

s: 23 Nov 2026Pages on Anders and Katie Christoffersen. Anders Christoffersen (1841–1921), the roll’s “Andrus Christofferson,” taken at Kington Fort and pardoned in 1863, and his wife Christiane Marie (Katie) Christoffersen (1846–1927), daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, now have their own pages, drawing on their Deer Lodge obituaries of 1921 and 1927, the 1862–63 court lists, the Reorganized Church register and censuses. Both obituaries are listed on the Newspapers page.

t: 22 Nov 2026A page on Peter Staffanson. Peter Staffanson (1823–1913), a…
s: 22 Nov 2026A page on Peter Staffanson. Peter Staffanson (1823–1913), a Swedish shoemaker who came to Utah as a Latter-day Saint in 1855, joined the Morrisites at Crescent City, Iowa, in 1869, presided over a quorum of Seventies in Montana and was bishop of William James’s Stake No. 1, now has his own page and an entry under Others named. It draws on the church’s records, the 1855 passenger register, censuses from 1860 to 1910, his 1913 obituary and his family’s history, and shows how his family, Daniel James’s and Andrew Hendrikson’s were joined by marriage.

t: 22 Nov 2026Who Lot Smith was, and where he was in June 1862. Lot Smith…
s: 22 Nov 2026Who Lot Smith was, and where he was in June 1862. Lot Smith, the Davis County sheriff who tried to collect the Morrisites’ drill fines, is now introduced where the Chronology first names him (Dec 1861): the militia officer famous among Latter-day Saints for burning the army’s supply trains in 1857. The Chronology adds Eardley’s account of the drill summons, the executions and the Parks horse (Gems of Inspiration, 1899), and the warrant Smith served after the hat affair (Anderson, Revisited). Was Lot Smith at the siege? is now In progress: from May 1 to August 16, 1862, he commanded the cavalry company guarding the mail and telegraph near Independence Rock, so he was very probably far from Kington Fort in June. County court minutes, as used by his 2018 biographers, show he was still sheriff in 1861, though the county’s list of sheriffs ends his term in 1859. Two new Bibliography entries.

t: 22 Nov 2026A page on Andrew Hendrikson. The Danish leader of the Morri…
s: 22 Nov 2026A page on Andrew Hendrikson. The Danish leader of the Morrisites at Omaha and in the Deer Lodge Valley, on whose land at Race Track the Lord’s House was built, now has his own page, the first for someone not on the 1861–62 roll. It draws on the church’s records, his 1921 obituary, which says George Johnson “of the Saints of the Most High church” conducted his funeral at the ranch, the censuses, the 1880 report of his daughter’s death, and his grandson Robert Staffanson’s memoir.

t: 22 Nov 2026Andrew Hendrikson in Montana. His entry on the People page …
s: 22 Nov 2026Andrew Hendrikson in Montana. His entry on the People page adds, from the church’s records, his wife Carrie’s baptism at Crescent City in 1871, his move to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1872 and his marriage that year, the choice of his land at Race Track for the Lord’s House in 1878, the children born in the valley, and the death of a five-year-old daughter in a yard fire in April 1880.

Sorensen, is very probably the roll’s John Peter Lorensen, and five were fined in March 1863. The question is now in progress. The question on the Evans and Thomas families of Gwendale adds that two sons of William Price Thomas married into Morgan Evans’s family.
