t: 21 Nov 2026A Council Bluffs question book. A miscellany folder among t…
s: 21 Nov 2026A Council Bluffs question book. A miscellany folder among the Morrisite records at the Church History Library holds Andrew Henriksen’s Danish notebook of questions for Williams, in which a Council Bluffs teacher counts William W. Davies among the “fallen spirits” (Teachings), and a manuscript copy of Morris’s revelation on young Joseph Smith with a different number and date from the printed one (Repositories). Eight more diaries and letters named in the library’s catalog are now listed as not digitized.

t: 21 Nov 2026John Parson and Joseph Smith III. Joseph Smith III’s letter…
s: 21 Nov 2026John Parson and Joseph Smith III. Joseph Smith III’s letterpress books, searched in the Community of Christ Library Archives’ database of transcripts, add his side of Parson’s years in the Reorganized Church: a letter of January 1885 quoting Morris’s revelation on the Reorganization and urging Parson to join; the baptism dates (1886); the Oakland dispute of 1888 over Dr. P. W. Poulson’s “Order of Messiah,” after which Parson returned his certificate; and his expulsion on April 1, 1890. See the roll note, the Chronology and How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? Smith’s letter to Kate Field of September 1, 1884, also confirms how Forscutt came to write his Sketch (Documents).

t: 21 Nov 2026The Cairo Democrat, 1867. The Illinois paper credited with …
s: 21 Nov 2026The Cairo Democrat, 1867. The Illinois paper credited with the November 1867 story of a Cairo woman who joined the Morrisites is not in Chronicling America, the Illinois Digital Newspaper Collections or Newspapers.com for that year, so the original is probably to be had only on microfilm. The Newspapers page now says so.

t: 21 Nov 2026The March 1863 term. The Deseret News reports of the court …
s: 21 Nov 2026The March 1863 term. The Deseret News reports of the court term in which the Morrisites were tried have now been read in full, not only the report of the verdict. Judge Kinney charged the grand jury on the case on March 9; twenty of the men bound over did not appear and forfeited their bail; ten were indicted for murder on March 19; the defence moved to quash the indictments; and Lot Smith testified for the prosecution and Mark Forscutt for the defence. The paper called Governor Harding’s pardon a “flagrant outrage.” See Documents, the Chronology (Mar 1863), Was Lot Smith at the siege? and the Newspapers page.

t: 21 Nov 2026George Morris on 1854. The rest of George Morris’s reminisc…
s: 21 Nov 2026George Morris on 1854. The rest of George Morris’s reminiscences (pp. 25–112) has now been read. One passage concerns Joseph: he lived with George through the winter of 1853–54, and in the spring went south “to his wifes Brother where she left him,” returning alone that summer. It agrees with the Sanpete divorce petition and Mary’s marriage at Ephraim, rather than with the Morrisite account that she went back to Salt Lake City. See the Chronology, March–April 1854, and Documents.

t: 21 Nov 2026Revelations not in The Spirit Prevails. The manuscript copi…
s: 21 Nov 2026Revelations not in The Spirit Prevails. The manuscript copies of Morris’s revelations among the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f1–f2) have now been checked against the printed book, and four texts were found that it leaves out. Three come from the week after the failed coming of December 31, 1861: on January 1, 1862, the dated promises “have failed, because they were intended to fail”; on January 5 and 6 Morris complains to the voice and is threatened with “many thousands of the inhabitants of this territory lying dead upon the ground.” The fourth is a letter to Brigham Young of December 11, 1860. See the Chronology (11 Dec 1860, 1–6 Jan 1862, 25–27 Feb 1862, Jun 1862), the timeline of the coming, failed prophecy and the Repositories. The Teachings page adds a paragraph, “Who rules this world,” on Adam as the “Loyal President” of this earth. Also new: W. W. Blair’s report in 1868 of “many old Saints (Morrisites)” in Nevada, friendly to the Reorganized Church.

t: 21 Nov 2026Woodruff at South Weber, February 11, 1861. Woodruff’s jour…
s: 21 Nov 2026Woodruff at South Weber, February 11, 1861. Woodruff’s journal for the meeting at which sixteen of Morris’s followers were cut off has now been read in full. Morris spoke for half an hour, claiming to be “the seventh Angel” with “six times more keys of the Priesthood” than Joseph Smith; Woodruff charged him with adultery to his face, and Morris denied it; Philo Allen was put over the rest of the branch. See the Chronology and the Glossary’s Seventh Angel. Correction: the Chronology said the journal records no exchange with Morris and does not name him, and so treated Whitney’s 1893 story as a late invention; the journal has the core of it. Also corrected: the Søndermarks were baptized at South Weber in 1861 “by Morrisen og Mikkelsen,” very probably Niels Morrisen and Jens Mikkelsen, not by Morris.

t: 21 Nov 2026Woodruff’s journal, June 1862. Wilford Woodruff’s journal, …
s: 21 Nov 2026Woodruff’s journal, June 1862. Wilford Woodruff’s journal, read in full for the siege and after, records Judge Kinney saying he took no step “without counciling President Young” and Brigham Young saying he would have left the Morrisites alone; Burton’s sworn account at the hearing of June 18, that he shot Morris with his revolver; the yellow tin crown and the scepters shown in Salt Lake City; and the bodies of Morris and Banks laid out at the City Hall before a crowd of nearly 2,000. See the Morrisite War and the Chronology, June 16, 18 and 29. A garbled sentence in the June 24–25 entry is also corrected.

s: 21 Nov 2026Twelve new Glossary entries. The Glossary now explains Seth, the Order of Sevens, Seth’s Diagram, birthright, the robe, crown and scepter, the Soldiers of Israel, the two Montana stakes, the Court of the Lord’s House, the women’s offices, the Josephites, Gems of Inspiration and the posse comitatus.

s: 21 Nov 2026Foreshadowing Day in the Glossary. A new Glossary entry describes the procession of May 30, 1862, from the Morrisite history and the two eyewitness letters.

s: 21 Nov 2026Foreshadowing Day, in a letter of that evening. A Welsh letter of W. P. Thomas in the Church History Library, written at Kington Fort on May 30, 1862, describes the procession: two sets of seven circuits, the descending crowns from Morris to John E. Jones, twelve mounted priests with rods, and the horse whose mane he plaited. The Chronology adds it, the roll notes for W. P. Thomas, W. W. Thomas and John E. Jones are updated, and Rees Howels and John Morris join the People page as Welshmen at the fort not on the roll.

s: 21 Nov 2026John L. Bear’s later life. The rest of Bear’s autobiography (Church History Library, MS 10240), now read, gives his death at Independence on December 14, 1919, and records that Mark H. Forscutt preached the funeral sermon for his wife in 1891; his roll note adds both.

t: 21 Nov 2026The source of The Spirit Prevails. The Documents entry on t…
s: 21 Nov 2026The source of The Spirit Prevails. The Documents entry on the book now notes that its own history of the revelations chest implies, without stating, that Joseph Taylor’s chest supplied the 1886 text, with James Dove’s account of publishing the revelations “in their crude state.”

t: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s Danish wife. The roll’s Karen Morris now has a not…
s: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s Danish wife. The roll’s Karen Morris now has a note: she was probably Karen Marie Olsen, born at Melby, Denmark, in 1843, daughter of Ole and Anne Olsen, who came with her family on the William Tapscott in 1859 and is in their Salt Lake County household in 1860. “Mary Olsen,” as the movement’s history calls Morris’s wife, would be her middle name. No record yet names her as his wife. The notes for Mary Morris, Ole and Anne Olsen, the People entry for Morris and Who died at Kington Fort? are changed to match. The note for Karen Morris also adds the movement’s own account that Morris’s widow kept the chest of revelations and that her father sold it to Abraham Taylor after her death: so she died by the mid-1860s and her father outlived her, as Ole Olsen did.

t: 21 Nov 2026Fuller, George Thompson and Mrs. Olsen. A new item in Commo…
s: 21 Nov 2026Fuller, George Thompson and Mrs. Olsen. A new item in Common errors in print: Acting Governor Frank Fuller was not a Latter-day Saint. The roll notes for George Thompson and his sister Jane Higham now give their deaths, after a runaway near present-day Ririe, Idaho, in June 1894. The “Mrs. O. Olssen” killed at Kington Fort is now identified as very probably Anne Olsen, wife of Ole Olsen and mother of Josephine Johnson; the notes for Anne Olsen and Mary Morris and Who died at Kington Fort? are changed to match. Correction: the guide had said that the “mother-in-law of the new prophet” whom Stenhouse reported killed was very probably Mrs. O. Olssen; that now holds only if Morris’s wife was Anne Olsen’s daughter (see Morris’s Danish wife).

t: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s first family across the guide. The entry for Morri…
s: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s first family across the guide. The entry for Morris on the People page, the roll note for Mary Morris and the Documents entry for George Morris’s reminiscences now agree with the records: Morris’s birth in 1823, his marriage to Mary Thorp in 1847, the children who died young, the 1854 divorce petition, and Mary’s later life at Ephraim. The family history and county history behind them are in the Bibliography, and Henry Beal’s 1911 obituary is on the Newspapers page.

t: 21 Nov 2026Four more common errors. The Common errors in print list ad…
s: 21 Nov 2026Four more common errors. The Common errors in print list adds the thousand-man posse, the infants said to have survived the first cannon ball, the story that church leaders turned Morris’s first wife against him, and the 1824 birth year, each with what the records now show.

t: 21 Nov 2026What became of Mary Thorpe. Morris’s first wife married Hen…
s: 21 Nov 2026What became of Mary Thorpe. Morris’s first wife married Henry Beal at Ephraim on July 4, 1854, three months after the Sanpete divorce petition, which the Chronology now ascribes to Morris without qualification. She raised his daughter Ann Eliza in the Beal household, died at Ephraim in 1905, and was the grandmother of Thorpe B. Isaacson, a counselor in the First Presidency (1965–70). A family history names the three children she and Morris lost in infancy, in Cheshire and St. Louis.

t: 21 Nov 2026Morris in the records: 1841, 1847, 1850. The 1841 census fi…
s: 21 Nov 2026Morris in the records: 1841, 1847, 1850. The 1841 census finds Joseph, fifteen, already a coal miner in his father’s household at Dukinfield with George; the Mottram parish register records his marriage to Mary Thorp on February 15, 1847, a collier of twenty-three who signed with a mark; and the 1850 census finds the couple in St. Louis with Mary’s mother and brother. These ages point to a birth on December 15, 1823, which the Chronology now gives, with 1824 and 1822 as the other dates in print. Their daughter Ann Eliza’s death certificate places her birth on the trail, at Greenwood, Wyoming, in September 1853. The city death register gives the cause of death for Morris, Banks and Wahler as “Resisting Federal Warrant” (Where is Joseph Morris buried?), and a new note sets the 2006 monument’s account beside the eyewitnesses’ (How has the Morrisite War been remembered?). Correction: earlier the same day the Chronology gave December 15, 1824, the date in The Spirit Prevails.

t: 21 Nov 2026The Church History Biographical Database on Morris. Its ent…
s: 21 Nov 2026The Church History Biographical Database on Morris. Its entry gives his birth as December 15, 1822 (two years earlier than the Morrisite history; the Chronology notes both), his marriage to Mary Thorpe on February 15, 1847, a daughter, Anna Eliza, and the Moses Clawson company of 1853 for Mary and the child. It also lists a Joseph Morris in the 1856 handcart rescue; that is entered as not confirmed.

t: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s birth and early life. The Chronology now gives Mor…
s: 21 Nov 2026Morris’s birth and early life. The Chronology now gives Morris’s birth, at Burwardsley, Cheshire, on December 15, 1824, from the opening pages of The Spirit Prevails, missing from the scan the guide usually links. Read against his brother George’s reminiscences, the Morrisite history agrees on almost everything: one mine explosion, Mary Thorp, the St. Louis steamboat, Pittsburgh, the 1854 separation at San Pete, a marriage to Elizabeth Mills in 1855, and a rebaptism at Provo in 1857. They differ on the year of his baptism.

t: 21 Nov 2026Wells directs the siege; “call it South Weber.” Daniel H. W…
s: 21 Nov 2026Wells directs the siege; “call it South Weber.” Daniel H. Wells’s letters to Burton of June 14–16, 1862, from his copy book, are on the Morrisite War page: rifle pits and “a little fasting,” “meet them with lead,” no rush on the works, and “treat them kindly.” Wells struck the word “Morrisite” from the dispatches (Glossary), and recalled Brigham Young’s son Joseph A. Young and Briant Stringham from the posse. The Chronology adds a mission president’s report of Morrisite “representatives” in Denmark in 1868.

t: 21 Nov 2026Rumor before the siege, and Soda Springs in 1870. A mission…
s: 21 Nov 2026Rumor before the siege, and Soda Springs in 1870. A missionary letter of July 1862 shows the stories told about Morris before news of the siege reached England, including a meeting with Brigham Young that no other source records (Did Brigham Young ever answer Morris?). John L. Bear’s autobiography adds that about ten of some thirty Morrisite families were left at Soda Springs by 1870, a threat made to RLDS missionaries at Bear Lake (RLDS question), and that Mark H. Forscutt led the singing at Bear’s wedding on the ship Underwriter in 1860 (roll).

s: 20 Nov 2026Morris in Salt Lake City, 1859. A new Chronology entry: George S. Dove moved Morris from American Fork to Salt Lake City in November 1859, where he received “Keys of the Priesthood,” from the Morrisites’ own histories of 1879 and 1886 (the 1886 pages, missing from the Berkeley scan, were read in a second copy at the Internet Archive).

s: 20 Nov 2026The posse’s names. The Data page adds a new file, morrisite-posse-1862.csv: the 341 entries on the posse’s militia returns (MS 33041, Church History Library), by company, with ranks, horses and arms where given. They are the posse, not Morrisites, and many readings are uncertain. See the posse chart.

t: 20 Nov 2026A Voice from the West found, and new eyewitnesses. The Dove…
s: 20 Nov 2026A Voice from the West found, and new eyewitnesses. The Doves’ 1879 pamphlet, long on the Wanted list, is digitized at the Church History Library and now listed in Documents; it is the first printing of the “History of Events,” and dates the Doves’ church to July 2, 1876. From diaries and reminiscences at the Church History Library: John L. Bear’s own account settles that his baby was killed with his wife, and is a third witness that the second woman shot at the surrender was Svend Hegg’s wife (Who died); Daniel H. Wells’s 3 a.m. letter to Burton, and the views of a posse diarist and a neighbor, on the Morrisite War page; Lot Smith and the Parks horse; Soda Springs in 1863 and Bear’s pamphlet against Morris’s revelations (Chronology); “the Eternal Rounds” shown to visitors in 1899 (Teachings); and new Repositories entries. Correction: the guide had dated the Doves’ church to about 1874 (correction of November 11); the movement at a glance chart now reads 1876 as well.

s: 20 Nov 2026The posse, by unit. A chart on the Morrisite War page shows the makeup of Burton’s posse from the militia returns in the Theodore McKean family collection at the Church History Library: about 520 men, from Salt Lake County, Centerville, and the Davis and Weber companies that joined at the fort.

s: 19 Nov 2026Mary Anderson in 1873, and Mr. Wood of Walla Walla. Wood is found: the Chronology, the Walla Walla question, Teachings, Newspapers, Others named and the Davies roll note add it.

s: 19 Nov 2026Woodruff’s story, and its problems. The Chronology under February 11, 1861, adds Wilford Woodruff’s later account of his exchange with Morris, as Orson F. Whitney printed it in 1893, with the reasons it cannot be taken at face value. Whitney’s History of Utah is added to the Bibliography.

s: 19 Nov 2026“The Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called.” The question When was Arthur Davies first called the “Walla Walla Jesus”? is answered: the Walla Walla Watchman used the name at the boy’s death in February 1880, so it was current in his lifetime (reprinted in the Seattle Daily Intelligencer, March 4, 1880). From Washington Digital Newspapers, the Chronology adds the press campaign against Davies in 1879–81 and the hearings of 1880–81; Teachings adds what former members testified he taught; the Newspapers page lists the Walla Walla items; and the roll notes for Peter C. Klemgard, George Lee and William W. Davies add their parts.

s: 19 Nov 2026The posse’s side, and the Soldiers of Israel. From Richard W. Young’s “The Morrisite War” in The Contributor (1890): Documents adds the roster of the Morrisites’ armed companies, formed May 16, 1862, with the oath (the men on the roll are linked from the Name index); The Morrisite War adds the posse’s account of the first shots and the surrender beside the Morrisites’, the writ of May 22, and the jury at Burton’s trial; and Young’s note that the Morrisite eyewitness Stenhouse quoted in 1873 was believed to be Mark H. Forscutt is added to the June 13 entry and Forscutt’s note. Also: the Chronology (May 16 and 30, 1862), Teachings, Was Lot Smith at the siege? and the Bibliography.

t: 19 Nov 2026Harding’s pardons. Documents adds the texts of Governor Har…
s: 19 Nov 2026Harding’s pardons. Documents adds the texts of Governor Harding’s two pardons of March 31, 1863, from Tullidge’s History of Salt Lake City (1886): seven men for murder and sixty-nine for resisting an officer, compared with the court’s list, and the grand jury’s presentment of Harding. The pardoned men are linked from the Name index. From Stenhouse’s Rocky Mountain Saints (1873): Who died adds the earliest naming of Mrs. Marsh and the death of Morris’s mother-in-law, and The Morrisite War adds an eyewitness’s account of the first shot, Brigham Young’s instruction to the posse officers and Marshal Lawrence’s warning.

s: 19 Nov 2026The earliest books. From Catherine V. Waite (1866), J. H. Beadle (1870) and Governor Harding’s statement in Hickman’s confession (1872): the Chronology dates Morris’s walk from Slaterville to November 19, 1860; The Morrisite War adds Harding’s account of the pardon and of Burton’s excuse at the 1863 trial; the roll notes for Maria Christofferson, Abraham Taylor, John Banks and Alexander Dow add what these books say of them; the Walla Walla question moves the first printed mention of the Davies child back to 1870; and the Bibliography adds Waite, Beadle and Bancroft.

s: 19 Nov 2026Morris as Davies saw him. The Chronology adds, under the fall of 1860, Davies’s 1882 description of Morris (“seven ringlets upon his shoulders” and “a mild blue eye”), the windstorm at Slaterville, and his meeting with John Cook on the road to Salt Lake City.

t: 19 Nov 2026Gabriel and Hur; Davies’s own story. From the same 1882 his…
s: 19 Nov 2026Gabriel and Hur; Davies’s own story. From the same 1882 history: the Teachings page adds Davies’s and Livingston’s report that Morris claimed the spirit of Gabriel, once Seth and Moses, and called John Banks Hur, and Livingston’s word that Morris taught a body could not be killed while its mission was unfinished. The William W. Davies page adds his own account of his life: his birth in Denbighshire in 1833, Willard, Soda Springs, Virginia City and the Deer Lodge Valley, the births of Arthur and David, and his second marriage.

t: 19 Nov 2026Mrs. Swanee identified. Frank T. Gilbert’s 1882 history of …
s: 19 Nov 2026Mrs. Swanee identified. Frank T. Gilbert’s 1882 history of Walla Walla County, written from interviews with William W. Davies and R. J. Livingston, both eyewitnesses of the surrender, names the second woman killed there as Mrs. Anna Swen O. Hegg: very probably the “Mrs. Swanee” of the 1879 testimony. Who died at Kington Fort? adds Gilbert’s list of the killed and Livingston’s account; the roll notes for the Heggs, R. J. Livingstone and Lebrecht Bar, and the Walla Walla Jesus question, cite it.

t: 19 Nov 2026“The Wound That Never Healed.” Peter Anderson’s 1965 Fronti…
s: 19 Nov 2026“The Wound That Never Healed.” Peter Anderson’s 1965 Frontier Times article on his mother, Mary Christoffersen Anderson, has been read. It adds her own memories of the surrender, the handkerchief she held over her mouth for the rest of her life, the family’s emigration and their reasons for leaving the church, the wedding at Soda Springs by Lieutenant Frank Shoemaker, and the names of the two women killed by the first cannon ball. See the roll notes for Niels Anderson, Maria Christofferson and Peter Christoffersen, Who died at Kington Fort? and the Bibliography.

t: 19 Nov 2026The Prophet Daniel of Genoa. The Carson Valley News, read f…
s: 19 Nov 2026The Prophet Daniel of Genoa. The Carson Valley News, read from its page images, names the preacher who brought word of the Walla Walla child to the Morrisites of Carson Valley: Robert Roberts, William W. Davies’s missionary, “the Morrisite Mormon who claims to be the Prophet Daniel.” It also reports a Morrisite meeting in the Genoa court house on June 18, 1876, at which R. J. Livingston spoke, the day Livingston left for Walla Walla (May 28, 1877), and his letter of March 1878 from his new farm on Mill Creek. See the Chronology, the roll note for R. J. Livingstone, People and Newspapers.

t: 19 Nov 2026Burton’s trial: the verdict, and witnesses on the siege. A …
s: 19 Nov 2026Burton’s trial: the verdict, and witnesses on the siege. A reading of the newspaper reports of Burton’s 1879 trial, checked against the page images, adds the verdict to The Morrisite War and the Chronology. The jury was out forty-six hours and found him not guilty on the morning of March 7, 1879; the second case against him had begun with his arrest in July 1877. Did one posse member die, or two? adds Joseph J. Romney’s account of the second death, a man he called “a Danishman,” shot in the doorway of the house the posse took on June 15. The roll notes for William J. Jones, Mark H. Forscutt and Abraham Taylor add their parts in the trial testimony: Jones’s own account of his capture, the log chain, his release on June 13 and his place in the posse; Forscutt as Morris’s “secretary and translator,” one of the captains, and among those who surrendered on Saturday, June 14; Taylor as a captain and a witness for the prosecution. Lars Christian Geertsen’s page adds Jones’s sentence on the escape: “Gearson got away without his shoes.”

s: 19 Nov 2026Emma Just on the stand, 1879. Who died at Kington Fort? now gives Emma Thompson Just’s testimony at Burton’s trial as the newspapers reported it: her father, George Thompson, sitting on Morris’s body and asking to be killed, and her account of the man on the dark horse, which the defence turned against her. The roll notes for George and Emma Thompson add the same. Correction: Emma Thompson’s roll note now cites the Agnes Just Reid papers at the University of Utah’s Marriott Library (MS 0365), not Utah State University.

t: 19 Nov 2026Lars Geertsen’s obituary. The Lemhi County Historical Socie…
s: 19 Nov 2026Lars Geertsen’s obituary. The Lemhi County Historical Society found the Idaho Recorder’s obituary of Lars Christian Geertsen, the man who escaped from the Morrisites’ log-house jail in 1862 and brought word to Salt Lake City. He died at his homestead on Geertson Creek, near Salmon, on October 3, 1925, aged 93; his funeral was held at the Methodist church, and a daughter was then living in Anaconda, Montana. See his page.

t: 18 Nov 2026A register of the Montana Morrisites. The People page now l…
s: 18 Nov 2026A register of the Montana Morrisites. The People page now lists in one place the 96 people the sources so far place in the Morrisite church of the Deer Lodge Valley, from Davies’s group of the 1860s to the Lord’s House at Racetrack. Most joined after 1862 and are not on Morris’s roll; the main source is the church’s record of members of 1874–87, with the minutes that record who voted in 1883 and 1886. Rows can be searched and filtered by status, and the open questions, such as names that may be the same person spelled two ways, are marked in their rows. See People.

t: 18 Nov 2026More dates for the coming, 1861–62. A reading of The Spirit…
s: 18 Nov 2026More dates for the coming, 1861–62. A reading of The Spirit Prevails for November 1861 to June 1862 adds seven entries to the timeline on the Teachings page: a deliverance promised in early December 1861 and “deferred a few days,” the revelation of February 20, 1862 explaining the “blank disappointments, time after time,” and promises tied to the Oath, the Foreshadowing and “the test.” See Teachings.

t: 18 Nov 2026Looking for the coming, 1861–1891. A new timeline on the Te…
s: 18 Nov 2026Looking for the coming, 1861–1891. A new timeline on the Teachings page sets out thirty-one moments when the time of Christ’s coming was set, tied to a condition, refused, or explained after it passed: from the deliverance promised and “deferred a few days” in December 1861 and Morris’s “to-morrow morning” of December 30, through Cainan’s refusals to set a date, to the year 1891 in Montana. Select a mark to read the entry and its source. See Teachings.

t: 18 Nov 2026The Copper Village organ, photographed. Jim Furshong, a vol…
s: 18 Nov 2026The Copper Village organ, photographed. Jim Furshong, a volunteer at the Copper Village Museum and Art Center in Anaconda, showed the editor the Mason & Hamlin organ said to have come from the Lord’s House at Racetrack. The medals printed on its nameboard date it to 1885 or later, after the church was built. The museum also showed two dolls that belonged to Myrtle and Evelyn Staffanson, of a Morrisite family of the valley. See Images and the open question. Jim and Barbara Furshong are now named throughout the guide for the photographs, clippings and pages they shared.

The High Priests Quorum’s membership record enters a Joseph Morris as ordained and enrolled at Great Salt Lake City on July 5, 1854, matching Morris’s own statement in Gems of Inspiration that he was ordained a high priest in that quorum. Jones; and Who they were notes that Allred names James Bowman’s wife as Sarah and has her killed by the first cannon shot, against the contemporary accounts of Isabella Bowman.

s: 17 Nov 2026A divorce petition, 1854. The Sanpete County probate court minutes record “Joseph Morris vs Mary Morris, Petition for Divorce,” heard before Judge George Peacock on April 6, 1854; the outcome is not recorded. Two Deseret News seventies lists of March 1854 that name a Joseph Morris of Great Salt Lake City are noted with it, unconfirmed. See Mar–Apr 1854 in the Chronology. Found by Kirk Watson.

s: 16 Nov 2026After the surrender. The Church’s Journal History for June 1862 adds three things to the Chronology: the posse reached Salt Lake City with “about 85 prisoners” on June 17 (the prisoner list counts 98 or 100); on June 24 John Parson was reported telling the Morrisites they had been “grandly humbugged” and urging them to take work Brigham Young offered through the bishops; and on June 25 Young sent a doctor to dress the prisoners’ wounds and flour to feed them.

s: 16 Nov 2026Morris preached against at Manti. A reading of the Manti ward minutes for 1861 finds four Sunday sermons against Morris between May and August, from David Candland’s warning against “Little Joseph” and a “man named Morris” to John Eagar’s report that the “New Prophet” was “at his Zenith and would now begin to go down.” See the Chronology, May–June 1861.

See John Garrett. The roll notes for Emma and her father, George Thompson, add her 1870 marriage to Nels Just and his plan, in 1891, to rejoin her in Idaho.

s: 15 Nov 2026Morris at Provo, 1857. A new Chronology entry draws on the Provo stake minutes, found by Kirk Watson: in the Reformation winter of 1857 Morris confessed, was cut off from the church “for lying,” was restored, and by April was telling the High Priests that he spoke by the Holy Ghost. His first revelation in The Spirit Prevails is headed “Provo, Utah, Spring of 1857.” Also corrected: James Brighouse’s vision, now dated July 21, 1885.

LeRoy Anderson’s view that Morris took the idea from Charles B. Thompson, and his finding that the belief usually arose from revelation rather than borrowing; who Morris, George Williams and William W. Davies believed they or others had been (Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from? and Teachings); and Thompson’s followers who carried the belief into the RLDS Church (How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church?).

s: 14 Nov 2026The Reorganization’s first notice of Morris. Two items from the RLDS True Latter Day Saints’ Herald are added to Teachings and the Chronology. In July 1861 the Herald printed an address to Morris and an editorial that quotes his revelation of May 25, 1861, the earliest known printing of one of his revelations.

t: 13 Nov 2026Forscutt’s Sketch: its last leaf, and page citations. A che…
s: 13 Nov 2026Forscutt’s Sketch: its last leaf, and page citations. A check of the manuscript on microfilm adds to the Repositories entry: the Historian’s Office bought the “Sketch of Joseph Morris” from Forscutt in June 1902, the manuscript breaks off at p. 54, and on its last leaf Forscutt writes that he burned a longer history of forty-six chapters. Corrections: page citations to the Sketch now follow Forscutt’s own numbering: the passage on an attack “Mountain Meadow fashion” is on p. 40 (not pp. 40–41); his dating of the first revelation is on pp. 7–11 (not 8–12); and the court-martial passages are on pp. 28–29 and 34–35.

t: 13 Nov 2026Forscutt’s diary at the fort, and the date of his Sketch. M…
s: 13 Nov 2026Forscutt’s diary at the fort, and the date of his Sketch. Mark H. Forscutt’s journals (Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University) have been read for their Morrisite content. His pocket diary kept at Kington Fort adds to the Chronology for December 1861 to April 1862: Lot Smith’s demand for the court-martial fines, the revelations of mid-December, the posse that could not be raised, the consecration vote of December 29, the Richards abduction, Merrill’s “Starve ’em out,” and the whipping of Christian Lundgreen. His later journals date the “Sketch of Joseph Morris” to 1884–85, written for Kate Field’s book on Mormonism (see Repositories). New roll notes for Lundgreen, Peter Moss, Niels Jacobson, William Richards, William Harris and James Mather; Almerin Grow’s converts at St. Louis in 1867; and a new research question, What does Forscutt’s shorthand diary say about the spring of 1862?, which credits Alan Bernthal-Hooker for working out Forscutt’s shorthand.

t: 13 Nov 2026Morris on the resurrection and the worlds; the two Montana …
s: 13 Nov 2026Morris on the resurrection and the worlds; the two Montana stakes. Two Morris pieces copied into Swedish by Emanuel Strom in 1872 are now on the Teachings page: an explanation of the diagram given at Weber in 1861, which puts Joseph Smith in the Terrestrial world presiding over the spirits of the dead, and an article teaching that the resurrection “takes place by birth” to immortal parents, close to the “baby resurrection” Brigham Young rejected (see also Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from?). The movement at a glance notes now describe the two Montana stakes and their agreement of May 10, 1877, and add two mentions of Nels Damander. The Omaha & Council Bluffs entry under Places notes the Reorganized and Adventist missions among the Danes who stayed, and S. P. Guhl’s letter of November 1871 is now cited as Andrew Hendrikson’s copy of March 1872. Translations from the Swedish and Danish are generated by Claude.

t: 13 Nov 2026The Morrisites and Mountain Meadows. Morris’s catechism “Ke…
s: 13 Nov 2026The Morrisites and Mountain Meadows. Morris’s catechism “Keys of the Priesthood” names George A. Smith as Cain’s heir and a Judas among the apostles, and Forscutt says Morris made Smith “the moving spirit” of the Mountain Meadows Massacre (Teachings). The Morrisite War page adds the camp’s fear in 1861 of an attack “Mountain Meadow fashion,” and, from Burton’s trial of 1879, a Morrisite’s testimony that Mrs. Swanee cried out “is this going to be another Mountain Meadows Massacre” before she was shot, the prosecutor’s argument that the camp expected to be killed, and the prosecution’s link to the federal case against John D. Lee. The two 1879 reports are added to Newspapers and John Codman’s The Mormon Country (1874) to the Bibliography.

t: 13 Nov 2026Where the dead of Kington Fort were buried. The Salt Lake C…
s: 13 Nov 2026Where the dead of Kington Fort were buried. The Salt Lake City Cemetery interment register lists John Banks (no. 1470) next to Joseph Morris in the strangers’ ground, but none of the Morrisite women killed at the fort, by the first cannon shot or at the surrender; they were presumably buried elsewhere, perhaps at the fort or in South Weber. See Who died at Kington Fort?

t: 13 Nov 2026A split in the Montana church. The movement at a glance cha…
s: 13 Nov 2026A split in the Montana church. The movement at a glance chart now shows the group that followed William M. James after the April 1886 assembly elected George Thompson president. James, who claimed the presidency for life on the strength of Williams’s envelope “I leave you in charge,” was suspended for “usurpation of authority”; with the officers of Stake No. 1 he kept meeting at Warm Springs, told the court in May 1890 that he and his followers were “as much a part of the church,” and would rejoin only on his own terms (Church History Library, MS 32226 and MS 31876). The chart’s description also notes S. P. Guhl’s break with Williams in 1871, and, in a new paragraph under the chart, the breaks and rival claimants that left no lasting body, among them Nels Damander, who turned against Williams in 1873, and Joseph Warner, who in 1875 prophesied a gathering to Weber (see Who was “Brother Warner”?).

t: 13 Nov 2026The Morrisite War, on its own page. A new page gathers what…
s: 13 Nov 2026The Morrisite War, on its own page. A new page gathers what the guide has on the siege of Kington Fort, June 13–15, 1862: why the posse came, the three days, the dead, the prisoners and the 1863 trials, and Burton’s trial of 1879, with sources. The Glossary adds Consecration, the Oath of 1862 and the Adam–God teaching, and the site search now suggests the likely name when a search is misspelled (“Chrisoffersen” finds Christoffersen). See The Morrisite War.

t: 13 Nov 2026Where they went: Omaha, Council Bluffs and Montana. The map…
s: 13 Nov 2026Where they went: Omaha, Council Bluffs and Montana. The map now places members of the roll at Omaha and Council Bluffs in 1869 from the two congregations’ Danish registers (Church History Library, MS 32226), among them Rasmus Rasmussen, Christian Lundgreen, Anders and Karen Maria Sørensen, S. P. Guhl and Hans Knudsen; four in the Montana church’s membership record begun in 1874; Josiah D. Price in Oneida County, Idaho, in 1867; and John R. Eardley at Salinas, California, in 1878. Most of the register matches rest on name, birthplace and a South Weber baptism, and are shown as probable. Stops in England (William P. Thomas, 1869; Eardley, 1873) are pinned at the map’s right edge. Three uncertain matches, Elisa Christensen, “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” and a “Mary Larsen” in Montana, are drawn with dashed outlines so that anyone who can settle them will see them; please write if you can. See Where they went.

t: 13 Nov 2026Josiah D. Price, the “431st person.” Price’s journal (Commu…
s: 13 Nov 2026Josiah D. Price, the “431st person.” Price’s journal (Community of Christ Library Archives, P26-22 f1) records his baptism on December 3, 1861, by William Davies and Edward Lloyd, as the 431st person in the church, more than the 430 names on the printed roll; the consecration of property on December 30, 1861; and the oath sworn twelve at a time on February 12, 1862. He also put Morris’s ordinances and oath into Welsh. See the Chronology, Teachings and the roll. Also new: Brigham Young’s rejection of the “baby resurrection” in the At a glance table, and Kenneth Godfrey’s papers, with his article on Robert T. Burton’s trial, in Repositories.

The Morrisite entries link to their sources on the page; on phones the table shows as cards.

t: 13 Nov 2026What Williams kept and changed. Teachings now opens George …
s: 13 Nov 2026What Williams kept and changed. The note on the Adam–God teaching now traces part of it to Morris’s own catechism on Genesis.

t: 13 Nov 2026The siege revelation, the 1863 prophecy, and two correction…
s: 13 Nov 2026The siege revelation, the 1863 prophecy, and two corrections. The Chronology adds Morris’s revelation of June 15, 1862, promising deliverance that day, and a prophecy in tongues given at Great Salt Lake City during the trials of March 1863, both from the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f5). Teachings notes the manuscript copies of Morris’s rod inscription and the formula shared by the numbered rods and the bishop’s robe. Corrections to yesterday’s Repositories entry: the letter on the tides was written from Camp Douglas in 1869 (San Leandro was the dateline of the newspaper it answered), and the sceptre inscription is the text already known from Morris’s rod, not a new one.

t: 12 Nov 2026Morris’s undated instructions. A folder of copies among the…
s: 12 Nov 2026Morris’s undated instructions. A folder of copies among the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f6) was checked against The Spirit Prevails. From it: the marriage covenant “for time” of August 1861, set beside the prophet’s sealing “for time and all eternity” (Questions); the prophecy of December 21, 1860, of no endowment “in this place” and a law to govern the nations (Chronology); and an inscription for the prophet’s sceptre that is not in the book (Repositories).

t: 12 Nov 2026The move into the RLDS Church. The question on why some Mor…
s: 12 Nov 2026The move into the RLDS Church. The question on why some Morrisites joined the Reorganized Church is rewritten as How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? It now traces the move in four stages, from Utah and Idaho soon after the siege to the last generation at Race Track around 1919–20, drawing on new items from the Community of Christ Library Archives: Charles W. Wandell’s letters of 1873 on the “about twelve Morrisites” at San Juan, California, and their St. Ann’s Hill records; Joseph Warner’s letter of 1877 to the Saints’ Herald; and the RLDS Deer Lodge Branch register, which shows three former Omaha Morrisites baptized in 1887–90. The chronology adds 1873 and 1881–90, the lineage chart now runs to the 1920s, and Repositories lists the new items. The People page adds the three Omaha Morrisites, Peter Nielsen, Niels Jensen and Niels Thorkelsen.

t: 12 Nov 2026Correction: “The Lord’s Supper.” The Teachings page quoted …
s: 12 Nov 2026Correction: “The Lord’s Supper.” The Teachings page quoted Williams’s 1881 ruling on the sacrament as “none partake of it but the Church in fair standing.” Both manuscripts read “outside the Church in fair standing”; the quotation is corrected. The page now dates the ruling to his answer to the council’s meeting of November 10, 1881, and adds his teaching in the same answer that the bread and wine were Christ’s “real body and blood,” by a principle “beyond the conception of men in mortality,” to be taken “even every week if it could be.” Repositories notes the copy made by John R. Eardley.

t: 12 Nov 2026The last of the Montana minutes. The remaining pages of the…
s: 12 Nov 2026The last of the Montana minutes. The remaining pages of the 1881 council minutes show that Sister Rasmussen, ordained High Priestess in 1877, had died by March 1881 with no successor appointed (Questions), and that Emanuel Strom refused the sacrament from Erik Eliason that spring (People). Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

t: 12 Nov 2026The Race Track council, 1876 and 1880. The rest of the coun…
s: 12 Nov 2026The Race Track council, 1876 and 1880. The rest of the council minutes for 1876 and 1880 add to the chronology the first recorded keeping of the 14th of February in Montana (1880), the council’s decision to hold Danish and English meetings in turn, and the arrival of Williams’s daughter Adelaide in Montana in 1880 (also in the Prophet Cainan entry); and, on the People page, more on Emanuel Strom and Johan Helström, who both sat on the council. Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

t: 12 Nov 2026The Danish and Swedish copies; a correction. Correction: th…
s: 12 Nov 2026The Danish and Swedish copies; a correction. Correction: the chronology dated Williams’s instructions for organizing in Montana to the spring of 1872. Hendrikson’s Danish copy shows they were written on August 2, 1871; the surviving English pages, filed with the 1872 letters, are the second half of the same letter. The entry now stands under 1871 and adds Williams’s answer on “the object of gathering together in Montana.” Also new: on the Teachings page, Williams’s charge of November 1871 that Brigham Young had “a fearful reckoning to answer for causing to be slain” Morris; in the chronology, a letter of 1875 to the Omaha Morrisites from Barnet Moses Giles, another claimant; on the People page, Emanuel Strom (1846–1929) and his father-in-law Johan Helström, very probably the Johan Helström baptized at Fremont in 1871; Williams’s August 1871 counsel in the roll note for John Merrick; and fuller descriptions of Strom’s and Niels Jensen’s record books in Repositories.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letter to “Bro. Robert” dated. The letter the Te…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letter to “Bro. Robert” dated. The letter the Teachings page quoted as written to “Bro. Robert” about 1871 is headed “Loughboro, Feby 7th 1871, My dear Bro. Robert (Ford)” and called the “First Epistle of Cainan to Robert Ford”; the citations are corrected, and Repositories notes the likely link to the Robert Henry Ford of MS 5576. The Teachings page also adds Williams’s letter of April 1866 on an account for the sisters of “their position in the Priesthood … their equal privileges … their voice in their own assemblies,” held back for the time.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–81, finished. The chron…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–81, finished. The chronology for January 1879 adds Williams’s hope of still coming to Montana and his word that the Lord’s House was “not the only House of Prayer for Montana”; the Teachings page adds George Thompson’s report of a saying of Morris, “Stick no stake but what you can easily pull up again,” and the Jordan as the setting of the Mahomet interview in Williams’s 1877 retelling.

t: 12 Nov 2026“Writings of Cainan, circa 1867–1872.” This folder dates Wi…
s: 12 Nov 2026“Writings of Cainan, circa 1867–1872.” This folder dates Williams’s “Interview with Mahomet” to his journal of 1867 and places it at the mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon, and holds the English original of the first chapter of the St. Ann’s Hill records, a Deer Lodge copy of March 1872, and the third chapter, “Chambers of the Dead” (see Teachings and Repositories).

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–77, finished. The Teach…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–77, finished. The Teachings page adds his reading of Brigham Young’s death in 1877 (“some for John, some for Orson, some for Wilford”), his rule that new members be baptized “to the lesser priesthood” and their genealogy sent to him, and his account of early opponents as “almost Apostles.” The chronology for 1877 adds music and “little schools,” and the Nez Perce scare at Deer Lodge; the roll note for S. P. Guhl, Williams’s charge that Guhl and Poulsen sought St. Ann’s Hill chapters to “gain favor with young Joe.”

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1872–73 to Andrew Hendrikson. The las…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1872–73 to Andrew Hendrikson. The last folder of his letters to Hendrikson places Williams at Stockport, Cheshire, in the spring of 1873, with John R. Eardley’s family (Prophet Cainan and the roll note for Eardley). The Teachings page adds his search in 1872 for a successor (“the longing for my mantle is amusing”) and his list of those “visited by these immortals”; the chronology, his instructions of spring 1872 for organizing in Montana; and the roll note for John Merrick, Merrick’s earlier visit to him at Cottonwood.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1871 to Andrew Hendrikson. The Teachi…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1871 to Andrew Hendrikson. The Teachings page adds his teaching of February 1871 that a high priest becomes a God by “taking one Daughter of each God” over 144,000 missions, beside his statement of the same years that he “never taught the doctrine or counselled the practice” of polygamy; his Paradise of partial faiths (“the Pope … Luther … Swedenborg … Brigham … young Joseph”); the high priests “not after the order of Seth nor Melchisedec” who bring the sciences; and the first chapter of the St. Ann’s Hill records, sent to Montana in July 1871, the earliest date found for them. The chronology adds Williams reading the Salt Lake Tribune, and the RLDS question under Questions his approval of the Omaha council’s action on Marie Mortensen. Correction: the earlier item today called Mortensen’s 1870 title seven years earlier than any High Priestess the guide had found; Theodora signed herself “High Priestess in England” in 1874, so it is four years earlier. The item is corrected.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1870 to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams c…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1870 to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams called Marie Mortensen the Omaha congregation’s “High Priestess” in 1870, four years before Theodora, the “High Priestess in England” of 1874 (corrected the same day; the item first said seven years) (see Teachings, the Omaha entry under Places, and the RLDS question under Questions). The Teachings page adds his account of Morris as the one who “gave the Diagram & revealed the two Priesthoods,” and the living raising or lowering their dead; the chronology adds “Abel’s Priesthood,” the English meetings of 1870, Almerin Grow’s own letter on his mission to Turkey, and Williams on the Godbeites; the Prophet Cainan entry adds the grasshopper year of 1870.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1869 to Andrew Hendrikson and the Oma…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1869 to Andrew Hendrikson and the Omaha church. A Danish record of January 26, 1869, is now the earliest witness that Enos meant Joseph Smith, and Williams’s own letters of that autumn speak of “Joseph the first, Joseph the second and the Lord’s Servant” (see Teachings, where the great and the common salvation is now dated from June 1869). The chronology adds Williams near Betchworth Castle, Surrey, in the autumn of 1869 and, apparently, in Wales by December. His family was in the 8th Ward by December 1869, not first in 1871 (Prophet Cainan). The roll notes for S. P. Guhl and the list entry for Andrew Hendrikson are expanded.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1874–75. The rest of the fol…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1874–75. The rest of the folder adds to Teachings Williams’s teaching that “all will be saved except the fallen spirits or Sons of Perdition,” his doctrine of mortality as the purification of spirits “not valiant” in the first estate, his reply of September 1874 to his family’s accusations, and his call for a presiding sister in each stake; to the question on Brother Warner, Williams’s own warning of February 1875; and to the chronology, his plan of 1874 to come to Montana.

t: 12 Nov 2026George Thompson’s letters and the Montana minutes, 1881–84.…
s: 12 Nov 2026George Thompson’s letters and the Montana minutes, 1881–84. Thompson’s letters to William P. Thomas (1869–83) identify the “Gudmanson” of 1868 as Gudmund Gudmundson, give an 1869 witness that Seth and Enos meant Morris and Joseph Smith, and add his expectation of Morris’s return “about the year 1902” an endowment-like rite at Derby in 1869, and his memory that Morris “fell by the School house” (see Teachings). The Race Track minutes add the council’s removal of the dissenters on May 26, 1883, George Johnson’s appointment as bishop that day, the council’s vote of January 1882 upholding Thompson as Williams’s writer, and Cainan’s counsel against dance places (chronology). A roll note for George Thompson is new.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s marriages checked. The Rotherham parish register…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s marriages checked. The Rotherham parish register records Williams’s marriage to Susannah Woolfitt at Rotherham Minster on September 8, 1846, and the 1860 census lists him, Susannah and Louisa in one Salt Lake household; the 1857 marriage to Louisa King given in Family Tree is still without a record (see Teachings).

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s household and Adelaide. FamilySearch Family Tree…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s household and Adelaide. FamilySearch Family Tree records two marriages for George Williams, to Susannah Woolfitt at Rotherham in 1846 and to Louisa King at Salt Lake City in 1857, and the 1880 census finds the two women in one Salt Lake household (see Teachings and Prophet Cainan). His daughter Adelaide never married the son of William James; she died at Los Angeles in 1947. Correction: the guide gave two forms of Adelaide’s name. The census and the California death index show she was Adelaide M[atilda] Williams; “Susanna Louisa Adelaide” named the household’s three women.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s last letters, 1880–82. His daughter Adelaide joi…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s last letters, 1880–82. His daughter Adelaide joined the Montana church and lived with the Daniel James family, and William James proposed a match with his son (see the chronology, 1882–83); Williams spent 1880–81 at Wrawby, Lincolnshire (Prophet Cainan); and George Thompson wrote in 1882 that baptisms at Weber needed no repeating (Teachings).

t: 12 Nov 2026Brother Warner identified. A letter of John R. Eardley of N…
s: 12 Nov 2026Brother Warner identified. A letter of John R. Eardley of November 1875 names the prophet of the 1876 gathering to Weber as “Bro. Warner—the German brother,” who claimed “the Presidency of the Apostleship” and to be “President of Germany.” He was almost certainly Joseph Warner of South Weber; the question under Questions is now marked answered, with only his manuscript still unaccounted for.

s: 12 Nov 2026Williams’s letters of 1870–73. They add help sent by the Omaha and Montana Saints to his family in Salt Lake City, his requests for hymns from Margaret Thomas and John Bowen (see Teachings), and notes on Guhl, Bowen, Eardley and Moss in the roll.

s: 12 Nov 2026A letter from Eardley, 1878. John R. Eardley’s letter to Williams from Hollister, California, in May 1878 adds to the roll notes for Joseph Moss (who froze to death near Austin, Nevada), R. J. Livingstone (Davies’s spokesman at Walla Walla, already doubting him), Svend Hegg, John Bowen and William W. Davies, whom Williams had ordained; and to the chronology, Almerin Grow’s turn to George Dove.

t: 12 Nov 2026Williams in 1868. His letters of 1868 to Montana add to the…
s: 12 Nov 2026Williams in 1868. His letters of 1868 to Montana add to the chronology: money carried to him by W. P. Thomas, “the rebels Dow, Davies, Gudmanson” whom he had sent out as ministers, and a plot against his life that he gave as the reason he did not go to Montana. Correction: the guide quoted Williams in 1875 as writing that Parson, Livingstone and “Davy Dove” “attempted a Priesthood of their own”; the manuscript reads “Davy, Dove [or Dow]” and “attempted a business of their own.”

t: 12 Nov 2026A poem on the siege, 1865. In a letter of November 1865 Geo…
s: 12 Nov 2026A poem on the siege, 1865. In a letter of November 1865 George Williams wrote an unfinished poem on the siege, “The Mormons came down like a wolf on the fold,” now quoted in the chronology. His letters of 1866–67 add a failed invitation to Montana in 1867, S. P. Guhl presiding at Virginia City, and an early mention of “the female Priesthood” (see Teachings).

s: 12 Nov 2026The Anderson family. A portrait of Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson with their eight children is now under Images, beside the photograph of their house.

t: 12 Nov 2026Joseph Warner, visionary. At Burton’s trial in 1879 Joseph …
s: 12 Nov 2026Joseph Warner, visionary. At Burton’s trial in 1879 Joseph Warner of South Weber testified that a vision of Joseph Smith had got him cut off from the Latter-day Saint church before he joined Morris in 1861, and read the court a sermon of his own; he died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September, “an indigent person” who left “no relatives” and a manuscript, according to the county court minutes. He was very probably the “Brother Warner” who prophesied in 1875 (see Questions). Mary Anderson’s testimony at the same trial adds a name to Who died at Kington Fort?

t: 12 Nov 2026The Beck family. The entries for Lars P. Beck and his wife …
s: 12 Nov 2026The Beck family. The entries for Lars P. Beck and his wife Maria, members of the Montana church from their baptism at Fremont, Nebraska, in 1871, now give their marriage, dates and children, and a new entry adds Lars’s brother Nels J. Beck, a trustee of the Lord’s House in 1887. With thanks to the Richardson family, who shared a family tree compiled by descendants.

t: 12 Nov 2026The Andersons at Soda Springs. A photograph of Niels Anders…
s: 12 Nov 2026The Andersons at Soda Springs. A photograph of Niels Anderson and Mary Christoffersen Anderson in front of a log house at Soda Springs, with a young woman believed to be their daughter, is now under Images.

t: 12 Nov 2026Letters to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882. Willi…
s: 12 Nov 2026Letters to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882. Williams’s letters to the Thomases of Warm Springs (Church History Library, MS 31876) add to the chronology a revelation of 1866 in the Deer Lodge Valley, Eardley in England in 1874, Rasmus Rasmussen there in 1876, and Williams’s last letter of March 1882; to Teachings, the presidency of “Seth, Enos & Cainan,” celestial names, the robe, the St. Ann’s Hill chapter “Chambers of the Dead” and the Masons; and to the Prophet Cainan, the break with his family in Salt Lake City. A new open question asks who “Brother Warner” was, who prophesied in 1875 that the Saints would gather to Weber in 1876; a likely candidate is Joseph Warner of South Weber, whose marker is in the photographs and who was living there in 1880. Correction: the guide said Williams gave his daughter Adelaide’s full name as “Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams.” In April 1871 he named her Adelaide Matilda, thirteen, and gave “Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams” as the address; but about 1870 he had addressed her as “Miss Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams,” writing out “all the Christian names.” The two letters do not agree, so the guide now gives both. (Updated the same day.)

t: 12 Nov 2026The letters of “The Elder,” 1891. The Salt Lake Tribune’s M…
s: 12 Nov 2026The letters of “The Elder,” 1891. The Salt Lake Tribune’s Morrisite letters of 1891 turn out to be part of a series of ten, “Charity for the Mormons,” printed on Sundays from May 31 to August 2 and signed “The Elder”; John R. Eardley wrote that they were John Parson’s. All ten are now listed on the Newspapers page with free links to Utah Digital Newspapers. The three on the Morrisites add to the Chronology (the meeting of February 11, 1861; the opening of the siege; Howard Egan at Deep Creek in 1863) and to Who died at Kington Fort?, Was Lot Smith at the siege? and the Farmington court-martial question. Correction: the Chronology and Parson’s roll note said the letters began in June and announced that his work would be “established this year”; the series began on May 31, and those words come from a private letter of Parson’s to Eardley.

s: 12 Nov 2026Data release 1.2. The data files are now release 1.2. It adds four people to the list of others named as Morrisites (Anders and Karen Søndermark, Hans Knudsen and Carleton Fellows), expands the entries for Joseph Morris, Andrew Hendrikson and the Bowmans, corrects George Williams’s entry, and records Josiah Price’s later affiliation with the Reorganized Church. It is archived at Zenodo with the earlier releases (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24154693).

t: 12 Nov 2026Why William James went to Nevada. A copy of a revelation of…
s: 12 Nov 2026Why William James went to Nevada. A copy of a revelation of August 20, 1872, among the letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas (Church History Library, MS 31876), shows that James’s mission of 1872 was to help John D. Bowen of Austin, Nevada, keep his property; Bowen’s own letter of 1874 says he lost it anyway. Added to the Chronology under September 22, 1872, with Andrew Hendrikson’s baptism in the Missouri River at Omaha in January 1869 under 1869, and a roll note for John Bowen.

t: 12 Nov 2026The Council Bluffs register. The Council Bluffs congregatio…
s: 12 Nov 2026The Council Bluffs register. The Council Bluffs congregation’s register of 1869–71 (Church History Library, MS 32226) shows S. P. Guhl baptized at South Weber on August 7, 1861, by Peter Klemgaard and Jens Mikkelsen and confirmed by Morris, Richard Cook and John Banks, and identifies further roll members baptized at South Weber: Niels and Maren Larsen, Mikkel Christensen and probably Elisa (Lese) Christensen, and a Maria Guhl, later Fellows. See the roll notes and Who they were (Hans Knudsen, Carleton Fellows). Corrections to the Omaha entries of earlier tonight, from the draft of that register: Rasmus Rasmusson’s birthplace reads “Akkerup,” not “Akkrup”; Christian Lundgreen’s baptism (June 30, 1861) and confirmation by Morris are now certain; the Søndermarks were baptized by Morris and Mikkelsen and are entered in the draft as Anders and Karen Maria Sørensen; and Hans Petersen’s exclusion is dated only to 1870.

t: 12 Nov 2026The Omaha register. The Omaha congregation’s own register o…
s: 12 Nov 2026The Omaha register. The Omaha congregation’s own register of members, 1869–1872 (Church History Library, MS 32226), lists forty-two members with their birthplaces and baptisms, five of them at South Weber in 1861. It adds roll notes for Christian Lundgreen, Hans Petersen and Kershon (Kjersten) Peterson and to the note for Rasmus Rasmusson, and two Morrisites not on the roll, Anders and Karen Søndermark, baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, to Who they were. The register is described on Repositories.

s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church organized, 1872. The Montana council’s first minutebook (Church History Library, MS 32226) records the meeting of September 22, 1872, at William P. Thomas’s house on Warm Spring Creek that organized the church there under Williams’s instructions, with William James as president and Margaret Thomas as “Lady elect to preside over the Female Order.” See the Chronology, the Teachings and the roll notes for W. P. Thomas and William James.

t: 11 Nov 2026Williams on polygamy, Idaho and Abel. A letter of George Wi…
s: 11 Nov 2026Williams on polygamy, Idaho and Abel. A letter of George Williams of about 1871 in the Church History Library’s MS 32226 adds to the Teachings: his statement that he “never taught the doctrine or counselled the practice” of polygamy, a gathering “in Idaho” that was not permitted, the washing of feet, counsel on eating and drinking, an earlier account of Grow’s mission, and Adam’s future government with Abel as “the next Jesus Christ.”

t: 11 Nov 2026Morris’s apostles in California, 1874. A letter of S. P. Gu…
s: 11 Nov 2026Morris’s apostles in California, 1874. A letter of S. P. Guhl from Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874 (Church History Library, MS 31876), reports that Morris’s apostles had organized in California under John Parson, with R. J. Livingston and Alexander Dow as counselors. It is added to What became of the California congregation? and to the roll notes for Parson, Livingstone, Dow and Guhl.

11 Nov 2026Letters of 1872–1878. Hendrickson’s letters for 1872–1878 (Church History Library, MS 31876) show James Bowman, whose wife Isabella was killed at the surrender, still a believer at Soda Springs in 1878 and receiving Williams’s epistles, and mentioning “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” nearby; and John R. Eardley at Salinas City, California, in December 1878. See Who they were and the roll note for Eardley. Correction: the entry for George Williams on Who they were still said that he prophesied in 1879 that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming; it now follows his letter, as the Chronology does.

t: 11 Nov 2026Reports from inside the camp, 1861–62. Informers’ reports t…
s: 11 Nov 2026Reports from inside the camp, 1861–62. Informers’ reports to Brigham Young in his office files (Church History Library, CR 1234 1) add to the Chronology for May–December 1861: Morris’s claim, on May 12, 1861, to be “the Seventh Angel”; the revelation of May 11 calling believers to gather at South Weber; and a diagram already in use that spring. An onlooker’s letter describes the procession of May 30, 1862, and acting governor Frank Fuller’s letters of June 14 and 16, 1862, are added to the days of the siege. The Teachings page adds the confirmation by three men, the Holy Ghost as a “redeemed being,” a form for ordaining an “elect lady,” and the inscriptions on the numbered rods of office, copied on June 19, 1862. See also Where did the rituals come from? and the Glossary.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Danish mission. Letters to Andrew Hendrickson of 1869–1…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Danish mission. Letters to Andrew Hendrickson of 1869–1871 (Church History Library, MS 31876) show a congregation of Williams’s followers in Copenhagen in 1871 and S. P. Guhl’s letter of November 1871 breaking with Williams; see the Chronology and the roll note for Guhl. The Places page now ends with a short note on places beyond the American West: England, Denmark and Constantinople.

t: 11 Nov 2026The siege, day by day. A posse member’s account of the sieg…
s: 11 Nov 2026The siege, day by day. A posse member’s account of the siege and the lists of prisoners in the Church History Library (CR 100 397, CR 1234 1) let the Chronology give the siege a day at a time, June 13–17, 1862. New: 149 men were taken, of whom 100 were brought to Salt Lake City and 49 released at the fort, among them eight, Mark H. Forscutt and John R. Eardley with them, who had given themselves up during the fighting. The posse member, John G. Chambers, gives a third account of the rolling battery and writes that Banks was killed with Morris at the surrender; both are noted under Who died at Kington Fort? and on the Kington Fort page. The files are described on Repositories.

t: 11 Nov 2026Williams on Mahomet, the eight estates and the August feast…
s: 11 Nov 2026Williams on Mahomet, the eight estates and the August feast. The rest of the record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879 (Church History Library, MS 31876), has been read. New on the Teachings page: Williams’s account (1877) of a message from Mahomet to the Sultan, carried by Almerin Grow; his teaching (1880) of eight estates and of Adam as the savior of an earlier planet; a Montana copy of two chapters of the records he said he translated, with the “Mighty Goddess”; and his confirmation (1880) of William James’s proposal that the anniversary of the Lord’s House be kept as a feast, also in the Glossary. Correction: the Repositories page called Emanuel Strom’s 1872 copies of Williams’s epistles Danish translations; they are in Swedish.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in the 1880s. Hendrickson’s letters for …
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in the 1880s. Hendrickson’s letters for 1880–1889 add to the Chronology: the dispute over the yearly election in 1884; the officers of Stake No. 1 who held out for William James in 1886; the Doves’ return to Montana in March 1887; John R. Eardley’s contacts with David Whitmer’s followers in 1887–89 and his journey to England in 1887; and George Thompson’s letters from Epping. See also How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another? and the roll notes for Eardley and John Parson.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church, 1893–1901. From the last of the letters…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church, 1893–1901. From the last of the letters to Andrew Hendrickson: Eardley watching the Salt Lake Temple dedication against a prophecy he attributed to Morris, baptisms at Race Track on August 9, 1893, a shared meeting house in 1894, and the “threatened collapse” of 1901 (Chronology); and Hendrickson’s own view of the Son and the Father, 1897 (Teachings).

t: 11 Nov 2026George Thompson’s sister. Jane Higham, on the roll with her…
s: 11 Nov 2026George Thompson’s sister. Jane Higham, on the roll with her husband Charles, was the elder sister of George Thompson, Williams’s companion in England and later president of the Montana church; Thompson settled near the Highams in Bingham County, Idaho, in 1891.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1891. Eardley’s letters of 1891 add t…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1891. Eardley’s letters of 1891 add to the Chronology: John Parson’s weekly letters in the Salt Lake Tribune and his visit to the Deer Lodge Valley, the November court in the year “expected,” and the first open break at Warm Springs in December.

t: 11 Nov 2026Morris’s diagram of the worlds. The Teachings page now show…
s: 11 Nov 2026Morris’s diagram of the worlds. The Teachings page now shows “The Rounds of Eternity: Joseph Morris’ First Diagram,” from Eardley’s Gems of Inspiration (1899), and “Seth’s Diagram” from Williams’s record of letters of the 1870s, a hand-colored version with Swedish labels. A third version, a drawing in Josiah D. Price’s journal, is described there.

t: 11 Nov 2026Records from the Community of Christ Library Archives. Josi…
s: 11 Nov 2026Records from the Community of Christ Library Archives. Josiah D. Price’s journal names the six men Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, and describes the drill and the four horsemen of May 1, 1862, the soldier’s oath of May 26 and the Foreshadowing procession of May 30. The Joseph Morris Papers, which appear to be Alexander Dow’s, add his account of the siege and his later life in St. Louis. See the Chronology, the Teachings page, Where did the rituals come from? and the Repositories.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Doves and Davies. The movement at a glance chart now dr…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Doves and Davies. The movement at a glance chart now draws a line from William W. Davies to the Doves’ California congregation, as the chart’s description already said. James Dove’s A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites shows him joining Davies’s followers in San Francisco in 1868; the Chronology under 1873 now gives his account.

t: 11 Nov 2026Correction: when the Doves organized. The movement at a gla…
s: 11 Nov 2026Correction: when the Doves organized. The movement at a glance chart said the Doves’ California congregation was a Church of the Firstborn “from 1873,” following Watson. James Dove’s own A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites places the organizing after April 7, 1874, and shows the church still active in 1892; the chart now reads “from c. 1874; active 1892,” and the Chronology gives both accounts. The chart’s description also now names the Emmonses, who joined the Reorganized Church in 1890.

t: 11 Nov 2026Letters of 1890. Hendrickson’s letters for 1890 show a Mont…
s: 11 Nov 2026Letters of 1890. Hendrickson’s letters for 1890 show a Montana family, the Emmonses, joining the Reorganized Church that year, and John R. Eardley conceding that Williams “was mistaken” in calling himself Daniel’s stone. See How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another? and the Teachings.

t: 11 Nov 2026W. P. Thomas and the Evans family. The roll note for W. P. …
s: 11 Nov 2026W. P. Thomas and the Evans family. The roll note for W. P. Thomas now records that Find a Grave links him as the father of Evan Price Thomas (1845–1891), and that a 1945 account places him on Warm Springs Creek before Morgan Evans’s party arrived in 1865. The same account dates the Evans family’s arrival to August 1865 and their move to the site near Opportunity to the spring of 1866 (see the Bibliography entry for In the Shadow of Mount Haggin).

t: 11 Nov 2026Letters of 1892. Hendrickson’s letters for 1892 include a p…
s: 11 Nov 2026Letters of 1892. Hendrickson’s letters for 1892 include a printed copy of James Dove’s A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, so it comes off the Wanted list. From it, the Chronology now has the Doves’ 1885 mission to Utah and Montana and their account of how The Spirit Prevails came to be printed. Refined date: John Parson’s death is now dated June 13, 1892, at the Larsens’ ranch near Deer Lodge (his page gave only the year and place). The Teachings add Thompson’s and Eardley’s hopes in 1892, and the Lord’s House glossary entry notes that it was still in use at the end of 1892.

t: 11 Nov 2026The revelation of the two stakes, 1874. Williams’s epistle …
s: 11 Nov 2026The revelation of the two stakes, 1874. Williams’s epistle from Ashby of April 6, 1874 (Church History Library, MS 31876) contains the revelation that divided the Montana church into “two Stakes under one Head,” James and Hendrikson each to take charge of “those that are convenient unto him,” the source of the word disputed in 1876. The same letters show “the Sides of the North” in use by 1874 (the guide had said 1877), the first robe for William James and a “thanksgiving day” with singing and dancing. See the Chronology under the 1870s, the Teachings page and Where did the rituals come from?

t: 11 Nov 2026Correction: who was Enos? The Teachings page said that Seth…
s: 11 Nov 2026Correction: who was Enos? The Teachings page said that Seth and Enos in Williams’s vision of 1862 were very probably Morris and John Banks. A letter of Williams’s of December 1881 says that Morris called Joseph Smith Enos, meaning that he “represented” him; Seth is Morris. The page is corrected.

t: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–1881. They give Thompso…
s: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–1881. They give Thompson’s written appointment to act for Williams (July 14, 1881), sent to Montana for the Saints’ approval; the ladder of 144,000 names and Christ’s return of the kingdom to “the Father of the family, even Adam,” with a note on the Adam–God teaching; rites for blessing children and the sacrament; the Lord’s House as “a Temple in miniature”; and Beck’s visit to Williams at Cottonwood, which supports the phrenology fragment. See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1880–81, the Glossary, and the questions on phrenology and on government by vote.

t: 11 Nov 2026Correction: the charge against William P. Thomas. Earlier t…
s: 11 Nov 2026Correction: the charge against William P. Thomas. Earlier today the Chronology placed the charge against Thomas in 1877 and said no record of it had been found. The New North-West shows that a Deer Lodge grand jury indicted “Wm. P. Thomas” in December 1876 for assault with intent to do great bodily injury, and that a jury found him not guilty on December 21, 1876. The account is now under 1876 in the Chronology.

t: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–1878. His letters to Wi…
s: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–1878. His letters to William James and the Montana Saints (Church History Library, MS 31876) give the High Priestess ordained for Stake No. 2 in 1877; the white robe; the founding of the Court of the Lord’s House; the first request, in October 1877, for a building “to carry out Temple ordinances” and the words for its dedication in 1878; the October 1877 motion consigning Davies, Guhl and the Doves to “outer darkness”; the charge against William P. Thomas; his own words on the “keys of detection”; and his mockery of “come to Walla Walla and see my little Jesus.” See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1876, 1877 and 1878–79, the Glossary, and the questions on women, on phrenology and on government by vote.

t: 11 Nov 2026Correction: how the Church History Library folders are cite…
s: 11 Nov 2026Correction: how the Church History Library folders are cited. The catalog does not number the folders of MS 31876, and this guide’s folder and item numbers counted them in two different ways, so some led to the wrong folder. Every MS 31876 citation now names the folder by its catalog title, for example “Minutes, 1876.”

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church, 1882–1891, and Seth’s Diagram. The rema…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church, 1882–1891, and Seth’s Diagram. The remaining Montana minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1882 to Minutes, 1891) have now been read, with the first letters of Williams to William James of 1876–77. New: the doctrine of birthrights set out by the church’s court in 1887; how the church met 1891, the year it had been taught to expect the Second Coming; prayer standing with hands raised; the 1887 election and the Lord’s House trustees; a proposal of 1891 to move the Lord’s House; Eardley as “first Counselor to Cainan in England”; and a description of “Seth’s Diagram.” See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1876, 1886, 1887 and 1891, and the Glossary entries for the Lord’s House and the Prophet Cainan.

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1880–81. The Danish council minutes f…
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1880–81. The Danish council minutes for 1880 and 1881 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1880 and Minutes, 1881) have been read in part. They give a robed William James administering the sacrament and looking for the coming of Christ in 1891, the first August 9 conference, word of the death of a son of Williams, Thompson writing Williams’s epistles by September 1881, Eardley preaching against brandy and tobacco, and a ruling of 1881 against speaking in tongues in public meetings. New in the Chronology under 1880–81, on the Teachings page under George Williams, and as first findings for What became of the spiritual gifts?

t: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1876. The Danish council minutes for …
s: 11 Nov 2026The Montana church in 1876. The Danish council minutes for 1876 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1876) have been read in part. They show William James away on a mission for Williams, the dispute over the two stakes when he returned in August, Williams’s call in November for proposals on a form of government, and the exclusion of a member who had lost faith in Cainan. New in the Chronology under 1876, with notes under Marriage on the Teachings page and on Dempsey Creek under Places.

t: 11 Nov 2026George Morris on his brother Joseph. The reminiscences of M…
s: 11 Nov 2026George Morris on his brother Joseph. The reminiscences of Morris’s elder brother George (Church History Library, MS 1614) have now been read for this guide. They give Joseph’s life before Utah (England, St. Louis, Pittsburgh), his arrival in 1853, his early marriages, a private revelation offering George an apostleship, Brigham Young’s 1876 permission for proxy ordinances, and George’s verdict on Burton’s 1879 trial. See Documents and the Chronology.

s: 11 Nov 2026The editor’s photographs are free to reuse. Photographs taken by the editor are now licensed under CC BY 4.0, like the guide’s text and data: credit “Eric Paul Rogers, Morrisite.org.” Photographs from other people and institutions still belong to their owners.

t: 11 Nov 2026When the Montana church ended. Correction: the guide said, …
s: 11 Nov 2026When the Montana church ended. Correction: the guide said, citing Anderson, that the Montana church disbanded in 1969 after a last annual gathering on August 6, 1969. Anderson dates the end to George Johnson’s death in 1954, when the Lord’s House was boarded up, and records a feast-day gathering of surviving Morrisites on August 9, 1969 (Revisited, pp. 212, 214, 218); the 1969 date for a formal disbanding comes from Utah State University’s finding aids. The guide also now credits the reading of the Deer Lodge prison as Ezekiel’s temple to Leland Jensen rather than to Neal Chase (pp. 216–18). See the Chronology and How and when did the Montana church end?
