s: 11 Nov 2026Watson’s Writings and Revelations among the essential works. Start here now lists Kirk Watson’s 2026 collection of writings by Morris, Williams, Davies and the Doves.

t: 11 Nov 2026“Walla Walla Jesus.” The Glossary now explains the name, la…
s: 11 Nov 2026“Walla Walla Jesus.” The Glossary now explains the name, later given to William W. Davies’s son Arthur, whom Davies proclaimed the Messiah; a new question asks when the name was first used.

t: 11 Nov 2026Teachings across the guide. Following the new Teachings pag…
s: 11 Nov 2026Teachings across the guide. Following the new Teachings page: the failed-prophecy, marriage and reincarnation questions have new first findings; the Chronology adds the consecration revelation of December 30, 1861, Davies’s “third dispensation” of 1866, George Dove’s Church of the Firstborn of 1873 and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation of 1892; the Glossary adds “Sides of the North” and the order of seven angels; and the lineage chart now dates the Doves’ church from 1873.

t: 11 Nov 2026A new page: what the Morrisites taught. Teachings summarize…
s: 11 Nov 2026A new page: what the Morrisites taught. Teachings summarizes the movement’s beliefs period by period, with sources: Joseph Morris on the coming of Christ, consecration, reincarnation, the spiritual gifts and marriage; George Williams, the Prophet Cainan, and “the Sides of the North”; the Montana church; William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven; the Doves; and later echoes. It draws on The Spirit Prevails, Gems of Inspiration, Kirk Watson’s new edition, and Williams’s letters at the Church History Library.

t: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s 1879 prophecy, from his own letter. Correction: …
s: 11 Nov 2026Williams’s 1879 prophecy, from his own letter. Correction: the guide said that in January 1879 George Williams prophesied that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming. His letter of January 6, 1879 (in a copy made by Andrew Hendrickson in 1883, Church History Library, MS 31876) names no county and no date: it calls the region where the Montana Saints lived “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming. The Chronology and the Glossary entry for the Prophet Cainan now say so.

t: 11 Nov 2026Three new questions from the Deer Lodge Valley. The Questio…
s: 11 Nov 2026Three new questions from the Deer Lodge Valley. The Questions page now asks where the Copper Village organ came from (a 2013 recording describes it as a Mason & Hamlin built about 1892, too late to have come from Utah or to date from the building of the Lord’s House), whether Gwendale was named for Gwenllian Evans, and whether the Evans and Thomas families of Gwendale were connected to the Morrisites.

t: 11 Nov 2026Willow Glen Ranch in 2013. The Images page has seven photog…
s: 11 Nov 2026Willow Glen Ranch in 2013. The Images page has seven photographs of the Willow Glen Ranch east of Anaconda, taken on July 8, 2013, by Jim Furshong. They show the barn, a cobblestone pillar, the stone cottage and the lane. This is the later stock farm of that name, not the Morrisite Willow Glen of the 1880s on Warm Springs Creek.

t: 11 Nov 2026A new question: Morrisite teaching and Chad Daybell. The Qu…
s: 11 Nov 2026A new question: Morrisite teaching and Chad Daybell. The Questions page now asks whether there is a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s. It compares Williams’s 1869 assignments of earlier lives with Daybell’s past-life claims and notes the differences, above all Daybell’s “zombie” teaching, which has no counterpart in the Morrisite records. No evidence of descent is known.

t: 11 Nov 2026Data release 1.1. The data files are now release 1.1. It co…
s: 11 Nov 2026Data release 1.1. The data files are now release 1.1. It corrects John Peter Lorensen’s entry, which had given a death in Nevada in 1870 that the records do not support, and adds George Johnson’s birth in Denmark in 1856. It is archived at Zenodo alongside release 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24139092).

t: 11 Nov 2026Building the Lord’s House; Montana in 1873–74. Correction: …
s: 11 Nov 2026Building the Lord’s House; Montana in 1873–74. Correction: the guide said the Lord’s House was begun in 1877. The council minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876) show the site was chosen only on February 24, 1878, when a joint council voted ten to five to build on Andrew Hendrikson’s land at Race Track. The House was built under Peder Jansen, used for Sunday meetings from the summer of 1879, and nearly paid for that October; the Chronology and the Glossary now say so. Also added to the Chronology: Stake No. 2’s founding meeting of July 12, 1874; the church in 1873, with William James on a mission in Nevada and the quarrel between William P. Thomas and Daniel James; a Fremont, Nebraska, branch, 1871–73 (now also shown in a small locator inset on the Omaha & Council Bluffs map, with Lincoln); and Sven Olson Hagg’s letter of March 1866, which shows Morrisites meeting in the Deer Lodge Valley that winter and William W. Davies already claiming spiritual gifts there. See also the roll notes for Hegg, Davies, Thomas, James and Eliason. The Danish passages are translated by Claude and not yet checked.

t: 10 Nov 2026About the Danish translations. The translations of the Dani…
s: 10 Nov 2026About the Danish translations. The translations of the Danish minutes, the 1869 record book and the Omaha minutebook quoted in this guide were generated by Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, from the Church History Library’s page images (MS 31876). No Danish reader has checked them yet, so treat them as provisional. Each citation now says so, and so does the collection’s entry under Repositories.

t: 10 Nov 2026Omaha in 1871. The last pages of the Omaha minutebook show …
s: 10 Nov 2026Omaha in 1871. The last pages of the Omaha minutebook show the congregation giving up Latter-day Saint-style conferences in March 1871, a leader of its sisters, Marie Mortensen, joining the Reorganized Church that May (the earliest such case yet found among Williams’s followers), and the book closing on June 4, 1871, as members prepared to move west. Its companion record book of 1869 records the earlier lives Williams assigned to the men he anointed. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the RLDS question under Questions, and Reincarnation in the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Omaha minutebook. The Danish minutebook of the Omaha an…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Omaha minutebook. The Danish minutebook of the Omaha and Council Bluffs church (Church History Library, MS 31876) tells how it was organized in February 1869, while George Williams passed through Omaha on his way to England, and names the Welsh missionary who went with William P. Thomas in 1869 as Daniel James, settling the question corrected earlier today. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the Chronology, and the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, S. P. Guhl and W. P. Thomas.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Lord’s House dedicated August 9, 1879. The Danish counc…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Lord’s House dedicated August 9, 1879. The Danish council minutes of the Race Track stake (Church History Library, MS 31876) date the dedication of the Lord’s House: in July 1882 the council planned to celebrate August 9 as the third anniversary of its dedication. They also show the council keeping February 14 as Williams’s birthday, and the Danish members’ debate before the 1883 vote. Added to the Chronology and the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: which James went to England. Earlier today th…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: which James went to England. Earlier today the Chronology said that William James went with William P. Thomas to join Williams in England in 1869–70. George Thompson’s letter of July 29, 1869, addresses the two as “W. P. and D. J.,” so the Brother James was probably Daniel James, not William M. James; the entry is corrected. Thompson’s letters to Thomas (Church History Library, MS 31876) also place Thompson with Williams at Ashwicken in 1869 and give Williams’s age and the cause of his death, now in the Chronology and the Glossary.

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams’s letters…
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s letters to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams’s letters of 1869–73 to Hendrikson and the Omaha church (Church History Library, MS 31876) show that William P. Thomas and a Brother James went to England to be with him and returned to Montana in 1870, give Williams’s own account of Almerin Grow’s mission to Constantinople and Jerusalem, and trace the move from Omaha to Montana in 1871–72. Added to the Chronology and to the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, John Merrick and S. P. Guhl; John Merrick’s identification is raised from “Check” to “Probable.”

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams in England, 1869–73. Williams’s letters of 1870–73…
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams in England, 1869–73. Williams’s letters of 1870–73 in the Church History Library (MS 31876) show that he left America about January 1869, leaving his family in Salt Lake City, and that his “Ashby” was Ashby by Brigg, Lincolnshire; they also name his daughter Adelaide. In 1873 he called “Burton and Lot Smith” “the murderers at Weber”; whether Lot Smith was at the siege is a new open question under Questions.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Montana by 1868. The Glossary said the Montan…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Montana by 1868. The Glossary said the Montana church regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s. A letter of George Williams dated December 14, 1868, is addressed to “Bro. James & Saints of the Most High in Montana,” so William James’s group was there, under that name, by 1868 (Church History Library, MS 31876). The Glossary is corrected and the Chronology has a new 1868 entry, which also notes that Williams was living in George Thompson’s house at Walthamstow by 1876. The roll note for Charles Higham adds his visit to Thompson in England about 1877.

t: 10 Nov 2026Thompson at Williams’s side. In March 1882, as George Willi…
s: 10 Nov 2026Thompson at Williams’s side. In March 1882, as George Williams lay dying at Walthamstow, George Thompson answered the Montana church’s questions for him, explaining that Williams “was not really Cainan the son of Enos” but represented him, and promising to confirm the church’s choice of officers (Church History Library, MS 31876). Added to the Chronology, the Glossary and the Questions.

t: 10 Nov 2026Thompson in England. George Thompson, elected president of …
s: 10 Nov 2026Thompson in England. George Thompson, elected president of the church in Montana in April 1886, was writing to the members that December from Thornwood Common, Epping, Essex, open to Joseph Smith III being “called through our Joseph” but not yet calling him a prophet. The letter is in the Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) and is now in the Chronology and the Questions. The same letters show John R. Eardley planning, in February 1880, to open a store in Montana (see the roll note).

t: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s last instructions. The Church History Library’s …
s: 10 Nov 2026Williams’s last instructions. The Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) hold George Williams’s own note of January 29, 1882, directing that William James be put before the church a year after his death, and an envelope to James inscribed “I leave you in charge after my decease,” the words James later relied on in claiming the presidency for life. Both are now in the Chronology. The same letters add to the roll notes for S. P. Guhl, who disputed James’s authority from Omaha in 1874, and for John Parson, William White and John Merrick, whom John R. Eardley reported on from California in 1875.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Montana elections. This guide said, follo…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Montana elections. This guide said, following Anderson, that William James was sustained as president in Montana in May 1882 and that George Thompson was elected president of the church on May 10, 1886. The Montana minutebook at the Church History Library records both elections at the yearly general assembly on April 25, the anniversary of George Williams’s death: James in 1883, by 19 votes to 10, and Thompson in 1886. The May dates are those of council meetings. The Chronology and Questions are corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026The Montana church’s own records. The Church History Librar…
s: 10 Nov 2026The Montana church’s own records. The Church History Library’s Church of the Firstborn records, now on the Repositories page and readable online, include the membership record kept from 1874 and the council minutes for 1881–1890. They give the date of Williams’s death in England (April 25, 1882), the two stakes on Warm Spring Creek and at Race Track, the meeting house at Willow Glen, the schisms of 1883 and 1886, the council’s notice in the New North-West of November 13, 1885, disowning the Doves of the California congregation (now on the Newspapers page), and an invitation in 1886 to use the Reorganized Church’s new meeting house in Deer Lodge City, which settles who built the church a newspaper had called Morrisite, now a first finding on one of the open questions. The membership record also strengthens the notes on several names on the roll: Ole Olsen, W. P. Thomas and Erick Eliason, and new notes for William James, Christian Anderson and Rasmus Rasmusson.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Zbaraschuk paper. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 …
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: the Zbaraschuk paper. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 paper on William W. Davies was written at Walla Walla College, not Whitman College as this guide said. Its acknowledgments thank his thesis advisor at Walla Walla College, and the Church History Library catalogs it the same way. The Bibliography is corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026Citations for your reference manager. The Bibliography and …
s: 10 Nov 2026Citations for your reference manager. The Bibliography and the Newspapers list can now be downloaded for Zotero, EndNote or Mendeley, as RIS, BibTeX or CSL-JSON: 109 books, articles, theses and media items, and 66 newspaper articles and reprints, each reprint noting the paper it was copied from. Each record keeps the citation exactly as it appears here.

t: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Johan Peter Lorentzen. Earlier versions of th…
s: 10 Nov 2026A correction: Johan Peter Lorentzen. Earlier versions of this guide gave his death as 1870 in Nevada. Family Tree says only that he died before 1870, probably in Nevada; the date was an estimate misread as a year. His death date is now left blank on the roll, the people and Movements pages and in the data files, and a new roll note explains the evidence, including the 1870 census, which finds his children Charles and Josephine at Treasure City with no father in the household. The same misreading had crept into the new roll note on Ole Olsen’s wife Anne, which gave Family Tree’s date for her death as 1870; the tree, too, says only “before 1870,” with no source, so the 1902 account of her death in Wyoming in 1862 stands uncontradicted. That note is corrected.

t: 10 Nov 2026George Johnson in 1902. A county biography of about 1902, P…
s: 10 Nov 2026George Johnson in 1902. A county biography of about 1902, Progressive Men of the State of Montana, says of George Johnson, later the last leader of the Montana church, that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” It also confirms that his wife, Josephine V. Oleson, was a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. Both entries are updated: Johnson under others named, and Ole Olsen on the roll.

t: 10 Nov 2026Free to reuse, with credit. The guide’s own text and data a…
s: 10 Nov 2026Free to reuse, with credit. The guide’s own text and data are now licensed under CC BY 4.0, and the data files carry a release number and a list of changes, so a figure can be traced to the version it came from. Release 1.0 is archived at Zenodo with a permanent identifier, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24100263. Every name on the roll now has its own link (hover over a name and click #), pages can be saved to Zotero with one click, and pages print without menus and buttons. The About page now explains how corrections are made and what the guide does for accessibility.

t: 9 Nov 2026The guide’s data, to download. A new Data page offers the li…
s: 9 Nov 2026The guide’s data, to download. A new Data page offers the lists behind the roll, the person pages and the Where they went map as CSV files: the 1861–62 roll with FamilySearch matches, birthplaces, emigrating companies and later affiliations; documented whereabouts after 1862; family ties on the roll; and others named as Morrisites. Each comes with a description of its columns and their limits, and all four can be downloaded together. The page also shows how much is known so far about the people on the roll, where they were decade by decade, a table of the roll that can be sorted, filtered, shared by link and downloaded, and a tool for counting the roll by any two characteristics, with the unknowns shown.

t: 9 Nov 2026Birthright by phrenology? A typescript fragment in the Morri…
s: 9 Nov 2026Birthright by phrenology? A typescript fragment in the Morrisite collection at USU, printed in Kirk Watson’s edition of Morrisite writings (pp. 90–91), says that a prophet in hiding at Cottonwood read men’s priesthood by feeling their heads, and that no descendant of Cain would enter the Church. Watson, who brought it to the guide’s attention, identifies the prophet as the Prophet Cainan. The page also names a Niel Beck. See the new question of interpretation.

t: 9 Nov 2026The Racetrack church in 2020. Ten photographs taken inside a…
s: 9 Nov 2026The Racetrack church in 2020. Ten photographs taken inside and outside the Lord’s House on August 16, 2020, from the Marcus Daly Historical Society Museum and Archives and identified by Jim Furshong, extend the condition record between 2018 and the videos of 2026. They show the pulpit, benches and table still in place, and the hymnals and a 1931 Reorganized Church lesson quarterly left in the building. See Images. The Bibliography adds In the Shadow of Mount Haggin (1975), on the Evans family at Gwendale, and an Anaconda Standard article of 1935 that Patrick F. Morris cites.

t: 8 Nov 2026Corrections. A check of the guide against its sources led to…
s: 8 Nov 2026Corrections. A check of the guide against its sources led to several fixes. The chronology no longer gives a single death toll for the siege, and now says that John Banks died in custody on the evening of the surrender. The Glossary explains that “Church of the Firstborn” was not the name of Morris’s church in 1861: his revelations call it “my Church,” and Anderson gives the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High. The roll no longer lists Joseph Morris’s wives as Mary and Karen: his wife Mary Olsen is probably the roll’s Mary Morris, and Karen Morris is not identified. Notes on Anne Bar now record that the sources disagree on whether her baby died. Citations of The Spirit Prevails have been checked against the 1886 text; the account of the surrender, the trials and the pardons is on its p. 8, not p. 7, and it names the second woman shot at the surrender “Mrs. O’Hagg” (see Who died at Kington Fort?). The counts on Who they were now include all 178 people linked to Family Tree.

t: 7 Nov 2026Where Gwendale was. Notices in the New North-West place Gwen…
s: 7 Nov 2026Where Gwendale was. Notices in the New North-West place Gwendale, the Montana settlement renamed Morristown in 1878, in the upper Deer Lodge valley near Warm Springs and Lost Creek; by 1883 its school district was called Willow Glen. Gwendale is now marked on the valley map, with roll notes for W. P. Thomas and William W. Thomas. The four Warm Springs homestead claims named in a March 1880 land-office notice (Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen, Daniel James and W. P. Thomas) were all patented in 1880–81 and are now drawn on the map. The paper also settles the link between the names: in March 1882 it reported John R. Eardley’s appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was”; his store stood at “Daniel James’ corner.” See Deer Lodge Valley and Newspapers.

s: 7 Nov 2026The Deer Lodge paper. Seven items from the New North-West of Deer Lodge (1877–86), free on Chronicling America, are now on the Newspapers page. Among them: a Montana post office renamed Morristown in 1878 because many of its people were Morrisites, a description of Davies’s colony in 1877, and the Doves’ visit to preach at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1885.

t: 7 Nov 2026Isabella and James Bowman. Isabella Bowman, killed at the su…
s: 7 Nov 2026Isabella and James Bowman. Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender and the woman Burton was tried for killing in 1879, is now listed among the others named in the sources, with her husband James, who testified at the trial. James was earlier taken to be the John Bowman of the roll; the sources show they were different men. The timeline now gives both of Burton’s indictments: 1870, voided in 1872, and 1877.

t: 7 Nov 2026Newspapers. A new Newspapers page lists the press coverage b…
s: 7 Nov 2026Newspapers. A new Newspapers page lists the press coverage by event, from the Sacramento dispatch of June 16, 1862, and its reprints as far as England and Australia, through the 1870 dispute over who commanded at Kington Fort, Burton’s arrest in 1877 and the Salt Lake Tribune letters of 1891, to recent retellings. It also has tips for searching the newspapers. A first pass through Utah Digital Newspapers added the Salt Lake Herald’s daily reports of Burton’s 1879 trial, where former Morrisites testified and gave their homes at the time, and a 1907 interview with Presto Burrell of Connor’s command, who helped escort the colony to Soda Springs.

t: 5 Nov 2026The Walla Walla court files. The Washington State Archives s…
s: 5 Nov 2026The Walla Walla court files. The Washington State Archives scanned the two lawsuits against William W. Davies for this guide. The 1880 case brought by three former followers ended in a judgment of $3,225 and the sheriff’s sale of the community’s livestock and its eighty acres in 1881. Its depositions add to the record of several people on the 1861–62 roll: Peter C. Klemgard, who lived at Davies’s camp from 1870 to 1872; Swen O. Hagg, who came to Walla Walla with the first five families in 1867; Niels R. Beck, probably the “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” who sent money toward the land; and R. J. Livingstone, who left the Carson Valley for Walla Walla in 1877, as the Carson Valley News reported. Witnesses also describe the community’s teaching of reincarnation. Thanks to Lee Pierce of the archives’ Eastern Region Branch. See Repositories, the roll notes and the reincarnation question.

t: 5 Nov 2026The man who went for help. Lars Christian Geertsen, one of t…
s: 5 Nov 2026The man who went for help. Lars Christian Geertsen, one of the men the Morrisites held in their log-house jail in 1862, escaped and carried word to Salt Lake City. A Church History Department profile now confirms that he is the same man who settled at Salmon, Idaho, where he ranched at Geertson Creek and built a log house, later listed on the National Register of Historic Places, whose upstairs dance hall served the community into the 1920s. Readers in Salmon pointed the way. See Lars Christian Geertsen.

s: 4 Nov 2026Where did the reincarnation teaching come from? With help from Kirk Watson, the question now sets out C. LeRoy Anderson’s theory that Morris took the idea from Charles B. Thompson, and the case against it: the idea was already current among Latter-day Saints in the 1850s, and Morris dated it to a revelation of 1859. It also adds Israel A. J. Dennis, who founded a reincarnationist “Church of the First Born” with no known Morrisite tie, and corrects the chronology on James Brighouse, whose ideas have not been traced to the Morrisites. Dansk

Morrisitterne: en vejledning på dansk En kort indføring for danske og skandinaviske forskere i morrisitterne og deres kilder, med henvisninger til vejledningens engelske sider, hvor kilderne er citeret i detaljer. Denne side er skrevet på dansk af Claude, Anthropics AI-model, ud fra vejledningens engelske tekst, og den er endnu ikke gennemlæst af en dansk læser. Ved tvivl gælder de engelske sider. This page was written in Danish by Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, from the guide’s English text, and has not yet been checked by a Danish reader. The English pages govern. Hvem var morrisitterne? Morrisitterne var tilhængere af Joseph Morris, en engelskfødt konvertit til Jesu Kristi Kirke af Sidste Dages Hellige, som i Utah modtog åbenbaringer og den 6. april 1861 organiserede sin egen kirke, Den Førstefødtes Kirke (Church of the Firstborn), ved South Weber nord for Salt Lake City. Hans tilhængere samledes i Kington Fort, et forladt nybyggerfort, og ventede Kristi snarlige genkomst. En strid om indviet ejendom og om tre medlemmer, der blev holdt fanget i fortet, førte til arrestordrer, og fra den 13. til den 15. juni 1862 belejrede et territorialt opbud under Robert T. Burton fortet (Morrisitkrigen). Morris blev dræbt ved overgivelsen, og bevægelsen blev spredt. De overlevende drog i 1863 til Soda Springs i Idaho under beskyttelse af oberst Patrick E. Connors soldater, og senere til Carson Valley i Nevada, Californien, Omaha og Council Bluffs og Deer Lodge-dalen i Montana. Mange fulgte George Williams, “profeten Cainan,” og i Montana byggede de Herrens Hus ved Race Track, indviet den 9. august 1879. Se kronologien, stederne og kortet og læren. De danske morrisitter Dansktalende var fremtrædende fra begyndelsen. Bedømt alene efter navnet har 168 af de 430 personer i den trykte medlemsliste fra 1861–62 skandinaviske navne, og blandt de medlemmer, hvis fødested er kendt, er Danmark det næsthyppigste fødeland, efter England (Hvem de var). Flere kom til Utah med det danske emigrantkompagni i 1859. Morris’ åbenbaringer cirkulerede på dansk; menighederne i Omaha og Council Bluffs førte deres protokoller på dansk fra 1869; og i Montana skiftede man mellem danske og engelske møder. Andrew Hendrikson, født i Ondrup i Jylland i 1843 og aldrig selv sidste dages hellig, ledede morrisitterne i Montana fra 1886 til sin død i 1921. Da Joseph Smith III besøgte Soda Springs i 1889, fandt han de gamle morrisitter at være mest svenskere, nordmænd og danskere. Blandt de dræbte ved overgivelsen var en dansk kvinde, kaldet “Mrs. O’Hagg” eller “Haag” (Hvem døde i Kington Fort?). Personsider for danske og svenske medlemmer Niels Anderson (1835–1926), i fortet under belejringen, siden i Soda Springs. Niels Rasmussen Beck (1823–1888), senere landmand i Deer Lodge-dalen. Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925), der undslap fra fortets fængsel i 1862. Søren Peter Guhl (1821–1883), leder af morrisitterne i Council Bluffs. Jacob Carl Klingbech (1812–1897) og Karen Marie Klingbech (1824–1898), med det danske kompagni i 1859. Svenskfødte: Erik Eliasson og Karin Caroline Eliasson; Sven Olasson Hägg. Alle 430 navne står i medlemslisten. Navnene er trykt i amerikansk form: søg både under Hanson og Hansen, Peterson og Petersen, Christiansen og Christensen, Sorenson og Sorensen. Danske kilder Church History Library, Salt Lake City, MS 31876 og MS 32226: Den Førstefødtes Kirkes protokoller, blandt andet minutbogen for Omaha og Council Bluffs (1869–1871), medlemsregistre for Council Bluffs og Omaha, rådsprotokoller fra Race Track-staven i Montana, danske afskrifter af Williams’ breve og Andrew Henriksens spørgebog fra Council Bluffs. Mange er tilgængelige som billeder i bibliotekets katalog (Arkiver). Utah State University, Caine MSS 10: C. LeRoy Andersons samling, med et indbundet bind af Morris’ åbenbaringer på dansk, som ikke synes at findes andre steder. Det er hverken oversat eller sammenholdt med The Spirit Prevails (et åbent spørgsmål). I Danmark og blandt emigranterne: den skandinaviske missions emigrantprotokoller, emigrantbreve og dansksprogede aviser kan kaste lys over, hvorfor så mange skandinaver sluttede sig til Morris (Hvorfor var så mange morrisitter skandinaver?). Danske læsere søges De danske passager, der citeres på vejledningens engelske sider, er transskriberet og oversat af Claude fra katalogets billeder og er endnu ikke kontrolleret af en dansk læser. Den, der læser dansk håndskrift fra 1800-tallet, kan hjælpe ved at efterprøve læsningerne eller ved at tage fat på de danske åbenbaringer i Utah. Skriv gerne på dansk eller engelsk til contact@morrisite.org; bidrag krediteres (Del arkivalier). Vejledningens data, herunder medlemslisten med fødesteder, kan hentes som CSV-filer på engelsk (Data). Citér gerne denne side som: Rogers, Eric Paul, red. “Morrisitterne: en vejledning på dansk.” Morrisite.org. https://morrisite.org/dansk.html.
About

About this guide Where the material comes from, how it is checked, and how to cite it. How the guide was compiled The guide brings together work done over more than two decades. Its foundation is the research of C. LeRoy Anderson, whose files at Utah State University (Caine Coll. MSS 10) remain the largest body of Morrisite records. The editor assisted Anderson with the 2010 edition of his history and has studied the Morrisite apostle and later RLDS minister Mark Hill Forscutt since at least 2001, when his first article on Forscutt appeared, including transcribing Forscutt’s journals. Photographs of the sites were taken by the editor from the early 2000s onward. Kirk Watson’s 2026 edition of Morrisite writings, published scholarship, and records shared by descendants fill out the rest. A family connection. The editor is not descended from the Morrisites, but his children are: through their mother, they descend from Morrisite families who settled at Soda Springs and in the Deer Lodge Valley. Those families are treated in the guide like any others. Standards Citations follow The Chicago Manual of Style. Every work in the bibliography has been examined by the editor in at least one edition; where a page reference comes from an edition not seen, the entry says so. A work known only from another source’s citation will be marked Not yet checked. Facts are drawn from published works with citations; their text is not reproduced. Videos and photographs by others are linked, not copied, unless they have been shared for this guide; those are credited. Dates marked provisional, approximate, or “ca.” are flagged as such and revised when better evidence turns up. Membership rolls and other records naming private individuals are cited but not republished, with one exception: the 1861–62 South Weber roll, printed in 1886 and naming only people baptized more than 160 years ago, is given in full on the Roll of membership page. Changes are listed under What’s new. Oral and field sources Records of the editor’s own fieldwork, cited in this guide. Rogers, Eric Paul. “Memorandum of Recollection: South Weber Door-to-Door Visit.” Signed memorandum, November 1, 2026, recalling an unrecorded canvass of South Weber residents made before February 2004 in preparation for the editor’s 2006 John Whitmer Historical Association paper. PDF Privacy The guide counts visits with GoatCounter, an open-source service that uses no cookies and collects no personal information. It records which pages are read, how visitors arrived, and what words are typed into the search box, so the editor can see what readers look for and where the guide falls short. No one is tracked from one site to another, and the counts are not shared or sold.

Questions. When what you type into the search box is a question, GoatCounter records only that a question was asked, not the question. On the Ask the guide page, the editor’s reviewed answers and the lists of people are looked up in your own browser and send nothing. If you ask for a written answer, your question is sent to the guide’s answer service, run on Cloudflare, which sends it with passages from this guide to Anthropic’s Claude model to write the answer. The answer service does not keep your question. To prevent abuse it counts questions for an hour under a scrambled form of your internet address, and a Cloudflare Turnstile check confirms that you are a person. How Anthropic handles what is sent to it is set out in its privacy policy. Please don’t put personal details in a question. How to cite this guide Rogers, Eric Paul, ed. Corrections Errors are corrected as soon as they are found. A correction that changes a fact, a date or an identification is listed under What’s new, and person pages show the date they were last updated. Corrections, with the source they rest on, are welcome at contact@morrisite.org, and contributors are credited unless they prefer not to be.

Accessibility The guide aims to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2) at level AA. Pages can be read with a screen reader and used with a keyboard alone, images carry text descriptions, the text can be enlarged without loss, and the layout adapts to phones and to the reader’s light or dark setting. Charts are accompanied by the numbers behind them, and every page prints cleanly. If anything is hard to read or use, please write to contact@morrisite.org, and it will be fixed.
Contribute

Share records and corrections Much of the record is still in private hands. This site is noncommercial and does not ask for or accept money. Write to the editor at contact@morrisite.org. Descendants If your family kept letters, diaries, photographs, or church papers, they can be described here, and digitized or placed in a repository if you wish. Nothing is published without your permission. Researchers Send citations, corrections, and new finds. Theses, conference papers, and local histories are especially welcome, since they are the hardest to locate. Forscutt papers For the forthcoming edition of Forscutt’s “Sketch of Joseph Morris,” the editor would be glad to learn of other writings by Mark H. Forscutt: letters, diaries, sermons, or the earlier Morrisite history he is said to have written, whether in repositories or in family hands. His diary shows him at work on “the History” at Kington Fort in February 1862, quoting from “Rev. Book No 1” (Mark H. On the roll Erik Eliasson (1817–1893) A Swedish convert baptized into Joseph Morris’s Church of the Firstborn at South Weber, who stayed with the Morrisites at Soda Springs, joined the RLDS Church in 1870, and died among the Morrisite families of the Deer Lodge Valley. (Family Tree) 1861–62Baptized with Karin into the Church of the Firstborn at South Weber; both names are on the roll of membership. His name is not on the list of men taken at Kington Fort and brought before Judge Kinney (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); whether he was at the fort in June 1862 is not known. May 1863Comes to Soda Springs with the Morrisites under General Connor’s escort. Shupe’s early list of those families names “Eric Eliason” and “Mrs. Caroline Eliason,” and also his brother Elias and Elias’s wife. (Shupe, p. 13) 2 Aug 1863Daughter Anna born at Soda Springs; Shupe calls her the first white child born there. (Shupe, p. 29; Family Tree) 1 Sep 1867Son John Eric born at Soda Springs. (family account) 9 Jun 1870Baptized into the RLDS Church at Soda Springs by Lars Edler, on the same day as Karin, who is entered as Caroline Eliasson, born March 7, 1830, in Sweden. (Black, vol. 2) After 1870Takes the twins, Jacob and John, to the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, leaving part of the family at Soda Springs, and settles on the ranch near Racetrack that his grandson still held in 1989. The grandson’s account gives 1868, but the twins were born in 1867 and Isaac at Soda Springs in 1869, so the move came later. (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109) 3 Jun 1877At the Race Track stake’s council at Deer Lodge the clerk notes “Bro. O. Olsen og Eliason, som var ankommet fra Soda Spring” (“who had arrived from Soda Springs”; the place name is a probable reading). The date fits the family account: the twins, born in 1867, were ten. (council minutes, June 3, 1877, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude) 24 Feb 1878At a joint council at Race Track he votes with the majority, ten to five, to build the Lord’s House on Andrew Hendrikson’s land. (council minutes, February 24, 1878, MS 31876) Jul 1879Leads the meetings at Race Track until July 24, 1879. That day the council agrees, and Eliason with it, that a brother who speaks English better should lead them, and asks Hendrikson to take them over. (council minutes, July 24, 1879, MS 31876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude) June 1880The census counts Erik three times: as a married farmer living alone in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana; as a rancher living alone at Soda Springs; and, as “Alexr. Eliasson,” 63, at the head of the family at Soda Springs with “Carrie,” 50, and all six children, including the thirteen-year-old twins. He was already working land in Montana while the family’s home was still at Soda Springs. (1880 U.S. census) 14 Jan 1888Receives the patent for his 40-acre homestead in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T6N R9W, sec. 4), Homestead Certificate 560 at the Helena land office. The Homestead Act required five years’ residence before final proof, so he was on the land by about 1882 at the latest. His son Joseph patented the adjoining 40 acres in 1889. (BLM General Land Office records) 1893Dies at Racetrack, Montana, on March 6. (Family Tree) Karin dies at Soda Springs in 1902. (Family Tree) His brother Elias Erik’s younger brother Elias Eliasson (born 1819) also came to Soda Springs with the Morrisites in 1863; Shupe lists “Elias Eliason” and “Mrs. Elias Eliason” beside Erik and Karin (p. 13). Neither is on the roll of membership. Elias’s wife was Margreta Nilsdotter (1816–1900), and the family was in the Deer Lodge Valley by 1870, some years before Erik. The Family Tree records for Elias are tangled: one (LVXJ-L2R) has his Swedish baptism, and another, which carries his wife and children, has been given Erik’s birth and death dates. An Eliason household in 1889 When Joseph Smith III, president of the RLDS Church, visited Soda Springs in 1889, he stayed in the house of an Eliason family whose head was a widow, then away at Blackfoot (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 437). Erik was still living in 1893, and Elias’s widow lived in Montana, though one of Elias’s daughters later died at Blackfoot. Who that widow was is an open question. Open questions Where were Erik and Karin between the siege of June 1862 and the move to Soda Springs in May 1863? Who was the Eliason widow at Soda Springs in 1889? In what year did Erik move to the Deer Lodge Valley, and did Karin ever join him there? The 1880 census finds him farming there alone, with the family still at Soda Springs. His homestead case file at the National Archives (Helena land office, Homestead Certificate 560) should give the date he entered the land. If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. On the roll John Parson (1829–1892) President of the Morrisite apostles, who gave the order to raise the white flag at Kington Fort in 1862, later a Morrisite leader in Nevada, and joined the RLDS Church. On the roll Parson, John, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born January 1829, England (Family Tree) Died 1892, Montana (Family Tree) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “John Parsons” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed Morrisite, later joined the RLDS Church. In the Morrisite presidency with Richard Cook and John Livingstone that worked and baptized in Nevada; at the 1864 meeting of apostles there (Anderson, pp. 178, 180); listed among the contenders for Morrisite leadership (Anderson, p. 181). Later baptized into the RLDS Church at Oakland by Joseph Smith III (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 432). Family Tree FamilySearch L7YM-D5Y, John Parson (1829–1892). Wife Elizabeth (roll: Elizabeth Parson); died at Deer Lodge, Montana, the later Morrisite center. Identified by editor (FamilySearch search). Connected names on the roll Farley, Robert E.; Cook, Richard; Brown, Alonzo; Parson, Elizabeth Places in this guide Kington Fort, Carson City & California, Omaha & Council Bluffs, Deer Lodge Valley What the sources say Living up Weber Canyon when Morris began his mission (Gems, p. 16); called by revelation to move to South Weber, February 1861, with Robert Farley (Spirit Prevails, pp. 60–61); president of the apostles (Anderson, p. 65; Spirit Prevails, p. 77). Gave the order to raise the white flag at the surrender (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137); named in the writ and contempt citation (Anderson, p. 108; Gems, p. 20). Carried Governor Harding's pardon to the penitentiary and demanded the seven prisoners' release (Gems, p. 31). Later a leader in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178–81). A member of the First Council; summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28, 51). In November 1857 he served as a private in the same Weber District militia company and platoon as Robert Farley, mustered at Ogden in the Utah War call-up (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, Utah State Archives); in July 1860 the two were next-door neighbors near Ogden, both tanners (1860 U.S. census, Weber County, p. 155, as "Jno Parsons"). On January 25, 1885, after a meeting between them that had left Parson “deeply pained,” Joseph Smith III wrote to him quoting Morris’s revelation No. 64 on the Reorganization, asked who had represented the Weber body after Morris, and urged him to join the Reorganized Church; Smith wrote that he neither attacked Morris’s work “nor accept[ed] it as binding on me” (Joseph Smith III Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, pp. 148–51, Community of Christ Library Archives). He later joined the RLDS Church: Joseph Smith III baptized him at Oakland, California, over the protests of some of his brethren (December 12, 1886, in the church record; February 23, 1886, in the Oakland branch record: Henry A. Stebbins to Richard Ferris, November 20, 1891, Stebbins letterbook HASLB7, pp. 236–37, Community of Christ Library Archives), and on July 29, 1889, Parson showed Smith and Brother Anthony the site of the camp at Weber (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, pp. 432–33). In 1888 H. P. Brown of Oakland, editor of the Expositor, accused him of holding séances and pressed Smith to disown him; Smith refused to sanction Dr. P. W. Poulson’s book “Light of Messiah” and its “Order of Messiah,” in which Parson had been offered the place of “Third general,” and told him to leave Oakland, and in July 1888 Parson returned his certificate of appointment (Joseph Smith III to Brown, June 28, to Parson, July 2, and to Heman C. Smith, July 3 and 23, 1888, Letter Press Book, P6, JSLB4, pp. 287–99, 303–12, 318–19). He was expelled from the Reorganized Church on April 1, 1890, as reported to its recorder (Stebbins to Ferris, 1891). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Parsons”). At the March 1863 term the jury found him not guilty of murder; he then pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). A John Parson received a patent for 40 acres near Genoa in Carson Valley on September 20, 1873 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, sec. 15; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0020__.043). John R. Eardley wrote from Hollister, California, on November 9, 1875, that “John Parson & family have moved to Iron County,” after a “Kingdom building in San Francisco” had failed (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23). In 1888 and 1889 the Montana council discussed Parson’s mission “as appointed him by a new prophet called Dr. Poulson of Oakland, Cal.,” while he still held membership in the Reorganized Church (Church of the Firstborn records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 40, 44). He died of pneumonia on Monday, June 13, 1892, at the Larsens’ ranch about eight miles from Deer Lodge City, “the 30th anniversary of the mob coming up to Weber against us,” and his remains were shipped to Portland, Oregon; Eardley, who had promised to fetch him but was stopped by floods, wrote that he had shown “faithfulness to his imprisoned brethren at Salt Lake, after he himself had been liberated from prison” (John R. Eardley to James Dove, June 18, 1892, copy, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1892). Eardley says he read of the death in “the paper” on June 17; that paper has not been identified, and no notice has been found in the Helena Independent of June 17 or the Deer Lodge New North-West (Anaconda Recorder and New Northwest) of June 18, 1892, read from the page images, or by keyword searches of the Montana and Portland papers of June 13–30. The Reorganized Church’s Saints’ Herald printed the news that July, from a letter of “Bro. John Eardley, of Helena”: Parson, “formerly of Nevada, more recently of Oakland, California, and later still of Salt Lake City, Utah,” had died at the ranch of Christian Larsen in the Deer Lodge Valley on June 13, 1892. The editor added that Parson “became strongly imbued with Spiritist philosophy in the last three or four years of his life, but died within reach of some of those who retained the memory of Joseph Morris as a prophet,” that “Elder John Livingston, formerly of the Morrisite Camp,” was also dead, and that he had hoped both men would in time become “fully identified with the Reorganized Church” (Saints’ Herald 39, 1892, p. 438). A revelation of April 4, 1861, names him and Richard Cook as the first two men called, Parson to preside over those who would hold the apostleship (Spirit Prevails, No. 56, pp. 78–79; manuscript in the Joseph Morris Papers, P11-1 f5, Community of Christ Library Archives). On May 1, 1862, he rode the pale horse carrying the book of revelations, and on May 30 he rode as the fourth general (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1). In 1891 he wrote to Eardley from Salt Lake City that the work under his charge would be “established this year,” and that he would have a long letter in each Sunday’s Salt Lake Tribune; Eardley described the second as “upon the difference existing between a church and a kingdom.” By October he had been among the Saints in the Deer Lodge Valley (Eardley to Hendrickson, June and October 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1891). The letters are the Tribune’s series “Charity for the Mormons,” ten letters signed “The Elder” and printed from May 31 to August 2, 1891; the second, “Church of God and Kingdom of God” (June 7), is the one Eardley described. Letters 7–9 (July 12, 19 and 26) tell the Morrisite story, and the ninth give

On the roll John Banks (1806–1862) Joseph Morris’s counselor and the movement’s orator, wounded at the surrender of Kington Fort on June 15, 1862, who died that evening in custody. On the roll Banks, John, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born February 1806, England (Family Tree) Died 1862, Utah (Family Tree) Later path Killed at Kington Fort, June 1862. Mortally wounded at Kington Fort, June 15, 1862 (FamilySearch KWJC-XYW; Wikipedia, "Morrisite War"). Family Tree FamilySearch KWJC-XYW, John Banks (1806–1862). Family Tree records his role as Morris's counselor and his death at South Weber on June 15, 1862. Identified by editor (FamilySearch search). Connected names on the roll Cook, Richard; Klemgard, Peter C.; Jones, William J.; Smith, John Places in this guide Kington Fort What the sources say Joseph Morris's counselor in the church presidency and, in Forscutt's words, the movement's orator; a member of the First Council (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 24, 51); signed letters with Morris and Richard Cook (Spirit Prevails). Named with Morris, Cook, Parson and Klemgard in the May 1862 writ over the three imprisoned dissenters (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20). Wounded at the surrender on June 15, 1862, and died that evening in custody (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Anderson, p. 137); Eardley reports he seemed to be recovering in a wagon, then was dead within the hour, citing William Jones, who went to the wagon (Gems, p. 28). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 1668). On May 1, 1862, he rode the black horse carrying a pair of balances, and on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, he rode as the third general (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). His son Franklin Cyrus Banks (1847–1922) settled at Pleasant Grove; two of Franklin’s sons wrote about him: John Ray Banks (1881–1940), in his University of Utah thesis of 1909, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” and Karl Banks (b. 1889), in an essay and in talks of 1958–72 (see the Bibliography, Repositories and Newspapers; family links from FamilySearch Family Tree, KWJC-LR7, KWVR-2WN). J. H. Beadle tells, as Governor Harding’s story, that “the widow of Banks, the murdered Morrisite,” came to Harding with a Danish woman to warn him of a plot to compromise him with a woman, which she said her husband’s spirit had revealed to her (Life in Utah, Philadelphia, 1870, pp. 423–24). No other source for it has been found. T. B. H. Stenhouse wrote in 1873 that Banks was wounded at Morris’s death “but not fatally”: “In the evening he was well enough to sit up and enjoy his pipe. Suddenly he died.” Stenhouse thought him “foully dealt with” and gave a short life: an early English convert, a former Chartist, a president of large conferences and once of the presidency of the church in Britain (The Rocky Mountain Saints, New York, 1873, p. 600). Joseph Smith III, who counted him an early friend, preached his funeral at Nebraska City in October 1903 (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 433). His "Sketch of Joseph Morris" (Church History Library, MS 702) is the subject of the editor's documentary edition, in preparation. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (44 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 36981). He was one of eight men who “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). At Burton’s trial in 1879, James Unsworth, his brother-in-law, who lived at the fort without joining, testified that Forscutt “was living there. I believe he was one of the twelve apostles. He was Morris’ secretary and translator” (Salt Lake Herald, February 25, 1879, p. 3). Hans Oakason named him among the captains of the armed companies: “Niels Tragrup, Seers, Forscutt, Klemguard, and Abraham Taylor, I think” (Salt Lake Herald, February 26, 1879, p. 3). James Bowman said Morris’s revelations “were written over again afterwards by Mark H. Forscutt and John Parsons” (Salt Lake Herald, February 21, 1879, p. 3). Burton himself testified that “on Saturday,” June 14, “several other persons came out of the fort and surrendered. Forscutt, Eardly and women and children were among them” (Salt Lake Herald, February 27, 1879, p. 1). Richard W. Young, writing on the Morrisite War in 1890, says that the unnamed Morrisite eyewitness account of June 13, 1862, printed by T. B. H. Stenhouse in 1873 (the revelation read in the bowery, the first cannon ball, no man armed) “is believed to have been written by Mr. Mark H. Forscutt, then one of the Twelve Apostles of the Morrisite sect, and now a prominent member of the Reorganized Church” (The Contributor 11, no. 10 (August 1890): 371 n.; Stenhouse, The Rocky Mountain Saints, pp. 597–98). Young also has him in No. 7 Company, the apostles, of the Soldiers of Israel formed on May 16, 1862, and among those who surrendered on Saturday, June 14 (no. 8, p. 284; no. 11, p. 429). At the March 1863 term he and John Smith testified for the defence in the trial of the Morrisites for resisting process (Deseret News, March 25, 1863, p. 5). He died at Nebraska City early on the morning of October 18, 1903, thirteen days after his wife. The Saints’ Herald gives his birth as June 19, 1834, at Manchester; his baptism into the Reorganized Church by David Pudney on January 1, 1865; his ordination as a high priest (1868) at Plano by Joseph Smith, William Marks and Isaac Sheen; missions to England and the South Sea Islands; and his founding of Zion’s Hope. Joseph Smith III preached at the funeral, Columbus Scott in charge, with a guard of honor from the Grand Army of the Republic (Saints’ Herald 50, 1903, pp. 982, 1027, 1046). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Robert Farley”). On the roll Peter C. Klemgard Leader of the armed party that captured the three dissenters in 1862, sentenced in March 1863 and pardoned. On the roll Klemgard, Peter C., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “Peter Klemgaard” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, remanded to prison Connected names on the roll Jones, William J.; Banks, John; Cook, Richard Places in this guide Kington Fort, Morristown, Carson City & California, Kingdom of Heaven What the sources say Led the armed party of about thirty that captured William Jones and his companions (Anderson, p. 99, as Klemgaard); named in the writs and the contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); appointed to take charge of the firearms (Spirit Prevails, pp. 527–29). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree for the deaths of the posse men and sentenced to fifteen years at hard labor, the heaviest sentence (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); Governor Harding pardoned him a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31). He later followed William W. Davies. Testifying at Walla Walla in 1881, he said that he and Davies had withdrawn from the Latter-day Saint church under Morris at Weber, that he next met Davies at Soda Springs in 1865, where there were “about sixty of us Morrisites” and the camp broke up for want of a leader, and that he then went to San Francisco, where Davies’s missionaries won him over. He lived at Davies’s camp near Walla Walla with his wife and four children from April 1870 to April 1872, and added that “the doctrine taught at the Davies camp is not like the Morrisite religion” (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). The Walla Walla Statesman reported his testimony before the referee, given over more than two days: “I have known Davis for over 16 years; I made his acquaintance first in Utah, at a place called Weber; in 1864 [so printed] Davis, myself and others withdrew from the Mormons under the leadership of Morris; I next saw Davis at Soda Springs, Idaho.” He had believed “that Davis was the Holy Ghost, and his son the Messiah,” and began to doubt him when Davies quarrelled with his wife and lived well “when the people were starving” (Walla Walla Statesman, February 5, 1881, pp. 3–4; checked against the page images). On the roll Niels Anderson (1835–1926) A Danish-born Morrisite who was at the fort during the siege, stayed at Soda Springs, and married Mary Christofferson there in 1863. On the roll Anderson, Niels, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born October 1835, Denmark (Family Tree) Died 1926, Idaho (Family Tree) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “N. Anderson” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed with a Morrisite group. Among the few Morrisites who stayed at Soda Springs (Anderson, p. 162); listed with the Morrisite families who came with Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Family Tree FamilySearch LC37-Q71, Niels Anderson (1835–1926). Birth and death dates (October 3, 1835 – March 4, 1926) match the Andersons' gravestone plaque at Soda Springs; husband of Mary Anne Christoffersen (KWJN-1KY). The tree also has duplicate records for him (PQ7X-PXV, 9JDV-BD2). Identified by editor (FamilySearch). Connected names on the roll Christofferson, Maria; Christofferson, Maria 2 Places in this guide Kington Fort, Morristown, Omaha & Council Bluffs What the sources say At the fort during the siege; later said the posse allowed too little time to surrender (Anderson, p. 114). Married Mary Christofferson (probably Christofferson, Maria), wounded by the first cannon shot of the siege, on July 30, 1863, and was among the few Morrisites who stayed at Soda Springs (Anderson, p. 162); Shupe gives the date as July 20, 1863, calls theirs the first marriage in Idaho Territory, and says he was the blacksmith at Connor's post (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Their son Abraham C. Anderson was born on February 20, 1865 (Shupe, p. 16). The family's gravestone plaque at Soda Springs calls him “the father of the Anti-Mormon Party” in Idaho, and a National Park Service marker there says he and other Morrisites began the anti-polygamy campaign that ended in the Idaho test oath barring Mormons from voting. He bought 160 acres near Soda Springs as a cash entry at the Oxford land office, patented January 20, 1882 (Boise Meridian, T9S R41E, sec. 3; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-ID0010__.029). The 1880 U.S. census finds him at Soda Springs, “Nels Anderson”, born in Denmark about 1835 (1880 U.S. census). He died in 1926 (FamilySearch LC37-Q71). His 1903 letter to Joseph F. Smith is cited in Anderson's bibliography (Anderson, p. 237). At Burton’s trial in February 1879, after his wife had testified for the prosecution, the defense offered to prove that he had written to Burton offering, for payment, to keep her out of the way, as compensation for the loss of her chin, and that she knew of the letter; the court sustained the objection and the letter was not admitted (Ogden Junction, February 22, 1879, p. 4, as reported). His son Peter, writing in 1965, says he was born in Denmark in 1835, came with his family in 1860 and pulled a handcart from Florence, Nebraska; that Lieutenant Frank Shoemaker of Connor’s command married him and Mary two months after the colony reached Soda Springs, with a dance on canvas spread on the ground; and that Shoemaker later married Mary’s sister and is buried at Blackfoot, Idaho (Peter Anderson, “The Wound That Never Healed,” Frontier Times, June–July 1965, pp. 29, 46). John Codman, at Soda Springs in July 1873, took his account of the surrender from the wounded girl, now married, “and her husband, who was also present” (John Codman, The Mormon Country (New York, 1874), p. 157; see Maria Christofferson). On the roll William J. Jones (1825–1909) One of Morris’s first converts, whose capture and confinement at Kington Fort in the spring of 1862, after he left the camp, led to the writs and the posse. On the roll Jones, William J., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born March 1825, Wales (Family Tree) Died 1909, Utah (Family Tree) Spring 1862 Probably the William Jones whom the Morrisites captured and held in a log house at Kington Fort; chained in the log-house jail until the posse came on June 13, 1862 (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 97–100). See the cabin in Images. Family Tree FamilySearch K2W1-SRR, William J. Jones (1825–1909) (probable match). Welsh convert, emigrated 1855; Family Tree's life sketch says he joined the Morrisites in April 1861 and escaped from the fort. Wife Ann Haddock and mother Margaret, probably the Ann and Margaret Jones listed after him on the roll. Died at South Weber. Identified by editor (FamilySearch search). Connected names on the roll Jones, Ann; Jones, Margaret; Geertsen, Lars Christian; Klemgard, Peter C.; Banks, John Places in this guide Kington Fort What the sources say The William Jones whose departure from the camp led to the siege: the man who testified at Burton’s trial as William J. Jones said he had joined the Morrisites in April 1861 and told of his own capture with Jensen and Gearson (see below). One of Morris’s first converts, he left the fort in the spring of 1862, was captured with John Jensen and Lars Gurtsen by an armed party under Peter Klemgard, and was held in a log house at the fort, chained, until June 13, 1862; the writs issued over his detention brought the posse (Anderson, pp. 97–100, 107). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 503–5. Forscutt says that in 1861 he was arrested by Constable Burton and rescued by his brethren, and that he later left the camp (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 39, 44). Eardley names him as the man who went to John Banks’s wagon after the surrender (Gems, p. 28). Family Tree identifies him as William J. Jones (1825–1909), a Welsh convert who emigrated in 1855; a family life sketch there says he joined the Morrisites in April 1861 and escaped from the fort, and later testified for the defense at Burton’s trial. His wife Ann (Anne Haddock) and his mother Margaret are probably the Ann and Margaret Jones listed after him on the roll; Anderson says his wife, mother and three children stayed in the fort when he left. He farmed at South Weber from 1864 and died there in 1909 (FamilySearch K2W1-SRR, probable match). Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households, from local recollection, puts “Welsh Billy” Jones and his wife Ann Haddock in a log house at South Weber from 1861 and says that he “tried to leave but was held prisoner” and later testified at the Morrisite trial (Allred, South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952, 2004, nos. 67–68). His own account, given for the defense at Burton’s trial on February 27, 1879: he smuggled his clothes out of the fort by wearing two suits at a time to a neighbor’s house, and escaped with his cattle; about May 8 or 10, 1862, “thirty men, all armed, came to Kaysville after me and took me, besides also Jensen and Gearson, back to camp in a wagon; I was chained with a log chain.” He was held five weeks; the prisoners cut a hole in the wall with a pocket knife, and “Gearson got away without his shoes.” Hewitt once whispered to him that “they were going to kill us,” and he heard preached that hypocrites and prisoners were to be drawn up in a line facing the faithful in three lines, each line to kill those who refused. On June 13 Klemgard told him a revelation freed the prisoners; he went out under a flag, then served with the posse, “one of a party of 16 men that took the log house at the west end of the fort,” and “the first man to enter that house.” After the surrender he told James Bowman, “Don’t you know your wife is shot?” (Ogden Junction, February 28, 1879, p. 4). Henry Codlam of the same party also put Jones in the house with them (Salt Lake Herald, March 1, 1879, p. 3). On the roll Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925) A Danish convert held with William Jones in the Morrisites’ log-house jail in 1862, who escaped through its wall and brought word to Salt Lake City; he became a cattle rancher and pioneer at Salmon, Idaho, where his log house stood for well over a century. On the roll Geertsen, Lars Christian, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born May 1832, Denmark (Family Tree) Died 1925, Idaho (Family Tree) Spring 1862 The Lars (Lewis C.) Gurtsen whom the Morrisites captured and held in a log house at Kington Fort; escaped through the log wall after several days and went to Salt Lake City for help (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 97–100). See the cabin in Images. Family Tree FamilySearch LHN8-BJ8, Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925). Born in Denmark; reached Utah September 1861; a Montana county marriage record spells the name L. C. Gurtson, the 1880 census Louis C. Died at Salmon, Idaho. The Church History Department profile identifies him as the Lars Geertsen who escaped from Kington Fort in 1862. Identified by editor (FamilySearch search; Church History Department). Connected names on the roll Jones, William J.; Klemgard, Peter C. Places in this guide Kington Fort, Deer Lodge Valley Kington Fort, 1862 In the spring of 1862 Lars Gurtsen, also called Lewis C. Gurtsen, left the Morrisite camp. A party under Peter Klemgard captured him with William Jones and John Jensen, and the three were held in a log house at the fort. After several days he and Jensen cut a hole through the log wall; Gurtsen got away, and Jensen was caught and brought back (Anderson, Revisited, pp. 98–100, 105). William J. Jones, testifying at Burton’s trial in 1879, gave the escape in a sentence: “during this time we made a hole in the wall with a pocket knife to escape; Gearson got away without his shoes” (Ogden Junction, February 28, 1879, p. 4). Judge Kinney’s writ of habeas corpus of May 22, 1862, as Richard W. Young printed it in 1890, names the prisoners as “John Jensen, Louis Christian Jensen, [Lars Christian Gurtsen] and Wm. Jones”; the bracketed name appears to be Young’s gloss on the writ’s “Louis Christian Jensen” (The Contributor 11, no. 9 (July 1890): 350). By his account the three had been taken from Kaysville about May 8 or 10, 1862, by “thirty men, all armed,” and brought back to the camp in a wagon. The Church History Department’s profile of Lars Christian Geertsen adds that he went to Salt Lake City and told the authorities that Jones and Jensen were being held against their will, and that the posse followed: the detention of these men is what brought the writs and the siege of June 1862. Salmon, Idaho The spellings of his name trace his road north. A Montana county marriage record calls him L. C. Gurtson, and the 1880 census lists him as Louis C., the “Lewis C.” of Anderson’s account; in Salmon he was known as Lars. He and his Danish wife came to the Salmon area in 1866 or 1867, as the town grew up around the gold strikes of 1866. In 1868 he homesteaded a 160-acre ranch, raising cattle to supply the miners, and a small community called Geertson Creek grew up nearby. He served for a time as a territorial justice of the peace, and he was one of the original shareholders of the Salmon City Cemetery Association. Between 1872 and 1883 he built a two-story house of hewn logs, square-notched and chinked. It also held the ranch commissary, which served settlers and travelers on the Red Rock–Salmon City stage line, and its upstairs dance hall was a gathering place for the community into the 1920s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 3, 1980, as the Lars Geertson House (later the Herb Aldous House). A Salmon resident reports that it was damaged by fire years ago and torn down in 2025. He died on the evening of October 3, 1925, at the family homestead on Geertson Creek, aged 93, after a month’s illness. His funeral was held at the Methodist church, and he is buried in the Salmon Cemetery. His wife had died about ten years before, while the family was away for a few months. The obituary names six surviving children, among them a daughter, Mrs. Kelly, then living in Anaconda, Montana, and remembers him as “a student not only of science, religion and politics, but of nature and plant life,” credited with raising the first raspberries, strawberries and other small fruits in the valley (Idaho Recorder, October 9, 1925). Its figure for his age, 93 years, 2 months and 19 days, puts his birth about July 14, 1832; Family Tree gives May 1832. Sources Anderson, C. LeRoy. Davies (1833–1906), born in Denbighshire, Wales, who came to Utah in 1855 (FamilySearch LRMD-8L5). With his wife Anne Elizabeth, also on the roll, he joined Morris; he was held to bail after the siege as “Wm. Davies” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). He told the Walla Walla historian Frank T. Gilbert in January 1882 that he was born at Eglwysfach, Denbighshire, on August 9, 1833, to William and Ermyn Davies, Wesleyan Methodists; learned his father’s trade of stonemason; joined the Latter-day Saints at sixteen and preached from about eighteen; married Sarah E. Jones in 1854; and sailed for America with her and a sister in the spring of 1855, settling at Willow Creek (Willard), about fifty-five miles north of Salt Lake City. The Mountain Meadows massacre and other acts of the church made him doubt, and he joined Morris in 1861. He was at the surrender and saw Morris killed, and his account of it is the one Gilbert printed. Afterwards he went with a few families to Soda Springs in 1863, near Virginia City, Montana, in 1864, and to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1865, where on January 24, 1866, after long prayer, he had the vision with which his new era began; in 1867 he went by the Mullan Road to Walla Walla County and bought eighty acres. His son Arthur was born on February 11, 1868, and named “Messiah Son of David” on the eighth day; David, “Our Father,” was born on September 28, 1869. Sarah E. Davies died on May 19, 1879, and was buried with the two boys in the northeast corner of the yard; on September 1, 1881, he married Cornelia S. Perkins, and their infant daughter he believed to be his first wife returned (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, Whitman, Columbia and Garfield Counties (Portland, 1882), pp. 369–77; also Watson, p. 189) and from 1867 led the Morrisite community near Walla Walla, Washington, known as the Kingdom of Heaven, until it broke up after the lawsuit of 1880–81 (Anderson, pp. 157, 187–92). He later lived in San Francisco, where James Dove found him in 1892 (Anderson, p. 192), returned to Walla Walla County shortly before his death on November 25 or 26, 1906, and is buried in the Lyons Cemetery above the old community (FamilySearch; Find a Grave 15969383). In 1880 Asa B. Cilley, Thomas W. Evans and A. J. Courtney sued him, his son Alfred (William Alfred Davies, born 1858) and W. Wood in the territorial district court at Walla Walla to collect wages and debts, the case the state archives index calls the “Walla Walla Jesus” case (Washington State Archives, Frontier Justice, WAL-3153). The 1880 U.S. census, taken that June, lists him at Walla Walla as “William W. Davis”, 47, a mason and a widower, with eight children from Grace, 25, to Seth, 4; Arthur and David are not among them. The census mortality schedule for the year records the deaths of Arthur Davis, 12, and David Davis, 10, of diphtheria in February 1880, and, in May, of “Sarah E. Davis”, 43, born in Wales. She was evidently his wife Anne Elizabeth: Family Tree records her birth on March 29, 1836, and her death at Walla Walla on May 19, 1879, which fits her age but falls just before the census year that began June 1, 1879 (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c, and mortality schedule, ED 50, p. 3; FamilySearch LRMD-NG6). His neighbors on that census page include Swin O. Hagg, David Park, Rachel Jones, two McCue boys and Cornelia S. Perkins, 30, who became his second wife (Find a Grave memorial 15969383). Watson prints his writings and the record of his community (Watson, pp. 111ff.). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 16 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 35854). In 1881 Davies testified that he had come to Walla Walla from Montana in the fall of 1867 with his family and the James, David Thomas and Sorenson families; Swen O. Hagg put the first party at five families, about forty people. Davies also said that “the association commenced in 1866 in Montana” and that “the doctrine of reincarnation is taught and believed”; a list he put in evidence names forty-three members in March 1881 (Watson, pp. 111ff.; Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). The community dated its era from January 24, 1866. On May 25, 1881, the court gave Cilley, Courtney and Evans judgment against Davies for $3,225; the sheriff sold his livestock and equipment on June 11, and on July 16 the community’s eighty acres, the west half of the northwest quarter of section 34, township 7 north, range 37 east (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). In 1885 the First National Bank of Walla Walla won a default judgment against him and his son over nine notes of 1879, made out to Lewis H. Bowman (First National Bank v. Davies, 1885). A letter of March 4, 1866, from Sven Olson Hagg at Deer Lodge City says that the first in the Deer Lodge Valley to receive “this power” of the Spirit was “his servant William D.”, president of the Aaronic priesthood, standing “in Abel’s place” by birthright (MS 31876, Letters from Sven Olson Hagg, 1866, 1869; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). It is the earliest known record of his spiritual claims. John R. Eardley wrote in 1878 that Davies had been ordained “under your [Williams’s] hands” and had written letters acknowledging Williams’s mission even “after his so-called Millenium reign set in” (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880). With Edward Lloyd he baptized Josiah D. Price on December 3, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). The Walla Walla Watchman ran an exposé of him in August 1879, and at his elder son’s death in February 1880 called the boy “the Walla Walla Jesus Christ, so called” (reprinted in the Seattle Daily Intelligencer, March 4, 1880, p. 3). The Walla Walla Statesman reported the testimony against him before the referee in 1880–81 under headlines such as “The Trinity” and “A Fiery Furnace Fraud” (January 1 and February 5, 1881). His follower S. W. Wood, passing through New York in November 1878 on his way to proclaim the Messiah in England, told the Sun that “in 1866, W. W. Davies, when in Montana, had it revealed to him that he was the Standard of Israel,” and then that he was the Comforter; that the society, which “some call … Redemptionists,” had a tabernacle and a meeting house; and that the Messiah, “the Father’s Son,” was “born in 1868 in Walla Walla … now 10 years old,” and could print and set type (“Mr. Wood of Walla-Walla,” The Sun (New York), November 14, 1878, p. 1; checked against the page image).
