Places in this guide Kington Fort, Omaha & Council Bluffs, Deer Lodge Valley What the sources say Soren Peter Guhl (1821–1883), born in Jutland, Denmark, who came to Utah in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJ8-9RQ). Held to bail after the siege as “S. P. Guhl” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Leader of the Council Bluffs group; sustained as Cainan’s first counselor on January 24, 1869, having come to Omaha on January 22 “from Montana, where he had lived some years”; he organized the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations on February 7, 1869, and presided over them until May 30, 1869 (Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876); and sent on a mission to Denmark, where he broke with Cainan (Anderson, pp. 193–94); in October 1869 Williams wrote that “the important request from Denmark for money is altogether against my wishes,” and that Guhl “likes to take some other way,” to which Williams consented only because of “his often importunities” (Williams to the Omaha church, October 13, 1869, MS 31876); Cainan had written ahead to Deer Lodge to receive him on his way to Scandinavia (Anderson, p. 187), and later named him among the “traitors” (Anderson, p. 204). He died at Council Bluffs, Iowa, in 1883. In a letter of November 24, 1874, from 678 14th Street, Omaha, to William James and the Saints in Montana, Guhl wrote that Cainan had ordered him and “Bro. Poulsen” to organize the church at Omaha and had told him, in a letter of October 3, 1874, that his mission stood “under his especial direction” and not under Deer Lodge. He refused to recognize Andrew Hendrikson’s calling at Deer Lodge, since neither he nor Cainan had ordained him, and asked James to return the church’s books (“Protocoles”) and diagram, which he said belonged to the Omaha church (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23). In Copenhagen, with J. P. Lorentzen, he founded a congregation of “the Most High Saints” that preached publicly from January 1, 1871, and with Lorentzen and C. B. Berg formed a committee to publish tracts. In a letter of November 5, 1871, to Mikkel Christiansen, he renounced Williams over his oaths, his succession of appointments “to further his speculations to get money,” and his claim to the Urim and Thummim (known from Andrew Hendrikson’s copy, made at Fremont in March 1872: Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1869–1871; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Back at Council Bluffs in August 1874, he reported a split in the Omaha congregation between Poulsen, who claimed the presidency by Cainan’s appointment, and its bishop, Andersen; he was treating “patients” in Omaha, had forgiven Lorentzen and Poulsen “provisionally” until “the first 12 Apostles” could meet, and remained “jealous” of Williams until Williams explained “why he has written evil about me” (S. P. Guhl to Andrew Hendrickson, Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). The Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists him first: born at Horsens, Jutland, on August 19, 1821, baptized at South Weber on August 7, 1861, by Peter Klemgaard and Jens Mikkelsen, and confirmed by “J. Morris, R. Cook, J. Banks” (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In December 1867 Williams wrote that Guhl had promised to send his expenses if he would visit the Montana Saints that winter, but had sent neither the money nor an answer; in the same letter Williams appointed him “to preside this winter in Virginia & elsewhere” (Williams to William James, December 12, 1867, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and John R. Eardley, 1864–1867). Early in 1868 Williams wrote that Guhl had not sent for him because “his horses were stolen,” and cleared him of the charge laid against “the rebels Dow, Davies, Gudmanson” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1868). In an epistle of 1873, after their break, Williams charged that Guhl had “caused the Great offence in writing to the innocent at Omaha to send him money to live in Idolatry and Sin in Denmark,” and that his scorn had “ended in his becoming a castaway”; this is Williams’s accusation (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873). On June 1, 1869, from Ashwicken, Williams rebuked him for passing on stories, among them one of “five young men going to Salt Lake thirsting for my blood,” and for breaking his promise to pay as the Saints did: “you want … my seat and chain and crown; this is not mine to give but it is reserved for one elected to it before this mortality commenced.” He called him again to his mission to Denmark, “but come alone” (Williams to Guhl, June 1, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869). In September 1876 Williams wrote that Guhl and Poulsen had begged for chapters of the St. Ann's Hill records, "no doubt to make profit & gain favor with young Joe" (Williams to Hendrikson, September 26, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1876–1877). Connected names on the roll Hegg, Ann Places in this guide Carson City & California, Deer Lodge Valley, Kingdom of Heaven What the sources say Held to bail after the siege as “S. Hagg” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Probably Sven Olasson Hägg (1832–after 1882), born in Sweden, who came to Utah in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJF-86P, probable match). Family Tree gives his wife as Anna Lundsten (1833–1862), who may be the roll’s Ann Hegg. The Spirit Prevails names the second woman shot at the surrender on June 15, 1862, after Isabella Bowman, as “Mrs. O’Hagg” (p. 8), and Alexander Dow’s affidavit calls her a Danish woman (Anderson, p. 148); she was very probably Anna: William W. Davies and R. J. Livingston, both eyewitnesses and later at Walla Walla with Swen Hagg, named her “Mrs. A. S. O. Hegg” and “Mrs. Anna Swen O. Hegg” (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, 1882, pp. 372–73), and the “Mrs. Swanee” of the 1879 trial testimony is probably the same name. The 1870 U.S. census lists Swen Hagg, 37, farming in Walla Walla County, Washington Territory, with John, 10; as Swen O. Hagg he proved up a homestead of 170.62 acres there, patented July 24, 1890 (BLM General Land Office records, accession SER-WAWWAA 016765). In June 1880 “Swin O. Hagg”, 48, born in Sweden, a laborer and a widower, was living in William W. Davies’s dwelling at Walla Walla, with an Ole Hagg, 72, born in Sweden, two houses away (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c). Testifying for Davies in 1881, Swen O. Hagg said he had known him “ever since the fall of 1861,” had joined his association in 1866, and had come to Walla Walla in the fall of 1867 with the first members, five families of about forty people; in Davies’s teaching he was the central figure of the second of the circles around the Trinity. Ola Hagg, 73, who had come to the camp in July 1868 and also testified for Davies, was probably his father (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81). His own letters survive in the Montana church’s records. On March 4, 1866, he wrote from Deer Lodge City that he had wintered there with his little son in the house of L. C. Larsen, which he had helped build and where the Morrisites now held their meetings; the first to receive the Spirit there, he said, was “William D.” (Davies). On January 22, 1869, he wrote from 926 Washington Street, San Francisco, as a missionary. He had left “Israels Camp” on December 19, 1868. His father lived at its “Hovedquarter” (headquarters) with his sister and her husband Jens Mortensen (the James Mortensen of Davies’s camp), his own son was in their care, and “Israels Standard” (Davies) cared for them all; David M. Thomas was then on a mission at Portland, Oregon (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 22; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Until about 1877–78 he was Davies’s spokesman at Walla Walla, when R. J. Livingstone took his place (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880). John L. Bear, an eyewitness, also wrote that after Mrs. Bowman “a Danish woman, Br. Sven Fleg’s wife, was shot” (“Fleg” evidently for Hegg; autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, p. 27). On the roll Niels Rasmussen Beck (1823–1888) A Danish convert who served as sergeant of the guard in his 1855 pioneer company, farmed at Moroni, was held to bail after the siege of Kington Fort, and by 1870 was farming in the Deer Lodge Valley of Montana, where his is the earliest Morrisite land patent yet found. On the roll Beck, Niels R., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886 Born February 26, 1823, Tørring, Skanderborg, Denmark, son of Rasmus Nielsen and Anne Nielsdatter (Family Tree) Died July 21, 1888, Deer Lodge, Montana; buried at Deer Lodge (Family Tree) Wife Maria Simonsen Thompson (1834–1898), married February 3, 1851, at Tønning, Skanderborg, Denmark; she stayed in Utah, remarried, and died at Castle Dale, Emery County, on September 5, 1898 (Family Tree; Life history, MS 2735 275) Children Four in Family Tree: Erastus (1853–1914), Simon Thomsen (1855–1926), Margaret Anna (1857–1942) and Annie Serena (1859–1940) June 1862 Taken at Kington Fort: printed as “N. R. Beck” in the Deseret News list of June 25, 1862, held to $1,500 bail for the March 1863 term Later path Stayed with the Morrisites. Family Tree describes him as a Morrisite; died at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1888. Beck” with $4,839 over these years, and Davies testified that he had received “over $1500 from Mr. Beck to pay for land,” $300 for a printing press and more than $3,000 besides, adding that “Mr. Beck is not a member.” Probably the same man. (Cilley v. Davies, 1880–81) 1870Farming in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana, as “Nelson Beck,” 48, born in Denmark (real estate $550, personal property $1,350), next to the households of Ole Olsen and Lars C. Hansen, both also on the roll. The household is Ellen C., 49, Chris, 11, and Anna, 8, the children born in Utah. (1870 U.S. census) 1 May 1871Receives the patent for 160 acres in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, secs. 34–35), a preemption cash entry at the Helena land office (certificate 230). It is the earliest Morrisite land patent found in the valley. Lars C. Hansen patented land in the same section in 1873. (BLM General Land Office records) 1880Farming alone at Cottonwood Creek in the Deer Lodge Valley, aged 57, the first household on the census page. His neighbors include Lars C. Hansen and his family and Lars C. Larson, whose children were born in Idaho in 1864 and in Montana from 1866, the path of the Morrisites from Soda Springs to the Deer Lodge Valley. (1880 U.S. census) c. 1875His sons Simon, then about twenty, and Erastus visit him at Deer Lodge; he gives them eighteen cows and eighteen calves, which they drive home to Utah. A daughter and her husband later stay with him for a year. (Life history, MS 2735 275) 21 Jul 1888Dies at Deer Lodge, Montana, and is buried there (the family account gives July 22). By the family account his will left money to his children, friends and churches, the Latter-day Saint church receiving the most. (Family Tree; Life history, MS 2735 275) A household that does not match Family Tree gives Niels a wife, Maria (born 1834), and four children born between 1853 and 1859; the 1860 census at Moroni agrees, with Maria and four children. The 1870 census in the Deer Lodge Valley lists a different household: Ellen C., aged 49, and two children, Chris, 11, and Anna, 8. Ellen may be a second wife, or the enumerator may have taken the names down wrongly. Neither Ellen nor Chris appears in Family Tree, and where Maria was in 1870 is not known. By 1880 Niels was living alone. The later Becks of the valley In 1884 an eighteen-year-old Dane, Soren R. Beck, born July 9, 1866, the son of Anders and Annie (Sorenson) Beck, came alone to Deer Lodge and for three years worked on “a ranch belonging to Nels R. Beck, adjoining the city of Deer Lodge.” In 1889 he leased land on the Little Blackfoot and went on to raise horses, cattle and sheep (Progressive Men of the State of Montana, 1902, p. 1637). The biography does not say how the two were related. Family Tree makes Soren (FamilySearch 9MKM-NJF) a son of Anders Rasmusen Beck (1830–1905), whom it lists as Niels’s younger brother, both children of Rasmus Nielsen and Anne Nielsdatter of the Tørring area; if so, Soren was Niels’s nephew, which would explain why he came to work on his ranch. A third Beck family, Nels Jensen Beck and Maria Helena (Hansen) Beck, who came from Denmark in 1872, is distinct from both. What the family accounts say A family history held at the Church History Library, as summarized by Julie A. Wright, says that Niels was baptized a Latter-day Saint in Denmark in 1851 and came to Utah with his wife in 1855; that she accepted plural marriage, which he could not; and that when he left the church and joined the Morrisites she would not leave Utah with him. It adds that he became a wealthy cattle rancher in Montana and left most of his estate to the Latter-day Saint church he had left (Eva and Evelyn Sorenson Jacobsen, “Life History of Niels Rasmussen Beck,” cited in Wright, “Mormon Movement to Montana,” 2004, pp. 34–35). The Church History Library catalogs it under Eva Sorensen Jacobsen as an undated photocopied typescript of four leaves (MS 2735 275); its catalog summary describes the same story of conversion in Denmark, joining the Morrisites, the move to Deer Lodge and success as a rancher. The family history has now been read for this guide (November 2026). It is in two parts: a narrative compiled by two great-granddaughters from Andrew Jenson’s history of the Scandinavian Mission and the emigration records, and a shorter account by a granddaughter. On the roll John Garrett (1815–1899) Probably the Gloucestershire shoemaker who crossed to Utah in 1853, lived at Moroni beside other Morrisite families, and ended his life near Blackfoot, Idaho, where he took up land under four different federal land laws. On the roll Garrett, John, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886, with Thurza, Fenetta E., Hennage, Richard W. and Jane Garrett Identification Probable: the Family Tree person fits the roll’s family by his children’s names, and the 1880 census finds him at Blackfoot with his wife Thirza Born June 11, 1815, Gloucester, England, son of William Garrett and Rachael Jones (Family Tree) Died May 9, 1899, Blackfoot, Bingham County, Idaho (Family Tree) Wives Finetta Nancy White (1815–1853), married January 1, 1845, at Bedminster, Somerset; then Thurza, the roll’s Thurza Garrett, aged 55 in 1860 and 75 (as “Thirza”) in 1880. Family Tree records a second marriage in 1855. (Family Tree) 1 Jan 1845Marries Finetta Nancy White at Bedminster, Somerset. (Family Tree) 1851A shoemaker in Gloucestershire. (1851 census of England and Wales, in Family Tree) 1853Crosses to Utah in the Joseph W. Young Company with his children Richard and Heneage. Finetta dies the same year. (Church History Biographical Database; Family Tree) 1860A shoemaker at Moroni, Sanpete County, Utah, with real estate worth $200 and personal property worth $250. The household is Thurza, 55, Richard, 14, Phenetta E., 12, and Amelia, 10 (Heneage Amelia). Niels R. Beck, also on the roll, is on the same census page. (1860 U.S. census) 1861–62John, Thurza, Fenetta, Hennage, Richard and a Jane Garrett are on the roll of membership. John is not on the list of men brought before Judge Kinney after the siege (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). 1870Probably the “Jno. Garrett,” 50, born in England, a fur trader, with Martha, 50, at a mining camp in the Snake River district of Oneida County, Idaho, enumerated August 4, 1870. His daughters were in the next district, Upper Snake River, counted by the same enumerator, A. J. Borland, a week earlier: Fenetta, married to F. S. Stephens, and next door Heneage, entered as a 19-year-old man working at mining (read as “Hemage Jarret” and, by the USGenWeb transcribers, “Honage Ganet”). (1870 U.S. census) 1874His son Richard (“Dick”) dies in Idaho, of typhoid fever, after about three weeks’ illness, by Emma Just’s account in a letter dated May 5, 1874. (Family Tree; Reid, Letters of Long Ago, p. 34) 1880Living at Blackfoot, then in Oneida County, Idaho, with his wife Thirza: John, 65, and Thirza, 75, both born in England. (1880 U.S. census) 1882–92Receives four federal land patents near Blackfoot, all in the same township (Boise Meridian, T3S R35E), each under a different law: 158.45 acres by cash entry (January 20, 1882, Oxford land office); a 160-acre homestead (April 18, 1888, Oxford); 200 acres under the Desert Land Act of 1877, which required the claimant to irrigate the land (September 23, 1890, Blackfoot land office); and a Timber Culture Act claim, granted for planting trees (March 17, 1892). (BLM General Land Office records) 9 May 1899Dies at Blackfoot, Idaho. (Family Tree) Thurza, not Martha The roll names John’s wife Thurza, and the 1860 census at Moroni has Thurza, aged 55. The 1870 census in Oneida County gives the wife of “Jno. Garrett” as Martha, aged 50, which raised the question of a second wife. The 1880 census answers it: John Garrett, 65, and his wife Thirza, 75, were living together at Blackfoot. The 1870 “Martha” was most likely the enumerator’s mistake. The land at Blackfoot John’s four patents lie close together in one township near Blackfoot, more than 500 acres in all. Using cash entry, the Homestead Act, the Desert Land Act and the Timber Culture Act together was a common way to put together a larger farm than any one law allowed. A homestead normally needed five years’ residence before final proof, so John was probably living on that land by about 1883, when he was in his late sixties. The case files at the National Archives would show when he made each entry and who witnessed his proofs. Neighbors of Emma Just Emma Thompson Just, who was a girl among the Morrisites in 1862, settled on the Blackfoot River in 1870, and the Garrett children were among her nearest friends there. The letters her daughter Agnes Just Reid published in 1923, written in Emma’s voice to her father, name three of them. “My good Nettie,” very probably Fenetta, came to help at the birth of Emma’s son in 1871 and later had a fine new house with furniture her husband “Steve” shipped from Ogden; that fits Fenetta’s marriage to F. S. Stephens in the 1870 census. Heneage, “just married to a young Southerner,” left her husband for some weeks in 1876 to help nurse Emma’s sick child, and her brother Dick died of typhoid fever in 1874. In 1880 Emma named twin daughters, who died that September, Finetta and Heneage, “for my two best friends” (Reid, Letters of Long Ago, pp. 18, 34, 38, 79, 104). The book is a late family account, shaped by the daughter, but these details are incidental to it and fit the census and Family Tree. Open questions Who is the Jane Garrett on the roll? Did family members help him work the Blackfoot land, or join him there? Where were the Garretts between the siege of 1862 and 1870? Did they go to Soda Springs with the other Morrisites before moving north toward Blackfoot? If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. On the roll David Park (1809–1884) A Scottish farmer who came to Utah by way of Canada and Missouri, joined Joseph Morris with his wife and five of their children, took up one of the first Morrisite land claims in the Carson Valley, was living in William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven at Walla Walla in 1880, and died back in the Carson Valley. On the roll Park, David Sr., in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886, with Ann, David Jr., Hugh, Martha, Ellen and Joseph Hyrum Park Identification Probable: Family Tree’s David Park, husband of Ann Brooks, whose record carries the 1880 Walla Walla census and the family’s Carson Valley deaths Born June 12, 1809, Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, Scotland, son of James Park and Marion Allen (Family Tree) Died July 22, 1884, Mottsville, Douglas County, Nevada; buried in Mottsville Cemetery (Family Tree) Wife Ann Brooks (1811–1889), married March 1829; the roll’s Park, Ann (Family Tree) Children Thirteen in Family Tree, born in Scotland, Canada, Missouri and Utah between 1830 and 1854; five are on the roll: David Jr. (1839–1908), Hugh (1843–1924), Martha (1845–1920), Joseph Hyrum (1849–1929) and Ellen (Margaret Ellen, 1852–1925) Family Tree FamilySearch LLQF-CF6, David Park (1809–1884) Connected names on the roll Park, Ann; Park, David Jr.; Park, Hugh; Park, Martha; Park, Ellen; Park, Joseph Hyrum; McCue, Unity (David Jr.’s wife) Places in this guide Kington Fort, Carson City & California, Kingdom of Heaven Life 12 Jun 1809Born at Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, Scotland. (Family Tree) Mar 1829Marries Ann Brooks. Their first children are born in Scotland; Mary Ann (1837), David Jr. (1839), Hugh (1843) and Martha (1845) are born in Canada, and Joseph Hyrum in Missouri in 1849. (Family Tree) 1850Crosses to Utah in the Smith Humphrey Company with Ann and their children. (Church History Biographical Database) 1860Farming at Kaysville, Davis County, Utah, with real estate worth $200 and personal property worth $690, with Ann and their children. (1860 U.S. census) 1861–62He, Ann and five of their children are on the roll of membership of Joseph Morris’s Church of the Firstborn. Their son Hugh’s name was later found inscribed on one of the Morrisite scepters. June 1862A “David Park” is among the men held to $1,500 bail after the siege of Kington Fort; whether it was David or his son David Jr. is not known. (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) 10 Dec 1864Receives the patent for 160 acres in the Carson Valley, Nevada (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, secs. 1–2), a cash entry at the Carson City land office: the earliest federal land patent yet found for any Morrisite. (BLM General Land Office records) 1870Living in Nevada. (Family Tree) 1874–78Gives $320 to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, according to a list of donations filed in a lawsuit against Davies. (Cilley v. Davies, 1880–81) June 1880At Walla Walla, Washington, among the members of William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven: “David Park,” 71, born in Scotland, a laborer, sharing a house with Ole Hagg, 72, two doors from Davies, in the months after the community’s collapse began. Ann, listed as “Annie Park,” born in Scotland, was counted the same year in the Carson Valley, living as the mother in one of her sons’ households; David Jr., Hugh, Joseph H. and William Park were all farming there. (1880 U.S. census) 22 Jul 1884Dies at Mottsville in the Carson Valley and is buried there. Ann dies in 1889. (Family Tree) Carson Valley and Walla Walla Most of the Park family stayed in the Carson Valley: David Jr. married Unity McCue, also on the roll, and he and his brother Joseph Hyrum died in Douglas County, Nevada. David himself appears in 1880 hundreds of miles to the north, at Walla Walla, as one of a cluster of former Morrisites living around William W. Davies near Walla Walla: Sven Hagg in Davies’s own house, two young McCue boys, Rachel Jones and her children, and Scandinavian families with children born in Utah. Ann was not with him: the same census finds her in the Carson Valley with their sons. Whether he went north to join Davies’s community, or for some other reason, and how long he stayed, are not yet known. Open questions Which David Park, father or son, was held to bail in June 1862? When did David go to Walla Walla, and why did he go without Ann? His 1864 cash entry was made within about eighteen months of the Morrisites’ arrival in Nevada. His land entry file at the National Archives (Carson City land office) should show when he settled on the land. If you can answer one, write to contact@morrisite.org. The Montana church Andrew Hendrikson (1843–1921) A Danish immigrant, never a Latter-day Saint, who joined the Morrisites at Omaha in 1869, led the Danish-speaking stake at Race Track in Montana, gave the land for the Lord’s House, and presided over what remained of the Montana church until his death in 1921. The letters sent to him over half a century are the core of the church’s surviving papers. Not on the roll He joined in 1869, after the 1861–62 roll was drawn up. See his entry under Others named. Name Anders Henriksen in Danish; written Hendrikson, Henrickson and Hendrickson in the records, and Hendrickson by his family Born July 29, 1843, at Ondrup, Jutland, Denmark (Council Bluffs record of members, MS 32226); his obituaries give 1844 Came to America 1866, by the censuses of 1900 and 1910; “when he was about 20 years of age,” by his obituary Married Carrie (Karen) Jensen (1853–1936), in 1872 in Montana Children Eleven, ten of whom outlived him: Maryann (Mrs. Ben Goldie), Henry, James, Margaret (Mrs. J. B. Hare), Victor, Julia (Mrs. George Staffanson), Kate, Clarence, Peter and Agnes; a daughter, very probably Maggie, died in 1880 Church offices Keeper of the book for the Omaha and Council Bluffs fund, 1869; counselor in the Montana presidency, 1872 and 1883; president of Stake No. 2 at Race Track from 1874; president of the Montana church from 1886 (Anderson); still signing as “Minister in Church of Saints of the Most High” in 1904 Civil office Justice of the peace for the Cottonwood district of Deer Lodge County in 1888 (deeds of June 25 and July 9, 1888) Died July 3, 1921, at the home ranch at Race Track, aged 77; buried in Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge (Butte Daily Post, July 6, 1921) Family Tree FamilySearch LCS1-BZ1. The Montana church Peter Staffanson (1823–1913) A Swedish shoemaker who came to Utah as a Latter-day Saint in 1855, joined the Morrisites in Iowa in 1869, as George Williams organized the church at Council Bluffs, and moved to Montana in 1872. He presided over a quorum of Seventies, then served as bishop of William James’s English-speaking Stake No. 1, and stood with James in the presidency dispute of 1886. He farmed on Lost Creek near Anaconda for forty years, and his family and Andrew Hendrikson’s were joined by marriage. Not on the roll He joined in 1869, after the 1861–62 roll was drawn up. See his entry under Others named. Name Pehr Staffansson in Swedish; written Staffenson, Staffensen, Steffanson, Stoffenson and Stevenson in the records, and Staffanson by his family Born November 22, 1823, in Skåne, Sweden (Council Bluffs record of members, MS 32226; 1900 U.S. census); family records name the village as Östra Torn, near Lund Came to America 1855, on the James Nesmith, Liverpool to New Orleans, with his wife and three children (Saints by Sea) Married Cecilia Nilsson (1827–1897), at Lund in 1851 (family records) Children Ten: Emma Caroline (Mrs. Oliver Barrett), Sophia Wilhelmina (died at sea, 1855), Nels Peter, Ephraim, Joseph, Hiram, Jacob, Nephi (died in infancy), John and William Henry Church offices President at Crescent City, Iowa, 1870; president of the second quorum of Seventies in Montana, 1872–78; first counselor to Bishop Rasmus Rasmussen, 1875; bishop of Stake No. 1 by 1883 and in 1886 Died June 16, 1913, at his ranch on Lost Creek, Deer Lodge County, aged 89; buried in the Staffanson family cemetery there, beside his wife Family Tree FamilySearch KWJK-LWP; his wife Cecilia is LQ55-QW4. Family members have added to his Memories there the 1855 ship register, his portrait, a photograph of him with his seven sons and the family history “From Sturdy Stock” (viewing Memories needs a free FamilySearch sign-in). On the roll Anders Christoffersen (1841–1921) A Danish emigrant who came to Utah with his parents in 1859, joined Joseph Morris with them, and was taken at Kington Fort in 1862. After the trials he went north with the Morrisites to Soda Springs, mined and farmed in Montana and Idaho, joined the Reorganized Church in 1870, and settled at last north of Deer Lodge, where he farmed and raised stock for forty years. On the roll Christofferson, Andrus, in the 1861–62 roll of membership printed in 1886; listed with his parents and his brother and sisters Name Anders Pedersen in Danish records; Andrus, Andres, Andrew and Anders Christofferson (Christoffersen, Christopherson) in American ones Born October 1, 1841, in Denmark, by his obituary (the Reorganized Church register has 1842, Family Tree October 11); Family Tree and Find a Grave place his family at Klinte, on Funen Came to America 1857, at fifteen, on the Tuscarora, Liverpool to Philadelphia, with his parents and six brothers and sisters (Saints by Sea); at Burlington, Iowa, until 1859, then to Utah in the Neslen company Married Christiane Marie (Katie) Hansen, daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, at Camp Floyd, Utah, on July 26, 1862, by her Saints’ Herald obituary (Family Tree has February 1862, his obituary 1863). See her page Children Twelve, by the censuses of 1900 and 1910 (eleven living in 1910): William (Peter William), John, Frank (Benjamin Franklin), Nettie, Minnie, Effie, Andrew James, Nephi (called Levi in 1910 and in one obituary), Lucy, Emma, Alma and Edward. The obituaries of 1921 and 1927 count Alma among the daughters, but the 1900 and 1910 censuses list Alma as a son, and Alma, from the Book of Mormon, is a man’s name among Latter-day Saints June 1862 In the fort through the siege, aged twenty; his sister Mary was wounded in the jaw by the first cannon fire on June 13. Taken prisoner at the surrender and held to $1,500 bail; fined $100 in March 1863 for resisting an officer, and pardoned by Governor Harding Later path Reorganized Church from March 6, 1870; ordained an elder at Deer Lodge, October 10, 1887 (Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District, #228, Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 43) Citizenship Declared his intention to become a citizen in the Deer Lodge County court, May 29, 1883, aged 41, renouncing Christian IX of Denmark (declaration of intention, Deer Lodge County) Died October 20, 1921, at his ranch four miles north of Deer Lodge, aged 80; buried in Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge, Protestant section 2 (Find a Grave memorial 82390205) Family Tree FamilySearch L2XW-JS2. Christopherson, 70, with Marie A., 64, next to his son Christian and Christian’s wife Bertha, and his son Andrew and Katie; Mary Anderson and Matilda Hansen and their families are nearby. (1880 U.S. census, Soda Springs, Oneida County, Idaho, enumeration district 25, dwellings 386–397) 21 Oct 1884Abelone dies at Soda Springs. (Find a Grave memorial 26408751) 20 Sep 1891Dies at Soda Springs and is buried in Fairview Cemetery beside Abelone, under a stone inscribed “Peter Christoffersen.” (Find a Grave memorial 26408752; Church History Department pioneer database) What the sources say Peder Christoffersen’s family is one of the largest on the roll: he, his wife and five of their children are listed, and four of the children married four children of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, also on the roll. The Church History Department’s database records that he and his son Andrew signed the Morrisite oath in May 1862, and the prisoner list of June 1862 includes them both. Why he left the Latter-day Saints is told only by his grandson Peter Anderson, writing in 1965 from his mother Mary’s stories: the lost stove and, above all, the pressure on his daughters to enter plural marriage. A 1989 county history, drawing on the family’s own account, says much the same: plural marriage did not suit them, and for safety they joined the Morrisites going north. After 1863 he stayed at Soda Springs, near his daughters Mary and Matilda and his son Christian, while Anders and Katie moved on to Montana. No obituary has been found. The sources disagree on small points: Family Tree and Find a Grave give his wife’s birth year as 1816 and 1817, and the 1870 census index misreads his name. On the roll Abelone Maria Christoffersen (1816–1884) Abelone Maria Andersdatter, wife of Peder Christoffersen, came from Denmark with him and their children in 1857 and reached Utah in 1859. She is very probably the roll’s “Abelone Anderson,” listed under her own surname. Her daughter Mary was wounded by the first cannon shot at Kington Fort. From 1863 she lived at Soda Springs, Idaho, where she died in 1884. On the roll Rasmus Hansen (1809–1890) A Danish farmer from Funen who came to Utah with his wife, Lena, and seven of their children in 1859 and joined Joseph Morris with them. He was discharged at Kington Fort the day after the surrender. After the Morrisites left Utah he lived at Soda Springs, Idaho, and by 1870 in Montana, where he died at Deer Lodge in 1890. The roll has two men named Rasmus Hanson, and Rasmus is identified as the first because he is listed beside Lena; the Rasmus Hansen of the armed companies could be either man, but the “Erasmus Hansen,” 55, discharged on June 16 was very probably he. His daughter Katie’s obituary of 1927 says only that she was with her parents in “that unfortunate band under Joseph Morris at Weber Canyon.” Lena and several of their children joined the Reorganized Church in Montana between 1870 and 1896. No record of Rasmus’s own joining has been found, but his funeral in 1890 was held from the “Latter Day Saints’ church” near Deer Lodge, which in Montana then meant the Reorganized Church. His only known notice is a three-line death announcement in the Anaconda paper. Her obituary in the Reorganized Church’s Saints’ Herald, written by the elder who baptized her, says plainly that she and her husband “soon left the Utah people and united with Joseph Morris,” and after his death moved to Soda Springs and then to Montana. It gives her birth as March 4, 1809, at Strarup, as do the Deer Lodge branch register and the Silver State Post’s correction; her modern gravestone and Family Tree have February 26. Her family shows the movement’s path in miniature: from the Latter-day Saints in Denmark and Utah to Joseph Morris, north to Soda Springs and Montana, and, over a generation, into the Reorganized Church, whose Deer Lodge branch built its chapel that same year under a committee that included her son-in-law. Places Kington Fort South Weber, Utah. The fort at South Weber where Morris gathered his followers in 1861–62, and the siege of June 1862. MO-IMG-001 · Monument, December 2008 Built in 1853 and abandoned in 1858, then reoccupied by the Morrisites. Nothing of the fort survives; a monument to the Kington Fort–Morrisite War site, Sons of Utah Pioneers marker no. 128, was erected in August 2006 at 6600 South and 475 East (N 41.14677, W 111.96884), sponsored by the South Weber chapter of the Daughters of Utah Pioneers, the Ogden Pioneer chapter of the Sons of Utah Pioneers and All Build Construction and Landscaping, with the site designed by Douglas B. Stephens (Barlow, 2022). The fort was named for Bishop Thomas Kington, and “Kington” is the correct spelling. The monument itself notes that the earliest sources (the notebook kept by Kington’s wife, his gravestone, Wilford Woodruff’s journals, and early church records) all spell it that way; recent scholarship such as Holley (2008) follows them. Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century accounts, and some modern references, including the Utah History Encyclopedia and Wikipedia, write “Kingston Fort.” Insiders used both: Forscutt, who lived in the fort, wrote “Kingston’s Fort” and called it “the proper name” of the place (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702). Search under both spellings. Not all the people in the fort were from South Weber. Holley (2008) names eleven men from Slaterville and Marriott, about nine miles to the northwest, among the prisoners of June 1862, and two of the family groups on the roll, Cowan–Bull and Higham, were Slaterville families (see “Families on the roll” on the roll page). A log cabin nearby, which the local historian Ed Cooper, from oral accounts of older South Weber residents, identified as the building Morris used to hold the three departing members whose detention led to the siege, is shown in MO-IMG-046–049; it has been moved from its original site, and the identification rests on local tradition. About 200 yards south, on the west side of the road, in the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery, a marker reads “Joseph Werner, ‘Morrisite,’ about 1870” (MO-IMG-021). The date cannot be his death: a Joseph Warner, sixty-two, born in Germany, a widowed laborer, was living at South Weber in 1880 (1880 U.S. census, South Weber, Davis County, ED 16), and he died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September (Davis County Court minutes, October 2 and October 30, 1893, pp. 462, 470 (County court minutes, 1852–1893, FamilySearch film 484601, item 2, DGS 7579269)). The date is a modern guess. In 1979 Werner’s grave was unmarked (Standard-Examiner, May 9, 1979, p. 75); Leonard Bowman of South Weber said in 1983 that he had learned two years before where Werner was buried and had a marker made for him (Salt Lake Tribune, April 28, 1983, p. 75), and in 1984 that marker read “Joseph Werner Morrisite, died about 1870” (Lakeside Review, North Edition, May 23, 1984, p. 2). The present flat markers were laid by a Boy Scout troop copying the older ones, about twenty years ago by the city’s account (the photograph is earlier than February 2004), and the date came over from Bowman’s marker. The city’s cemetery records do not support it: Mattie G. Ray’s compiled list, typed in 1998, enters “Werner, Joseph” with no dates, as the “only Morrisite to stay in South Weber,” and the plot map puts him in lot 20, on the south row. The city, drawing on Norma Earl Allred’s compilation of South Weber families, also regards the date as an error; Allred adds that several people she talked to had been told stories about “the old Morrisite that lived by or at the fort” (Norma Earl Allred, comp., South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952 (2004), Attachment 3) (South Weber City cemetery records, sent to the editor by Lisa Smith, November 16, 2026). He was almost certainly the “Brother Warner” who in 1875 prophesied a gathering to Weber (see Who was “Brother Warner”?). The same records place other Morrisites in or by the cemetery. Two were buried outside the fence near its northeast corner, because residents did not want them inside; one was “Bella Bowman,” very probably Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender (see Who died at Kington Fort?). Charles Patton Bowman (1865–1872), son of John and Agnes Bowman, both on the roll, is buried in lot 40. Bendt Nielsen, who died on July 15, 1862, a month after the siege, is buried in lot 24 (same records). He was not a casualty of the siege: a family history by his granddaughter May Nielsen Christensen makes him a Latter-day Saint convert from Denmark who died on his farm at South Weber, the second burial in the cemetery (Lakeside Review, September 18, 1990, p. 9). The city’s history of the cemetery notes “at least one burial” from the war of 1862. In 1908 Henry Firth, who had lived at South Weber in the Morrisite years, showed John Banks what was left of the fort wall and the site of Morris’s house, and pointed out fifteen unmarked mounds in the old village cemetery that he said held Morrisites killed in 1862 (Banks, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” 1909, p. 2). The name lingered locally. In the early 2000s, while the editor was going door to door in South Weber, a woman then in her sixties said that elementary-school classmates had called her “Morrisite” as a taunt because of where in South Weber she lived; she said her family had no Morrisite connection. (Editor’s memorandum of recollection, written November 1, 2026; the conversation was not recorded at the time.) Two traditions of the siege survive in undated papers kept by the city, their authors unknown, and neither has been found in a contemporary account. Local tradition: a dissenter was chained in a log shed for three weeks and escaped his Danish guard near Weber Canyon; the story may echo the detention of the three departing members. Places Morristown Soda Springs, Idaho. The settlement at Soda Springs founded in May 1863 under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor. MO-IMG-061 · Anderson gravestone, October 2018 The Morrisites were among the founders of Soda Springs, one of the oldest towns in Idaho. Connor reported bringing 160 settlers (53 families, seven single men, and four widows), who arrived May 20, 1863, and were given building lots on a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River, beside the military reservation of Camp Connor (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). A later marker describes a 200-acre survey west of Soda Creek, lots of 25 by 130 feet, and one-room log homes with dirt floors. The Morrisite “Lower Town” stood below the military “Upper Town”; Soda Springs was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. After the troops left in 1865, hard winters and failed crops thinned the settlement; John L. Bear, who left for Missouri in 1870, remembered “about 30 families” when they first came and “about 10” by then, and sold his two log houses, stables and yards to Erick Eliason for $350 (Johann L. Baer, autobiography, circa 1908, typescript, MS 10240, Church History Library, p. 47). Many Morrisites moved on, some north to the Blackfoot area, and others sold to miners and to Latter-day Saint settlers, whose new town site dates from Brigham Young’s visit of 1870–71. Most of the old town now lies under Alexander Reservoir. Those who stayed, led by Niels Anderson, carried their quarrel with the Mormon hierarchy into territorial politics; the Niels Anderson Homestead marker credits his anti-polygamy campaign with helping deny Mormons the vote in Idaho. Accounts differ on some details: most give 160 settlers (one popular account says about 325), Camp Connor’s founding is dated May 20 or May 23, and the National Park Service marker wrongly calls Morris Welsh-born. Markers stand in town, including the Park Service’s Morrisite settlement marker in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse (HMDB), the state’s Camp Connor marker (HMDB), and “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor’s probable site near the hospital (HMDB). Descendants held a reunion in Soda Springs on August 3, 2013. Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson, married at Morristown on July 20, 1863 (the date on their gravestone; some accounts give July 30), are buried in Fairview Cemetery at Soda Springs. Their gravestone carries a long bronze inscription giving a Morrisite account of the 1862 siege, in which Mary, then fourteen, lost her jaw to the first cannon shot fired into the fort. Forscutt, who was present, described her lower jaw “hanging only by a narrow strip of skin,” with two women dead beside her (“Sketch of Joseph Morris,” CHL MS 702; MO-IMG-061, with transcription; MO-IMG-062; HMDB; see also the Niels Anderson Homestead marker). VisitThe markers and the Anderson gravestone in Fairview Cemetery are publicly accessible. The townsite is largely under Alexander Reservoir. Places on the ground The 1863 settlement and the land the Morrisite families later took up. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate; squares are land patents, drawn at the quarter-section or smaller part they name. Most of the old town lies under Alexander Reservoir. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. The patents are drawn from their legal descriptions on the BLM section grid; marker positions are from the Historical Marker Database. The Morrisite settlement markers Located today map Three National Park Service panels stand together in the parking lot of a Latter-day Saint meetinghouse at 290 South 3rd Street West: “A New Beginning…” on the Morrisite settlement, “Law & Order on the Frontier” on Camp Connor, and “First in Soda Springs” on Niels and Mary Anderson. Public. Sources: Historical Marker Database, 106709, 106710, 106726. The Park Service panel says it is believed to have stood near the Caribou Memorial Hospital, just south of the markers; a settler recalled that Connor later moved the fort a little farther east, on the hill. The marker follows the panel. Sources: Historical Marker Database, 106710; Connor’s report, June 2, 1863. Morristown (Lower Town) Approximate 1863–1870s map The Morrisite town site, surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River west of Soda Creek, below the military “Upper Town”: about 200 acres in lots of 25 by 130 feet, with one-room log houses. It was the first seat of Oneida County, 1864–66. Most of it now lies under Alexander Reservoir. The marker shows the general area only. Places Carson City & California Nevada · California. The western congregations in Carson Valley and San Francisco, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails. The western congregations, where George Dove published The Spirit Prevails and led the California church after 1882. In May 1863 Connor gave 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City in an empty quartermaster’s train bound there for stores (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, OR). VisitNo surviving sites identified for this guide. Information welcome. In the chronology Nov 1859George S. Dove moves Morris from American Fork to Salt Lake City, where, by the Morrisites’ own history, he stays “in a vacant house and lot in the First Ward” and receives “the revelation called the Keys of the Priesthood” (The Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” p. 3). The Doves’ earlier printing of 1879 dates the move to November 1859, says that George’s father, James Dove, had refused several times to allow it, and places the revelation “in an old wagon box covered with canvass, in the same lot with the house he [George] occupied, in the first Ward”; it adds that of the church’s leaders only Heber C. Kimball urged Brigham Young to hear him (George S. and James Dove, A Voice from the West, San Francisco, 1879, p. 6). Both accounts then send him to Slaterville, in the spring of 1860 (The Spirit Prevails) or the fall of 1859 (1879). The date of “Keys” is uncertain: Emanuel Strom’s Swedish copy dates it at South Weber, December 12, 1860 (see the Teachings). May 1863Many Morrisites leave Utah under the protection of Patrick Edward Connor, commanding the District of Utah. On May 5 a party of 160 (53 families, seven single men, and four widows) sets out with a company of California Volunteers; it reaches Soda Springs on May 20, where Connor has a town site surveyed on the north bank of the Bear River beside a new military post, Camp Connor (established by order of May 23). The Morrisites call their town Morristown. Connor also gives 150 Morrisites passage to Carson City, Nevada, in an empty supply train. Others settle in California. (Connor’s report, June 2, 1863, Official Records, ser. 1, vol. 50, pt. 1, 226–29.) A writer who camped beside that train at Deep Creek, the Overland Mail station kept by Howard Egan, remembered six-mule army wagons carrying two Morrisite families each, bound for Fort Churchill under a lieutenant, with Richard Cook among them; Egan, who had been with the posse in 1862, gave them a supper and a dance (“The Morrisite Movement,” letter 7 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 12, 1891, p. 3). Some Morrisites had spent the winter at Camp Douglas, cutting wood for the troops. John L. Bear, driving a Swiss brother’s ox team, reached Soda Springs “on the 3rd of June, 1863,” to snow that night; the settlers lived in dugouts, Captain Black’s men brought logs, flour and bacon, and “all felt happy to be out of Brigham’s dominion.” James Bowman, who had lost his wife at Weber, helped Bear start a Sabbath school, and later kept a store on the lot Alexander Dow left when he moved to St. Louis (Johann L. Baer, autobiography, MS 10240, Church History Library, pp. 31–36). 1860s–Some Morrisites return to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, in Utah and elsewhere. The 2006 monument at South Weber notes that a few were rebaptized and remained there. Others find a home in the Reorganized Church (RLDS): the former Morrisite apostle Mark Hill Forscutt joins it in Salt Lake City in 1865, and John L. Bear (Johann Lebrecht Bär, 1838–1919), a Swiss convert from Affoltern am Albis who emigrated from Zürich in 1860 and lost his wife and child at Kington Fort, later serves as an RLDS missionary to Switzerland and Germany, dies in Independence, Missouri, and publishes his autobiography in the RLDS Journal of History. In 1865 RLDS missionaries at Malad, Idaho, baptize several people who appear on the roll. Others join only after years in the Morrisite groups: Erick and Caroline Eliason are baptized together at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870; Margaretta Cook leaves the Morrisites in Nevada in 1870 and is baptized RLDS in 1873; and Lena Hanson, at Soda Springs and then Deer Lodge, in 1895; Bear himself was baptized into the Reorganized Church at Malad on November 29, 1869, organized a branch at Soda Springs, and wrote a pamphlet, one copy for each Morrisite family still there, on “the fallacy and non fullfillment of many of Joseph Morris revelations”; some burned it unread, but by his account most of the Soda Springs Morrisites joined the Reorganization in time (autobiography, MS 10240, pp. 41–42; no copy of the pamphlet is known); in 1890 John R. Eardley reported that Brother Emmons of the Montana church had been baptized and that Mrs. Emmons meant to follow (see the roll). Oct 1868W. W. Blair, president of the Reorganized Church’s Pacific mission, tells its California conference at San Francisco: “In Nevada I saw many old Saints (Morrisites). As a general thing they are good people who have been deceived,” led astray “by seducing spirits,” but now “beginning to look at the matter in a favorable light,” and “friends to our cause.” The word in parentheses is cramped and its reading not certain (minutes of the semiannual conference, California District, October 6–9, 1868, p. 7, P19 f34, Community of Christ Library Archives). The conference’s Carson City District then had branches at Carson City, Franktown and Jack Valley, where Cook’s and Parson’s Nevada Morrisites lived. 1869George Williams leaves Utah for England, passing through Omaha from January 18 to February 5, where the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations are organized on his authority (see Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places); a year later he writes from Loughborough that it was “now one year since I left the continent of America”; his wife and children stay in Salt Lake City, and he asks the Montana members to send help for “my little ones” (Williams to the Saints of the Most High in Montana, Janu

Places Omaha & Council Bluffs Nebraska · Iowa. Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive. Danish-speaking congregations whose 1869 membership and account books survive in translation. Their own minutebook, written up at Omaha in May 1871, tells how they began. Jens Jacob Poulsen, “a High Priest of the Weber House,” was sent ahead by George Williams to gather the scattered Morrisites, and spent about a year there. Williams himself arrived in Omaha on January 18, 1869, “from his home in South Cottonwood in Utah,” on his way to England, held meetings in Omaha and Council Bluffs, and left on February 5 with Poulsen and a Brother Mortensen, who went on to Denmark. On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, S. P. Guhl, newly come from Montana, organized the church on Williams’s authority: Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, under Carlton Fellows, with Hans Nielsen over the Scandinavians at Crescent City, since the Danes “were not satisfied” to have an American president; and Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for all the Saints west of the Missouri, under Jens Jensen, with a district at Florence under Niels Jensen. Rasmus Rasmussen became the first bishop. A conference at Omaha on April 6, 1869, sustained “George Williams, called of the Lord Cainan,” as “our Prophet, Seer and Revelator,” and on May 30, as Guhl left on a mission to Denmark, Andrew Hendrikson was appointed to preside, with Jens Jensen and Hans Nielsen as counselors (minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In March 1871 the church gave up its yearly conferences, which Hendrikson said Guhl had brought in “in likeness with the Mormons’ custom” and Williams had never commanded, and met instead in councils in members’ houses and in “social gatherings.” That May one of its leaders, Sister Marie Mortensen, whom Williams had called the congregation’s “High Priestess” in 1870 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870), joined the Reorganized Church, and Hendrikson had the early records copied into a book, “for many of us must be called hence and go to other places.” The last entry is dated June 4, 1871, at Jens Jensen’s house in Omaha. Most of the congregation moved to the Deer Lodge Valley in 1871–72. Those who stayed were courted by other churches: by 1874 Danish “Josephites” of the Reorganized Church were challenging S. P. Guhl to debate, and a Danish Adventist missionary had baptized several “of our brothers and friends”; O. P. Andersen wrote from Omaha that spring that one of the sisters had taken up Adventist teaching and lodged a Danish Adventist preacher (Guhl to Hendrikson, Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874, and O. P. Andersen to Hendrikson, Omaha, March 10, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878; translations from the Danish and Swedish generated by Claude). VisitNo sites identified; the record survives in documents only. Places on the ground The two congregations organized at Council Bluffs on February 7, 1869, and their districts, as the Omaha minutebook names them. All the markers are approximate: they show the towns, not buildings. No meeting place has yet been located. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Towns are placed at their old centres. The river is drawn roughly along its present course; it has moved since the 1870s (the Carter Lake bend was cut off by the flood of 1877), so its exact line then is not shown. The minutebook made the river the boundary: Omaha City Congregation No. 2 took in “all the Saints west of the Missouri.” The inset at upper left shows where Fremont and Lincoln lie, beyond this map; its rivers are drawn only roughly. Council Bluffs: Congregation No. 1 Approximate 1869–1872 map Council Bluffs City Congregation No. 1, organized on February 7, 1869, at a conference held in Council Bluffs, with the High Priest Carlton Fellows as president. The Danish members “were not satisfied” with an American president, so Fellows was kept as president “for the English” and the Scandinavians were given their own district (see Crescent City). Councils met in Brother Damander’s house, and in 1871 Williams wrote to Andrew Hendrikson in care of Damander at P.O. Box 610, Council Bluffs. The house has not been located. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; Williams’s envelopes, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1870 and 1871. Crescent City: the Scandinavian district Approximate 1869–1870 map A district of Congregation No. 1 for the Scandinavian Saints at Crescent City and round about, under Hans Nielsen from February 1869 and, after he stopped holding meetings, under Peder Staffanson from March 1870. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library. Omaha: Congregation No. 2 Approximate 1869–1872 map Omaha City Congregation No. 2, for “all the Saints west of the Missouri,” organized on February 7, 1869, under the High Priest Jens Jensen. Its conferences were held in Omaha, among them the one of April 6, 1869, that sustained Williams as prophet. Rasmus Rasmussen, the first bishop, had his post office box here (P.O. Box 40). The minutebook was written up at Omaha in May 1871. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–1871, Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, MS 31876, Church History Library; Williams’s envelope to Rasmussen, June 1869, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869. Florence: a district of No. 2 Approximate 1869–1870 map A district of Congregation No. 2 for the Saints at Florence and round about, under Niels Jensen “from Florence.” Florence, now part of north Omaha, was the site of the Latter-day Saints’ Winter Quarters of 1846–48 and a later outfitting point for emigrants to Utah. Sources: Minutebook, 1869–

t: Deer Lodge Valley, Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana
s: Places Deer Lodge Valley Powell and Deer Lodge counties, Montana. The longest-lived center of the movement, and the Lord’s House at Racetrack, the last Morrisite church standing. MO-IMG-014 · Racetrack church, November 2018 The longest-lived center of the movement. The wood-frame Morrisite church, built in 1878–79, still stands on private land at Racetrack, about 8 miles south of Deer Lodge: on the north side of Dempsey Road, just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (Exit 195; about 46.29° N, 112.75° W; NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County; until 1901 this was Deer Lodge County, the county named in older records and in this guide’s photograph captions). The county lists it as a frame building of 18 by 36 feet (Montana Cadastral, Montana State Library, consulted November 6, 2026). In the 1870s the council also met in members’ houses on Dempsey Creek, near the site: in December 1876 it set its next meeting for Peter Jansen’s place on Dempsey Creek (council minutes, December 3, 1876, Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1876; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). It was last photographed for this guide in August 2020. Called the Lord’s House, as the panel over its doors reads, it was the church’s meeting place: George Thompson was elected president of the church there in 1886, and Andrew Hendrikson (1886–1921) and George Johnson (1921–1954) presided over the Montana church from it. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive, and its condition has worsened markedly since 2009. See the condition record under Images. Everyone the sources place in the Montana church is listed in the register of Montana Morrisites on the People page. The Deer Lodge paper, the New North-West, spoke well of its Morrisite neighbors. In June 1878 it reported that the post office at Gwendale, Deer Lodge County, had been renamed Morristown, and that “as many of the people are Morrisites” they would likely take to the name. In 1883 it called the settlements on Warm Springs Creek and the upper Deer Lodge River “largely composed” of Morrisites and praised them as industrious, hospitable and law-abiding; in 1885 it noted “a large number of Morrisites in this valley” (New North-West, June 7, 1878, p. 3; April 13, 1883, p. 2; October 30, 1885, p. 3; see Newspapers). The paper’s notices place Gwendale in the upper Deer Lodge valley, near Warm Springs and Lost Creek. It was school district No. 6; in April 1875 “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” met at the Gwendale school house on the railroad question, with Morgan Evans in the chair and a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee; Gwendale primaries were held at Wier’s store; and a smelter there began work in August 1877 (New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2; June 18, 1875, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3). Morgan Evans, whose land later became Anaconda, gave Gwendale as his address. By 1883 the same school district, No. 6, was called Willow Glen, with Peter Jessen, a Gwendale man since the 1870s, as a trustee and J. I. Eardley as clerk (New North-West, May 4, 1883, p. 3). In March 1880 the land office listed Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims were held up while it decided whether the ground was mineral land; among them were Daniel James and William P. Thomas, on Warm Springs Creek east of where Anaconda was built (secs. 33 and 34, T5N R10W), and Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen, in sec. 9, T4N R10W, near today’s Opportunity (New North-West, April 30, 1880, p. 4); all four claims were patented as homesteads in 1880–81. In January 1882 the paper reported that John R. Eardley, formerly of San Francisco, had built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and that the neighborhood had petitioned for a post office there “to be called Willow Glen”; in March it reported his appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was” (New North-West, January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3). Gwendale, renamed Morristown in 1878, and Willow Glen were thus successive post offices for the same neighborhood, between Anaconda, Opportunity and Warm Springs. The exact site of the Gwendale school house is still not known. View onlyThe church is privately owned, unsafe and not open to the public. View it from Dempsey Road or the frontage road; do not enter the property. Places on the ground Sites named in the sources, with how precisely each can be placed. Solid markers are located; outlined markers are approximate; squares are land patents, drawn at the quarter-section or section the patent names. Sites not yet located are listed without a marker. Most of these places are private land today. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. “Willow Glen Ranch” near Opportunity, shown in gray, is the later company stock farm of that name (burned in 1963), not the Willow Glen of 1882. The Lord’s House, Racetrack Located 1878–1969 map The church of the Montana Morrisites, built in 1878–79 and dedicated on August 9, 1879, on the north side of Dempsey Road just west of the railroad and the Interstate 90 frontage road (NE¼ sec. 8, T6N R9W, Powell County). George Thompson was elected president of the church here on May 10, 1886. It is the only Morrisite church building known to survive. Don Cornelius, who saw it in 1962, dated it to 1878 and described a building of planed lumber, once painted white, with “THE LORD’S HOUSE” lettered above its double doors, standing in a pasture; Julie A. Wright gives its dedication as 1879. Privately owned and unsafe: view it from the road only. s: Places Kingdom of Heaven Walla Walla, Washington. William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. William W. Davies's commune near Walla Walla, 1867–1881. Its site lay on the west side of Mormon Grade Road, a few hundred yards south of Scenic Loop Road, near Russell Creek (Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026). An interpretive sign that Walla Walla 2020 put up at the corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. The road name and Davies’s grave in Lyons Cemetery remain. VisitLyons Cemetery is public. The colony site is not marked. Places on the ground Sites of Davies’s community, 1867–1881, and of what remains of it. Solid markers and tracts are located; outlined markers are approximate; sites not yet located are listed without a marker. The colony land is private today. If you know where one of these places stood, please write. Tracts are drawn from their legal descriptions on the BLM section grid. The corner of Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads is from OpenStreetMap. The colony’s eighty acres Located 1867–1881 map After the 1881 judgment against Davies, the sheriff levied on his land, “the W½ NW¼ sec. 34, T7N R37E,” less one acre, and sold it at the courthouse door on July 16, 1881, for $1,975. A witness in the case spoke of the eighty acres “where he resides,” so this was almost certainly the camp. The tract lies on the west side of Mormon Grade Road just south of its corner with Scenic Loop Road, which matches Dan Clark’s placing of the site near Russell Creek. Private land; the site is not marked. Sources: Washington State Archives, Eastern Region Branch, Walla Walla Frontier Justice, case 2373 (WAL-3153); Dan Clark, Walla Walla 2020, correspondence with the editor, November 2026; section lines from the BLM National PLSS dataset. Scenic Loop and Mormon Grade roads Located today map The road named for the colony. Walla Walla 2020 put an interpretive sign about Davies’s community at this corner; it was shot up, replaced, shot up again and finally stolen. Sources: Walla Walla 2020; OpenStreetMap. Swen O. Hagg’s homestead Located patented 1890 map Swen O. Hagg (the roll’s Svend Hegg), who came to Walla Walla with the first five families in 1867 and was living in Davies’s house in 1880, patented a 170-acre homestead about three miles east-southeast of the camp in 1890 (S½ SE¼ sec. 1, T6N R37E, and lots in sec. 6, T6N R38E). The square shows the part in section 1. Sources: Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov); section lines from the BLM National PLSS dataset. The Davies cabin, Fort Walla Walla Museum Located today map A cabin in which Davies and his family lived has been moved to the grounds of the Fort Walla Walla Museum. Public, during museum hours. Sources: Wikipedia, “William W. Davies”; OpenStreetMap. Davies’s other land Not yet located 1870s A witness in 1881 listed 160 acres on Mill Creek, 160 acres “on the mountains” in Oregon or near the line, and 40 to 80 acres more. These tracts have not yet been found in the land records. Sources: Deposition of V. D. Lambert, case 2373. Davies’s grave, Lyons Cemetery Not yet located 1906 Davies died in 1906 and is buried in Lyons Cemetery, north of Mill Creek Road. Public. Its position is not yet on this map. Sources: Wikipedia, “William W. Davies.” In the chronology 19 Nov 1860Morris leaves Slaterville for South Weber. Catherine V. Waite, writing in 1866, gives the date: on November 19, 1860, Morris set out on foot “from Slatersville, a settlement in Weber County … to the Holy City” to deliver two letters to Brigham Young, his life having been threatened and he driven from his home, and on the way met John Cook, brother of Bishop Richard Cook (C. V. Waite, The Mormon Prophet and His Harem, Cambridge, MA, 1866, p. 122). By the account William W. Davies gave in 1882, the people of Slaterville, northwest of Ogden, had set a day to drive Morris out; he would not go at their order, but prayed, and the day brought “a destructive wind that blew down houses,” so that night found him still there, which he and his followers took as an answer to prayer. The next day he set out for Salt Lake City and on the road met John Cook, brother of Bishop Richard Cook, who invited him to South Weber, “late in the fall of 1860.” Davies says Morris had been driven from seventeen homes in three years; that of the church’s leaders only Orson Pratt would receive him; and that he was called “the Dreamer, or Praying Joe.” He described him as “a stout, square built, powerful man, about five feet six inches in hight,” whose dark brown hair, never cut, “hung in seven ringlets upon his shoulders,” with a small mouth, thin lips, an aquiline nose and “a mild blue eye”; meek, slow of speech, never known to laugh, though he would smile “in a way that made one like the man” (Frank T. Gilbert, Historic Sketches of Walla Walla, Whitman, Columbia and Garfield Counties, Portland, 1882, pp. 370–71; Davies’s recollection of twenty years later. Other accounts have Morris brought to South Weber after John Cook met him near the Warm Springs; see the roll note for John Cook). 1867–1881William W. Davies, who in an 1867 pamphlet declared that a third dispensation had been opened through him on January 24, 1866, setting baptism aside for a covenant vow (Watson, p. 124), leads a Morrisite offshoot, the Kingdom of Heaven, near Walla Walla, Washington. He declares his infant son Arthur to be Christ returned, the “Walla Walla Jesus.” Lawsuits by former members end the community: in 1881 a court awards three of them $3,225, and the sheriff sells the community’s livestock and its eighty acres to satisfy the judgment. 1873The Montana council minutes, kept in English this year, show the church at Warm Springs while its leaders are away.
